title: Landmark trial puts social media addiction theory to the test
description: The theory that tech giants intentionally targeted and manipulated young minds for profit will soon be put to the test, with the first in a series of trials set to begin next week in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom.
preview:
The theory that tech giants intentionally targeted and manipulated young minds for profit will soon be put to the test, with the first in a series of trials set to begin next week in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom.

For years, lawsuits against the major social media platforms have hit the same wall — a federal law that shields them from liability for what their users post.

searchText: Landmark trial puts social media addiction theory to the test The theory that tech giants intentionally targeted and manipulated young minds for profit will soon be put to the test, with the first in a series of trials set to begin next week in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom. The theory that tech giants intentionally targeted and manipulated young minds for profit will soon be put to the test, with the first in a series of trials set to begin next week in a downtown Los Angeles courtroom. For years, lawsuits against the major social media platforms have hit the same wall — a federal law that shields them from liability for what their users post. But a new legal playbook has taken shape, one that shifts the focus away from content and toward what plaintiffs say are deliberate design choices made by Big Tech to get kids hooked on their products, despite internal warnings about the risks. The companies have long maintained that such claims rest on third-party content protected by Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act. The trials will instead turn on the platforms’ design choices, and whether those choices can support negligence claims tied to foreseeable harms. Jurors will begin grappling with that question next week, as the first in a series of trials opens in downtown Los Angeles. At the center is a young woman known as K.G.M., who was six when she began using YouTube, eight when she started uploading videos, and nine when she joined Instagram, according to court documents. Snapchat followed at 11 and TikTok at 14. By age 10, she was checking social media from the moment she woke up — while eating meals, in the bathroom, and late into the night. In high school, she would ask to be excused from class to use the restroom, where she would scroll through Instagram and Snapchat. Her mother observed that her daughter seemed unable to live without her phone, and any effort to curb her use would trigger a confrontation, or, as her sister put it, “a meltdown as if someone had died.” K.G.M. says she realized by the age of nine or 10 that she was addicted to social media. “I was on it all the time when I didn’t want to be, and I would freak out if my mom tried to take my phone away,” she testified. The incessant social media use coincided with a cascade of mental health problems. Her anxiety spiked and she developed body dysmorphia. She became obsessed with grooming and hygiene, as she was served a steady diet of posts featuring people “way skinnier” and “way prettier.” Healthy food also became a fixation, along with “what I eat in a day” videos that encouraged eating as little as possible. Cutting videos continually surfaced on her feed, despite her attempts to block that sort of content, and she struggled through suicide attempts in 2019 and 2020. She was also bullied relentlessly online and at school, to the point where a vice principal recommended that she “remove herself from social media to decrease frequency of bullying by peers.” Now 20 years old, K.G.M. is taking the platforms to court, where her lawyers intend to show that social media’s manipulative algorithm and design features were the wellspring of these harms. “It’s impossible to tell K.G.M.’s story without mentioning social media,” said her lawyer Joseph VanZandt. — The plaintiff — K.G.M.’s trial is the first in a succession of bellwethers involving personal injury plaintiffs who accuse Meta Platforms, YouTube, Snap and TikTok of developing products designed to maximize engagement while negligently disregarding foreseeable psychological harms to kids. Snap and TikTok reached confidential settlements with K.G.M. just before jury selection got underway this week, leaving Meta and YouTube as the sole remaining defendants (see here and here). “Two down, two to go!” lead plaintiff counsel Mark Lanier told MLex in an email response to a request for comment on the TikTok agreement. Eight other jury trials have been scheduled for later this year in Los Angeles, as well as a set of three federal jury trials set for this summer in Oakland. TikTok and Snap remain defendants in those cases, along with thousands of other suits brought by state attorneys general, school districts and individuals. The claims mirror state lawsuits brought against tobacco companies in the 1990s, which alleged that the industry targeted young people, concealed known health risks, and fueled public health problems that burdened the healthcare system. In November, Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn B. Kuhl rejected arguments that the companies are shielded by the First Amendment and Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, finding that features like endless scroll, autoplay, likes and comments, beauty filters and push notifications are not content-based, but design choices that must be weighed by a jury. searchText: Papers, please: Can online age verification be compatible with privacy? Age verification is increasingly seen as a way to keep children away from harm online, as seen with versions in place in the EU, UK and the US. But there are widespread fears that proving your age necessarily means handing over sensitive personal data that is vulnerable to exploitation. Can age verification work effectively without eroding privacy for children and adults alike? Age verification is increasingly seen as a way to keep children away from harm online, as seen with versions in place in the EU, UK and the US. But there are widespread fears that proving your age necessarily means handing over sensitive personal data that is vulnerable to exploitation. Can age verification work effectively without eroding privacy for children and adults alike? This article is part of an MLex online safety special series running this week. Other stories focus on US-specific regulation, algorithmic content and video gaming (see here). Across Europe, and more lately the US, governments are turning to age verification as a practical way to shield children from online harm. But can the verification tools out there strike a balance between protecting children and protecting privacy? It's tricky, and there's no obvious playbook that stands out. “The absence of any safeguards whatsoever has led to a whole generation of kids who have basically been experimented on and fed huge amounts of harmful content,” says George Billinge, who helped draft regulatory guidance underpinning the UK’s emerging online safety regime. Billinge, now a tech consultancy CEO, sees it as about establishing values: “Trying to think about how nation states can exert some kind of social contract onto previously completely ungoverned online spaces is a worthwhile activity,” he told MLex. For privacy advocates, though, the rapid pace of regulation is a concern. A fervor for bringing in age verification risks masking a less visible threat to both children and adults by requiring everyone to give up their ability to browse the web anonymously, they fear. “We think about it as identifying minors, but it is really about identifying adults,” Alice Marwick, director of research at New York-based institute Data & Society, told MLex. Legal scholars share this concern. Eric Goldman, Associate Dean for Research at California’s Santa Clara University School of Law, is skeptical about whether age verification can ever work effectively without eroding privacy for both children and adults. Laws that force platforms to separate adults from children end up sweeping in everyone, he says, creating a gated system where access depends on showing your digital “papers” and requires surrendering a significant degree of privacy and data security. He expounds on this idea in a paper published this summer in the Stanford Law Technology Review on what he calls “Segregate and Suppress” laws, a regulatory model in which governments first compel platforms to separate adult users from minors, then restrict or censor what minors can access. Such laws are incompatible with privacy, Goldman contends. — Europe’s early lead — The debate has been under way for some time in Europe, where the Digital Services Act in the EU and the Online Safety Act in the UK have ushered in some of the world’s most stringent age-verification requirements. In the process, they have been instrumental in raising questions about just how far regulators can go in curbing online harms without undermining privacy. The UK’s requirement, ushered into force in July by online safety regulator Ofcom, effectively compels platforms that allow pornography and are “likely to be accessed by children” to ensure only adults can get in. But it doesn’t specify how sites should go about doing this, only that whatever method they use be “proportionate, highly effective and privacy-protective.” Most are outsourcing the task to third parties, drawing criticism from some privacy groups who say Britons are being forced to entrust an array of sensitive data — such as facial scans, identity documents and financial information — to overseas age-verification providers with dubious track records on privacy. The rollout hasn’t been without its bumps, says Iain Corby, executive director of the Age Verification Providers Association. “Ofcom has done a pretty good job, but they still haven't required any sort of independent certification,” he told MLex. “There’s a lot of newcomers into the market doing very poor-quality age checks. And also, we don't know whether they're behaving well in terms of your personal data.” While Ofcom hasn’t set specific accuracy thresholds, the enforcer's expectation that companies clearly show that their age-verification methods are effective and designed to preserve privacy has proved a tall order. “I don't think that anybody is getting it right yet,” Ofcom’s online safety policy director, Almudena Lara, told a recent conference (see here). title: Mississippi’s online child-safety law faces high-stakes constitutional test
description: Mississippi is enforcing the toughest online-safety law in the nation, and so far, neither the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit nor the US Supreme Court has said why they've allowed it to go forward. A forthcoming a hearing on whether HB 1126 can remain in force, which has triggered a wave of amicus briefs challenging its constitutional footing, may clarify whether the law is likely to survive First Amendment review.
preview:
Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit nor the US Supreme Court has said why they've allowed it to go forward. A forthcoming a hearing on whether HB 1126 can remain in force, which has triggered a wave of amicus briefs challenging its constitutional footing, may clarify whether the law is likely to survive First Amendment review. The US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit gave no explanation for why it allowed Mississippi to impose the toughest restrictions for children’s access to online platforms in the nation back in August. Nor did the US Supreme Court when it upheld that decision, though Justice Brett Kavanaugh said it likely violates the First Amendment (see here). . . .

description: In closing arguments today in a high-stakes privacy trial, a lawyer for a class of women who used the Flo period-tracking app urged a federal jury to tell Meta Platforms that "they don't get a pass" for secretly recording sensitive reproductive health data. Meta pushed back in its own closing arguments, saying it never recorded, only received, strings of code created by Flo.

title: Google fights to exclude privacy scandals, 'ambush' witnesses in app-tracking trial
description: Google is seeking to bar jurors from hearing what it calls irrelevant or highly prejudicial evidence and testimony — and to split an upcoming privacy trial into two phases — in a high-stakes case that could expose the company to billions in damages and reshape how it tracks user activity through apps. The tech giant asked a federal judge today to exclude references to prior data scandals, reproductive and health apps, and testimony from executives and former engineers that it says would confuse
preview:
testimony — and to split an upcoming privacy trial into two phases — in a high-stakes case that could expose the company to billions in damages and reshape how it tracks user activity through apps. The tech giant asked a federal judge today to exclude references to prior data scandals, reproductive and health apps, and testimony from executives and former engineers that it says would confuse or inflame the jury during the liability phase of the trial. Google fired another salvo in its battle to narrow the scope of evidence a jury will get to see in a trial this summer over whether it secretly tracked app activity from users who explicitly opted out. . . .

title: FBI violated ex-Google engineer's rights in AI espionage case, US judge rules
description: A US federal judge suppressed statements made by a former Google engineer accused of stealing AI trade secrets after finding that FBI agents violated his Miranda rights during a pre-dawn interrogation. But evidence from his electronic devices can be used at trial, as the judge found that he voluntarily gave agents his passwords and did not clearly invoke his right to a lawyer.

description: A US federal judge ruled that Adobe and two of its executives must face the US Federal Trade Commission’s lawsuit accusing them of duping customers into enrolling in its priciest annual subscription plan and then saddling them with onerous "stealth" cancellation fees and hurdles. The agency alleges the software maker turned its hefty early termination fee into a "retention tool" to trap customers in subscriptions they didn’t want. Adobe cannot escape claims that it trapped customers in onerous subscriptions for Photoshop and other software products in violation of the Restore Online Shoppers’ Confidence Act, a US federal judge ruled today....

title: Prosecutorial Flip-Flop in Bribery Case of Ex-Cognizant CLO Highlights Confusion Over Trump Executive Order
description: The DOJ installed a new top prosecutor in New Jersey on Monday night, and hours later he asked a judge to put the trial on hold. His predecessor last month had told the judge the trial should proceed as scheduled, with jury selection starting this week.
preview:
Confusion over the implications of President Donald Trump’s executive order pausing Foreign Corrupt Practices Act enforcement is so thick that even officials within the Justice Department disagree on what it means.

That became apparent Tuesday after the newly installed U.S. attorney for the District of New Jersey asked a judge to delay the bribery trial for former Cognizant Chief Legal Officer Steven Schwartz and former Cognizant President Gordon Coburn for 180 days to give his office time to assess how Trump’s Feb. 10 FCPA order applies to the case. Jury selection had been set to begin this week.

searchText: Trump bid to eject privacy board Democrats spurs EU-US data-transfer questions The Biden-era data deal between the U.S. and European Union, designed to enable billions of dollars in transatlantic digital trade, faces its first major test under President Donald Trump. (January 24, 2025, 23:08 GMT | Comment) -- The beginning of the second Trump administration brought renewed questions this week about the future of transatlantic data transfers after President Donald Trump demanded the resignation of Democratic members of a key privacy oversight board. More than 3,000 companies, many of them smaller firms ranging from Abacus Information Technology to Zywave, are registered with the EU-US Data Privacy Framework, the legal mechanism that since 2023 has allowed participants to legally transfer personal data between Europe and the US. The Privacy and Civil Liberties Oversight Board isn't a high-profile privacy watchdog, but within the Data Privacy Framework (DPF) it has a key role in overseeing the critical legal redress system that hears privacy complaints filed by Europeans about issues caused by US intelligence agencies or other elements of the US government. Soon after his inauguration on Monday, Trump demanded that three Democratic members of the five-member PCLOB resign by Thursday, raising questions in the view of European privacy advocates who twice successfully challenged two earlier transatlantic data transfer mechanisms. Max Schrems, the privacy advocate whose legal challenge to the EU-US Privacy Shield led to Europe’s top court annulling that data bridge in 2020 (see here), said this week that Trump’s action shows that the new DPF is a deal built “on sand” (see here). Despite that weak legal basis for the DPF, Schrems said, “the EU business lobby and the European Commission wanted it anyways. Instead of stable legal limitation, the EU was agreeing to executive promises that can be overturned in seconds. Now where the first Trump waves hit this deal, it may soon dissolve in seconds and bring many EU businesses into a legal limbo.” The reassuring news for companies that rely on the DPF is that it could take years for any legal challenge filed by Schrems or anyone else to work its way up to the European Court of Justice, and for the apex court to rule on that challenge. Until then, the DPF would remain in place. In short, there is no immediate crisis that data flows between Europe and the US might be disrupted because of Trump’s actions with the PCLOB. When the European Court of Justice annulled the EU-US Privacy Shield in July 2020 following a complaint by Schrems (see here), in large part because of the lack of a binding legal redress system for Europeans, it kicked off three years of legal uncertainty for data transfers between Europe and the US as the two jurisdictions worked out a successor dealing, including creation of the new redress court by the US Department of Justice. Like the DPF, Privacy Shield was meant to guarantee European residents equivalent protection for their data even when held inside US data centers. Privacy Shield was the successor to the EU-US Safe Harbor Framework, which was used by more than 5,000 US companies but which the European court invalidated in 2015. In its decisions on both Privacy Shield and Safe Harbor, the European court questioned the mechanism’s ability to protect Europeans’ data from US intelligence agency surveillance. The commission’s first annual review of the DPF, issued in September, notes that it will pay “particular attention to the upcoming reports of the PCLOB on the implementation” of the DPF in evaluating the transfer mechanism, and that review will include watching “the nomination and appointment of members to the PCLOB to fill upcoming vacancies." PCLOB members are chosen by the president and confirmed by Congress for six-year terms. There are currently four: Chair Sharon Bradford Franklin, who was appointed by Biden in 2022; Travis LeBlanc, a Democrat appointed to his first term by Trump and reappointed in 2022 by Biden; and Ed Felten, a Democrat appointed by Trump in 2018. The fourth member, Beth Williams, was appointed by Biden in 2022. But her Republican affiliation spared her from receiving an e-mail asking her to resign or be fired by end of day. LeBlanc is a lawyer who is a former enforcement director for the US Federal Communications Commission; Felten is a prominent Princeton University computer scientist. Trump’s resignation request was confirmed to MLex this week. As of today, the Democratic PCLOB members have not yet resigned, MLex has learned. PCLOB didn't respond to a request for comment from MLex today on the resignation demand. Trump’s purge of the Democrats on the independent advisory board, which must have at least three members to keep functioning, makes it unclear how the board could continue to function for the immediate future. title: Washington AG sues T-Mobile over 'avoidable' 2021 data breach
description: Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson says T-Mobile's lax security practices resulted in a 2021 data breach that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million Washingtonians.
preview: By Maria Dinzeo
excerpt: Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson says T-Mobile's lax security practices resulted in a 2021 data breach that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million Washingtonians.
searchText: Washington AG sues T-Mobile over 'avoidable' 2021 data breach Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson says T-Mobile's lax security practices resulted in a 2021 data breach that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million Washingtonians. By Maria Dinzeo (January 6, 2025, 21:30 GMT | Insight) -- The State of Washington is suing T-Mobile over lax cybersecurity practices in the lead up to a massive data breach back in August 2021 that exposed the personal information of more than 2 million residents, including their social security numbers and driver’s license information. "This significant data breach was entirely avoidable,” Washington Attorney General Robert Ferguson said in a statement announcing the lawsuit. “T-Mobile had years to fix key vulnerabilities in its cybersecurity systems — and it failed.” Those vulnerabilities allegedly stemmed from inadequate risk management and security monitoring, including failure to store customers’ personal data in legacy Sprint databases maintained by T-Mobile after the two telecoms merged in 2020, according to the complaint filed in King County Superior Court today (see here). "T-Mobile knew of the risks from cyber-attacks and decided to accept the risks rather than adequately implement safeguards,” the lawsuit says. The complaint notes that T-Mobile even admitted in a securities filing that the merger introduced additional security risks. Security problems also preceded the merger, however, dating back to 2017 when an “ethical hacker” uncovered an Application Programming Interface vulnerability that could have exposed personal identifying information like customer names, email addresses and account numbers, just by knowing or guessing a customer’s phone number. Vulnerabilities persisted for years, the lawsuit says, resulting in several instances where hackers stole customer PII in 2018 and 2019. Employee credentials were also stolen by hackers in 2021 and 2022 and used to access call logs and proprietary source code. In August 2021, T-Mobile alerted customers that it had suffered a massive cyberattack. It eventually came out that the personal data of more than 79 million customers had been exposed and that PII had been posted for sale on the dark web. T-Mobile initially disclosed the breach to customers via text message, but the messages allegedly misled customers about its seriousness and omitted critical information like the fact that social security numbers were included in some of the leaked data. Ferguson’s office has been investigating the breach for years, though the office claimed in a 2023 court filing that T-Mobile impeded its efforts by failing to respond to numerous requests for documents and information related to its cybersecurity practices, past breaches and the revenue it derives from collecting user data. Ferguson’s office did not reply to questions from MLex about whether it ever received the requested documents. The 2021 data breach sparked a firestorm of privacy lawsuits across the country that were eventually consolidated in Washington federal court. Bellevue, Washington-based T-Mobile agreed to settle with the consolidated class for $350 million in a 2022 deal (see here) that was approved in 2023 (see here). T-Mobile also reached a $31.5 million settlement with the Federal Communications Commission last year. A T-Mobile spokesperson told MLex in an email that the company has had multiple conversations with the Washington AG's office about the 2021 data breach over the last several years "and even reached out in late November to continue discussions, so the office’s decision to file a lawsuit today came as a surprise." They added, "While we disagree with their approach and the filing’s claims, we are open to further dialogue and welcome the opportunity to resolve this issue, as we have already done with the FCC. We also look forward to sharing how T-Mobile has fundamentally transformed our approach to cyber security over the past four years to further protect our customers." The spokesperson did not address MLex's inquiry about whether it complied with Ferguson’s document requests prior to the lawsuit filed today, which seeks civil penalties and restitution, improved security practices and more transparency in T-Mobile’s communications about cybersecurity to its customers. title: Wave of US state privacy bills taking effect in January
description: California's privacy regulator is gearing up to institute new rules for businesses in 2025 aimed at tightening protections for consumers' personal data and bolstering defenses against cybersecurity incidents.
preview:
A wave of state privacy laws taking effect in January will expand an already complicated patchwork of US privacy regulations and reflects an escalating trend among states to continue raising the bar for consumer privacy protections.

searchText: Wave of US state privacy bills taking effect in January California's privacy regulator is gearing up to institute new rules for businesses in 2025 aimed at tightening protections for consumers' personal data and bolstering defenses against cybersecurity incidents. A wave of state privacy laws taking effect in January will expand an already complicated patchwork of US privacy regulations and reflects an escalating trend among states to continue raising the bar for consumer privacy protections. 23 Dec 2024 | 23:48 GMT | Comment By Maria Dinzeo California's privacy regulator is gearing up to institute new rules for businesses in 2025 aimed at tightening protections for consumers' personal data and bolstering defenses against cybersecurity incidents. Regulations on annual cybersecurity audits, or CSAs, in the making since mid-2023, could finally get over the finish line this year. As currently written, the regulation requires that companies hire a third party to evaluate the strength of their cybersecurity programs and identify any gaps or weaknesses in baseline cybersecurity like multi-factor authentication, zero-trust architecture, account access controls, penetration testing and disaster-recovery plans. For any missing elements, the business and its auditor must explain why the component is not necessary to protect personal information. Stacey Higginbotham, a cybersecurity expert and policy fellow at Consumer Reports, said it’s remarkable how many companies currently don’t employ best cybersecurity practices. That became even more apparent earlier this year when Change Healthcare suffered one of the largest known data breaches of protected health information in a ransomware attack that exposed the personal, financial and healthcare records of some 100 million Americans. “That happened because someone didn't put multi-factor authentication, which is a bare bones best practice, on a remote admin server with data on it,” Higginbotham said. “It's bonkers that in the Year of our Lord 2024 that people aren't using MFA on a remote server. That's like leaving the house with the door unlocked and announcing on social media that you’ll be in Europe for the next two weeks.” She said California’s CSA requirement will get companies thinking about minimum standards at a time when so much consumer data is being disseminated across the dark web. “Broadly speaking, a CSA is a tool to help ensure that people are actually paying attention that they're taking the steps they need to,” Higginbotham said. “It's not going to magically prevent cybersecurity intrusions. It's going to ensure that they're employing best practices that will help prevent an intrusion or data extraction. It would be nice if anyone did this anyway, but you really need regulations to ensure people are doing them.” Data breaches also have staggering business costs. IBM’s 2024 data breach report puts the global average cost of a data breach at $4.88 million, up 10 percent from last year and the highest total ever. Customers suffer too. IBM’s report says that 63 percent of organizations said they planned to raise the price of goods and services following a data breach, up from 57 percent last year. But economic researchers from Berkeley and California State University Sacramento anticipate that Calfiornia’s CSA regulations will save companies money in avoided annual losses, approximately $734 million in 2027, and more than $32 billion by the end of 2036. The researchers also believe that absent a cybersecurity audit, businesses will be less likely to catch issues in internal controls and processes. But over time, the CSA will result in them being “more proficient in dealing with data breaches swiftly and effectively.” The rules apply to businesses that derive at least 50 percent of their revenue from selling data, or make $28 million or more in annual revenue and process the data of 250,000 consumers or the sensitive personal information of 50,000 or more consumers in the preceding calendar year. The California Privacy Protection Agency estimates that roughly 25,000 companies will be impacted by its CSA regulation. Importantly, the rules require that the company’s highest ranking executive or a member of the board sign off on the audit and attest that they have reviewed and understand its findings. Jeewon Serrato, a partner at Pillsbury Winthrop who handles enforcement actions and advises clients on complex security incident investigations, said regulatory agencies are asking more from C-suite executives. “The trend I’m seeing is personal liability,” she said. “We often talk to clients about how privacy and cybersecurity is now a C-suite and board-level responsibility.” While California’s CSA regulations do not penalize executives for cybersecurity failings, they demand that the most senior people in a business be informed about its security posture. “That there has to be executive-level sign off is really putting it onto the individual executives to be respo

title: Tech giants must face largest personal injury litigation in US over social media harm
description: Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward.
preview: 14 Dec 2024 | 00:25 GMT | Insight
excerpt: Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing...
searchText: Tech giants must face largest personal injury litigation in US over social media harm Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward. 14 Dec 2024 | 00:25 GMT | Insight By Maria Dinzeo Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward. Social media giants will have to face claims that they designed their platforms to get kids hooked, as a California appellate court denied their bid to vacate a trial court judge’s ruling allowing negligence and fraud claims to move forward. Meta Platform’s Facebook and Instagram, ByteDance’s TikTok, Google’s YouTube and Snap’s Snapchat petitioned the appellate court last December, asking the judges to review Los Angeles Superior Court Judge Carolyn B. Kuhl’s October 2023 ruling that the companies aren't shielded by the First Amendment or Section 230 of the Communications Decency Act, which provides online platforms immunity from liability over third-party content. The plaintiffs, a group of individuals, school districts and local governments, claim Facebook, Instagram, TikTok, YouTube and Snap are all designed to get young people addicted without regard for the deleterious consequences for kids’ mental health. They’ve also used a unique tack to skirt Section 230 and First Amendment protections by alleging that social media platforms are defectively designed products. Kuhl reasoned that the platforms are not “products” in the product liability sense, but the plaintiffs nevertheless sufficiently alleged that the companies were careless about the design of their algorithms. “Plaintiffs have adequately pled a cause of action for negligence that is not barred by federal immunity or the First Amendment,” Kuhl wrote in her 89-page ruling (see here). In their petition (see here), the social media giants argued that Kuhl had violated the “core principles” of Section 230 and the First Amendment as a means of immunizing platforms from protracted litigation, “not just from liability.” California’s Second Appellate District rejected the petition in a two-sentence order last week, saying it had read and considered the petition for writ of mandate and that “the petition is denied.” The companies didn't respond to messages seeking comment on the brief order. In a statement, Beasley Allen, which is representing the plaintiffs, said it was pleased with the most recent development in the litigation, saying the appellate courts’ refusal to weight in puts the case “one step closer to trials seeking to hold the tech giants liable for the mental physical harm suffered by youth as a result of social media addiction.” Kuhl is overseeing the largest personal injury litigation in the nation against the social media giants, encompassing 1,900 cases from 44 states, which has been consolidated into a Judicial Council Coordination Proceeding — the state equivalent of multidistrict litigation in federal court. Meanwhile, a massive MDL is playing out in the US Northern District of California before U.S. District Judge Yvonne Gonzalez Rogers, who in November largely denied the social media companies’ motion to dismiss nuisance claims. title: Three Reasons CLOs Are Critical to the Successful Adoption of Generative AI

searchText: Lawyers Drowning in Cases Are Embracing AI Fastest—and Say It's Yielding Better Outcomes for Clients “This is the first technology wave that no lawyer can ignore," said Aaref Hilaly, a partner at Bain Capital Ventures, which invests in legal document automation companies. Lawyers with sky-high caseloads are adopting generative artificial intelligence with the greatest zeal—embracing the technology to screen cases, draft demand letters, pull together medical records and refine litigation strategies. And they're finding it's giving them a big advantage over those mired in traditional ways of working. They’re able to do more with less, resolve cases faster and achieve better outcomes. It’s also supercharging their output. “It's an advantage available to both sides, and it’s sort of an arms race to a certain extent, where when one side gets equipped with one advantage, the other side will have to essentially respond,” said James Lee, a former litigator at Quinn Emanuel Urquhart & Sullivan and at Morgan, Lewis & Bockius who two decades ago started his own boutique firm, LTL Attorneys. He said litigation departments have historically been the least productive in terms of producing revenue. An old-timer at Morgan Lewis once told him this all changed with the advent of the Xerox machine. “Because when the Xerox machine was invented, people made copies of copies of copies of documents, memos, and reports, and guess who had to review them all? Litigators. And then at that point you had the number of billable hours on litigation cases go up.” Email and e-discovery likewise increased the volume of data lawyers had to deal with, and now AI is amping things up even more. Which can be good for lawyers who know how to exploit it. “If you truly are part of the elite, you're going to do fine. If you truly admit that you are a commodity firm, you're going to do fine. These firms in the middle are going to struggle, and at some point they'll just disappear." Lee saw the revolution coming six years ago when he attended a week-long program for AM Law 200 partners and practice heads at Harvard Law School. “On one of the days, they talked about how AI had already started to take over portions of the medical world, and it was just a matter of time before it would start taking over portions of law,” he said. Lee remembered looking around the room. “I could see the look of fear in their eyes,” he said. “Lawyers are motivated by two things, fear or greed. Mostly fear. And you could just see the fear in their eyes. And I had that fear too, by the way—that I thought these bigger firms were going to steal our lunch.” 'This Is Nuts' When Lee returned to LTL's Los Angeles headquarters, he told his partners to experiment with AI platforms. Soon, they were able to do work in two minutes that junior lawyers required eight hours to complete—answering a lawsuit, coming up with affirmative defenses, and drafting very targeted discovery questions based on the complaint. “Six years ago, people were going, ‘This is nuts,' because it really is replicating the work of what a junior lawyer would be doing,” Lee said. But it became so successful that he and LTL partners Enoch Liang and Thomas Suh spun out those services into a new company, LegalMation, which provides AI tools that automate the creation of legal documents, streamlining the early phases of a lawsuit. Walmart became its first client. Later, U.S. auto companies and large insurance companies signed on, as did a handful of high-volume litigation firms. Lee said the services make the most sense for litigators with high-volume caseloads. “I'm doing dishes one night, and my wife says, ‘Hey, you run an automation company. Why aren't you using a dishwasher?’ And I couldn't answer this question, and it took me two weeks before I realized I just don't do enough dishes. ... I see automation the same way.” Automation has been a particular game-changer for insurers. “There's one large national insurance carrier where, in 33 states, we are handling all of their motor vehicle accident claims,” Lee said. “That works out to about 60,000 cases. That’s a lot of dirty dishes. And it’s where it begins to make sense, getting a number of these dishwashers all over the country for their teams.” LegalMation launched in 2016 as the first AI company to automate and enhance litigation tasks. Today, the landscape is vastly different, with more than 500 legal document automation companies globally, 85 of which have received venture capital funding, according to the technology research firm Tracxn. The 85 firms have raised $27.3 billion, with LegalMation scooping up nearly $24 million, including $15 million in a funding round last year. Investors are wowed by the sector's potential. “This is the first technology wave that no lawyer can ignore. He added that hackers “are having a field day leveraging it for everything from phishing attacks and password cracking to producing malware and deepfakes.” The report, released Tuesday, also predicts that AI will increase insider fraud, teen hacker gangs, and attacks on large data centers that power commercial use of generative AI. Bruemmer told Law.com that he isn't surprised AI is playing an increasing role in online fraud, but another trend highlighted in the report—that FBI data shows the average age of someone arrested for a cybercrime is 19—did catch him off guard. The average age for all other crimes is 37. “We've seen a lot more activity with gangs that are powered by teenagers, and it makes sense because the teens are being recruited because they're tech savvy, they're into gaming, they know about AI. They can be easily recruited either on the dark web or on the internet,” he said. With the rise of AI use in the workplace, Experian also anticipates an increasing amount of fraud will be pulled off by corporate insiders. "It could be anything, including stealing personal identity information, giving elevated access credentials to an outsider, embezzlement," Bruemmer said. Experian's report notes that companies training their employees on how to use AI responsibly could have unintended consequences. "We could see a marked increase in the use of that AI education by those very same employees for internal theft, sensitive information sourcing, and much more," its report says. "Next year may see at least one global brand impacted by fraud perpetrated by an insider to whom it provided educational AI training." AI is also fueling demand for data centers, making them a prime target for hackers. "Within the next year, cyber attackers could successfully jeopardize a nation-state’s cloud infrastructure through a attack on the power needed to run it," Experian predicts. Bruemmer noted that one ChatGPT query requires 10 times the amount of electricity as a regular Google search, and Goldman Sachs expects a 160% increase in data center power demand by 2030. "By 2050 in Texas, which now consumes 13% of the U..S power grid's power, they need to have a doubling of the 342 data centers by 2050, to almost 700 data centers, just to keep even with where we are today," he said. The growth projections make data centers particularly vulnerable. "The hackers are going to pick a point that's going to be most impactful in that supply chain to be able to shut things down, and what's driving the power-hungry data center prediction is the fact that there's so much demand because of AI," Bruemmer said. Ransomware and supply chain attacks will continue to plague companies heading into 2025. Experian serviced more than 4,000 events this year, Bruemmer said, and 50% involved some kind of ransomware, particularly in health care. "If you shut down a hospital, you denied patients access to emergency care, let alone elective surgeries and the like. So ransomware hasn't gone away," he said. The same goes for supply chain attacks, as companies continue to feel the downstream effects of cyberattacks, such as one that exploited a flaw in the MOVEit managed file transfer service in 2023. "There are some companies that just recently announced data breaches from over 18 months ago because they didn't know that they were impacted. So supply chain hacks represent almost a third of all the breaches we service," Bruemmer said. "There's stuff that we're working on right now that's well beyond 6 months old, but will be announced coming up that people have just discovered. They're doing the best they can, but if they aren't told by the third party or they don't see any direct indication, unless the company reports to them, they have to figure it out on their own." Bruemmer said it's incredibly important for procurement and legal teams to be very involved in any contracts with third and fourth parties. title: CFIUS Is Locked and Loaded, but What Lies Ahead for CFIUS Enforcement Activity?
description: The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (“CFIUS”) has published new details and guidance on its enforcement activities on the Department of Treasury’s website, including, for the first time, a comprehensive list of civil monetary penalties it has imposed.
preview:
The Committee on Foreign Investment in the United States (“CFIUS”) has published new details and guidance on its enforcement activities on the Department of Treasury’s website, including, for the first time, a comprehensive list of civil monetary penalties it has imposed. CFIUS also provides insight on factors informing the issuance of Determination of Noncompliance Transmittal (“DONT”) Letters, which CFIUS sends to parties that CFIUS has determined violated CFIUS’ regulations or a national security risk-mitigation agreement.

Enforcement Actions That Resulted in Penalties and DONT Letters
CFIUS recently provided new insight into its new enforcement era by publishing on its website a list of eight enforcement actions involving monetary penalties pursuant to Section 721(h) of the Defense Production Act of 1950. CFIUS took into account the objectives of enforcement and national security, among other factors, when assessing these penalties. CFIUS also provided significant new insight via its website regarding its use of DONT Letters, with which CFIUS notifies parties of its determination that they have violated CFIUS’ regulations or a mitigation agreement. A DONT Letter itself does not impose a penalty, but could be a pre-cursor to CFIUS’ issuing a penalty, and will either inform the parties that CFIUS has elected not to issue a penalty or that CFIUS requires additional information to determine whether a penalty is warranted. Even if the DONT Letter does not result in a penalty, CFIUS at a later date could consider the existence of a violation identified in a DONT Letter as an aggravating factor in a subsequent enforcement proceeding.

The truism that law school doesn’t prepare you to be an in-house lawyer in tech is quickly changing. Didday, an associate general counsel of product and privacy at Zendesk, grew up in the Bay Area and was familiar with the boom-and-bust cycle of tech. But it wasn’t until he went in-house at cloud-based electronic health record company Practice Fusion after four years in Big Law that he got a crash course in how those companies actually operate, and what being an “effective and helpful” in-house lawyer really means. “Listening to how the business operates and advising on how they can comply with the law is the core definition of what it is to be a lawyer.” Didday said. The product counsel's job is to figure out what the company is planning to do and ensure that the path to that goal from idea to launch is legal, he added. Didday said lawyers tend to think of the world as “two sided”: There are plaintiffs and defendants, winners and losers; someone is right and someone is wrong. “A tech company is more complex," he added. "It's not my job to say finance is right and engineering is wrong. It's more like, 'What are all those departments, and what are they trying to do as a company?' That skill set of learning about and being curious about and communicating with those departments is the crux of the skill that I realized was going to be so important.” Fortunately, Didday had a mentor early on “who knew everybody at the company really well who really took me under her wing,” he said. “She literally moved my desk so I sat in the middle of the engineers, product managers and designers and took me into every meeting she went into. By necessity that experience made me listen.” Embedded in the Business In-house teams have long been organized by disciplines—IP, employment, commercial contracts and litigation. While legal departments need that specialized expertise, they also need lawyers to advise companies on the products and services they offer, said Adrienne Go, former associate general counsel at eBay. “While we absolutely have to have that expertise, at the same time, the real question is, 'Who is looking after the goods and services?' That's what the company is built on. That's what their brand is built on. It's not necessarily built on that great lawsuit that they just won. It really is built on providing excellent products, things that make people happy,” Go said. “With our rapid product life cycles in the past 20 years, businesses are being led more and more by their products. And it’s not just a just a brand campaign; it really is how much they are delivering value to their customers," Go added. title: How Marsh McLennan's Small But Mighty Legal Innovation Team Builds Solutions That Bring Joy

preview:
LIT Lab started as a concept. Now it’s a verb. Liu reminded him that it was right around Christmas when The New York Times sued OpenAI and Microsoft last year. Palmer said that kind of timing is not unusual, as 30%-40% of lawsuits are filed against the company between Thanksgiving and New Year's. “I think plaintiffs lawyers in particular think that they're being tricky or that they're somehow getting some advantage by doing that,” he said. “It’s become a joke in my family—it’s the holidays, what's gonna make Dad be on the phone for 12 hours straight? LIT Lab started as a concept. Now it’s a verb. For Marsh McLennan chief legal innovation counsel Farrah Pepper, there’s no higher praise for the Legal Innovation & Technology (LIT) framework she helped launch in 2019 to drive new ideas for how to better run legal and compliance at a global company. Legal has long suffered under the sometimes unfair designation as the “place where good ideas go to die.” But it’s recently started to turn that label on its head. For Pepper, who was hired back in 2018, it’s about finding better ways of working. “Innovation doesn't have to always be a moonshot," she said. "I define it as incremental change that adds value. And that's what our LIT Lab is doing all the time; looking at the processes we have now. How do we make them better?” Marsh McLennan’s commitment to modernizing its legal and compliance department through its own innovation lab earned it this year’s Corporate Counsel award for Best Use of Technology. She and other Corporate Counsel winners were recognized for their achievements on Nov. 13 at The American Lawyer Industry Awards in New York City. (Read the full list of winners here.) With the blessing of General Counsel Kate Brennan, Pepper said she and her team have gone about rooting out mundane, repetitive tasks and cumbersome processes, and applying practical, streamlined solutions. "It is possible to teach an old lawyer new tricks," Brennan told Law.com for a LIT Lab profile back in 2022. "I think it's easy when you're in-house for a number of years to just become complacent and resort to 'that's always just how we've done it and it works fine, so don't break it.'" Projects have to meet four principles—save time, save money, improve quality and bring joy. “That last one is my personal favorite,” Pepper said. “Is it making our colleagues day better? Is it making them enjoy their job more?” Though some might think of Pepper’s role as primarily data- or tech-based, she said that it’s really about people. “I will have conversations all day long with colleagues, and I will hear them say something which embedded in their statement is a hope or a wish," she said. "Maybe something like, 'I wish this process were easier, but it's not.' And to me, that's the antenna up moment where I say, 'Well, maybe we can help you. Let's have a LIT Lab conversation about whether there's something we can do to make that better.’ And we find opportunities everywhere.” She said one of the recurring pain points her team heard from legal colleagues was translation services. Microsoft already has translation capabilities embedded in its software suite, Pepper said, “But we found that sometimes that wasn't enough, and people needed something that was more specific to legal terms.” So they also started using an artificial intelligence-based translation tool through Marsh McLennan’s own internal generative AI solution, dubbed “LenAI.” When legal wanted the tool to be able to learn specific legal terms and clauses, the company partnered with Alexa Translations to “build a translation brain for our department of key terms and clauses," she said. "That's one example of something that may sound simple, but in reality, it's a multipronged approach with different solutions depending on different use cases,” as well as “an external relationship and partnership where we are collaborating to add capabilities and features.” Another strategic partnership has been with Priori Legal to design and test a new outside counsel management program called Scout. Pepper said Scout pulls together all the data points on a firm, including billing, diversity initiatives and reviews, traditionally information that lives in a bunch of places, and puts them all together in one place. “You're looking at actual real matters and associated cost structures. We've also got reviews and testimonials,” Pepper said. “As much as we want to think our colleagues will stay with us forever, sometimes there can be a change in who those relationship leads are. We wanted to prevent a situation where years of excellent work from a law firm and institutional knowledge walked out the door with a relationship lead on the in-house side and vice-versa.” LIT Lab also created an ideas portal called FIRE, an acronym for “fabulous ideas, requests, and enhancements," where legal and compliance colleagues can submit ideas, crowdsource, and vote on one others' ideas about how to work better and smarter. “We have a simple intake form for our colleagues to present their idea, it gets posted into the portal, and others can review it, comment, vote on it,” Pepper said. searchText: Legal Chief of Retailer Beyond Exiting at Tumultuous Time The company recently said that its deal to invest $40 million in the ailing Container Store chain is on the rocks. Beyond Inc., the housewares giant formerly known as Overstock, is losing its legal chief on Dec. 31, according to a late Friday securities filing. E. Glen Nickle joined the company as associate general counsel in 2016 and became chief legal officer in 2021. The filing comes just days after Midvale, Utah-based Beyond announced that its $40 million investment in the Container Store was on the rocks due because of The Container Store's inability to “secure adequate financing to support the business going forward." One analyst recently said Container Store is in a "freefall." Beyond is struggling as well, having not received the financial boost it expected from buying Bed Bath & Beyond out of bankruptcy for $21.5 million last year. In the second quarter, the most recent available, Beyond lost $42.6 million on revenue of $399.1 million, down 6% from a year earlier. In October, Beyond, which started the year with 830 employees, laid off 20% of its workforce, including Chief Product Officer Carlisha Robinson. The company did not respond to a request for comment from Law.com on Nickle’s departure. Nickle, who earned $1.3 million in 2023, will be entitled to severance, according to Friday's filing, which did not disclose the amount. A May securities filing had said he would be entitled to $606,398 in severance in the event of his termination. After Nickle steps down at year-end, he will transition to an advisory role, the filing said. It did not indicate whether the company had found a successor or initiated a search for one. Nickle has spent his entire career in-house. After receiving his law degree from Brigham Young University, he was an associate general counsel at exercise equipment maker HealthRider, then served as general counsel at NordicTrack, a subsidiary of ICON Health & Fitness. He did not immediately respond to a message seeking comment on his departure.

It's now much more global thinking. We still have some cultural issues—you know, in China, lawyers are just seen as administrators, not really part of the whole process. But this is not how the company operates,” Colby said. When he came on board, Colby immediately realized that GOWell needed a serious overhaul of its contracting process. “When there was a document, they would have utter trust in the other side. They would sign these things that were just completely like, ‘Why did you sign this?’” Part of that had to do with the culture, he said. Contracts in China contain very little legal language. Colby had to teach the company it couldn’t just rubber-stamp the other party’s four-page contract, trusting that the other side would be fair, without any terms and conditions. “That was the first thing to attack and create, pretty much out of nothing,” he chuckled. “It was challenging but fun, too.” He also helped institute a strong compliance framework for its many global transactions and robust compliance training for employees, a necessity when your global footprint includes Azerbaijan, Egypt, Indonesia, Mexico, the United Arab Emirates and Indonesia. Scott Maberry, a partner at Sheppard Mullin who works closely with Colby on Foreign Corrupt Practices Act and other international compliance issues, said the legal terrain Colby navigates has land mines in every direction. "This is a company with operations in a lot of geographies. That includes not just sales in different companies but R&D labs and software engineers all over the place. They’re kind of far-flung. There's a lot of international trade law risk in any company like that," he said. “Of my clients, he’s in the top tier of compliance. He’s really good at that, and it’s a critical general counsel skill. Culturally speaking, if I was hiring a GC for a business I was trying to run, that's the No. 1 thing I’d look for: someone who really understands compliance and gets ahead of problems,” Maberry said. Colby is also particularly adept at issue spotting, Maberry said. “He may not know what the rules are or what the U.S. sanctions on a given country are as of today. But if he knows there’s a big sanctions regime and if they're going to start doing business with that country and they have an R&D lab in that country, he asks the right questions. Then he can go to the business unit and say, ‘This is easy, go ahead’ or ‘We have to expend some resources to make sure this can be done,’" he said. searchText: Porsche's Luxembourg-Based Venture Capital Arm Hires General Counsel From Clifford Chance Early-career attorney Lynn Nussbaum is taking the legal reins of Porsche Ventures as it hits the gas on its next phase of growth. Porsche Ventures, the Luxembourg-based venture capital arm of the luxury car maker Porsche AG, has hired Clifford Chance lawyer Lynn Nussbaum as general counsel, according to a LinkedIn announcement from Nussbaum. Nussbaum did not respond to a message from Law.com seeking comment on the move, and a Porsche spokesperson said the company "does not"comment on personnel matters at this level." The role marks the first in-house job for the young lawyer, who joined Clifford Chance in 2020 after short stints as a legal intern at Luxembourg-based law firms Kleyr Grasso SCS, Trialys and Elvinger Hoss Prussen. Porsche Ventures has been on an investing tear since launching in 2016, pumping funds into startups in such areas as mobility, e-commerce, battery technology and virtual reality. From launch through 2022, Porsche Ventures invested in 39 startups and provided financing to 13 others through Forward 31, a separate Porsche building its own portfolio of startups. Porsche Deputy Chairman Lutz Meschke called that 2016-2022 time frame "the first generation" of Porsche Ventures. In that span, it invested repeatedly in Croatian electric sports car maker Rimac, pumping in a a total of more than $100 million and building its stake to 20%. It also made big bets on WayRay, a Swiss company that makes holographic augmented-reality head-up display technologies for vehicles, Anagog, an Israeli startup specializing in artificial intelligence for mobile phones, and iMaker, a Chinese company that creates virtual influencers and digital ecosystems. In 2023, Porsche Ventures announced it was “shifting into high gear” and had earmarked €250 million (U.S. $263 million) for investments in new companies and its existing portfolio of about 60 startups. Last year, Stuttgart, Germany-based Porsche moved the headquarters of Porsche Ventures to Luxembourg. The VC arm also has offices in Berlin, Shanghai, as well as in Palo Alto, California. So far this year, Porsche Ventures has invested in companies producing technology for lithium-ion batteries, self-driving cars and semiconductors.

searchText: Companies' Dirty Little Secret: Those Privacy Opt-Out Requests Usually Aren't Honored “Ignoring privacy requests in states where they are legally obligatory creates a huge legal risk. Most companies that do so usually don't have evil intentions but haven't properly configured their consent-management tools," said Jules Polonetsky, Global privacy control lets computer users set privacy preferences in their browsers, automatically sharing those choices whenever users go to a site. It's supposed to give individuals more control over their personal data, allowing them to opt in or out of cookie usage, data sharing, data selling and targeted advertising. But they only work if companies honor them. And in most instances, they don't. Research from two major privacy compliance firms found that the vast majority of the most-visited websites in the United States and Europe do not honor GPC and opt-out preference signals. “It's not that they don't want compliance or they don't want to honor; it's just somehow it's broken,” said Vaibhav Antil, CEO of privacy software company Privado, whose State of Website Privacy Report 2024 found 76 of the top 100 websites in the United States do not honor opt-out consent signals, as the California Privacy Rights Act of 2020 requires. More than 80% of those sites were in the media, e-commerce and lifestyle industries, which rely heavily on ads to drive and monetize website traffic. The United Kingdom fared no better, with 74 of the 100 most-visited sites not honoring the opt-in preferences required under the Data Protection Act 2018, which mirrors the provisions of the European Union's General Data Protection Regulation of 2016. “In Europe, there is no signal. You have to interact with the banner. So, in our test, we actually interacted with the banner. We would go in, reject all cookies and see if still calls are being made or trackers are being fired or cookies are being stored,” Antil said. They were. And if these websites are not honoring GPC signals, it’s fair to assume that they are not honoring simple “do not sell/share” opt-out clicks. “We didn't explore it, but it should be similar because the thing is these are misconfigurations,” he said. Privado’s findings track with similar data from consent management platform DataGrail in its 2024 Data Privacy Trends Report. DataGrail audited more than 5,000 websites and found 75% of them do not comply with GPC requests. This comes as consumers are increasingly interested in protecting their privacy. DataGrail found more than a 200% increase in data subject access requests from 2021 to 2023. “When you actually engage with the cookie banner, and you're hopefully trying to address your preferences, you actually hope they work. Sorry to tell you they probably don't,” DataGrail CEO Daniel Barber said at his firm’s annual privacy summit in June. Why is that? It’s complicated, said Jules Polonetsky, internet privacy expert and CEO of the Future of Privacy Forum. “When you visit a website, a kaleidoscope of cascading things occurs. The second you request a webpage, your browser is requesting cookies from a website. Milliseconds later, the servers that have just been pinged are pinging companies and other companies and networks and multiple third-party plug-ins are loading,” he said. “Ignoring privacy requests in states where they are legally obligatory creates a huge legal risk. Most companies that do so usually don't have evil intentions but haven't properly configured their consent-management tools. Getting these tools to work properly can be hugely complicated, and we see even sophisticated companies dropping the ball, or shall I say, dropping the cookie,” he said. The nebulousness of an internet protocol address makes it more difficult to identify who is making the opt-out request. “An IP address could be you and your laptop at home or at a Wi-Fi on a university campus, and that's one IP address for the whole college,” said Ryan O'Leary, research director at International Data Corp. “It's hard to manage the consent, and after you leave that website, it's almost like you weren't there. When you have a known relationship with a brand—let’s say you log into your Apple ID or Target account—you're a known person" and have to manage the consent there," he said. "But it's virtually impossible to marry that ID to the IP address that clicked ‘do not track.’ If you're just bumping around from channel to channel or website to website, they don't have a duty to honor your choices.” GPC has some 50 million users worldwide. Currently, just three states—California, Colorado and Connecticut—require companies to comply with GPC signals. But laws requiring opt-out signals kick in in Delaware and Montana on Jan. 1, and in Oregon and Texas one year later. searchText: Shareholder Activists Poised to Pounce in 2025. Is Your Board Ready? Next year’s proxy season will be a wild one, as public companies face a surge of shareholder activism and more scrutiny around the composition of their boards. Next year’s proxy season will be a wild one, as public companies face a surge of shareholder activism and more scrutiny around the composition of their boards. Boardroom battles were one of the big topics at this week's Berkeley Law Fall Forum on Corporate Governance, where business and legal leaders convened to discuss a head-spinning array of regulatory and governance challenges. The event was co-hosted by Berkeley Law and Cooley. Activists Will Turn Up Heat Shareholder activists took their campaigns to new heights in 2024, with notable battles against Disney, News Corp., Norfolk Southern and Southwest Airlines. David Rosewater, head of Morgan Stanley’s shareholder activist defense practice, said public campaigns by activists shot up 40% from 2023, and he expects next year to be just as busy. “A lot of activity is going to continue,” he said, driven by the vast sums of uninvested capital held by private equity firms, a change in the presidential administration and what likely will be a more robust M&A market. “There is a tremendous amount of activity kind of under the surface that I expect to sort of ramp up more significantly into next proxy season." Steve Lipin, CEO of the strategic communications and investor relations firm Gladstone Place Partners, said it’s not a coincidence that activist fund Elliott Management made public its $5 billion stake in Honeywell this week. “A lot of these positions are going to be made public in coming days, and so we'll all be scrubbing the filings,” Lipin said. “Metaphorically, we have an activist in the White House and the perception is that, yes, all his friends happen to be activists and raiders. But the feeling is that there's a bit of euphoria from the activist side of the house.” Activists are also getting less predictable and more willing to go public, Lipin said. “There's a competition in effect to get out first with a particular name. Now we're seeing that the activists are less willing to sort of stay private because they're worried about other activists going public in the same name. And to be honest, they want all the glory and credit and they also sort of want to drive the initiative as opposed to competing with other activists.” Even controlled companies, where one investor holds more than 50% of the voting power, are likely to see more activist fireworks, said Sean Donahue, co-chair of the activism and takeover defense practice at Paul Hastings. “I think at some point you're going to see somebody actually run a slate at a controlled company, even though they can't win, and then claim victory if they get a substantial percentage" of the vote, Donahue said. That would allow the activist to essentially say, "Hey, we got 80% of the Class A. Ignore the Class B. This is a mandate. Four directors should resign, we should be appointed." Companies should prepare for attacks by addressing obvious vulnerabilities on their own and by taking control of the narrative, in part by developing well-crafted rebuttals in advance. “The activists are very press-savvy," Lipin said. "They know how to leak to the outlets. They're quite often quite good on CNBC. And CNBC becomes almost like their megaphone." Lipin said companies need to figure out their story and make sure they present it clearly in annual reports. “The criticisms may not be an economic one. It may be we don't like your dual class. It may be the makeup of your board,” he said. “In the world of universal proxy, it is not my slate against your slate. It's literally a fight for the individual directors. So part of the planning is not just defense of the board,. It's actually defense of every director who is either up for election or who would be targets in a universal proxy contest.” A board refresh can go a long way toward keeping activists at bay. But Rosewater said it's something companies are often slow to do. Or, if they do it, they might not clearly explain what they're trying to achieve. “The most important thing that you can do in your proxy statement or when you're talking about your board is, Why is every single person on that board? And what is the fundamental reason that that person needs to be on your board?" Rosewater said. Freshening the Board Venture capitalist Joanna Rees said companies should plan board refreshment and evolution well in advance, not when a company is caught short or in a crisis. Rees said board refreshment has contributed to the success of the credit-scoring company FICO, where she's been a director nine years. When she came aboard, the stock was at $89 a share. title: Regulatory Upheaval Is Coming. How Businesses Prepare and Respond Will Separate Winners and Losers
description: “Every regulation is going to be questioned. ... And that'll be a better environment for many businesses once the regulations are wiped away. But they're going to have to adapt their businesses to exploit that," said Sean West, co-founder of Hence Technologies.
preview:
The only constant is change, the adage goes. And it was particularly salient at Berkeley Law’s Fall Forum on Corporate Governance this week, where business and legal leaders convened to hear what they can expect in the year ahead, and how to navigate an ever-shifting regulatory environment.

Angeli Patel, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business, which hosted the event along with Cooley, said change management could be deemed the loose theme of Tuesday’s program. Attendees were treated to a slate of panel discussions on how to manage volatility and risk in areas such as artificial intelligence, climate and environmental, social and governance, and the incoming Trump administration.

searchText: Regulatory Upheaval Is Coming. How Businesses Prepare and Respond Will Separate Winners and Losers “Every regulation is going to be questioned. ... And that'll be a better environment for many businesses once the regulations are wiped away. But they're going to have to adapt their businesses to exploit that," said Sean West, co-founder of Hence Technologies. The only constant is change, the adage goes. And it was particularly salient at Berkeley Law’s Fall Forum on Corporate Governance this week, where business and legal leaders convened to hear what they can expect in the year ahead, and how to navigate an ever-shifting regulatory environment. Angeli Patel, executive director of the Berkeley Center for Law and Business, which hosted the event along with Cooley, said change management could be deemed the loose theme of Tuesday’s program. Attendees were treated to a slate of panel discussions on how to manage volatility and risk in areas such as artificial intelligence, climate and environmental, social and governance, and the incoming Trump administration. Here are highlights from Tuesday’s sessions: | The State of AI Regulation If change and uncertainty are the closest descriptors for the current state of corporate governance, “safety” is the buzzword most closely associated with regulating AI. But federal efforts to put up legislative guardrails have largely fallen flat. More than 120 AI bills have been introduced in Congress, but not one has passed. “Congress has deeply struggled for many years to regulate the tech sector,” California state Sen. Scott Weiner, D-San Francisco, noted at a panel on regulatory developments in AI. President-elect Donald Trump has vowed to repeal President Joe Biden’s sweeping executive order on AI, and members of the U.S. House of Representatives have expressed an interest in defunding the National Institute of Standards and Technology, Weiner said. “California more than ever has not just a role, but a responsibility to act,” he said. But California's Democratic governor, Gavin Newsom, recently vetoed SB 1047, an ambitious bill written by Weiner that required testing of large and expensive “frontier” AI models and held AI developers liable for catastrophic harms those models may cause. It also mandated a “kill switch” that could shut down AI models if they started to do anything “problematic.” “I think there were some in the opposition to SB 1047 who, I thought, were in a very flippant way dismissing any idea of regulating anything at the model level,” Weiner said. “They would refer to it as ‘regulating math.’ OK, sure. But it's math that has incredible power, and the power is at the model level. The model level is what allows those applications to happen.” Weiner said there’s no way to remove any chance of risk or force companies to certify that their AI models will cause no harm. “All we were asking is, 'Hey, can you please do a basic safety evaluation of your model to determine if there is a risk of catastrophic bargain? And if you do identify that risk, can you please take reasonable steps not to eliminate the risk, but to reduce the risk?'" Gerard de Graaf, the European Union's digital envoy to the United States, took a similar tack. “The keyword is safety here," he said. "You step into an airplane, you believe it's safe. Rigetti Computing, a Berkeley, California-based designer and maker of quantum computers, is saying goodbye to Rick Danis, its general counsel of five years. Danis informed the company last week that he plans to resign on Nov. 30, Rigetti announced in a securities filing. Danis joined Rigetti in 2019 after a little more than a year at satellite antenna company Kymeta. He also held leading in-house roles at Nokia, Yahoo, media company Leaf Group, and domain name provider Rightside Group, which he helped sell to the domain name registry Donuts for $213 million in 2017. Rigetti did not respond to an inquiry from Law.com about the reasoning behind his resignation. In a LinkedIn message, Danis said he is "moving on to another great opportunity," adding, "I have nothing but good things to say about Rigetti and will be a strong supporter of the company going forward." The company’s 8-K Securities and Exchange Commission filing says he will act as a consultant for the company through March 31, 2025. Founded in 2013 by a former IBM physicist, Rigetti Computing specializes in building quantum processors and the software necessary to harness quantum computing, an advanced area of computing that uses quantum mechanics to solve complex problems beyond the capacity of classical computers. It specializes in developing quantum processors and the software necessary to harness quantum computing for practical applications, helping scientists and engineers work on issues like climate change, drug development and discovery and artificial intelligence. Last year, it released its first commercially available quantum processing unit called Novera, designed to provide researchers and developers with hands-on access to advanced quantum computing technology. title: What to Expect From the SEC Under Trump 2.0
description: Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority.

Donald Trump's reclaiming of the White House could spell the end of one of the most aggressive SEC rulemaking and enforcement regimes in history.
