searchText: What to Expect From the SEC Under Trump 2.0 Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority. Donald Trump's reclaiming of the White House could spell the end of one of the most aggressive SEC rulemaking and enforcement regimes in history. Experts and legal observers say that Americans should expect a more measured Securities and Exchange Commission during Trump's second term; less gung-ho about testing novel legal theories and pushing the boundaries of its enforcement authority and more concerned with issues affecting Main Street and everyday retail investors. "We've already seen what the SEC in a Trump 1.0 administration looked like, where the SEC focused on bread-and-butter cases focused on addressing harm to retail investors, such as offering frauds, Ponzi schemes and excessive fees charged by investment advisory firms," said Jennifer Lee, a Jenner & Block partner who formerly spent 12 years with the SEC, rising to assistant regional director of its enforcement division. By contrast, the SEC under current Chair Gary Gensler has been more willing to bring individual compliance cases against public companies and investment firms it regulates, even if there is no investor harm," she said. In his three years as chair, Gensler has steered the commission into uncharted territory, pushing initiatives on climate change disclosure, environmental, social and governance investing and corporate greenwashing. Preemptive compliance measures were at the center of Gensler's ambitious regulatory agenda. Observers said he wanted to get ahead of issues that, if left unchecked, could lead to greater fraud or investor harm down the road. To that end, the commission expanded its authority into policing data-security incidents and cyber-risk disclosures, greenhouse gas emission reporting and regulating the use of AI and other types of predictive analytics by broker-dealers and investment advisers. "The SEC under Chair Gensler has been aggressive in terms of really putting in prospective requirements in emerging substance areas like cybersecurity, ESG and also AI," Lee said. She expects that, under the Trump administration, the SEC will likely pull back on rulemaking and adopt a less stringent stance on enforcement, particularly when it comes to pushing the bounds of existing rules. Trump already has vowed to fire Gensler "on day one" and appoint a replacement. One credible successor is Robinhood Chief Legal, Compliance and Corporate Affairs Officer Dan Gallagher, who was an SEC commissioner from 2011 to 2015, according to people familiar with the discussions, Also well-respected in the legal community and a potential to successor are Hester Pierce, who has been a Republican GOP commissioner since 2017 and is known for her incisive dissents, and Chris Giancarlo, a former chair of the Commodity Futures Trading Commission, who is now a partner at Willkie Farr & Gallagher. Legal observers say that, under a new chair, the SEC likely will abandon ESG rulemaking and will stop trying to implement its new rule requiring public companies to disclose greenhouse gas emissions. That rule is on holding amid challenges by industry groups and Republican-run states. Novel legal theories also likely will be out, including its controversial push to apply internal accounting controls to cybersecurity, legal observers said. In July, a federal judge sided with software firm SolarWinds on the question of whether the provisions of the the Securities Exchange Act that give the SEC authority to regulate accounting controls also give it authority over cybersecurity controls. The judge "resoundingly rejected" that premise, finding that the SEC was overreaching. Aravind Swaminathan, a partner at Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe, told Law.com at the time. Lee said the SEC under its next chair will be less likely to test its legal boundaries. "There will be more of a hewing to tried and true legal theories," she said. "The SEC under Trump will generally be more skeptical of novel theories in enforcement actions. The posture will also matter—the SEC may be more open to novel theories that will be litigated before a court or tried in front of a jury, versus theories that companies may feel they have to settle just to move on from an issue." She also anticipates that the SEC will be less exacting in its demands around cyber-incident disclosures and will shy away from bringing enforcement actions in instances where regulatory violations may have occurred but there is no evidence of consumers being harmed. Last month, the commission fined four companies that it said downplayed intrusions into their systems and misled investors about their cybersecurity risks, an action that brought a strong dissent from Pierce and fellow GOP commissioner Mark Uyeda. searchText: How Dana Rao Built a 'Yes' Culture at Adobe and Why He Walked Away When Dana Rao became general counsel of Adobe six years ago, he said he set out to recast the culture of a legal department known as a place where "good ideas go to die." Dana Rao has a collection of coffee mugs from all of the jobs he's had in his three-decade career, one of the most memorable of which features a slogan he created when he took the legal reins at Adobe six years ago. It says, "Yes starts here." Berkeley Law's Irene Liu, who interviewed Rao for a webinar Tuesday hosted by its executive education program, asked what the fine print underneath the asterisk said. "Except when it's a definite no," he said, drawing laughter from Liu. Rao explained, "We love the asterisk because not only is it true, even as yes-friendly as you want to be, there is this backstop. But it's also funny. And it's so stereotypically a lawyer thing." Rao recently stepped down as San Jose, California-based Adobe's general counsel and chief trust officer, capping his 12-year run with the maker of Photoshop, InDesign and other software tools for creatives. He told Liu that he felt it was the right time. "I've always had this framework in my career to force myself to think about what matters and how I'm spending my life," he said. "Life isn't just about one thing. Just being general counsel isn't like the sum of who I am. I'm a father. I'm a husband. I have friends. I have hobbies." In his conversation with Liu, Rao reflected on some of the greatest triumphs in his in-house career. Among them was changing Adobe's perception of its legal department. Rao had already been at Adobe six years before he was appointed general counsel, and he knew the in-house culture was pretty conservative. "People would say pejoratively, 'We're the department of 'no' and 'good ideas go to die there.' That's how people think about lawyers, unfortunately. But there were a whole bunch of us who wanted to change that culture." Rao said he knew that revamping the legal department's image as "solution-oriented" would require marketing. Two months into the job, he held an off-site with members of his team, where they figured out the principles they wanted to convey to the rest of the company. Then he talked a trademark lawyer into enlisting help from the marketing team and after some brainstorming came up with the now-internally famous tagline. "Both my CEO and my CHRO, both still carry that mug around to their meetings," he said. While the mug helped get the point across, Rao said it still took a lot of work to change legal's approach. "'Yes starts here' is more work than 'no starts here.' And the reason is that in order to say yes, you're taking on risk." He said it requires really knowing the business and how it makes money. "All the credit goes to my legal team. That was a fun change," he said. "But they also had to do more work as a cultural change in order to get to yes or a yes that we could accept. Our view has always been, like, 'We don't really care if you get the answer wrong as long as you understand all the questions.' And we get things wrong because we're taking risks, and that's fine. But you did have to do the work and understand all the risks before you made that recommendation." Rao applied that mindset to one of Adobe's riskiest ventures—developing safe and ethical AI products. Adobe launched its text-to-image and video model, Firefly, two years ago, but Rao had been thinking about issues like deep fakes and bias long before that. "Being a lawyer of color, I was pretty acutely aware that the last thing we all need is some kind of automated system furthering stereotypes." He also was very aware of the IP issues around training a foundation model. Rao said he told the CEO things could go one of two ways: "You can just go train on everything on the web, which is what everyone else is doing. The way I see that playing out, is there's going to be litigation for years on whether you can scrape the web and whether or not the output is going to infringe the copyright of someone from the input side. "And I said my opinion is in the United States fair use will eventually win, and you will be able to do these things. But I think that will go to the Supreme Court because there are millions of dollars at stake. "And so your enterprise customers may not be that excited about the uncertainty. And then our creators don't like this at all. They don't like getting screwed. We have creators who are customers, who are the ones who are getting copied. "That's not Microsoft's problem. That's not OpenAI's problem. It's our problem." So Rao suggested a different path, creating the product to be what he calls "commercially safe," with a lot of technical work underlying it to make it competitive and to differentiate it from other products working with a limited dataset. searchText: Ex-Twitter Exec Sues for $20M, Says Musk Fired Her as 'Petty Retribution' Leslie Berland was chief marketing officer until October 2022, when a meeting with advertisers went off the rails, leaving Musk embarrassed and looking for someone to blame, she says. Another former Twitter executive has joined the chorus of fired employees suing Elon Musk alleging unpaid severance. This time, it's ex-chief marketing officer Leslie Berland, who says she was fired so that Musk could avoid paying her $20 million in severance and benefits. Berland, who until October 2022 was Twitter's chief marketing officer, said Musk fired her in an act of "petty retribution" after a meeting with advertisers went off the rails, and also to "rid himself of her large compensation package." The fateful meeting happened on Oct. 31, just days after he completed his $44 billion takeover of the San Francisco-based social media company, now called X Corp. Its purpose was to preserve the platform's relationships with legacy advertisers. Because chief commercial officer Sarah Personette had just resigned, Berland recommended Musk connect with her successor, head of global sales Jean-Philippe Maheu. But Musk went "off-script," Berland says, suggesting in front of the advertisers that "he ought to send a Tweet teasing the reinstatement of Donald Trump's then-suspended Twitter account." Maheu suggested Musk not do this, which prompted an "embarrassed and angry" Musk to text Berland "JP is not going to work out. Bad recommendation," according to the suit. Musk ended up firing them both. The suit alleges that Musk blamed Berland for personally vouching for Maheu and terminated her "for cause" to get out of paying her the roughly $20 million in severance she would be owed for her nearly seven years at the company. Her lawsuit claims her firing was a "jarring reversal" from Musk's attitude the week prior to the meeting. At one point Musk's chief of staff, Jehn Balajadia, confided to Berland that she was "the only one here [at Twitter] that Elon trusts," the suit alleges. Berland says in the suit that Musk had a human resources employee call her to tell her that her computer access had been shut off and that security was outside her office door, ready to escort her out of the building. Confused as to why, Berland says she texted Musk, saying she was "rooting" for him and asking to talk about the situation. He did not respond, and the two never spoke again, according to her complaint. When Berland appealed the for-cause termination and denial of benefits, she was met with a host of reasons for denial, including that she violated Twitter's travel policy by taking chartered flights in her last week of employment that cost the company "approximately $200,000." Berland says the flights were a pretext, and that she had to fly to San Francisco at the last minute to assist Musk and his team. A commercial flight would not have gotten her there in time, her lawsuit claims. In addition to an undisclosed amount in cash severance, Berland says she was denied accelerated equity vesting and payment of COBRA premiums to cover health insurance for herself and two children. "Musk's belated characterization of Ms. Berland's termination as 'for cause' was done for the unlawful purpose of denying Ms. Berland these benefits. This is consistent with Musk's long pattern of not paying his bills," her lawsuit says. After leaving Twitter, Berland spent a year at Peloton before becoming Verizon's chief marketing officer in January, according to her LinkedIn profile. Musk's legal team did not respond to requests for comment on her case. The company did not respond to an inquiry sent to its reestablished press inbox. The billionaire is currently fending off a slew of lawsuits filed by ex-employees claiming they were cheated out of severance, including one brought by former CEO Parag Agrawal, CFO Ned Segal, CLO Vijaya Gadde and General Counsel Sean Edgett. On Nov. 1, U.S. District Judge Maxine Chesney denied Musk's motion to dismiss the case, rejecting Musk's argument that he was acting in his capacity as an employer, not as a fiduciary, when he terminated the foursome. The web-tracking litigation landscape is growing ever more frightening amid an onslaught of lawsuits targeting anyone with a website.

With no single statute governing website tracking, crafty plaintiffs' lawyers are haunting modern digital practices with a zombie horde of old laws, including ones aimed at videorecording, wiretapping and false advertising.

searchText: Old Laws, New Tricks: Lawyers Using Patchwork of Creative Legal Theories to Target New Tech The web-tracking litigation landscape is growing ever more frightening amid an onslaught of lawsuits targeting anyone with a website. The web-tracking litigation landscape is growing ever more frightening amid an onslaught of lawsuits targeting anyone with a website. With no single statute governing website tracking, crafty plaintiffs' lawyers are haunting modern digital practices with a zombie horde of old laws, including ones aimed at videorecording, wiretapping and false advertising. "Most of the litigation to date is novel, and a win in one court doesn't necessarily scare away the plaintiff's counsel from trying over and over again, or from flooding every website that their clients come in contact with and sending a demand letter," said Bethany Lukitsch, co-leader of BakerHostetler's class action defense practice. "So we see new lawsuits and new theories that are being developed throughout the year. Almost monthly, we come into contact with some new theory. Lukitsch made this observation at a recent Halloween-themed webinar hosted by the firm on website tracking litigation trends. Lukitsch said she would never have expected three years ago to see such a proliferation of website tracking litigation, particularly in California, where she practices. "Who would have thought that wiretapping would become such a big trend with website tracking?" Lukitsch said. "These are decades-old laws that were written to protect against spying or listening in on telephone conversations. They have now morphed into trying to be applicable to internet activity, and not just conversations like we think of in any sort of email communication or web chat or an actual textual communication, but literally any application of any website tracking technology to a website is subject to one of these wiretapping claims." Wiretapping claims started exploding in 2022 with Javier v. Assurance IQ, where the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit held that California's wiretapping law, the California Invasion of Privacy Act applies to Internet technologies. Lukitsch said these lawsuits argue that "when consumers come to your website, their actions on your web button clicks, whether they be chat, whether they be just visiting and browsing, constitute a communication for purposes of these wiretapping statutes." She noted that, just last month, the Massachusetts Supreme Court shot down a lawsuit brought under Massachusetts's state wiretapping law, a development she termed a bit of "good news" for corporate defendants, though certainly not a magic bullet. Lukitsch said a lot of the complaints she sees aren't alleging a single cause of action. "The plaintiff will throw in whatever they could possibly throw in in terms of legal theories," she said, adding, "I think one of the reasons that we're seeing all of these creative theories is because of a lack of private right of action in many of these different state privacy statutes." The federal Video Privacy Protection Act is another popular example of an old law being repurposed for a new legal theory. "If you're a retailer or somebody that has an occasional video on your website, you're probably in decent shape of escaping one of these or defending against one of these claims, but if you do have video content or streaming service as part of your customer contract, I think it's going to be potentially more difficult to evade these cases at an early motion stage," Lukitsch said. Marketers may love "session replay" technology for its ability to track how consumers interact with websites, but they have also become a major pitfall. Lukitsch recommended that companies delay recording a screen until a banner or notification secures user consent, or record sessions intermittently, providing only a random sample of user interactions. "So still helpful for your marketing team, but no one particular user is going to be able to say, 'Aha, this session was recorded when I was visiting,'" she said. She also counsels clients to avoid collecting sensitive data—such as names, addresses or chat content—or to mask such information in session replays. Every website tracking tool carries some risk, but some are necessary to make sure your website, and its opt-out mechanism, function properly. The term "necessary" hasn't yet been litigated. "What is absolutely required and where you need to provide opt-outs is a little bit squishy. So you don't have to provide some sort of opt-out right for every single type of technology," Lukitsch said, though she's not sure if that gets companies around the wiretapping claim absent some type of advance notice and consent. "This is the area that is being hotly litigated and tested," she said. Justin Yedor, a BakerHostetler partner who specializes in California privacy laws, said companies should focus on disclosure and consent as a way to push back. searchText: SEC Fines 4 Companies $7M for Downplaying Breaches Tied to Massive SolarWinds Hack The agency said Unisys, Avaya Holdings, Check Point Software Technologies and Mimecast provided misleading disclosures about the incidents, leaving investors in the dark about their "true scope." The U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission has levied civil penalties totaling nearly $7 million against four companies it alleges misled investors about their cybersecurity risks and downplayed intrusions into their systems by the same hackers behind the SolarWinds attack. In an order Tuesday, the SEC said Unisys Corp., Avaya Holdings Corp., Check Point Software Technologies and Mimecast all filed public disclosures that "minimized" cybersecurity incidents likely related to SolarWinds. The order follows the regulator's yearslong investigation into public companies affected by the SolarWinds breach in 2020, which ranks among the most devastating cyberattacks ever, compromising thousands of SolarWinds customers, including major companies and government agencies. The attack, known as Sunburst, is widely believed to have been carried out by hackers affiliated with the Russian intelligence service. Investigators say they pulled it off by covertly inserting malicious code into SolarWinds' flagship Orion software, which spread to the company's customers through a routine software update. The SEC began issuing sweep letters to potential SolarWinds hack victims back in 2021, and is currently suing the company and its security chief Tim Brown for civil fraud. "As today's enforcement actions reflect, while public companies may become targets of cyberattacks, it is incumbent upon them to not further victimize their shareholders or other members of the investing public by providing misleading disclosures about the cybersecurity incidents they have encountered," Sanjay Wadhwa, acting director of the SEC's Division of Enforcement, said in a statement Tuesday. "Here, the SEC's orders find that these companies provided misleading disclosures about the incidents at issue, leaving investors in the dark about the true scope of the incidents." Unisys, Avaya and Check Point all learned in 2020 and Mimecast learned in January 2021 that their systems had been accessed by a threat actor "likely behind the SolarWinds Orion hack," the SEC said. All four companies went about disclosing the incidents in different ways, though they all kept investors in the dark about the scope of the intrusions, the SEC alleges. The regulator said all four cooperated with the SEC's investigation and took voluntary steps to improve their cybersecurity controls. Unisys, which agreed to pay a $4 million civil penalty, described its cybersecurity risks from two SolarWinds-related intrusions as hypothetical, "despite knowing that it had experienced two SolarWinds-related intrusions involving exfiltration of gigabytes of data." "Downplaying the extent of a material cybersecurity breach is a bad strategy," Jorge Tenreiro, acting chief of the SEC's Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit, said in a statement. "In two of these cases, the relevant cybersecurity risk factors were framed hypothetically or generically when the companies knew the warned of risks had already materialized. The federal securities laws prohibit half-truths, and there is no exception for statements in risk-factor disclosures." Unisys referred Law.com to an 8-k it filed Tuesday announcing that it had resolved the matter, and declined to comment further. The SEC also said Avaya knew the hacker had accessed at least 145 files in its cloud-based file-sharing environment but stated only that it had accessed a "limited number of [the] company's email messages." Avaya will pay a $1 million penalty under the SEC's order. Check Point, which will pay $995,000, described its risks from intrusions in "generic terms," and Mimecast, which was fined $990,000, failed to reveal the specifics of the exfiltrated code or the number of encrypted credentials that were accessed by the threat actor. In an email, an Avaya spokesperson said the company is pleased to have resolved the matter and highlighted its cooperation with the SEC. "Avaya continues to focus on strengthening its cybersecurity program, both in designing and providing our products and services to our valued customers, as well as in our internal operations," the spokesperson added. Check Point, an Israeli company, noted in an email that the company disclosed last year that it was in settlement discussions with the SEC after cooperating with its investigation into whether it should have reported its 2020 intrusion in its annual report in 2021. "As mentioned in the SEC's order, Check Point investigated the SolarWinds incident and did not find evidence that any customer data, code, or other sensitive information was accessed," a spokesperson told Law.com. October 17, 2024 at 11:28 AM 7 minute read Artificial Intelligence By Maria Dinzeo "AI washing" is a relatively new addition to the regulatory lexicon, but it's really just plain-old grifting. Whether it's making bold, unfounded claims about your AI's capabilities or the accuracy of its outputs or downplaying the level of human involvement in an "automated" process, there is no AI exception to the consumer protection laws already on the books. "Whether you're in real life or in the metaverse or in some instance of the multiverse or it's all a giant computer simulation, guess what? Too bad. The FTC Act still applies," said Michael Atleson, senior attorney at the Federal Trade Commission's division of advertising practices. "Products and services that are new or innovative surely get no free pass." Atleson joined colleagues with the Securities and Exchange Commission and California's Office of Financial Technology Innovation Wednesday for a "Steering Clear of AI Washing" virtual panel hosted by Berkeley Center for Law and Business. While there's been some debate about whether AI hype has reached its peak, there's no question that the investing craze is still on the upswing. Talk of AI also dominated this year's annual report season, with more than 40% of S&P 500 companies mentioning AI in their 10-Ks, panel moderator Angeli Patel noted. Chrissy Filipp, assistant regional director for enforcement in the SEC's San Francisco office, said a wide array of actors are going to seek to exploit this level of interest for some time, and companies that tout their use of AI models to assist with investment recommendations or trades will remain high up on her agency's radar. She pointed to two recent enforcement actions against investment advisers as cautionary examples—that of Toronto-based Delphia and San Francisco-based Global Predictions. The agency charged both with making false and misleading statements, either in SEC filings or on their websites and social media, about their AI capabilities. "The basic idea here is that actors are going to seek to exploit the current interest in all things AI, including excitement about investing in companies in the AI space or retaining investment professionals using AI," she said. "The same risks and issues have come up in the past with respect to crypto, with respect to the ESG movement, where actors are capitalizing on strong waves of investor interest. It's just important to be mindful that the same statutory provisions and standards that the commission has applied for years in dealing with false statements, misrepresentations and deception by issuers and others, would also apply in instances of AI washing." "Artificial intelligence" is itself a marketing term coined in a paper by "the father of artificial intelligence," John McCarthy, Atleston said. Years after its publication, McCarthy acknowledged that he and his co-author "came up with it because they were using that document to get funding, and they wanted to get the attention of the people with the money, Atleston said. There's a "general lack of transparency" about how AI tools were built and how they work, Atleston noted, a topic that spawned a recent enforcement sweep. He said his favorite was against DoNotPay, a do-it-yourself legal and consumer services company that had advertised itself as the world's first robot lawyer "but was sadly, or happily for some of us who are lawyers, unable to support claims that it could substitute for the expertise of a human lawyer." searchText: When Law Firms Get Hacked, Are Their Corporate Clients on the Hook? Analysis "Law firms are being heavily targeted now because they have a lot of sensitive information and they need to operate," said Brian Levine, managing director of Ernst & Young's cybersecurity and data privacy practice. 8 minute read… October 15, 2024 at 03:37 PM 8 minute read Cybersecurity By Maria Dinzeo Cyber criminals are giving corporate litigation departments yet another reason to worry—that organizations could be on the hook for their law firms' data breaches. Global snack food conglomerate Mondelez found this out the hard way when it was sued over a data breach suffered by its law firm, Bryan Cave Leighton Paisner, in 2023. The plaintiffs, a proposed class of 1,100 current and former Mondelez employees, argued that the company had not properly protected their sensitive data by ensuring that Bryan Cave had "reasonable cybersecurity procedures" in place when intruders accessed its systems in February 2023, "including an area it used to store certain customer files." During the intrusion, which ran through March 1, 2023, hackers made off with a host of personal and financial data from Mondelez employees, including names, addresses, birthdates and Social Security numbers, as well as employment identification numbers and retirement plan information. Mondelez initially fought to have the case dismissed, arguing that it didn't have a duty to make sure that its law firm had adequate security, and it shouldn't be held accountable for a breach that didn't involve its own systems. U.S. District Judge Jorge Alonso of the Northern District of Illinois summed it up nicely: "Bryan Cave's information systems, not Mondelez's, were hacked, and Mondelez argues that there are no plausible allegations to support the claim that Mondelez should be held responsible for a breach not of its own systems, but Bryan Cave's." Alonso noted that neither side pointed to any previous cases where judges have directly tackled this theory in a similar situation, let alone decided for or against it. But rather than dismiss the claim, Alonso adopted a "let's see where this goes" approach, ruling, "To the extent that there is little precedent to guide the parties and the court as to plaintiffs' precise legal theory, there is all the more reason to develop the facts first, rather than to hastily proceed to a dispositive ruling." But that wasn't to be. Mondelez quickly settled with the plaintiffs a few months later for $750,000. This comes at a time of skyrocketing data breaches targeting the world's most prominent law firms. Brian Levine, managing director of Ernst & Young's cybersecurity and data privacy practice, said firms are attractive targets for breaches because they are a central repository of lucrative, non-public information. Their bill-by-the-hour revenue model also opens them up to ransomware gangs looking to exploit any shutdown in operations. "Law firms are being heavily targeted now because they have a lot of sensitive information and they need to operate. So from a ransomware perspective, law firms work on the billable hour. If their employees can't do their job and if their attorneys can't do their job, they're not earning revenue. But even more importantly, a high percentage of their documents are attorney-client privileged or confidential. They may contain trade secrets that are pre-patent. They may contain merger plans, acquisition plans, strategic plans that bad guys have actually taken—not to do ransomware or hurt the firm—but to trade on," he said. Law firms are also not specifically attuned to implementing sophisticated cybersecurity policies, procedures, and controls. "One sort of universal vulnerability that I would say probably applies to law firms different from other industry verticals, it probably has to be a sort of relative lack of security governance maturity," said Jack Freund, chief risk officer for cyber-risk-quantification platform Kovrr. Even with great security, attackers will always look for the easiest method of intrusion. Reused passwords, phishing emails, "very basic, stupid ways," Freund said. Hackers are also looking to exploit security flaws in software and products that "are in the wild" exist but haven't been fixed yet. "You can have very sophisticated security controls, but if you're leaving the back door open, well I'll just walk right in. And that tends to be the way a lot of security hackers tend to target," he said. And the amount of vulnerable is growing with the use of AI. "It's going to encourage organizations to record more, to save more. And then we come back to that data retention issue again," Freund said. "So when the pile of potentially explosive information becomes more interesting and larger, then you're going to see more attackers going after it." October 10, 2024 at 03:26 PM 12 minute read Foreign Corrupt Practices Act By Maria Dinzeo Federal enforcement agencies are prowling for instances of bribery and corruption around the world—scrutiny that can put general counsel in peril, even those who believe they've stayed on the right side of the law as they navigate the inevitable gray zones that come along. Many countries where American companies do business have an array of business practices and customs that might be frowned upon in this country, but whether they cross the sometimes-blurry lines of legality isn't always clear. The club enforcers wield is the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act, a 1977 law that bars companies from providing anything of value to foreign officials to gain a business advantage. "The Foreign Corrupt Practices Act is a tricky issue because it's omnipresent and business practices are different in different areas," said Laura Schumacher, the former chief legal officer at Abbvie. But it is the general counsel's duty to ensure that their company is operating responsibly, even in jurisdictions where payments to foreign officials might be expected. Executives are also navigating a landscape fraught with personal risk as the Justice Department steps up its whistleblower and self-reporting incentives. Legal chiefs in particular could find themselves facing unexpected scrutiny over what may seem like routine advice, and they could become potential targets of federal enforcement agencies bent on holding individuals accountable for misconduct. The high-profile prosecution of an ousted legal chief at a large tech company highlights the growing risk of personal liability over legal and business advice given years after the fact. For the last five years, Steven Schwartz has been awaiting trial on charges of violating FCPA, conspiracy, falsifying books and records, and circumventing and failing to implement internal accounting controls. He stands accused of authorizing a contractor to bribe foreign government officials in India. If convicted, he faces 180 years in prison. His indictment dates back to 2019, but the facts of the case go back even further. Schwartz was chief legal officer at Cognizant, a giant tech firm headquartered in New Jersey but with significant operations in India, including half of its 250,000 global workforce. One of its specialties is building call centers, and in 2014, Cognizant had a major project in the works in Chennai. The company had hired an Indian multinational construction firm, Larsen and Toubro, to build the 2.7-million-square-foot campus, a job that included securing the necessary permits. In April 2014, Schwartz was pulled into two videoconference calls with his co-defendant, former Cognizant president Gordon Coburn. It was on those calls, the government claims, that the pair authorized L&T to pay $2 million to an Indian government official who had demanded payment in exchange for a planning permit that would help keep the project on track. L&T allegedly asked to be reimbursed the money, and Coburn and Schwartz "agreed that cognizant would reimburse the construction company for the bribe payment through a change order request at the end of the project." According to the indictment, Schwartz agreed that this approach was acceptable "but cautioned that the reimbursement payment should not stand out in the change order request." The government was turned on to the allegations after Cognizant self-reported the incident following an internal investigation led by DLA Piper in 2016. The company ended up paying a total of $28 million in disgorgement and penalties to the DOJ and Securities & Exchange Commission in 2019 but received a nonprosecution agreement in exchange for its cooperation. The trial has been delayed multiple times due to difficulties in getting India to cooperate with the defense's effort to depose L&T executives, including CEO Sekharipuram Narayanan Subrahmanyan, who at the time was head of L&T's real estate division, was involved in the Chennai project and is under investigation in India for corruption. A new trial date has been set for March 2025, to "preserve the integrity of the truth seeking process," says an order by U.S. District Judge Michael Farbiarz, who took over the case from retiring U.S. District Judge Kevin McNulty in October 2023. title: In-House Lawyers Weigh In on How AI Will Revolutionize Dispute Resolution
description: For years, China has employed AI agents as online "robot judges." Could that happen here?
preview:
For years, China has employed artificial intelligence agents as online "robot judges" that can decide everything from copyright lawsuits to traffic tickets. Can such a thing be possible in America?

For Jo Levy, former general counsel of Asia Pacific at Intel, it could very well be.
excerpt: For years, China has employed AI agents as online "robot judges." Could that happen here?
searchText: In-House Lawyers Weigh In on How AI Will Revolutionize Dispute Resolution For years, China has employed AI agents as online "robot judges." Could that happen here? For years, China has employed artificial intelligence agents as online "robot judges" that can decide everything from copyright lawsuits to traffic tickets. Can such a thing be possible in America? For Jo Levy, former general counsel of Asia Pacific at Intel, it could very well be. "Concepts take a long time to be socially accepted. But there's a growing body of people in America who are ready and just want an answer," she said Thursday at Future Dispute Resolution, a conference at Stanford University hosted by the American Arbitration Association that explored how AI will revolutionize the dispute resolution process. In China, mobile courts are the norm. Litigants can even upload evidence to a mobile court on WeChat, China's ubiquitous messaging and payment app, and have a decision on their dispute in minutes. If they're not satisfied, the judgment can go directly to an actual judge to assess the AI's findings. Such a system is great for multinational tech firms like Alibaba, which has thousands of cases to deal with at any given time. Levy said people and companies alike love the system because it's fast, reliable and safe. Levy spoke on a panel of current and former in-house lawyers on how AI can help automate some of the most onerous parts of litigation and arbitration, arrive at decisions faster, and level the playing field between patent trolls and their targets. They came from companies large and small, but all had one thing in common: they have enormous litigation burdens and rely on arbitration to resolve disputes quickly. Matt Brown, associate general counsel and head of global litigation at peer-to-peer car-sharing startup Turo, said arbitration is crucial to managing all the issues that naturally arise when a stranger agrees to rent their car to another stranger via an app, from scratches and dents to a user smoking in someone else's car. "Without arbitration we wouldn't be able to deal with those issues at all," he said. Arbitration is a must for tech giants such as Cisco, where associate general counsel Bryan Sinclair heads its intellectual property litigation department. "We use mediation in 99% of our patent litigation matters as a vehicle to try to resolve disputes," he said. Lawsuits from so-called nonpracticing entities, or patent trolls as they're colloquially called, that buy up patents to use as fodder for infringement lawsuits are exploding thanks to the backing of litigation funders. "When I started at Cisco seven years ago we had one case on my docket that had about 75 cases on it that we knew was funded," Sinclair said. "We suspect today that about 45% are funded at some level." NPEs and litigation funders are increasingly using AI to help them evaluate their cases before they file. Ken Korea, a transactions attorney and mediator at Colev Law who formerly headed the Silicon Valley IP office for Samsung, said NPEs are just as cost-conscious as companies when it comes to picking their legal battles. "AI is at some level the great equalizer," he said. "NPEs are afraid of the cost and you have to pick the right patents to sue, so it levels the playing field." Levy, now a partner at The Norton Law Firm, said it's just a matter of time before in-house counsel ask their outside firms to also start using AI for early case assessments. "NPEs are already using it. We're already behind," she said. AI has other benefits in litigation too, especially in discovery. Korea said he was floored when he was at Samsung and one expert quoted $100,000 to go through an 80,000 patent portfolio. "Now the same thing can be done for half the cost with AI," he said. "Small-sized firms usually don't have the resources to effectively review the documents in patent litigation. Getting a million+-page document is par for the course. How are you going to analyze it? With AI you can do it very effectively." Levy said AI may soon enable companies to simulate jury trials more efficiently, particularly helpful as impartial jurors in popular patent litigation jurisdictions like Texas are getting harder to find. "Pretty soon you'll have AI mock jurors which will enable you to do a mock trial online. You can even have mock lawyers and have 12 different personas for jurors," Levy said, adding that such tools will help companies decide if they should defend a case or try to settle. Brown added: "You'll learn very quickly about how much they believe in their case if they're willing to submit it to an objective machine." He noted that companies might be hesitant to try AI if arbitration is binding, but if not, what's the harm? "If mediation is not binding, that's maybe one way you can see early adoption," he said. title: Disney's Black Eye Over Arbitration Gambit Likely to Linger, Underscoring PR Risks of Spurning Courts
description: The public relations drubbing that beset The Walt Disney Co. recently after the entertainment giant tried to force a wrongful-death lawsuit into arbitration for the quirkiest of reasons—in signing up for a Disney+ trial in 2019, the plaintiff had…
preview:
The public relations drubbing that beset The Walt Disney Co. recently after the entertainment giant tried to force a wrongful-death lawsuit into arbitration for the quirkiest of reasons—in signing up for a Disney+ trial in 2019, the plaintiff had agreed to settle all disputes with the company out of court—should serve as a cautionary tale for other companies, legal observers say.

Companies often prefer to resolve disputes through binding arbitration, rather than in court, in part because of the efficiency and confidentiality of the process. But in this matter, Disney found itself a social media punching bag because of the legal tactics it used in a dispute that otherwise might have garnered little or no public attention.

title: At DataGrail Summit, Legal Leaders Call for Transparency in the Age of AI

preview:
Kirsten Daru had a revelation after landing her first general counsel role. She had spent the previous 11 years as chief privacy officer at Electronic Arts, where she was the first privacy lawyer at the company.

She joined in 2008 just as privacy was blowing up, and built its program from the ground up. But even as she had much more on her plate as a GC—contracts, financing deals and partnerships, IP prosecution, patent litigation, employment and antitrust matters—she realized something that never occurred to her in those 11 years at EA. Privacy was still by far the most challenging legal discipline in existence. And now with AI exploding on the scene, it’s even more complicated.

title: FTC's Kroger-Albertsons Suit Premised on 'Fanciful' Definition of Grocery Market, Dissenting States Say
description: Attorneys general from Alabama, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio are urging a federal judge to allow Kroger’s $24.6 billion acquisition of rival Albertsons to go through, arguing that the Federal Trade Commission’s opposition to the deal is premised on an…
preview:
Attorneys general from Alabama, Georgia, Iowa and Ohio are urging a federal judge to allow Kroger’s $24.6 billion acquisition of rival Albertsons to go through, arguing that the Federal Trade Commission’s opposition to the deal is premised on an overly narrow definition of the grocery market that’s detached from reality and contradicts its own precedent.

In an amicus brief filed in Oregon federal court Friday, the attorneys general say the merger actually is “procompetitive” because “it can be expected to strengthen Kroger’s ability to compete more effectively in the wide-open market for consumers’ retail grocery dollars,” a free-for-all that includes far larger companies such as Walmart and Amazon.

preview:
“Happiness can be consciously cultivated through certain actions anyone can take which are not at all dependent upon your external circumstances, said Mark LoSacco, a former in-house leader at HSBC and American Express who now helps legal department attorneys find greater fulfillment.

August 12, 2024 at 04:57 PM
excerpt: “Happiness can be consciously cultivated through certain actions anyone can take which are not at all dependent upon your external circumstances, said Mark LoSacco, a former in-house leader at HSBC...
searchText: Chasing Goals Won't Give Frazzled In-House Lawyers Inner Peace, But a 'Mental Cleanse' Might | Corporate Counsel “Happiness can be consciously cultivated through certain actions anyone can take which are not at all dependent upon your external circumstances, said Mark LoSacco, a former in-house leader at HSBC and American Express who now helps legal department… “Happiness can be consciously cultivated through certain actions anyone can take which are not at all dependent upon your external circumstances, said Mark LoSacco, a former in-house leader at HSBC and American Express who now helps legal department attorneys find greater fulfillment. August 12, 2024 at 04:57 PM Maria Dinzeo When ALM polled in-house lawyers for its mental health survey this year, an overwhelming majority said they generally liked their jobs. But they also said they were physically and mentally overwhelmed, and found themselves feeling moody and irritable. Mark LoSacco, a longtime senior in-house leader who most recently headed litigation and regulatory enforcement at HSBC, said they deserve better. Many lawyers might mistakenly conclude that they are OK if they aren’t depressed, aren’t substance abusers, aren’t contemplating suicide or don’t have other widely discussed mental health conditions, he said. “These are huge issues, but sometimes people might go through that, that list of statistics, and just say, ‘Hey, I don’t have these, so I must be fine.’ And that’s where I think people make a mistake, especially in the legal profession. We go through our lives and we say, ‘Hey, you know what? I feel pretty good.’ But is that enough? And I would suggest that it’s not,” LoSacco said. He made these marks on a webinar hosted by In-House Connect Monday on how in-house counsel can cultivate happiness and find well-being, titled “Why ‘Not Being Miserable’ Is Not Enough.” Now an executive leadership coach, LoSacco previously spent 11 years leading a legal team of 25 at HSBC. Before that, he was chief litigation counsel at American Express. He said many in-house lawyers have fallen into the trap of thinking that achieving success will bring happiness, or that happiness is a goal to continuously strive for. But it’s actually a choice. “Don’t try to do things that will make you feel happy. Don’t try to get external things that will make you feel happy,” he said. “Happiness can be consciously cultivated through certain actions anyone can take which are not at all dependent upon your external circumstances.” So why is it so hard to be happy? LoSacco said it all goes back to our limbic system, the “legacy brain” that kept our ancestors alive thousands of years ago by constantly seeking sources of danger. “We’re not on the Serengeti. We don’t have those same survival needs to that extreme, but we still get stuck here. And while we don’t have the same survival needs, our limbic brain is working in the same way,” he said. “And so it senses things that are modestly unnerving to us, and it starts with cortisol, the anxiety, the stress and that is one of the largest causes of unhappiness.” Being anxious can help us perform better because it can keep us hyperfocused on the things we need to get done. But it can also drive us to obsess over situations outside our control, ruminate on the past or worry about the future. LoSacco said focusing on what he calls the “golden quadrant” can help people consciously nurture and encourage well-being, getting themselves to a place of safety that can make them happier. This includes downtime to care for the mind and body, meditation, spending time with family, calling friends, and, of course, lots of physical activity. The problem is we tend to put those things off. “You all have many things that matter to you that maybe you don’t spend enough time doing because you know they’re important, but you can always do it later, or you tell yourself you can always do it later,” he said. So put it on your calendar. “It may seem odd to put in your calendar, even on a weekend, to spend time with the family or whatever it is, but it will help. Put it on the schedule. It will make it real,” he said. LoSacco also recommends a seven-day “mental cleanse” to rewire the brain not to have strong emotional responses to every negative input. “Say to yourself for seven days, anytime I have a feeling of anger, rage, or judgmental, nasty feelings, like when somebody cuts you off, just say, I’m going to change the way I think about it. I’m going to take myself out of that state, and I’m going to say, ‘Oh, that’s curious. I wonder why they did that,’” he said. Doing so will help you let go of feelings of rage in response to external triggers. “If you don’t get through the seven days doing that, if just one time something sticks with you, you have to start the seven days over,” he said. “Spoiler alert, you never get past the seven days. But it is amazing what you’ll find if you give this a shot, just for a day or two. You will be happier.” LoSac

Competition regulators have been on high alert for risks posed by too much market concentration, where a single point of failure can disrupt business worldwide. A cascading information technology outage that recently grounded hundreds of flights, upended health care and halted banking across the globe has been no exception. The recent outage was triggered by a bug in a routine update to cybersecurity firm CrowdStrike’s flagship software Falcon, resulting in a “blue screen of death” across thousands of enterprise computer systems running on Microsoft Windows. Even though CrowdStrike had issued a fix within hours, some companies took days to recover. Lawmakers immediately pounced, calling on CrowdStrike CEO George Kurtz to testify before a House Subcommittee on Cybersecurity and Infrastructure. “Protecting our critical infrastructure requires us to learn from this incident and ensure that it does not happen again,” said a letter from Reps. Mark Green, R-Tennessee, and Andrew Gabarino, R-New York. The outage also drew the attention of the Federal Trade Commission, which lately has taken a keen interest in how competition issues across layers of the technology stack can cause resiliency problems that wreak widescale havoc. “All too often these days, a single glitch results in a system-wide outage, affecting industries from healthcare and airlines to banks and auto-dealers. Millions of people and businesses pay the price. These incidents reveal how concentration can create fragile systems,” FTC Chair Lina Khan posted on X shortly after the outage. Meanwhile, competition and cyber experts are wondering what to make of the debacle, and whether the market for threat detection software has become too heavily concentrated in a few dominant players. “If the market doesn’t have competition, then essentially what you find is that one standard, one dominant way of doing it kind of emerges. And that’s exactly what you’re seeing with CrowdStrike,” said Ramnath Chellappa, a professor of information systems and operations management at Emory University’s Goizueta Business School. He said CrowdStrike, which works on the cloud and on-prem, has become an industry standard for remote and local monitoring of computer systems throughout a company. “CrowdStrike has just become a nice way to put a little sensor on every single machine and monitor that nobody’s changing anything. Basically, they almost become like a monopoly when it comes to thinking about what is a good way to address these things,” he said. Microsoft Blames European Competition Regulator for Meltdown Chellappa explained that CrowdStrike’s Falcon runs at the deepest level of the Windows operating system, the kernel, which gives it privileged access to the system’s core functions and memory. This should allow Falcon to provide stronger protection because it can more closely monitor system activities and intercept threats before they can cause harm. But it also means that an entire system can be brought down if one little thing goes wrong. Chellappa said this unique level of access also means that while Microsoft computers crashed, Macs were unaffected. “Apple is very tight with its ecosystem,” he said. Microsoft has said that it’s not allowed to wall off Windows the way Apple has because it agreed to give third-party developers greater access to its operating system under a 2009 agreement with the European Union. “Microsoft is saying that it cannot legally implement the same protections as Apple, simply because it’s opened it up so much,” Chellappa said. He noted that the outage also didn’t affect computers that run on Linux, which has a completely open operating system. However, he said that could be because most companies don’t use Linux. Ironically, the EU agreement designed to promote competition may have caused a bigger problem, said Anant Raut, Meta’s former director of global competition policy and a public adviser to the National Institute of Standards and Technology. “If it exposed Microsoft Windows at a more dangerous level that would be an argument against mandated interoperability.” CrowdStrike Dominates in the Cybersecurity Services Market CrowdStrike is a behemoth in the cybersecurity world. Security chiefs nationwide found solace in a federal judge’s recent gutting of the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission’s civil fraud lawsuit against SolarWinds, a case that marked the first time the regulator took a public company to court over its handling of a cyberattack. The turn of events has drawn varied reactions from legal and security experts. While some see the dismissal as a blow to the SEC’s efforts to police companies’ cybersecurity practices, they’re not expecting regulators to back off their quest to force firms to provide greater transparency about their cybersecurity risks and how they’re managing them. “While the dismissal of most of the SEC charges against SolarWinds will be viewed as a win within the [chief information security officer] community, it is premature to think regulatory pressure and litigation against companies and individuals will desist in the future,” said Steve Martano, a faculty member at cybersecurity consulting firm IANS Research. Martano said that every cyber incident and response is unique, and while the SEC may pull back in the short term, it’s clear that regulators are willing to push boundaries and pursue cases premised on novel legal theories. The SEC’s suit, filed in October 2023 in the Southern District of New York, accused the Austin, Texas-based information technology software company and its CISO, Tim Brown, of concealing cybersecurity red flags and filing a “boilerplate” disclosure that cast as hypothetical cyber threats that its employees and Brown knew to be real. And once SolarWinds became aware of the breach, which occurred in 2020 and ranks among the most devastating cyberattacks ever, the SEC alleges the company misled the public about its magnitude. But in his 107-page ruling last Thursday, U.S. District Judge Paul Engelmayer threw out the SEC’s claims that SolarWinds’ disclosures to investors before the attack were overly general and that disclosures afterward failed to convey its gravity. He said those disclosures represented the risks and the fallout from the attack accurately, observing that antifraud laws “do not require cautions to be articulated with maximum specificity.” An SEC spokesperson did not respond to Law.com’s request for comment on whether the ruling would have an impact on the agency’s cyber agenda. ‘Generic’ Filings and ‘Gamesmanship’ Cyber professionals had warned that overly detailed disclosures about vulnerabilities could have the unintended consequence of giving bad actors a road map to carry out attacks. Engelmayer agreed, writing that “spelling out a risk with maximal specificity may backfire in various ways, including by arming malevolent actors with information to exploit.” The ruling comes as companies wrestle with how to comply with SEC rules adopted last year requiring them to promptly disclose material cyberattacks and to detail their cyber risks and vulnerabilities in their annual reports. In advocating for the rules, SEC officials said they’d become fed up with “generic” filings and “gamesmanship” from public companies more concerned with protecting their reputations than their shareholders and customers. Even in the wake of Engelmayer’s ruling, “bare minimum statements aren’t going to cut it,” said Michael Daniel, who serves as CEO of Cyber Threat Alliance and formerly was cybersecurity coordinator for the National Security Council, as well as special assistant to President Barack Obama. He said the SEC’s frustrations were well-founded. “A lot of companies would make a statement about their cybersecurity risk, which is just along the lines of ‘We have cybersecurity risk,’ which is not helpful to investors. The SEC does have an interest in ensuring that disclosures are accurate and useful to investors,” Daniel said. “The key thing is it has to be somewhere in between ‘we have some risk’ and ‘here are the holes in our controls.’ There has to be some kind of happy medium. In-house and outside counsel are going to have to figure out what is the language that will get you to the right place.” Ed McNicholas, co-leader of Ropes & G

The Federal Trade Commission said Tuesday that it is investigating a little-known ecosystem of middlemen, including corporate giants Accenture, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Mastercard and McKinsey & Co., to explore how it helps clients set different prices for different consumers based on browsing histories, past purchases, credit histories and other personal information.

searchText: FTC Probing Use of Browser Histories, Other Personal Info to Individualize Product Prices Editor’s note: Uber’s and Lyft’s variable-pricing strategies reflect a broader push by businesses ito optimize pricing. But their practices do not fall within the scope of “surveillance pricing,” The story below has been updated to make that clear.… Editor’s note: Uber’s and Lyft’s variable-pricing strategies reflect a broader push by businesses ito optimize pricing. But their practices do not fall within the scope of “surveillance pricing,” The story below has been updated to make that clear. The Federal Trade Commission said Tuesday that it is investigating a little-known ecosystem of middlemen, including corporate giants Accenture, JPMorgan Chase & Co., Mastercard and McKinsey & Co., to explore how it helps clients set different prices for different consumers based on browsing histories, past purchases, credit histories and other personal information. The FTC calls the technique “surveillance pricing,” which it describes as a “new frontier” made possible by advances in artificial intelligence and machine learning. The agency says it wants to learn how surveillance pricing affects privacy, competition and consumer protection. “Firms that harvest Americans’ personal data can put people’s privacy at risk. Now firms could be exploiting this vast trove of personal information to charge people higher prices,” FTC Chair Lina Khan said in a statement. “Americans deserve to know whether businesses are using detailed consumer data to deploy surveillance pricing, and the FTC’s inquiry will shed light on this shadowy ecosystem of pricing middlemen.” In addition to Accenture, JPMorgan Chase, Mastercard and McKinsey, the commission sent examination letters to Bloomreach, Pros, Revionics and Task Software, all of which are players in marketing automation, dynamic pricing or related fields. The common thread among the eight is that they advertise their use of advanced algorithms and AI to set personalized prices, the FTC said. The FTC has not accused any of the firms of wrongdoing. Law.com reached out to all eight for comment. Among those responding, Mastercard said it is reviewing the letter and would cooperate with the inquiry. Revionics, which bills itself as an “AI-powered retail price optimization software” firm, said in a statement that it does not recommend pricing for specific consumers and “does not, in any manner, use individual consumer data.” The company added: “Our software ingests data from various sources, most often, directly from our retail partners. Revionics does not, in any way, conduct operations related to the surveillance of consumers. We are confident that the FTC will affirm the benefits of Revionics’ AI price optimization software pending its research into this matter.” A spokesperson for Bloomreach said the company would help the FTC with its informational inquiry as it aims to more fully understand rapidly evolving AI technology and its use in ecommerce. “As a key player in the ecommerce AI space, Bloomreach welcomes the opportunity to assist the FTC’s industry inquiry, along with other industry leaders. We believe in fair competition and the protection and education of consumers, and are committed to that pursuit while providing the consumer with a better, more personalized experience.” For years, companies have been experimenting with innovative strategies to optimize pricing. In 2012, Uber introduced surge pricing, quickly followed by Lyft’s ‘Prime Time’ pricing, which adjusts fares based on consumer demand at specific times and locations. Similarly, airlines long have employed “dynamic pricing” to determine how much customers are willing to pay for fares. A Washington Post report from 2020 said carriers show different consumers different prices based on the data they’ve collected on them. The article noted that Pros was one of the companies developing dynamic pricing for the travel industry. In addition, some car brands are providing driver-behavior data to auto insurers, which they use to set personalized premiums. The surveillance pricing probe is the latest in a string of FTC investigations focusing on the collection of data without consumers’ knowledge that is then used in targeted advertising. In January, it dinged security software firm Avast for storing and selling users’ browsing information, and in February brought an enforcement action data aggregators X-Mode Social and InMarket for collecting consumers’ precise location data without consent. The commission also has taken a keen interest in any kind of algorithmic tool that could violate privacy or discriminate against certain groups. Last year, it ordered online therapy provider BetterHelp to pay $7.8 million for sharing users’ sensitive mental health information with third parties, such as Facebook and Snapchat, which used it for targeted advertising.

And I really love that,” said Sarah Tinsley, general counsel of Culture Amp. "You have a combination of doing the strategy and the management pieces, but also getting your hands dirty. And I really love that," said Sarah Tinsley, general counsel of Culture Amp. July 22, 2024 at 10:39 AM 8 minute read By Maria Dinzeo In-house lawyers eyeing the general counsel seat will find a limited number of options in the Fortune 500. But a growing number of aspiring GCs are finding opportunities abound in the sometimes-overlooked realm of private equity portfolio companies. While the number of public companies has waned since the late 1990s, the private equity industry has boomed, creating in-house opportunities at private equity-owned companies and companies backed by venture capital. The sector needs legal leaders with business savvy, a healthy appetite for risk and the ability to see the job as a long-term investment, said John Gilmore, co-founder and managing partner of the recruiting firm BarkerGilmore. Gilmore said his firm just finished six candidate searches for private equity clients. Portfolio companies see the general counsel role as a "mission critical hire," Gilmore said. With a base salary at around $300,000 and bonuses at 60%, compensation comes mostly in the form of equity, which can deter those seeking guaranteed higher upfront remuneration, Gilmore said. "You're not going to see the cash award windfall immediately, but more important than the cash is that you wind up with the title of enterprise general counsel and you can use that as a launching pad for your career," he said. "It's not about the money, it's about the opportunity to do something." That spirit of adventure is what led Sarah Tinsley in 2019 to become general counsel of the Australian human resource and employee feedback platform Culture Amp. After a decade working in-house, Tinsley said she was looking to step out of her comfort zone as a lawyer and "learn something completely new and different." The founders at Culture Amp "caught me at a moment where I was really contemplating what is my next move. I've been doing this for a while. Where's my next growth opportunity coming from?" Tinsley said. The job gave her the chance to be more hands-on in the business and manage projects that fell outside the legal scope. "You have a combination of doing the strategy and the management pieces, but also getting your hands dirty. And I really love that," Tinsley said. "I've done stuff that is very much outside of the conventional legal lane. So for my own growth and development, that's been incredible. And as a GC, every time I do something like that, I'm learning more about the business. So it makes me more effective because I really understand what's going on. And that is always powerful knowledge to get as a GC," she said. Others hire to replace a retiring outside counsel and may upgrade the position and responsibilities as the company grows. He said his clients are looking for lawyers with high emotional intelligence who deal well with pressure. "They want the lawyer who the first thing they do isn't call outside counsel. They want someone who can figure things out first—the person who can master things quickly," he said. "A lot of times, our series A companies will hire someone who isn't a GC and give them a broader title that encompasses more of the business side, something to do with strategy and operations, and it also encompasses legal because there isn't enough legal work to do," he said. title: The Morning Minute: Latest Big Law Layoffs Illustrate Inconsistency in Market
description: TOO MUCH, TOO FAST - Despite impressive gains at the top of the Am Law 200 charts and a mindset geared more toward growth, layoffs and cuts continue to rattle the industry. Productivity and utilization remain a problem, observers and analysts have…
preview:
TOO MUCH, TOO FAST  - Despite impressive gains at the top of the Am Law 200 charts and a mindset geared more toward growth, layoffs and cuts continue to rattle the industry. Productivity and utilization remain a problem, observers and analysts have told Law.com’s Andrew Maloney , as some firms expect deal work to improve only ”incrementally” and the tech sector in particular just hasn’t shown enough resilience. Those assessments come as Fenwick & West told employees on Tuesday that it was laying off “just under” 10% of its professionals, including attorneys and staff. The firm cited a surge in demand from 2020 through early 2022 that caused Fenwick & West to hire “quite aggressively,” said Richard Dickson, the firm’s chair, in a memo viewed by Law.com. “It felt necessary at the time. But, with the benefit of hindsight, it represented a deviation from our core principle of managing for the long-term,” Dickson said.

LEGAL ORGANIZATION - From the casinos on the Las Vegas Strip to Hollywood’s writing rooms, workers are turning to their unions to seek protections against the risks that emerging technologies like genAI may pose to their jobs. Could a growing movement by employees to prepare for the impact of generative AI spread to an industry that hasn’t traditionally been prone to unionization, like legal? As Law.com’s Cassandre Coyer reports , in many ways, the legal industry is now at an inflection point. Stuck between the prospect of roles being transformed, if not entirely threatened, by the technology, an ongoing push toward business-oriented structural changes, and questions around the longevity of the billable hour,  some believe this could be the industry’s first real opportunity to meaningfully consider collective bargaining.

title: I Got Royalties, Babe: L.A. Federal Court Sides With Cher On Income from Sonny's Song Interests
description: After Sonny died in a skiing accident in 1998, Mary Bono agreed to a confirmation of Cher’s continued rights under a 1978 marital settlement agreement. In 2016, Mary sent termination notices to music publishers to which Sonny had assigned his…
preview:
After Beach Boy Brian Wilson’s ex-wife Marilyn filed a request in Los Angeles Superior Court for an accounting and for payment, under the couple’s 1981 divorce judgment, of 50% of the monies Brian received from his 2021 sale of his song rights to Universal Music, Brian’s counsel had the case removed to Los Angeles federal court citing federal question jurisdiction. This was because the songs sale occurred after Brian had recaptured his copyrights under the 17 U.S.C. §304(c) copyright-assignment termination provision of the U.S. Copyright Act. Wilson v. Rutherford, 2:22-cv-01982 (C.D.Calif. 2022).

But Central District of California federal Judge Josephine L. Staton decided in Wilson that federal copyright law didn’t preempt Marilyn’s state law claim, then remanded the case back to the state superior court. In doing so, District Judge Staton noted, “Marilyn does not assert that she has a right to terminate any grants of copyrights in the [songs] ….” Judge Staton added: “Section 304(c) provides that ‘[t]ermination of a grant under this subsection affects only those rights covered by the grant that arise under this title, and in no way affects rights arising under’ state law.”

title: Limitations of Generative AI in Civil Jury Trials
description: Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using…
preview:
Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using generative AI for drafting opening statements, closing arguments, direct and cross-examinations, creating graphics, and assisting with trial motions is strong. This allure and the marketing hype ignores a fundamental truth: Generative AI is not yet ready for the courtroom.

A jury trial is a multifaceted event, involving distinct audiences: the judge, the jury, client representatives, and witnesses. Each of these audiences have different needs and will require a tailored approach that will dynamically change throughout the trial.

searchText: Limitations of Generative AI in Civil Jury Trials Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using… Generative AI has made significant strides in various fields, promising to revolutionize how we handle complex tasks. It’s no wonder that clients, attorneys, and law firms are drawn to its fast, inexpensive, and clear output. The allure of using generative AI for drafting opening statements, closing arguments, direct and cross-examinations, creating graphics, and assisting with trial motions is strong. This allure and the marketing hype ignores a fundamental truth: Generative AI is not yet ready for the courtroom. Diverse Audiences With Unique Needs A jury trial is a multifaceted event, involving distinct audiences: the judge, the jury, client representatives, and witnesses. Each of these audiences have different needs and will require a tailored approach that will dynamically change throughout the trial. The Judge: Judges are concerned with the trial record, the potential for appeal, maintaining courtroom control, and efficient time use. They require clear, legally sound arguments. Understanding the judge’s experience and background is crucial. A seasoned judge may have a firm view of how a trial should proceed, while a newcomer might still be shaping their approach. Each judge’s unique viewpoint, philosophy, and rules play a significant role in the trial’s dynamics. Generative AI, however, lacks the nuance to adapt to these individualized needs effectively. The Jury: Comprising individuals from diverse backgrounds, jurors have no personal stake in the case outcome but are tasked with delivering a fair verdict. They must understand complex legal rules and concepts, making clear and relatable presentation of evidence crucial. Emotional appeals, compelling storytelling, and witness credibility are vital here—subtleties generative AI often misses. Client Representatives: These individuals, whether in-house legal counsel focused on costs and expectations or high-ranking corporate officers viewing the trial as an extended negotiation, have different goals and concerns. Their anxiety over trial outcomes is heightened by their limited control over courtroom proceedings. Generative AI cannot provide the reassurance and strategic updates these clients need. Witnesses: Witnesses, who range from nervous laypeople to compensated experts, are critical to the case. Their testimony needs to be clear, concise, and compelling. Preparing and managing witnesses requires a human touch. Many factors outside the courtroom and concerns about the future can have significant impact on the emotions, preparation and cooperation of witnesses. title: Blockchain Domains: New Developments for Brand Owners
description: Blockchain technology has revolutionized numerous industries, including finance, supply chain management and digital identity verification. Blockchain domain names offer decentralized alternatives to traditional DNS-based domain names, promising…
preview:
Blockchain technology has revolutionized numerous industries, including finance, supply chain management and digital identity verification. One of its latest frontiers relates to the domain name system (DNS). Blockchain domain names offer decentralized alternatives to traditional DNS-based domain names, promising enhanced security, privacy and censorship resistance. However, these benefits come with significant challenges, particularly for brand owners seeking to protect their trademarks in these new digital spaces. This article explores the issues associated with trademark protection in blockchain domain names and examines new steps and policies that blockchain domain registrars should implement to safeguard brand owners.

Traditional DNS operates under a hierarchical structure managed by the Internet Corporation for Assigned Names and Numbers (ICANN). This centralized authority oversees domain name registrations and resolves disputes through established policies such as the Uniform Domain-Name Dispute-Resolution Policy (UDRP). Developed more than 20 years ago, the UDRP was ICANN’s first consensus policy and was intended to address cybersquatting in the DNS. Cybersquatting involves the registration of domain names that are identical or confusingly similar to trademarks with the intent of registering and using those names in bad faith.

title: The Increasing Value of Human Time in the Age of Advanced AI
description: In an era where artificial intelligence (AI) inches ever closer to limitless capabilities, the boundary between human creativity and machine-generated content becomes increasingly blurred. This technological frontier challenges traditional notions of…
preview:
In an era where artificial intelligence (AI) inches ever closer to limitless capabilities, the boundary between human creativity and machine-generated content becomes increasingly blurred. This technological frontier challenges traditional notions of authorship and invention, prompting key regulatory bodies like the U.S. Patent and Trademark Office (USPTO) and the U.S. Copyright Office to grapple with defining the essence of “human” contribution. Their recent guidelines endeavor to delineate the unique value of human creativity and contribution in a landscape increasingly dominated by AI’s expanding prowess, underscoring the legal and philosophical complexities in distinguishing between the outputs of humans and machines.

The advancements in AI have been groundbreaking, pushing the boundaries of what machines can achieve. These technologies have mastered complex tasks, from driving cars autonomously to diagnosing diseases with precision. In the world of creativity and invention, AI systems can now generate artwork, music, and literature that rival human creations, challenging traditional concepts of authorship. Robotics, for example, are not just executing manual tasks but are also engaging in activities requiring problem-solving and adaptability. These developments question the long-standing distinctions between human and machine capabilities, contribution and creativity.

title: Viewing AI Through Cheaper/Faster Lens Misses Its Full Potential

preview:
When Harvard law professor David Wilkins started teaching about technology and the law back in 2000, he invited a Massachusetts Institute of Technology professor to speak to his class. This was at a time when architects and engineers were starting to use software to create and build 3D models of physical structures, and computer-aided design and manufacturing were disrupting the world of design.

“He walked into the class, and the very first thing he said was, ‘Professionals always think that technology allows them to do what they already do cheaper and faster. But, in fact, what technology does is it redefines what it means to be a professional,’” Wilkins recalled the professor saying.
