Amid the initial burst of excitement around generative AI, companies invested vast sums into the technology. But now many say the results are falling short of expectations, according to a quarterly survey by Bain Research. Thirty-eight percent said they couldn't understand how to use generative AI tools, and 29% attributed their disappointment to the "low quality" of the vendor and its product. Sales, software development, marketing and customer service fared much better, with all of these business units reporting increased satisfaction with AI over the five months. And they don't like to admit that, but it's true," Winmill said. "Second, they often lack expertise to implement new technologies. title: All Eyes on Pennsylvania After Texas Court's Limited Injunction Against FTC Noncompete Ban
description: A first-in-nation ruling in Texas federal court casts serious doubt on the enforceability of the broad-reaching new Federal Trade Commission (FTC) noncompete rule. For any company seeking to legitimately protect its hard-earned competitive position,…
preview:
A first-in-nation ruling in Texas federal court casts serious doubt on the enforceability of the broad-reaching new Federal Trade Commission (FTC) noncompete rule. For any company seeking to legitimately protect its hard-earned competitive position, this opinion and the FTC’s rule must be considered and understood. While the Texas decision was limited to the parties before that court, the reasoning is important in predicting whether the FTC’s noncompete rule is likely to go into effect, and all companies need to be constantly reevaluating how they are protecting their corporate secrets.

On April 23, 2024, the FTC issued its noncompete rule, a rule that largely banned worker noncompete agreements with limited exceptions, based on the FTC’s position that nearly all noncompetition agreements constitute an “unfair method of competition” under Section 5 of the Federal Trade Commission Act, 15 U.S.C. Section 45(a). The FTC estimated that, upon the noncompete rule’s planned effective date of Sept. 4, 2024, the rule would invalidate 30 million contracts. Baker Donelson’s attorneys initially covered the decision and its significance for employers shortly after it was issued.

title: Hiring From a Law Firm for an In-House Position? Use Caution
description: Within my niche practice of recruiting attorneys exclusively for companies, 90% of the lawyers my search firm has placed in the past four years came with current or previous in-house experience. Our mix of placement backgrounds was closer to 60/40…
preview:
Within my niche practice of recruiting attorneys exclusively for companies, 90% of the lawyers my search firm has placed in the past four years came with current or previous in-house experience.  Our mix of placement backgrounds was closer to 60/40 just ten years ago, meaning almost half of our placements were lawyers moving into their first in-house position.

I think this is a meaningful observation that speaks to change that has occurred on a boarder scale.  Specifically, law firm career paths and in-house career paths are increasingly viewed as two divergent roads.  It used to be much easier for a law firm Partner to move in-house as, to stay with the metaphor, the transition was viewed more as just changing lanes.

Companies routinely work together, signing stock non-disclosure agreements (NDAs) before collaboration. title: Foreign Extortion Prevention Act (FEPA): How the New Law Creates Legal Risks and Opportunities for International Businesses
description: On December 22, 2023, President Biden signed into law the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which will give the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) new tools to prosecute foreign bribery. The Foreign Extortion Prevention Act (FEPA) will…
preview:
On December 22, 2023, President Biden signed into law the 2024 National Defense Authorization Act (NDAA), which will give the U.S. Department of Justice (DOJ) new tools to prosecute foreign bribery. The Foreign Extortion Prevention Act (FEPA) will amend the domestic bribery statute (18 U.S.C. § 201) to make it a criminal offense for foreign government officials to solicit or receive bribes from any person in the United States, any issuer, or any domestic concern. See H.R. 2670, 118th Cong. § 5101 (2023). This article describes the new law and assesses its likely effects on foreign affairs and anti-bribery and anti-corruption (ABAC) investigations.

While the Foreign Corrupt Practices Act (FCPA) focuses on the “supply side” of bribery, meaning those who offer or pay bribes, FEPA instead focuses on the “demand side” of bribery by subjecting the recipients of bribes, the payment of which would likely violate the FCPA, to prosecution under 18 U.S.C. § 201. The demand side has been a focus of DOJ policy statements and enforcement efforts. Enforcement, however, generally has been through other laws, like money laundering, wire fraud, and the Travel Act. In parallel to recent DOJ initiatives, the Organization of Economic Cooperation and Development recently called for member states to amend their criminal statutes to prohibit soliciting and obtaining bribes by foreign officials. By enacting FEPA, the United States joins countries like the United Kingdom, Switzerland, and France in making such revisions to its laws.

preview:
Tara Trantham was driving home after attending her 11-year-old son’s football game, a cheer bow still in her hair, when she looked up and saw flashing blue lights in the rearview mirror. Her son had gone home with his grandparents, which was good—he’d be spared the sight of his mom getting arrested.

I am excited to announce that headlining day two of this year’s Women, Influence & Power in Law conference will be tennis champion and New York Times best-selling author Venus Williams! With seven Grand Slam titles, including five Wimbledon championships, and four Olympic gold medals, Venus is one of the most accomplished and inspiring women in the history of sports. Beyond her accomplishments on the court, Venus has also been a steadfast advocate for equality throughout her career. In 2006, UNESCO, the United Nations’ cultural organization, titled her as the first “Promoter of Gender Equality.” In 2007, it was her unwavering fight which led Wimbledon to award women players the same pay as their male counterparts. Most recently, she launched an awareness initiative called the #PrivilegeTax to bring attention to wage inequality and unveiled a platform of resources for young women to get inspired and address the issue on a grassroots level. Register today to be part of this intimate conversation with Venus as she shares her journey of resilience, determination and the importance of celebrating individuality. Whether it’s overcoming self-doubt or providing tools to navigate a male-dominated industry, Venus’ unique insights will sure to inspire our WIPL community to not only discover that inner champion but unleash its full potential! We are also excited that this year’s WIPL conference will be held in Chicago at the Hyatt Regency McCormick Place. I hope to see you there!

The two companies on Monday said they decided to scrap the $1.7 billion deal, which had been in the works since August 2022, amid strong resistance from antitrust regulators in the European Union. In November, the EU’s competition authority said it was concerned that the acquisition, which would have added the Roomba to Amazon’s range of devices, would unfairly restrict competition in the market for robot vacuums. title: Law.com's Top 100 Verdicts of 2023
description: VerdictSearch strives to report as many jury verdicts, decisions and settlements as possible. Although a great many cases are submitted by attorneys, we also rely on a diligent team of assignment editors who scour docket lists, cultivate…
preview:
VerdictSearch strives to report as many jury verdicts, decisions and settlements as possible. Although a great many cases are submitted by attorneys, we also rely on a diligent team of assignment editors who scour docket lists, cultivate relationships with law firms, and search the internet and news sources, including the ALM family of legal publications. Our exhaustive efforts allow us to present what we believe is a comprehensive list of the top 100 jury awards of 2023. Nevertheless, we sincerely apologize to anyone whose case may have been inadvertently omitted.

The Top 100 verdicts are ranked by gross award calculated by the jury. They do not reflect reductions for comparative negligence or assignment of fault to settling defendants or nonparties; additurs, remittiturs or reversals; or attorney fees and costs, unless awarded by the jury. In cases in which awards were automatically doubled or trebled by statute, the doubled or trebled amount determined rank. We do not consider cases in which the jury only determined per-plaintiff or per-year damages that a judge later used to calculate the gross award, cases in which the jury’s instructions permitted it to determine damages against a party that it had already deemed not liable, or cases in which a jury awarded damages against one or more parties while one or more other parties awaited trial in the same matter. The editors retain sole discretion to make adjustments in rank when necessary to reflect statutes that provide for election of remedies or other types of overlapping awards.

On Monday, Canadian legal tech startup Alexi, which offers generative artificial intelligence-powered legal research and drafting tools, announced that it raised $11 million ($15 million CAD) in a series A funding round led by venture capital firm Drive Capital and including existing investor Draper Associates.

Founded in 2017, Alexi, formerly known as Alexsei, leverages generative AI models, including OpenAI’s GPT models, to help legal professionals automate a number of tasks. While the startup first focused on drafting research memos for users based on their questions, it has since expanded to offer an AI-powered litigation assistant called Alexi Chat and a tool that uses AI to help lawyers brainstorm legal arguments for desired outcomes called “Arguments.”

Audio Pod IP has filed three patent infringement suits against Amazon, AWS and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia. The plaintiffs allege that after a meeting to discuss sharing Audio Pod's technology with Audible went nowhere, the company started using their innovations without permission. An audiobook company represented by Chandran Iyer, Ronald Daignault and Kevin Sprenger of intellectual property firm Daignault Iyer recently filed three patent infringement lawsuits against Amazon, Amazon Web Services and Audible in the Eastern District of Virginia. The company, Audio Pod IP, alleges in one complaint that it invented “several key media streaming technologies” after it was founded in 2005, including segmenting and sequencing streaming files to work around long download times for large files, bookmarking digital content so it can be paused and played at a later time and a subscriber-paid streaming service launched in 2006. The complaint cited a January 2008 front-page article in the Ottawa Citizen to document its early trajectory.

title: National Law Firms Keep Shipping Up to Boston, Eyeing Well-Connected Local Dealmakers

preview:
Boston’s native legal market is sustaining aggressive recruiting by national firms, poaching homegrown transactional partners with the street credibility necessary for breaking through to the city’s tight-knit business community.

In the first half of the year, Am Law 100 firms Paul Hastings and Blank Rome and Connecticut-based midsize firm Wiggin and Dana started Boston offices by recruiting local dealmakers. title: How Do We Know Who 'Wins' the War for Talent?
description: Firms are engaging in a frenzied battle for top talent. Lateral hires get a lot of press, but departures fly under the radar. Paul Hastings offers one example of a firm hiring at a brisk pace. In an era of free-agent partner moves in Big Law, law…
preview:
In an era of free-agent partner moves in Big Law, law firms are hiring prominent laterals at a rapid clip this year. Elite firms like Kirkland & Ellis, Paul Hastings and Paul Weiss frequently garner headlines for the groups of laterals and individual partners they add in any given month.

At the same time, these law firms and others that have been particularly active on the lateral market have seen substantial U.S partnership exits, according to data obtained by Law.com, whether via lateral moves, moves to in-house roles or the government, or other types of departures. Other law firms have even seen net losses in U.S. partner moves.

title: Early Impact of the CHIPS Act
description: The CHIPS Act was driven in part by concerns among U.S. policymakers that the U.S. semiconductor industry had fallen behind other modern manufacturing hubs abroad. The Act provides for a total of $52.7 billion in appropriations from 2023 through…
preview:
The Creating Helpful Incentives to Protect Semiconductors Act (the CHIPS Act or the Act) was signed into law in August 2022, providing for a total of $52.7 billion in appropriations from 2023 through 2027. This article describes certain key developments in the period from passage of the CHIPS Act through the present day, including a summary of commitments by semiconductor companies to increase capital investment in the United States (possibly reflecting incentives created by the legislation). We also provide a brief survey of key grantmaking and investment activity by U.S. government agencies since passage of the Act. Finally, we discuss the Act’s likely future, as well as analogous policy developments in critical East Asian manufacturing centers.

The CHIPS Act was driven in part by concerns among U.S. policymakers that the U.S. semiconductor industry had fallen behind other modern manufacturing hubs, primarily in East Asia (e.g., South Korea, Taiwan, and, to some extent, China). See, id. at 2. In light of these concerns and others, the Act was structured in large part to provide incentives and financial resources to companies who wished to expand or develop semiconductor manufacturing operations in the United States. See, id. at 6 – 10. To this end, the Act earmarked up to $38.22 billion to provide financial incentives to build, expand, and equip U.S.-based semiconductor fabrication plants, as well as other manufacturing facilities, necessary for the overall supply and value chain (e.g., packaging). See, id. at 14, 16.

Business, labor and consumer interests expressed sharply differing views at a public forum Wednesday over proposed California rules that would govern how companies use customers' personal information for anything from hiring decisions to advertising. The California Privacy Protection Agency rules, in the works since the latter half of 2023, require companies that use automated decision-making technology to provide consumers with notice, a way to opt out, and a way to find out how the business uses ADMT to make decisions about them. Because California has established itself as a trailblazer on privacy policy, the evolution of the CPPA rules is being closely watched nationally. Since California in 2018 became the first to enact comprehensive privacy legislation, more than a dozen other states have done so, The proposed ADMT rules discussed at Wednesday's public hearing in Sacramento mandate that companies conduct risk assessments on how they use and protect personal information and what the consequences and benefits might be to consumers. They must comply if they use ADMT for "extensive profiling" for behavioral advertising or to observe people in public places using facial recognition, or make a "significant decision" about hiring or denying goods and services. They'll also be subject to the rule if they use personal information to train artificial intelligence or ADMT tools. The CPPA also wants to impose a separate cybersecurity audit requirement on any business that "presents significant risk to consumers' security" by processing personal information, a rule that will apply to companies that derive at least 50% of their revenue from selling or sharing consumers' personal information, as well as those that make at least $28 million in annual revenue and collect, use, disclose, retain or process the personal information of at least 250,000 consumers. The proposed rules have drawn widespread disquiet from business groups claiming they are both too onerous and broadly written, while labor and privacy advocates say the rules define automated decision-making too narrowly. "We're worried that it creates an easy way for businesses to sidestep these rules. This definition is the crux upon which all the rest of the rules reside," said Maggie Oates, a privacy researcher and consultant for Consumer Reports. The rule currently defines ADMT as "any technology that processes personal information and uses computation to execute a decision, replace human decision making, or substantially facilitate human decision making." Oates said the final rule should more strictly define ADMT or at least provide examples to clarify the meaning of "substantially facilitate." Matt Scherer, a senior policy counsel for workers' rights with the nonpartisan Center for Democracy and Technology, said the definition "would basically give companies a license to opt themselves out of the law's requirements." Companies have a strong incentive to hide their use of automated decision-making tools, Scherer said, "in large part because having an information monopoly gives companies a huge competitive advantage over consumers and workers." Once the company decides that its use of ADMT tools doesn't substantially facilitate human decision-making, it need not even disclose that such a tool exists. This makes it impossible for anyone to challenge that determination, and "threatens to make the ADMT regulations a dead letter, with companies largely ignoring them," Scherer said. As a cautionary tale, both Scherer and Oates pointed to New York City's AI ordinance that requires companies to disclose when they use algorithms to rank and review job applicants. A study published by Consumer Reports and Cornell University found that because it gave businesses wide latitude in deciding whether the law applies to them, only 18 out of 391 employers posted audit reports on how algorithms influence their hiring decisions. Meanwhile, a Society for Human Resource Management study found that 64% of companies use automation to make recruitment and hiring decisions. "It's essential that the CCPA rules be written in a way that ensures companies cannot use their information monopoly on ADMT to avoid transparency and accountability," Scherer said. Nursing groups are particularly concerned about ADMT being used to make staffing decisions or replace nurses altogether, said Brynne O'Neal, a regulatory policy specialist with National Nurses United. She pointed to Nvidia and Hippocratic AI's virtual health care agents that the companies say can outperform human nurses. title: Swelling Workloads Taking Toll on In-House Lawyers' Mental Health
description: In-house lawyers generally like their jobs but are nonetheless anxious, exhausted and stressed. according to Law.com and ALM Intelligence’s 2024 Mental Health Survey. It found that crushing workloads, understaffed teams and dysfunctional company…
preview:
In-house lawyers generally like their jobs but are nonetheless anxious, exhausted and stressed. according to Law.com and ALM Intelligence’s 2024 Mental Health Survey. It found that crushing workloads, understaffed teams and dysfunctional company culture are largely to blame.

Seventy-nine in-house counsel responded to the survey, up from last year’s two dozen. While it’s too small a sample to be statistically significant, the results are consistent with observations from in-house experts who say the job has grown increasingly demanding.

preview:
In no uncertain terms, 2023 was the year of pop icon and IP rockstar Taylor Swift. Snap Inc., the creator of messaging app Snapchat, was hit with a wrongful-death lawsuit on May 17 in U.S. District Court for the District of South Carolina. The lawsuit was filed by Griffin Humphries and Joe Cunningham Law on behalf of the estate of the teenager, Timothy Isaiah Barnett. Barnett died by suicide after being the victim of “sextortion,” which is the practice of a predator threatening to circulate the sexual images of an individual unless the predator is paid to keep the images hidden, according to the complaint. The complaint alleged that a predator posing as a young girl manipulated Barnett into sending sexually explicit photos. The predator then threatened to share the images unless certain demands were met, allegedly leading Barnett to commit suicide, the complaint said. Snap is accused of knowingly facilitating the exploitation via its defective practices and design, including features that make the platform dangerous for minors, such as the “My Eyes Only” and disappearing photos features. Snap allegedly failed to implement adequate age verification and additional safeguards to protect vulnerable minors from being exploited, and is instead accused of facilitating and exacerbating the risk of exploitation by implementing features which help sexual predators connect with children. “Defendant’s product is designed in unsafe ways—including, as to some or all Defendants, flawed age verification, lack of meaningful mechanisms to prevent sham accounts, default-public profiles, matching and recommending connections between adults and minors, promoting unsolicited messages and interactions from adults, and wholly inadequate and ineffective parental controls, among others—that allow children to be easily identified, targeted, accessed, and exploited,” the complaint said. The complaint brings claims for strict liability, design defect and failure to warn, negligence, and negligence per se. The estate requests more than $10 million in compensatory damages, punitive and exemplary damages, attorneys fees and costs, and pre- and post-judgment interest. Neither the estate’s attorney, James M. Griffin of Griffin Humphries in Columbia, nor Snap immediately responded to requests for comment. Counsel have not yet appeared for the defendant.

searchText: GC Searches Veer Away From Internal Hires, Upending In-House Promotion Tracks Succeeding as general counsel now requires a much broader range of skills, "making the step up for internal candidates from deputy to GC a much bigger gap to bridge," a report from the executive search firm Russell Reynolds Associates says. Roughly… Succeeding as general counsel now requires a much broader range of skills, "making the step up for internal candidates from deputy to GC a much bigger gap to bridge," a report from the executive search firm Russell Reynolds Associates says. Roughly two-thirds of companies are going outside to fill general counsel openings, a dramatic increase from past practice driven by the reality that few legal departments have candidates in the pipeline with the broad range of skills the job now requires. It’s not a shortage of sharp legal talent in the tiers of legal department leadership below the GC, say recruiters, general counsel and others involved in conducting GC searches since the pandemic. Instead, the two most-often-cited reasons for going outside are that internal candidates lack “the ability to inspire or lead others, or fall short serving as a business-minded, strategic adviser,” said John Gilmore, co-founder and managing partner of BarkerGilmore, which conducts GC searches for companies. Gilmore said it is unwise for “companies select a successor based on the resume alone and tolerate the lack of soft skills necessary to become general counsel by assuming gravitas, judgment and EQ can be trained.” Sixty-one percent of the 66 Fortune 500 companies filling GC openings in 2023 went outside, a study released in March by the executive search firm Russell Reynolds Associates found. That’s a big leap from 2020, when 50% of the 52 Fortune 500 companies filing GC posts did so. That trend isn’t just playing out at the nation’s largest companies. BarkerGilmore’s “Aspiring General Counsel Report,” released in January, found 71% of GC openings were filled externally. It was based on a survey of 607 legal department leaders at companies and nonprofits of various sizes. Technology was the industry most likely to go outside, while industrial/manufacturing was most likely to hire internally, the study found. The Russell Reynolds report noted that the shift in hiring strategy coincides with a recasting of the general counsel role to include a variety of nonlegal duties, many of them external-facing, such as policy, communications, public affairs and government affairs. “GCs are increasingly seen as true enterprise leaders, trusted to guide companies through the choppy waters of war, politics, inflation, reputational risk, and AI. The GC role is more complex today than ever before, and is certainly not for the faint of heart,” the report said. With the new duties, the average Fortune 500 GC now has “six times more responsibility than any of their direct reports, making the step up for internal candidates from deputy to GC a much bigger gap to bridge,” the report said. To gain comfort a candidate can handle the role, companies increasingly are filling GC openings by hiring candidates who already hold the role elsewhere. From 2022 to 2023, the percentage of GC openings filled by current GCs leapt from 36% to 44%. High-Stakes Decision Many companies conducting GC searches have needs unique that make filling the role even more difficult. A firm planning an IPO might want a GC with IPO experience, for instance, or one with an entrepreneurial culture might want a GC who isn’t too buttoned down. Because getting the pick right is so important—and so difficult—Chicago-based TAG, parent of the nationwide Aspen Dental chain of clinics—spent nearly two years on the search that culminated with the November 2023 appointment of Hyung Bak, a former GC of Warby Parker, as chief legal and compliance officer. Spearheading the effort as he began to plot retirement was Richard Parr, who’d taken the legal reins in 2018. In the years since his arrival, the privately held company had tripled in size—a blizzard of growth that would have been out of the comfort zone for a typical Fortune 500 CEO. Parr said he concluded early on that “we didn’t really have an internal successor. We have some great attorneys but nobody who was quite ready.” As for possible outside candidates, “Somebody who had been part of a large legal department was not what we needed,” he said, noting that during his his six years as legal chief TAG dove into three new business lines, including veterinary care. “To do that, you have to be somebody who’s nimble and comfortable with growth and comfortable with building a department as opposed to just maintaining.” TAG eased Hyung into the job. Founded in 2023, Leya offers a generative AI assistant that looks to help streamline legal tasks such as document analysis, due-diligence review, data extraction, legal research and drafting legal documents like memos. A Leya spokesperson told Legaltech News in an email that the tool “integrates its AI system directly with the documents and knowledge that law firms have accumulated over the years, coupled with legal data from over 15 jurisdictions.” The AI assistant is already being used by a number of European law firms, including Spanish firms Pérez-Llorca and Araoz & Rueda, and Finnish firms Dittmar & Indrenius and Waselius, among others. “The company is currently being used by 70+ top law firms and companies in Europe with plans to expand to the U.S. in the future,” the spokesperson added. This funding will also be used to establish a local presence in many of the markets where Leya already serves clients.” Though there are a number of other legal-focused generative AI assistants on the market, Leya looks to stand out via its focus on the European legal system specifically. “Our decision to choose Leya was influenced by its foundation in European and Spanish legal documentation,” Marisa Delgado, the head of knowledge management at Pérez-Llorca told Legaltech News in February. “This specialization makes Leya particularly adept at delivering precise and relevant results for the contexts in which we operate, and sets it apart from other tools that might not be as finely tuned to our specific legal environment.”

The plan and award agreements provide for recoupment in the event an employee engages in misconduct, including criminal activity or violations of company policy, according to the May 13 opinion. However, Ellis rejected Grainger’s request for summary judgment on its claims that Witz breached his fiduciary duty and fraudulently concealed his conduct from the company. Grainger claimed Witz owed a duty of care and loyalty to the company as a corporate officer but placed Grainger in danger of potential liability through his illegal conduct. After Witz left the company in July 2021, Grainger received a request from law enforcement for Witz’s Grainger-issued laptop. It was later revealed that Witz stored the illegal content on his company-issued laptop. Witz pleaded guilty to one count of possession of child pornography, the opinion said. Grainger’s board determined that Witz’s conduct triggered the recoupment provisions in the award agreements and passed a resolution authorizing recoupment of certain incentive compensation of Witz’s. After notifying Witz of its intent to recoup the compensation, Witz’s counsel told Grainger that he would not agree to repay the compensation, resulting in Grainger initiating the action. Grainger argued that it was undisputed that the company was entitled to recoup the award agreements, while Witz argued against recovery because the compensation committee of the board of directors allegedly abused its discretion in seeking to take back the incentive compensation. Ellis concluded that the court didn’t need to definitively resolve the recoupment matter as to whether the covenant of good faith applied to the board’s decision. “Even assuming that the covenant of good faith limited the Board’s discretion, Witz has not created a question of fact as to whether the board violated the covenant,” Ellis wrote. “Because the award agreements provided that the board could authorize recoupment of Witz’s incentive compensation based on the board’s determination of whether Witz complied with applicable laws and Grainger policies, the parties expressly contemplated the situation at hand, an attempt at recoupment based on Witz’s violation of the acceptable use policy. In other words, Grainger did not act in bad faith when it exercised its discretion to recoup Witz’s incentive compensation for violating a company policy.” The court also rejected Witz’s argument because he violated Grainger’s acceptable use policy relating to the use of its technology and devices. “The parties agreed in the award agreements that the board had sole discretion in determining the extent to which it would seek recovery for any incentive compensation, meaning Witz cannot argue he did not contemplate the board pursuing recoupment if he violated a policy, regardless of its allegedly selective enforcement of the provision,” Ellis said. In regard to Grainger’s remaining claims, the court concluded that the company failed to set forth elements to support its argument that Witz breached his fiduciary duty and fraudulently concealed his conduct from the organization. Should Grainger pursue these claims, it may renew its request for summary judgment at the close of discovery, Ellis said. Witz also filed a counterclaim alleging that Grainger violated Section 2-103 of the Illinois Human Rights Act, failed to pay him certain compensation, and violated wage laws. Neither party sought summary judgment on those claims. A status hearing was set for Aug. 7. Grainger’s attorney, Ryan Hamilton Vann of Cooley in Chicago, declined to comment. Witz’s attorney, Dennis Ray Favaro of Favaro & Gorman in Lakewood, Illinois, did not immediately respond to a request for comment.

title: A Controversial Regulation: How the FTC Noncompete Ban Might Affect the Legal Industry
description: The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the…
preview:
The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the legal industry from across the Law.com Newsroom.

In a hearing Tuesday, agency staffers provided reassurance to rattled businesses, noting that other tools remain at their disposal to protect IP and investments in training.
excerpt: The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court...
searchText: A Controversial Regulation: How the FTC Noncompete Ban Might Affect the Legal Industry The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the… The Federal Trade Commission finalized a rule on April 23 banning noncompete agreements, and challenges from employers claiming the mandate exceeds the agency’s statutory authority quickly hit court dockets. Follow how the regulation might affect the legal industry from across the Law.com Newsroom. In House In a hearing Tuesday, agency staffers provided reassurance to rattled businesses, noting that other tools remain at their disposal to protect IP and investments in training. “Nonsolicitation agreements will be that much more important, that much more of a prevalent part of how private entities regulate … or manage the market for employment and employment mobility,” said John Siegal, a Baker & Hostetler partner. “If you take this to its natural extension, the FTC is invalidating hundreds and hundreds of years of a common law, of statutes being implemented on this topic,” Jason Tremblay, a partner with Saul Ewing, said. Regulatory “You’re going to still see enforcement by some states for time, space and scope-type noncompete roles,” said Gwendolyn Lindsay Coole, Wisconsin’s antitrust chief. “First, in my mind, the plain text of the FTC Act clearly gives the agency the authority to promulgate rules addressing unfair methods of competition,” FTC Chair Lina Khan said. Not everyone agrees. The Federal Trade Commission is scheduled to vote Tuesday on its rule that would prohibit noncompetes. The FTC said it would sue as early as Wednesday. “The freedom to change jobs is core to economic liberty and to a competitive, thriving economy,” Federal Trade Commission Chair Lina Khan said. Business of Law “If it did go into effect, certainly it’s going to create a demand for people to make sure their nonsolicitation provisions are tightly drafted,” said Ogletree partner Christine Bestor Townsend. Headhunting firms have used covenants to prevent their employees from leaving. Now these firms could become more vulnerable to poaching. Gibson Dunn, Sullivan & Cromwell Tapped to Challenge FTC’s Noncompete Ban Gibson Dunn’s Eugene Scalia, the former U.S. labor secretary, is representing tax services firm Ryan LLC. Sullivan & Cromwell is representing the U.S. Chamber of Commerce. Legal Technology Many in legal tech are split on if the FTC’s ban on noncompetes will bring massive changes in hiring and talent acquisition, or come up short. “I’m a defense lawyer primarily, but at the end of the day, noncompete agreements were not meant to be a tool to prevent your midlevel workers from going from Company A to Company B,” employment attorney Michael Elkins said.

The latest to do so is Everlaw, which announced on May 9 that it expanded its Everlaw for Good program to include its generative AI features, in a move to increase the number of cases supported by the program by 60% before the end of the year.

“If you think about all the ways you could try to address the [justice] gap, there are many ways that we can’t control as a company,” AJ Shankar, founder and CEO at Everlaw, told Legaltech News. “There are systemic issues, and it’s super complicated, but we can build the technology that can help facilitate some of this. And I think it’s actually really important to think about technology as a tool. Because you can imagine a world where, if it’s hard to access critical technology, then it can widen the access-the-justice gap.”

searchText: Everlaw Offers Free Gen AI Access Through 'Everlaw for Good' Program The latest to do so is Everlaw, which announced on May 9 that it expanded its Everlaw for Good program to include its generative AI features, in a move to increase the number of cases supported by the program by 60% before the end of the year. “If… The latest to do so is Everlaw, which announced on May 9 that it expanded its Everlaw for Good program to include its generative AI features, in a move to increase the number of cases supported by the program by 60% before the end of the year. “If you think about all the ways you could try to address the [justice] gap, there are many ways that we can’t control as a company,” AJ Shankar, founder and CEO at Everlaw, told Legaltech News. “There are systemic issues, and it’s super complicated, but we can build the technology that can help facilitate some of this. And I think it’s actually really important to think about technology as a tool. Because you can imagine a world where, if it’s hard to access critical technology, then it can widen the access-the-justice gap.” The program provides unlimited access to the Everlaw platform, including, now, its generative AI offering Everlaw AI Assistant, which is currently available in beta for select paying customers and is slated to be released for general availability some time this year. All tools accessed through the Everlaw for Good program are offered free of charge up to “a monthly cap,” with discounted rates for larger matters. Everlaw for Good is open to eligible 501(c)(3) organizations, pro bono practices and investigative journalists focused on access-to-justice issues. “We have made our eligibility very, very open. So if you’re a 501(c)(3) in good standing that operates in the legal space and has a use case for e-discovery, we have (six) broad program categories,” explained social impact expert Joanne Sprague, who joined Everlaw last October as the first-ever director of the program. In fact, Everlaw for Good seeks to support matters in the following categories: low-income populations, civil rights, civil liberties, human rights, public rights and environmental rights. The use cases between those different types of matters and organizations vary, but the overall needs often align. “Fundamentally in our field there’s two jobs: one, you have to go from a huge haystack of evidence to find a small handful of needles, and then two, you’ve got to take those needles and build a compelling narrative,” Shankar explained. “And in the corporate or the private-sector world, you solve those problems with a lot of human power. … When you’re a legal aid entity, you don’t have those resources.” The program has been running since 2017. In that time, Everlaw estimates it contributed approximately $2.75 million in platform services and served more than 125 organizations. While generative AI has sometimes been received with a bit of a sticker shock by the legal industry, Shankar noted that Everlaw was able to expand its beta program to nonprofit purposes for multiple reasons. On one side, the profitability of the rest of the organization is key to the sustainability of the program. “I want to emphasize that this program can only exist because we exist as a commercial entity, a for-profit entity that is allowed to invest in technology to serve lots of people. And so I think they go really hand-in-hand,” he said. But he also noted that once the technology is developed, expanding it to more users requires few additional resources. “We build software, and software is scalable in a way that human services aren’t quite scalable. I mean, you write some code once and you can run it many, many times. … So fundamentally, I think when you think about the benefits of technology, one of those benefits is scale,” Shankar added.

title: China Finalizes New Regulations to Relax Personal Data Exports
description: On the same day, the CAC also released guides which make corresponding adjustments pursuant to the New Regulations. The New Regulations significantly raise the threshold requiring the exporter to apply for a mandatory government security assessment.…
preview:
Nearly six months after the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) was first introduced for public consultation, with its draft regulations proposing to ease outbound data transfers from China (Draft Regulations) (see our article “China Releases Draft Regulation to Significantly Ease Cross-border Data Transfers,” Privacy World), the much-awaited final rules on Regulating and Facilitating Cross-border Data Flows were published and came into effect on March 22, 2024 (New Regulations). The New Regulations largely repeat the Draft Regulations, but now have further relaxed personal data exports from China.

The New Regulations largely implement exceptions set forth in the Draft Regulations, permitting certain cross-border transfers of personal data from China without the need to sign or file a standard contract (SC) or file a personal information privacy impact assessment (PIPIA) with the CAC. However, as compared to the Draft Regulations, the New Regulations further lessen export obligations requiring SCs and PIPIA filings by increasing the threshold from 10,000 individuals to 100,000 individuals for non-sensitive data.

searchText: China Finalizes New Regulations to Relax Personal Data Exports On the same day, the CAC also released guides which make corresponding adjustments pursuant to the New Regulations. The New Regulations significantly raise the threshold requiring the exporter to apply for a mandatory government security assessment.… On the same day, the CAC also released guides which make corresponding adjustments pursuant to the New Regulations. The New Regulations significantly raise the threshold requiring the exporter to apply for a mandatory government security assessment. We strongly encourage companies to swiftly identify their data exports from China. Nearly six months after the Cyberspace Administration of China (CAC) was first introduced for public consultation, with its draft regulations proposing to ease outbound data transfers from China (Draft Regulations) (see our article “China Releases Draft Regulation to Significantly Ease Cross-border Data Transfers,” Privacy World), the much-awaited final rules on Regulating and Facilitating Cross-border Data Flows were published and came into effect on March 22, 2024 (New Regulations). The New Regulations largely repeat the Draft Regulations, but now have further relaxed personal data exports from China. Exceptions to Signing Standard Contracts and Easing of Government Security Assessment Thresholds The New Regulations largely implement exceptions set forth in the Draft Regulations, permitting certain cross-border transfers of personal data from China without the need to sign or file a standard contract (SC) or file a personal information privacy impact assessment (PIPIA) with the CAC. However, as compared to the Draft Regulations, the New Regulations further lessen export obligations requiring SCs and PIPIA filings by increasing the threshold from 10,000 individuals to 100,000 individuals for non-sensitive data. The New Regulations also make important clarifications that are commonly of concern to multinational companies and businesses: Business/marketing/scientific data (other than personal data and important data) can be freely transferred.The specific list or catalogue of “important data” will be provided by the government, either through public announcement or notice to specific entities. Accordingly, businesses will not need to make a self-judgement as to whether they possess or process important data.Exports of personal data originally collected and generated outside of China, and then transferred into China for processing is exempted from a government security assessment, as well as the signing and filing of a standard contract, provided that no domestic personal data or important data is introduced during the processing.The validity period for a government security assessment is extended from two years to three years, with the possibility of extending the validity period for another three years.Free trade zones may establish whitelists to further relax data flows among applicable jurisdictions therein. The New Regulations took effect immediately upon their publication, i.e., March 24, 2024. We strongly encourage companies to swiftly identify their data exports from China, including the categories and quantities of data transferred in each scenario described above to evaluate their compliance with New Regulations. Companies should also keep in mind that even if they are exempted from having to pass a government security assessment or sign and file a standard contract, they are still required to fulfill their ongoing statutory obligations of providing the requisite notifications to and obtaining individuals’ relevant consents, as well as conducting PIPIAs for their data transfer activities. We would advise that these compliance measures be properly documented to demonstrate accountability with the PIPL and New Regulations.

title: CLOC 2024 Takeaways: Gen AI Is Changing Everything, and 'Data Is the New Gold'
description: "The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it," said Jenn McCarron, CLOC president.
preview:
More than 2,000 legal ops professionals descended on Las Vegas last week for the 2024 CLOC Global Institute, with generative artificial intelligence taking center stage.

Legal industry professionals are shedding their initial fears that the burgeoning technology will come for everyone's jobs. Now, the conversation has shifted to how legal ops and in-house counsel can put it to use to automate rote tasks and solve complicated business problems.
excerpt: "The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it," said Jenn McCarron, CLOC president.
searchText: CLOC 2024 Takeaways: Gen AI Is Changing Everything, and 'Data Is the New Gold' "The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it," said Jenn McCarron, CLOC president. More than 2,000 legal ops professionals descended on Las Vegas last week for the 2024 CLOC Global Institute, with generative artificial intelligence taking center stage. Legal industry professionals are shedding their initial fears that the burgeoning technology will come for everyone's jobs. Now, the conversation has shifted to how legal ops and in-house counsel can put it to use to automate rote tasks and solve complicated business problems. A few of the panels featured practical discussions on how legal departments have experimented with generative AI in the past year, and what they envision for the future. Law firms also will be challenged to think more deeply about the value they bring to their client relationships, as the technology displaces some of the services outside lawyers currently provide. Below are some observations and takeaways: Legal Ops 3.0 The Corporate Legal Operations Consortium appointed Jenn McCarron as president in January, making this the first CGI where she ran the show. McCarron used the platform to showcase her vision to move the profession beyond being simply a support function for legal with "sharply defined limits" into becoming a true strategic business adviser. In her opening keynote, McCarron said legal ops pros "have spent too much time on questions like 'what is the right contract life cycle management solution for my team?" instead of on the bigger picture. "We need to take control of the technology and innovation agenda. We can't solely rely on our product teams anymore. All this transformation we're talking about, it goes through the technology. So if we aren't pushing the software development life cycle, then we aren't creating the impact that we need fast enough," she said. McCarron went into more detail in a conversation with Law.com. Legal has always touched every aspect of the business, but is still siloed, she explained. McCarron said those who can use their positions effectively can deliver value beyond legal and grab the attention of the C-suite. "If some of us are doing this right, and I'm starting to see this now, with some real senior thought leaders in our industry, your role will transcend legal. You'll be pulled up into a C-suite, advising, strategic, focused capacity, because you are driving an impact that is hundreds of millions of dollars or whatever it equates to in big numbers for your business," she said. She pointed to Allison Silver, former head of legal ops at Zoom. Silver is now global head of operations and strategy and reports to Chief Operating Officer Aparna Bawa, who was herself chief legal officer before being promoted. Legal Ops 3.0 is still in the nascent stage, and many CLOC goers are still puzzled over what it means in practice. One attendee predicted a backlash from general counsel, who have been fighting for years for that same C-suite attention. Another was too focused on the day-to-day job—taking on more legal work with fewer resources—to fixate on other ambitions. And that's OK, McCarron said, noting that for a while there was a lot of buzz in legal ops around the chief of staff role. "I'm all of that, but that's not for me. That's not my archetype and I would not do well in that role," she said. "But I love doing the technologist work inside of the legal department. What are the other endpoints? So stay in legal if that makes sense, if that's where your role starts, and that's where you are for the foreseeable future. And it's OK if it transcends in time," she said. 'The Future Is Written in Data' Executive aspirations notwithstanding, everyone was talking about how to better use data. "Data is the new gold," McCarron told the CLOC audience in her keynote. "It's the entire point of all this technology we spend our lives deploying. The future is written in data. There's no way to engage with the challenges ahead of us if we don't become masters of collecting and exploiting it." Many of CLOC's panels focused on how legal can make the most of the swaths of data companies interact with every day. title: 'Walk a Fine Line': Managing Hyperpolarized Environment Zooms Up Employers' List of Worries
description: Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears. Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler…
preview:
Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears.

Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler Mendelson 12th Annual Employer Survey said they were moderately concerned or very concerned about managing divisive political or social beliefs in the leadup to the 2024 election.

searchText: 'Walk a Fine Line': Managing Hyperpolarized Environment Zooms Up Employers' List of Worries Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears. Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler… Companies are becoming more anxious about how to navigate political speech in the workplace as the Nov. 5 presidential election nears. Forty-nine percent of the 400 in-house lawyers, business executives and HR professionals responding to the Littler Mendelson 12th Annual Employer Survey said they were moderately concerned or very concerned about managing divisive political or social beliefs in the leadup to the 2024 election. Another 38% expressed slight concern, leaving just 13% of respondents who were “not at all concerned.” That’s a big shift from the start of the year, when 27% of respondents to Littler’s Inclusion, Equity and Diversity C-Suite Survey Report said they were ”not at all challenged” by managing divisive political beliefs among employees The employer survey, released last week, found anxiety levels were especially high among large employers, with just 6% saying they are not at all worried about the topic. Littler, which bills itself as the world’s largest management-side employment law firm, advised companies to “walk a fine line,” noting that those inclined to restrict politically toxic conversations face a legal minefield. It noted that the National Labor Relations Board—whose authority extends to most private-sector employers—has been interpreting the National Labor Relations Act in ways that expand the rights of workers to speak out. A September 2023 ruling, for instance, came down on the side of an employee who’d been fired after creating a brouhaha in the workplace advocating that her organization rehire a non-U.S. citizen it had earlier let go when her work authorization had expired. In February, the NLRB ruled a former Home Depot worker who’d resigned in protest after the retailer ordered him to remove “BLM” from his apron had been within his rights to display it. Meanwhile, some states also are expanding protections for political speech. In March, for instance, the Colorado Department of Labor and Employment bulked up protections for public employees. “Given the ramifications of the election’s outcome on employment law, as well as the labor-related statements offered by both candidates, employers attempting to limit contentious political conversations should be careful not to run afoul of the recently expanded interpretations of the NLRA and state laws, Littler’s report says. Political and social tensions already have boiled over at some workplaces. In April, Google fired 50 workers who held protests at the company’s New York and Sunnyvale, California, offices protesting the company’s cloud-computing contract with the Israeli government. Southwest Airlines’ yearslong legal battle over its 2017 firing of flight attendant Charlene Carter serves as a cautionary tale for other employers trying to manage discord in the workplace. The airline had said it fired Carter for violating a civility policy after she expressed her opposition to abortion by sending graphic videos and images of an aborted fetus to her union president. A jury in 2022, however, deemed her dismissal unlawful, finding that her opposition to abortion was rooted in her religious beliefs and that she was a victim of religious discrimination. The jury awarded her $5.1 million in punitive damages, though a judge later reduced the award to $800,000, citing federal limits on punitive damages. In 2020, both Basecamp and Coinbase grabbed headlines—and spurred dozens of employees to quit—by imposing outright bans on political speech. Other firms have taken a middle ground. Intuit, for instance, moderates company channels, flagging language “that could be hurtful or exclude.” In April, the DEI consultant Seramount issued an eight-page guide for employers titled “Managing Politics in the Workplace.” It recommends a proactive approach in which employers arrange discussions conducted in a respectful tone. Seramount noted that failing to engage on the topic can itself fan discord, noting that employees and other stakeholders increasingly expect their employers to engage on social and political topics. “It is important to allow employees the time and space to share their stories and perceptions in both formal and informal ways. Despite political differences, we can almost always find common ground and discover ways in which we are similar and share certain values and experiences,” the report says.

preview:
The legal industry's ambivalence about generative artificial intelligence is on the wane. And if it isn't, it should be.

That was the central message Thursday from Suffolk University Law School Dean Andrew Perlman, who provided the closing keynote for this year's CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas.

searchText: Think Gen AI Is Mind-Blowing Today? Next Decade's Advancements Will Be 'Momentous The legal industry's ambivalence about generative artificial intelligence is on the wane. And if it isn't, it should be. The legal industry's ambivalence about generative artificial intelligence is on the wane. And if it isn't, it should be. That was the central message Thursday from Suffolk University Law School Dean Andrew Perlman, who provided the closing keynote for this year's CLOC Global Institute conference in Las Vegas. He said the conversation has moved beyond the associated risks and pitfalls surrounding generative AI to how lawyers should be exploring it for their practice. The greatest risk, Perlman said, is in getting left behind. "I could say it will not be too long before we move away from concerns that the use of generative AI is incompetent to concluding that failing to use generative AI is incompetent," Perlman told an audience of several hundred legal professionals. He said people who compose legal documents using today's prevailing methods might be viewed in the future just as anachronistically as someone today who does so using a typewriter. "In the future, I believe anyone who opens up a blank screen and starts to type or goes to an old version of a document, saves it as a new one and does a 'find and a replace' will be similarly viewed as incompetent," Perlman said. OpenAI's chatbot is already capable of drafting a personal-injury complaint based on a slip and fall outside someone's home after a snowstorm with great precision. Perlman said he was surprised to see ChatGPT cite a Philadelphia code provision that imposes a duty on homeowners to keep their sidewalks clear after a snowstorm within a certain number of hours. At first, he thought it was hallucinating. But, sure enough, the provision exists. The GPT model was also capable of composing interrogatories, including one that asked the plaintiff to describe the footwear worn at the time the fall occurred. "It knew enough that it was a personal injury, slip-and-fall case, and that it should ask about the footwear of the plaintiff," he said. Perlman then asked it to "attack its own work" by drafting a brief in support of a motion to dismiss the complaint, and it gave him three decent arguments in response. "Now to be very, very clear, would I file this in court without looking at it? Not if I want to continue to be licensed in Massachusetts. Nor would I recommend that any lawyer do that. But can this give us guidance and a first draft of what we might use in the future? I think the answer is most certainly yes," Perlman said. ChatGPT and similar tools also can draft terms and conditions of a merger agreement between companies based in different countries. It can give suggestions on how to improve policy documents, suggesting edits or new language for a legal department to consider, while showing its reasoning for doing so. Perlman said he expects this will be the new way of working. There are still kinks to work out, such as algorithmic bias and hallucination. It also can try to get users to believe things they know to be untrue. "It is the best gaslighter you have ever met," he said. "It is a serious problem that we are going to have to consider in the future." But there is a plethora of customer solutions, dozens of which were featured at the CLOC conference this week, and the technology is only going to improve in the years ahead. Perlman said he's been talking to law firms, in-house counsel and bar associations, and across the board they agree that no one has figured it out yet. "At the same time, I'm a big fan of this quote from Bill Gates: 'We always overestimate the change that will occur in the next few years and underestimate the next 10.' "I think that describes generative AI and legal services perfectly. If I came back here two years from now, we'll see some changes, to be sure. But will they be dramatic? Will they be industry-changing developments? I think the answer is no. But if you come back 10 years from now, I think the changes are going to be momentous. In light of that. I think even though there's a lot of uncertainty, don't use it as an excuse to do nothing." Perlman urged audience members to experiment. "You can just ask generative AI to help you strategize what your plan should be inside of your legal department. I recently did that, and it can be an excellent road map. "And … it suggested some ways in which you might communicate your steps to the C-suite in your company. It even drafted an email for me along those lines," he said. "These are the ways in which we can use it, and they are nonthreatening and helpful. They enable us to think in new ways about the nature of the work that we do." While ChatGPT and its competitors have drawn comparisons to the advent of the internet and search engines, Perlman said this is bigger. ContractPodAi: On Monday, contract lifecycle management (CLM) provider ContractPodAi announced the general availability of Leah Helpdesk, its generative AI-powered application. The application will expand to provide legal support through Leah Draft—a generative AI-powered chatbot meant help structure and cleanly format legal documents. The expansion will automate contract drafting processes throughout the Leah tools. “In-house legal teams are increasingly taking on more work, and we’re excited that we can provide immediate relief to our customers, through Leah,” said Gabriel Buigas, EVP of legal and compliance solutions at Integreon. “With Leah’s new offerings and updates, customers can immediately take advantage, and reap the benefits, of GenAI services. These will enhance our ability to drive true transformation for our customers, at scale.”

Evisort + Icertis: On Tuesday, CLM and intelligence software provider Icertis announced a new alliance with CLM company Evisort. This strategic partnership platform will enable new and existing Icertis customers to leverage Evisort’s contract-specific AI engine, accelerating the ingestion and analysis of contract data to deliver insights and optimize workflows, according to the press release. Since Icertis works to transform the key contents of a contract into “strategic assets,” the ability to use software to extract the critical information contained in contracts, structuring it into a common data model, and connecting it with operational systems like ERP, SCM, CRM and HCM is key, the release stated. Indeed, Evisort’s contract-specific AI engine will work in concert with Icertis Discover Copilot to do just that. ”By integrating our contract-specific AI engine with the Icertis Contract Intelligence platform, we can enable joint customers to rapidly ingest and analyze both legacy and new agreements, accelerating insights that drive business performance. Our collaboration with Icertis will set new standards for how contracts are managed and executed, and deliver exceptional outcomes to our joint customers,” said Jerry Ting, CEO of Evisort, in the release.

description: But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins. Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely…
preview:
But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins.

Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely filing of their infringement suits, a divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled Thursday.
excerpt: But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins. Copyright holders can seek past damages for...
searchText: Copyright Infringement Damages Are Not Limited to Three Years, Supreme Court Says But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins. Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely… But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins. Copyright holders can seek past damages for infringement beyond the three years prior to the timely filing of their infringement suits, a divided U.S. Supreme Court ruled Thursday. But the court, in its 6-3 decision, left perhaps for another day a ruling on when exactly the three-year clock for filing an infringement case begins: when the infringement occurred or when the holder discovered or should have discovered the copyright was infringed. So, in its decision regarding damages, the court “assume[d] without deciding that a claim is timely” if brought within three years of the infringement’s discovery regardless of when the infringement occurred. “We have never decided whether that assumption is valid—i.e., whether a copyright claim accrues when a plaintiff discovers or should have discovered an infringement, rather than when the infringement happened,” Justice Elena Kagan wrote for the majority. Nevertheless, she stated that there’s no reason to limit the availability of money damages for infringing conduct that has only occurred in the three years prior to filing, as a federal district court did in the proceedings below. “There is no time limit on monetary recovery,” Kagan wrote. “So a copyright owner possessing a timely claim for infringement is entitled to damages, no matter when the infringement occurred.” To the three dissenting justices, the majority’s exercise of assuming when the three-year clock begins for filing an infringement claim was a waste of the court’s time and energy. “The trouble is, the [Copyright] Act almost certainly does not tolerate a discovery rule,” Justice Neil Gorsuch wrote in a dissent joined by Justices Clarence Thomas and Samuel Alito Jr. “And that fact promises soon enough to make anything we might say today about the rule’s operational details a dead letter.” The unusual procedural aspect of the case comes from the fact there is no acknowledged circuit split on the discovery rule, but there is one regarding how that rule is applied. Therefore, when the Supreme Court granted certiorari, or review, in the case, it assumed the existence of the discovery rule and asked whether the act allows for damages for “acts that allegedly occurred more than three years before the filing of a lawsuit.” The petitioner, Warner Chappell Music, had nevertheless encouraged the court to address the discovery rule, earning a mild rebuke from Kagan’s majority opinion Thursday. “Our reformulation of the question presented should have put an end to such arguments,” she wrote. Gorsuch, however, stated that the approach taken by the majority “does not strike me as the most sensible one.” “Nothing requires us to play along with these particular parties and expound on the details of a rule of law that they may assume but very likely does not exist,” he wrote. “Respectfully, rather than devote our time to this case, I would have dismissed it as improvidently granted and awaited another squarely presenting the question whether the Copyright Act authorizes the discovery rule,” Gorsuch wrote. “Better, in my view, to answer a question that does matter than one that almost certainly does not.” The lawsuit centers around a 1980s music venture between Sherman Nealy and Tony Butler called Music Specialist Inc., which recorded a number of songs during a brief period before Nealy went to prison from 1989 to 2008 for drug crimes. Butler later signed a deal with Warner Chappell Music to license Music Specialist Inc.’s works and found “quite a few takers,” as Kagan’s opinion explains. After a second prison term from 2012 to 2015, Nealy filed a copyright infringement lawsuit in 2018 covering alleged infringement acts that took place more than a decade prior. Nealy said his claims were timely because he did not learn of the infringement until after he was released from prison for the second time. A federal district court allowed the claims to proceed, but said Nealy could only seek damages for infringing conduct that occurred within three years of the lawsuit, a decision reversed by the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit. Warner Chappell Music appealed, but the Supreme Court affirmed the Eleventh Circuit’s ruling. Kannon Shanmugam of Paul, Weiss, Rifkind, Wharton & Garrison argued the case on behalf of Warner Chappell Music in February. Joe Wesley Earnhardt of Cravath, Swaine & Moore appeared for respondent Nealy. Assistant to the U.S. Solicitor General Yaira Dubin appeared on behalf of the federal government in support of Nealy

searchText: How Can Countries Prepare to Defend Against Deepfakes—and ‘Cheapfakes’—This Election Cycle? 2024 has been dubbed the year of elections—and for good reason. Voters from at least 64 countries and the European Union are preparing to vote in national elections, all against the backdrop of a staggering rise in disinformation and misinformation… 2024 has been dubbed the year of elections—and for good reason. Voters from at least 64 countries and the European Union are preparing to vote in national elections, all against the backdrop of a staggering rise in disinformation and misinformation increasingly fueled by artificial intelligence-generated content. Most parts of the world, including the United States, may not be prepared to face such waves of synthetic media, especially as investments in the development of large language models (LLMs) continue to outpace those made into detection-based approaches. As stakeholders from private companies and federal agencies start to collaborate to uncover robust solutions, experts during the “From Pixels to Policy: Defending Against AI-Generated Threats” session at the 2024 AI Expo for National Competitiveness in Washington, D.C., suggested it may be time to give up on the cat-and-mouse-game that has been the bane of many detection softwares and instead start to focus on content provenance. Retroactive Detection vs. Content Provenance Efforts to detect AI-generated content aren’t new. But more recently, they’ve involved steps from some of the leading AI providers. On May 7, OpenAI announced it joined the Coalition for Content Provenance and Authenticity Steering Committee (C2PA), a standard used to prove that content comes from a particular source. The AI provider noted it began adding C2PA metadata “to all images created and edited by DALL·E 3, our latest image model, in ChatGPT and the OpenAI API.” It also announced the upcoming integration of C2PA metadata for its video generation model Sora. Earlier this year, Meta had made a similar announcement, noting that it was building tools to identify visible markers, including the C2PA and IPTC standards to “label images from Google, OpenAI, Microsoft, Adobe, Midjourney, and Shutterstock.” “What that standard does is it simply exposes the origin and history of digital content over time, and it gives consumers the ability to view that, whether they’re looking at any photo or video, and understand and make their own decision around the credibility of that content,” explained Jeffrey McGregor, CEO at Truepic, a company which offers content transparency tools. There are currently two main approaches to content authenticity, McGregor noted. On one end, detection-based approaches often leverage some form of machine learning to analyze media retroactively and make what he called a “probabilistic determination” of whether it might be synthetic. “When you talk about the…pure scale of digital media, both synthetic and authentic, even a couple percentage points in terms of the model not being correct results in a massive amount of digital media that remains undetected as false,” McGregor said. “It’s also very much a cat-and-mouse game in terms of the ability for detection-based algorithms to keep up with the sheer investment into AI-generated content.” Instead, some are exploring approaches focusing on content provenance, meaning, the origin of a piece of media. This is akin to SSL (Secure Sockets Layer) certificates—digital certificates that authenticate a website’s identity and security—by binding trusted data to a file. In practice, a content provenance standard would assign security credentials to a picture or video to show its origin. As iterations to the content are made—whether it be a simple crop, or an AI-generated background—these changes can be tracked in the metadata. “The robustness, the scale, the security of that all far outweighs what we believe is possible with detection,” McGregor explained. “The downside is, of course, it does need to be adopted by an ecosystem.” Deepfakes, ‘Cheapfakes’ and Media Literacy A truly scalable ecosystem of content provenance standards may still be a few years away, as it will require buy-in from leading AI providers as well as developers of open-source models. But in the meantime, a combination of multiple approaches may still help shield some of the impact of synthetic content. In addition, for authenticity markers to truly be effective, the onus will also have to fall on consumers to look for such markings—a task which some suggest many aren’t ready to tackle. “From a global standpoint, we’re not prepared from a media literacy standpoint to truly look for authenticity markers,” McGregor said. searchText: Former Legal Exec at Hulu, Disney Joins Telecom Aiming to Narrow Digital Divide Lumen CEO Kate Johnson said that newly appointed Chief Legal Officer Chadwick Ho's "innovative and proven experience with large public companies and his ability to fuel growth in the technology sector makes him the perfect person to guide Lumen… Lumen CEO Kate Johnson said that newly appointed Chief Legal Officer Chadwick Ho's "innovative and proven experience with large public companies and his ability to fuel growth in the technology sector makes him the perfect person to guide Lumen through its ongoing transformation." Chadwick Ho, part of the leadership that launched the streaming service Hulu in 2007, is taking the legal reins of Lumen Technologies, an old-line telecom that has refashioned itself into a broadband provider for the masses. Ho served as general counsel of Santa Monica, California-based Hulu from 2007 to 2021, a span that included multiple transactions among the media giants that owned it. After The Walt Disney Co. gained control of the business, he jumped to the House of Mouse, where he spent a year as associate general counsel. In August 2022. Ho joined the travel software Sabre as chief legal officer. But by May 2023, he already had departed, a rapid exit that nether Ho nor the company publicly explained. Because of the short tenure, Ho forfeited most of his $2.5 million cash-and-stock signing bonus. Ho’s latest post will put him at the helm of a Denver-based company that hopes to rekindle investor interest in its stock—which has fallen from above $15 to below $1.30 over the last three years—by riding the wave of rural broadband investment. The company, founded in 1968, began as a copper-wire provider of phone service, and it grew over the years to become one of the largest providers of phone service in the rural United States. But with that legacy business sliding into decline, Lumen pivoted to building fiber-optic networks, and it now has 350,000 route miles of fiber-optic cable globally. It’s pinning its growth plans in part by tapping into the billions of dollars the U.S. federal government has anteed up to expand broadband service to rural communities, or to bolster existing service there. Ho will start as Lumen’s CLO in June, succeeding Stacey Goff, 58, who has been with the company for 26 years, the last 15 as general counsel. Goff received $2,7 million in compensation in 2023, including a $700,000 salary, according to a company securities filing. Lumen has not yet disclosed elements of Ho’s compensation package. “Chad’s innovative and proven experience with large public companies and his ability to fuel growth in the technology sector makes him the perfect person to guide Lumen through its ongoing transformation,” Lumen CEO Kate Johnson said in a statement. “I am confident in Chad’s ability to bring unique insights and drive results. In addition, his ability to motivate is a great cultural fit for this company. Lumen—which a year ago moved its headquarters from Monroe, Louisiana, to Denver—has 28,000 employees. In the first quarter, it reported revenues of $3.3 billion, down from $3.8 billion in the same period a year earlier.
