description: The U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), Damian Williams, began the year by announcing a call for individuals with knowledge of certain criminal conduct to join Team America. The district’s latest tool in white-collar criminal…
preview:
The U.S. Attorney for the Southern District of New York (SDNY), Damian Williams, began the year by announcing a call for individuals with knowledge of certain criminal conduct to join Team America. The district’s latest tool in white-collar criminal enforcement, SDNY’s Whistleblower Pilot Program, is the first of its kind, offering a non-prosecution agreement (NPA) to individuals in exchange for working with SDNY prosecutors to “figure out what [they] don’t know.” See SDNY Whistleblower Pilot Program.

Williams hopes the program will alert his office to “the next Madoff case” before extensive damage occurs. The promise of an NPA under the program provides significant benefits compared with SDNY’s stringent approach to negotiating cooperation agreements. SDNY intends for its program, which applies only to individuals, to “provid[e] clarity on the requirements and the benefits of [ ] self-disclosure” to motivate individuals to provide valuable information. With the program’s greater potential for leniency, however, may also come the potential to justify imposing harsher consequences on individuals aware of criminal activity who fail to come forward.

title: Why Progress on Law Firm Diversity Is 'Minimal at Best'
description: Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity.
preview:
Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity.

"Do in-house departments still care about improving diversity in the legal profession? The answer is yes, they do. They absolutely do. I don't think this has ever been a question of people not caring," said Akshay Verma, a former legal-ops chief at Meta and Coinbase. "But not much has changed. Everyone talks a big game, and nothing has happened."

searchText: Why Progress on Law Firm Diversity Is 'Minimal at Best' Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity. Legal departments' efforts to use their clout to get law firms to hire and promote more women and minorities appear to be stalling, even as firms say they're more committed than ever to diversity. "Do in-house departments still care about improving diversity in the legal profession? The answer is yes, they do. They absolutely do. I don't think this has ever been a question of people not caring," said Akshay Verma, a former legal-ops chief at Meta and Coinbase. "But not much has changed. Everyone talks a big game, and nothing has happened." Legal observers and DEI advocates attribute the disappointing results to many factors and say there's plenty of blame to go around. For starters, just 21% of legal departments are asking their law firms to report diversity data, a June Association of Corporate Counsel study found, and an even smaller percentage are demanding that firms staff matters with attorneys from underrepresented groups. And, while law firms do hire associates from underrepresented groups, they too often keep them in the background. One legal industry expert said there simply aren't enough diverse attorneys to go around, underscoring the need to expand the pipeline. The percentage of women and minority associates inched up in 2022, reaching an all-time high, according to data released last month from the National Association for Law Placement. Yet NALP, which has been tracking the data for 33 years, calls the progress "excruciatingly slow" and "minimal at best." Over the past decade, NALP data shows, the percentage of partners who are people of color has increased from 7% to 12%, and the percentage of partners who are women of color rose from 2% to 4%. One point of tension is whether legal departments should use a "stick" approach, punishing firms that fail to show meaningful progress on diversifying their ranks, or should instead take a "carrot approach," rewarding diversity gains with the opportunity to land more work. One cautionary tale for "stick" advocates is Bradley Gayton, who became general counsel of The Coca-Cola Co. in September 2020 after a nearly 30-year in-house career at Ford. The following January, he announced stringent new diversity guidelines for the beverage giant's outside firms, writing that diversity scorecards, summits and committees that were meant to drive meaningful change "are not working." Under his plan, 15% of a law firm's lawyers working on Coca-Cola's matters had to be Black, and at least another 15% had to be diverse. Firms that failed to meet the requirements would face reduced fees and could ultimately lose Coca-Cola as a client. The backlash was intense, and by April Gayton had resigned, with Coca-Cola putting the new system on hold and eventually scrapping it. 'Legally Thorny' Last year's U.S. Supreme Court ruling striking down affirmative action in higher education, as well as conservative groups' subsequent challenges to corporate diversity programs, caused some companies and law firms to pull back on DEI or at least reframe those efforts. A much-cited Littler Mendelson survey released in January found organizations are still committed to diversity, with 55% saying they're promoting more diverse employees to leadership roles. But the report also said they've been "slower to implement legally thorny" inclusion, equity and diversity goals. For example, only 34% of the 320 respondents said they were defining benchmarks and metrics to assess progress, "While executives are largely maintaining or increasing their IE&D commitments, more than one in three (35%) do not agree that their organizations have clear plans and goals in place related to IE&D," the report said. It noted that just 23% of companies are providing incentives to executives to advance diversity priorities. Diversity progress for both legal departments and law firms has been slow, acknowledged Jim Chosy, general counsel of U.S. Bancorp. "We have a lot more work to do as a broader profession," he said. "We've had a lot of organizations, whether they be diversity-focused organizations, law firms or corporate legal departments, just kind of doing their own thing. There's still just a bit of sort of us-them—we're doing this and they're doing that—and they don't always come together in the way that they should." Keeping Quiet Many law firms are reluctant to discuss what they're doing on the diversity front—perhaps spooked by conservative groups' assertion that the efforts often amount to reverse discrimination. Several law firms last year modified their diversity fellowships after activist Edward Blum filed lawsuits challenging their legality. Law firms see increasing opportunities to leverage both in-house and wider-market legal tech for their clients. But there are potential concerns, such as whether firms can support their own tech and whether partners will be willing to cede some degree of control over a client relationship to business teams. Big Law is exploring more tech solutions for clients, as law firms evolve to find business opportunities in generative AI, e-discovery tools and other software. But firms need to make sure their efforts in offering tech solutions to clients don’t upset the partnership and that the firm is capable of both scaling and supporting those tools for clients, according to law firm professionals and others speaking at a panel this week that focused on client-facing solutions that highlight firm expertise. title: The Rise of Counter-Disinformation Litigation and What It Means for Business
description: In the past year, viral lies and conspiracies have saturated our public discourse, with concrete results. The scale and speed with which falsehoods have spread about everything from the outcome of the 2020 election to the Jan. 6 attack to COVID-19…
preview:
In the past year, viral lies and conspiracies have saturated our public discourse, with concrete results. The scale and speed with which falsehoods have spread about everything from the outcome of the 2020 election to the Jan. 6 attack to COVID-19 vaccines, and much else, have led to real-world consequences for companies and people—ruined reputations, lost business value, security expenses, and death threats, to name a few. The prevalence of disinformation can impact all kinds of businesses by affecting corporate brands, sales, partnerships, employee and customer retention, physical security, and even stockholder activism.

Partly in response to the spread of false narratives, 2021 witnessed a new trend: the proliferation of counter-disinformation litigation. While many of these suits are still in the early stages, plaintiffs have seen notable (and surprising) successes thus far, suggesting the emergence of a specialized, potent tool to combat phony and harmful narratives. Both victims of false narratives and potential defendants should pay heed to these novel developments.

title: How Will the Federal Reclassification of Marijuana Affect New Jersey's Cannabis Industry?

preview:
Marijuana has been classified as a Schedule I drug since Congress enacted the Controlled Substances Act (CSA) in 1970. Under the CSA, Schedule I drugs are deemed to have a high potential for abuse and have no accepted medical use. For perspective, other drugs listed as a Schedule I drug include, but are not limited to, heroin, lysergic acid diethylamide (LSD) and ecstasy. However, as of the writing of this column, 38 states have legalized medical marijuana and 24 states have legalized recreational, adult-use marijuana.

Perhaps you are thinking—if 38 states have already legalized medical marijuana in the U.S., then the U.S. government must have previously recognized that there is at least some accepted medical use … right? Wrong.

title: Biden’s AI Executive Order: 6 Actions for Legal Leaders
description: In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology. “Artificial Intelligence must be…
preview:
In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology.

“Artificial Intelligence must be safe and secure. Meeting this goal requires robust, reliable, repeatable, and standardized evaluations of AI systems, as well as policies, institutions, and as appropriate, other mechanisms to test, understand, and mitigate risks from these systems before they are put to use. It also requires addressing AI systems’ most pressing security risks — including with respect to biotechnology, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, and other national security dangers — while navigating AI’s opacity and complexity.”

searchText: Biden’s AI Executive Order: 6 Actions for Legal Leaders In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology. “Artificial Intelligence must be… In October 2023, The Biden Administration issued an Executive Order on artificial intelligence (AI) that calls for federal agencies to develop new guidance around safe, secure, and trustworthy use of the technology. “Artificial Intelligence must be safe and secure. Meeting this goal requires robust, reliable, repeatable, and standardized evaluations of AI systems, as well as policies, institutions, and as appropriate, other mechanisms to test, understand, and mitigate risks from these systems before they are put to use. It also requires addressing AI systems’ most pressing security risks — including with respect to biotechnology, cybersecurity, critical infrastructure, and other national security dangers — while navigating AI’s opacity and complexity.” Much of the order pertains to U.S. government requirements and specific industries such as healthcare, financial services, and critical infrastructure owners and operators. However, it also reflects principles aligned with global regulatory efforts initiated by the European Union and others, which include: Transparency: Highlights new guidance and standards on disclosing to individuals and relevant regulatory agencies when and how AI is being used. Fairness: Calls for cabinet and regulatory agencies to set standards and guidance to minimize bias in areas such as hiring, housing, and healthcare. Human oversight: Recognizes the importance of having human oversight in AI decisions, especially higher-risk situations where discrimination or unintentional bias may pose an issue in automated decision making. Risk management: Introduces new risk management practices specifically for AI with a particular focus on third-party usage and monitoring. It also calls for an updated National Institute of Standards and Technology (NIST) risk framework. Privacy: Renews a call for federal legislation in this area and calls out specific privacy risks that are potentially exacerbated by AI.

title: Big Law Has 'False Sense of Security' as Clients Depart for Midsized Firms
description: Since the financial crisis of 2007-2008, "market power shifted decisively from law firms to the clients, rapidly moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market for legal services," a new report from Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law says. Thomson…

Since the financial crisis of 2007-2008, "market power shifted decisively from law firms to the clients, rapidly moving from a sellers' to a buyers' market for legal services," a new report from Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law says.

Legal departments are aggressively shifting work from the Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred to less expensive law firms, a new study found, a trend that began to take root during the 2007-2008 financial crisis but was partly masked by a decadelong boom in transactional work.

Thomson Reuters and Georgetown Law have released their 2024 legal market report. It notes that clients often don't inform Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred firms when they choose cheaper firms for new matters. That, plus the M&A boom that sustained Big Law for years, has obscured the extent of clients' move down market. Legal departments are aggressively shifting work from the Am Law 100 and Am Law Second Hundred to less expensive law firms, a new study found, a trend that began to take root during the 2007-2008 financial crisis but was partly masked by a decadelong boom in transactional work. With M&A activity down sharply the past two years, the extent of the shift is only now coming into full focus, according to a new legal market report by Thomson Reuters and the Center on Ethics and the Legal Profession at Georgetown Law.

title: All the News That's Fit to Pinch: NYT v. OpenAI
description: The emerging cases by authors and copyright owners challenging various generative AI programs for using copyrighted materials are certain to create new troubles for the courts being asked to apply the fair use doctrine to this important new…
preview:
Courts have said time and again that the fair use doctrine may be “‘the most troublesome in the whole law of copyright.’” See, e.g., Oracle Am., Inc. v. Google Inc., 886 F.3d 1179, 1191 (Fed. Cir. 2018) [internal citations omitted], rev’d on other grounds, 141 S. Ct. 1183 (2021). The emerging cases by authors and copyright owners challenging various generative AI programs for using copyrighted materials are certain to create new troubles for the courts being asked to apply the fair use doctrine to this important new technology. Several such cases to date have received considerable publicity, including two class actions by Michael Chabon, Ta-Nehisi Coates and others, Chabon v. OpenAI Inc., No. 3:23-cv-04625 (N.D.Cal.) and Chabon v. Meta Platforms Inc., No. 3:23-cv-04663, (N.D.Cal.); another class action involving several best-selling authors, Authors Guild v. OpenAI Inc., No. 1:23-cv-08292 (S.D.N.Y.), and another class action including Sarah Silverman, Kadrey v. Meta Platforms Inc., No. 3:23-cv-03417 (N.D.Cal).

Perhaps the most troublesome of all so far is the new complaint filed by The New York Times alleging that OpenAI, Microsoft and others committed copyright infringement in training its Generative Pre-Trained Transformer (GPT) systems and wrongfully attributing false information to The Times via the output from systems such as ChatGPT and Bing Chat. The New York Times Co. v. Microsoft Corp., No. 1:23-cv-11195 (S.D.N.Y.) The Times asserts claims for direct as well as vicarious and contributory copyright infringement, unfair competition, trademark dilution, and violation of the Digital Millennium Copyright Act — Removal of Copyright Measurement Information (17 U.S.C. §1202). Among other things, the complaint alleges that GPT not only copied published articles verbatim but could be prompted to offer up content that is normally protected by The Times‘ paywall. The complaint cites several such examples of nearly verbatim copying of large sections of articles and includes screenshots of GPT delivering up the first paragraphs of articles as well as ensuing paragraphs when prompted to do so. The complaint alleges that the “training” of the program included storing encoded copies of the works in computer memory and repeatedly reproducing copies of the training dataset, such that millions of The Times works were “copied and ingested — multiple times — for the purpose of ‘training” Defendants’ GPT models.” The Times further alleges that when OpenAI’s chatbots are not revealing verbatim copying, they instead (when actual content is not available) entirely fabricate “hallucinations” — inventing and misattributing to The Times content that it did not publish.

title: New DOL Regulation on Employees Versus Independent Contractors Restores Multifactor Test While Leaving Some Important Questions Unanswered
description: On Jan. 1, 2024, the Biden administration’s Department of Labor (DOL) issued its final regulation on who is an employee versus who is an independent contractor, Part 795 – Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor…
preview:
On Jan. 1, 2024, the Biden administration’s Department of Labor (DOL) issued its final regulation on who is an employee versus who is an independent contractor, Part 795 – Employee or Independent Contractor Classification under the Fair Labor Standards Act, 89 F.R. 1741, No. 7 (Jan. 10, 2024). The regulation rescinds the Trump administration rule because, according to the administration, it emphasized two factors—employer control over how the work is done and opportunity to engage in entrepreneurial activity—in a manner unsupported by the agency’s traditional multifactor view and case law, and was inconsistent with the DOL’s emphasis on “economic dependence” as a principal guidepost.

The regulation brings back the traditional, flexible multifactor approach but leaves some important questions unanswered.

title: Meet Yalonda Howze, the Chief Legal Officer of Codiak BioSciences
description: The first member of her family to attend college, Yalonda Howze, chief legal officer of Codiak BioSciences in Cambridge, Massachusetts, grew up in East Detroit. During that time, she watched many communities become ravaged during the war on drugs.…
preview:
The first member of her family to attend college, Yalonda Howze, chief legal officer of Codiak BioSciences in Cambridge, Massachusetts, grew up in East Detroit. During that time, she watched many communities become ravaged during the war on drugs. Witnessing this at an early age sparked her desire to find a way to help people that were suffering.

“Mine was a desperate neighborhood, at the time, a working-class neighborhood that had fallen, due to a raging crack epidemic that decimated families and communities,” she said. She compared that time to the pandemic that we’re suffering through now. “There are various kinds of epidemics that hit us,” she observed.

title: Looking for Your Dream Job? Don’t Follow Your Heart
description: This month’s column is inspired by an amusing commercial for one of the job posting sites. Cue a woman keyboarding away with a bored look on her face. Then we are treated to an image of the woman’s heart tearing itself out of her chest, marching into…
preview:
This month’s column is inspired by an amusing commercial for one of the job posting sites.  Cue a woman keyboarding away with a bored look on her face.  Then we are treated to an image of the woman’s heart tearing itself out of her chest, marching into the boss’ office, and resigning.  The tagline, of course:  “follow your heart.”  I loved it.

We get resumes every day from dissatisfied attorneys.  Those are usually the people we cannot place.  So, my first reaction to the ad, once I stopped laughing, was to verbalize my cynicism.  To my friends around the chip and dip bowls, I announced, “there is no Santa Claus, you are not going to win the lotto, and, most certainly, there is no such thing as a dream job.  Well, at least not for you lawyers.”  Yes, a lot of my friends are lawyers!  The reaction was general agreement, not protest.

title: Hackers Increasingly Infiltrate Software While It's Still in Development—Before Guard Is Up
description: "Not only is this terrifying because it can happen to any organization that's building software, but it's actually also incredibly difficult to detect," said Dan Draper, founder of CipherStash.
preview:
Imagine a lauded restaurant that attracts government officials and corporate elite. One day, someone sneaks into the kitchen and puts cyanide into a pot of stock used in its signature dish. The sitting U.S. president happens to be a guest that evening and consumes it. Now, the president is dead.

"That's kind of what's happened here, where SolarWinds are the cooks in the kitchen, and somebody has snuck in and put some malicious code into their software as they're building it. And nobody noticed," said Dan Draper, technologist and founder of Australia-based cybersecurity and governance platform CipherStash.
excerpt: "Not only is this terrifying because it can happen to any organization that's building software, but it's actually also incredibly difficult to detect," said Dan Draper, founder of CipherStash.
searchText: Hackers Increasingly Infiltrate Software While It's Still in Development—Before Guard Is Up "Not only is this terrifying because it can happen to any organization that's building software, but it's actually also incredibly difficult to detect," said Dan Draper, founder of CipherStash. Imagine a lauded restaurant that attracts government officials and corporate elite. One day, someone sneaks into the kitchen and puts cyanide into a pot of stock used in its signature dish. The sitting U.S. president happens to be a guest that evening and consumes it. Now, the president is dead. "That's kind of what's happened here, where SolarWinds are the cooks in the kitchen, and somebody has snuck in and put some malicious code into their software as they're building it. And nobody noticed," said Dan Draper, technologist and founder of Australia-based cybersecurity and governance platform CipherStash. Draper is referring to the 2020 hack of Austin, Texas-based SolarWinds, which sells network-management software to Fortune 500 companies, all U.S. military branches, the State Department and the Pentagon, the most infamous example so far of a sophisticated supply chain hack that pushed malicious code to thousands of customers through routine software updates. But what was so insidious about this hack, Draper said, is that it was so covert. "Not only is this terrifying because it can happen to any organization that's building software, but it's actually also incredibly difficult to detect," he said. Cybersecurity experts say such attacks are the latest frontier for hackers, a humbling reality for computer security leaders to confront just as they're getting better at shielding their enterprises from older methods of infiltration. Cybersecurity company CrowdStrike, one of several that assisted SolarWinds in its investigation of the attack, posted a breakdown on its blog of how hackers inserted malicious code into SolarWinds' network management software as it was being built, without arousing suspicion. Joe Sullivan, a former security chief at Uber, said it was almost fortuitous that CrowdStrike made the discovery. "When they discovered the compromise, it wasn't because they did an audit of the code and discovered it. It was because CrowdStrike had a good security team that had gotten an alert on lateral movement in their identity and access management infrastructure," he said. "So hundreds of companies and governments had run the software and it had gone through their third-party vendor software audit review process and [they had] blessed it. And nobody caught it." In a landmark enforcement action, the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission in October sued SolarWinds and its chief information security officer, Tim Brown, alleging that the company ignored red flags raised by employees and Brown himself about their ability to fend off cyberattacks. Draper said that while much of the public discussion has focused on the attack itself, and the vulnerability of the SolarWinds' system, the malware, dubbed "Sunspot" by security researchers, could end up playing a critical part in the case. "The SEC is out for blood," Draper said. "Was SolarWinds negligent in allowing an adversary to implant malicious code in their source code as they're developing the software? That's the question of the day, and for some reason it's the question that people are not talking about." In the aftermath of the SolarWinds hack becoming public in December 2020, the Biden administration issued an executive order stating that "the private sector must adapt to the continuously changing threat environment, ensure its products are built and operate securely, and partner with the federal government to foster a more secure cyberspace." But Draper said the success of the hack doesn't necessarily mean there were lapses in cybersecurity. "At the time, I'm not sure that there were any standard practices, certainly not that I'm aware of, that would have necessarily provided a high confidence that they would have detected this issue," he said. Cybersecurity professionals commonly refer to attacks that occur while software is being created and deployed, often in a series of automated processes known as continuous integration/continuous delivery pipeline, as "poisoned pipeline" executions. The CI/CD pipeline is meant to streamline development and cut down on errors, but it's also an area of vulnerability because attackers can inject malware into the CI/CD pipeline and manipulate the software to execute malicious commands. "This is a new, up-and-coming attack vector," said Saumil Patel, co-founder and chief technology officer of EchoLayer, a startup that helps companies resolve security vulnerabilities. "Now there's a billion things that happen in the CI/CD pipeline. And that makes this attack vector significantly more broad." He said bad actors are increasingly zeroing in on where the sausage gets made as security professionals become more adept at fending off common hack

title: NIST Cyber Framework 2.0: Doubling Down on Governance, Expanding Applicability

title: SEC Cybersecurity Rules Go Live in Days. Companies Still Aren't Sure What to Expect
description: The SEC's cybersecurity-disclosure rules kick in Dec. 18. Determining what to disclose will be tricky. Security chiefs may be inclined to disclose more, fearing personal liability for inadequate disclosures, while other C-suite executives might favor…
preview:
Any security professional who has dealt with a cyberattack can tell you that the early stages are often chaotic, with the extent of the damage and the magnitude of the intrusion difficult to immediately determine.

The stakes will become even higher when new U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission rules take effect in mid-December that demand prompt disclosure of material cyberattacks and annual reports about cyber risks and vulnerabilities. Tired of “generic” disclosures and “gamesmanship” from public companies more concerned with protecting their reputations than their shareholders and customers, the SEC says it’s time to get tough.

title: More People Are Bringing Politics, Religion to Workplace, Testing Employers on Civility
description: COVID-19 blurred the lines between home and work, upending long-established workplace boundaries. Meanwhile, a larger cultural push is encouraging employees to bring their whole selves to work. But the new environment can leave some employees feeling…
preview:
Southwest Airlines thought it was getting rid of a workplace bully when it fired a flight attendant for sending abusive messages to a colleague on social media. But her termination turned into a legal nightmare, with the airline ordered to reinstate the flight attendant, pay $5 million in damages and send a team of its top lawyers to “religious liberty” training.

The episode underscores the predicament companies face in maintaining a workplace culture of mutual respect and civility. While never an easy proposition, it’s getting even harder as employees shed reservations about loudly sharing their strongly held religious and political beliefs, emboldened by a larger cultural push to bring their “whole” selves to work.

title: Moving the Needle on Outside Counsel Team Diversity
description: The current profusion of outside counsel DEI surveys that law firms receive from their clients has hit an all-time high. While well intended, these surveys haven’t moved the needle at a rate commensurate with the work involved. And, at their worst,…
preview:
The current profusion of outside counsel DEI surveys that law firms receive from their clients has hit an all-time high. While well intended, these surveys haven’t moved the needle at a rate commensurate with the work involved. And, at their worst, they can actually work at cross-purposes with legal departments’ objective of fostering a culture of diversity and inclusivity by diverting valuable time from diversity leaders to repeatedly define the problem rather than working on solutions. This need not be the case.

Most legal departments have neither the resources nor the scientific expertise to craft and conduct an effective assessment of their outside counsel DEI that produces more inclusive teams. Many have told us they don’t know where to start other than perhaps the raft of firmwide data produced annually by dozens of reputable third-party organizations. And even then, it takes substantial time and ability to analyze the data and successfully operationalize the findings to align with organizational values.

description: Legal departments are starting to embrace generative AI to drive legal and business efficiencies. And just as in-house lawyers are under pressure to adopt new technologies, they're placing similar expectations on their outside counsel.
preview:

Certainly, caution reigns supreme in the ongoing dialogue between legal departments and law firms concerning the adoption of generative AI. Yet, in-house leaders are increasingly looking to outside counsel to at the very least understand the technology, if not use it to drive their own business efficiencies.

searchText: With the Rise of Generative AI, Legal Departments Lean on Law Firms as 'Business Partners' More Than Ever Legal departments are starting to embrace generative AI to drive legal and business efficiencies. And just as in-house lawyers are under pressure to adopt new technologies, they're placing similar expectations on their outside counsel. Legal departments are starting to embrace generative AI to drive legal and business efficiencies. And just as in-house lawyers are under pressure to adopt new technologies, they're placing similar expectations on their outside counsel. Certainly, caution reigns supreme in the ongoing dialogue between legal departments and law firms concerning the adoption of generative AI. Yet, in-house leaders are increasingly looking to outside counsel to at the very least understand the technology, if not use it to drive their own business efficiencies. "My growing expectation is that, if I'm going to outside counsel, they will be aware of [generative AI] and understand its use cases," said Colin Levy, director of legal at Malbek, noting he's looking for a combination of practicality and pragmatism. Even though law firms typically haven't been on the cutting edge of technology adoption, the way generative AI rushed into the public consciousness late last year has pushed client expectations higher, perhaps at a faster clip than ever before. "I'd hope a law firm in today's day and age would have the foresight to understand if they want to attract clients and retain their existing clients, they have to be up-to-date on the current state of tech as it pertains to the practice of law," Levy said. Laura Safdie, general counsel at CaseText, doubled down on the idea that law firms need to seriously consider the use of generative AI to improve their own business models for the benefit of their clients. "There's an expectation that outside counsel don't frivolously use human labor on the type of tasks that can be competently done by a machine," Safdie said, noting that there already is and will continue to be pressure from clients to keep billed time to a minimum on basic tasks. "If you see a 10-hour bill for a research memo where co-counsel can do the first draft in 10 minutes — it should be two hours. It should never be 10 [hours] anymore." Safdie said she's had conversations with several global firms that are asking important questions about how generative AI may change the practice of law, such as how associates are trained, the kind of substantive work that young associates can take on, as well as how quickly and efficiently they can produce a product or answer for the client. To the latter, Safdie said there is an awareness among law firms that generative AI can give them a competitive advantage by doing more work for their clients at a faster rate. "Being in-house, I can tell you there is nothing better than being able to provide a competent answer to the business stakeholder fast, as opposed to every contract review taking four hours," Safdie said. "When you can move at the speed of business, it creates a real opportunity to be seen as a business partner." Allen & Overy is one such law firm that embraced generative AI early on, as one of the first firms to adopt Harvey. Already, Karen Buzard, a partner and member of the firm's Markets Innovation Group, said Harvey is likely the firm's most utilized tool on a day-to-day basis. "It's becoming part of our day-to-day working and everybody is realizing that it didn't take their job, but it changed their job and took some mundane or low-value tasks off their plate," Buzard said. That early adoption spurred an immediate dialogue with clients, Buzard said, as companies reached to understand how Allen & Overy is using the technology and the challenges it encountered along the way. Generative AI is also contributing to a shift in discourse as it relates to law firm billing, as well as the quality and value of legal services, Buzard added. For instance, though it's still early days with respect to the adoption of AI, the cost of legal services has already been under pressure given the prevalence of alternative legal providers, she said. "Already, clients were starting to say I don't want to pay to have a first-year associate spending time on something that is not high value," she said. "That cost model of fixed fees (is) starting to become part of the vernacular," she said. "We haven't seen a complete shift. … But it is moving us in a direction that we can meet the demands of our clients at the pricing our clients were starting to demand." title: An In-House Revolution: Early Adopters of AI Reduce 'Rote Tasks,' Spend More Time on Strategy
description: Early generative AI adopters have reached an epiphany: It's going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days.
preview:
Generative artificial intelligence is triggering a range of emotions in legal departments—from anxiety to exhilaration—but early adopters already have reached an epiphany: It's going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days.

Whether they're the only lawyer at their company or part of a department of 1,000, in-house counsel are putting tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Bard to use for more than just drafting contracts and legal memos. They're using them to comb through vast repositories of data, summarize long, complicated legal documents and find opportunities to advance business.

Generative artificial intelligence is triggering a range of emotions in legal departments—from anxiety to exhilaration—but early adopters already have reached an epiphany: It's going to make them more effective strategic business advisers, the yardstick of success for in-house attorneys these days. Whether they're the only lawyer at their company or part of a department of 1,000, in-house counsel are putting tools like ChatGPT, Claude and Bard to use for more than just drafting contracts and legal memos. They're using them to comb through vast repositories of data, summarize long, complicated legal documents and find opportunities to advance business. "I have AI going out there and looking for new revenue development possibilities," said Kelly Slavitt, general counsel and head of corporate development at Sikka.ai, a cloud platform that makes applications for the health care industry. "There are some of us who are using it to control costs and save time, but I believe there is also a way to drive revenue. … It takes away some of those rote tasks, so you can use your business and legal teams to push for revenue-driving strategies and find new space where you can innovate." In interviews with more than a dozen in-house attorneys and other legal and technology experts, Law.com found legal departments in a broad range of company sizes and industries have moved beyond experimenting with the technology to integrating it into their day-to-day processes. At startups, for instance, legal chiefs are using tools like ChatGPT to beef up their negotiation skills and spot potential snags in business deals and contracts. Large legal departments like Ford Motor Co.'s are finding generative AI tools boost productivity and reduce the time attorneys spend tracking down answers to questions. "We jokingly say, 'It's like having a really solid first-year sitting next to you working on things with you,'" said Darth Vaughn, litigation counsel and managing director of legal ops for the automaker. Vaughn added: "We haven't seen a practice area where we don't think this is applicable yet," Slavitt said she uses public AI tools like Claude and Bard to study business trends, research competitors and find potential business partners. "I can look into companies that we want to go into business with. I can go out there and say, 'Hey we have this new partnership with Wells Fargo. What else can we be doing to match their needs? What initiatives do they have going on? How can we partner with them? Getting AI to go out there and do that research is very useful." AI also has helped Sikka.ai's privacy officer and head of IT better protect customer data, Slavitt said. "It can go out and find publicly filed data breach notifications, and it aggregates it and saves me the research time," she said. "The value-add for me is helping me with my compliance program. I use it to see if there are any trends or mistakes that were made that are now being publicly reported. It can save me the time in going out there and finding what data breach notifications that were filed. AI can go out there and find that information for me and bring it back to me." Legal and technology experts say in-house attorneys who seize on the benefits of AI are making themselves more valuable, paving the way for advancement opportunities at their current employer or to stand out in applications for plum jobs elsewhere. "Once you learn as a general counsel or in-house lawyer how to leverage AI in the work you do day to day, you're putting yourself in the position to identify opportunities in the business itself," said Laura Safdie, general counsel at Casetext, whose AI tool Co-Counsel was built using OpenAI's platform. "We have several large companies we've worked with closely, and we saw a general counsel or an associate general counsel take this path where they're like, 'Here's a huge business problem, and I understand how to leverage this technology.' And it's putting them in a position to advise the business in a way that's more powerful and more value-creating than what they were able to do before." searchText: Ex-Uber Security Chief Appeals Conviction That Shook Cybersecurity World "Joe Sullivan used tools and strategies that all CISOs utilize to protect the data of hundreds of thousands of Uber drivers, and was prosecuted for doing his job," Sullivan's appeals attorney said Former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan is appealing his conviction for covering up a 2016 data breach and obstructing a regulator's investigation into Uber's security practices. Sullivan was sentenced in May to three years of probation following a nearly monthlong jury trial in 2022. He faced up to eight years in prison for obstructing the Federal Trade Commission's ongoing investigation into Uber's security practices and misprision of a felony, a rare charge that involves taking active steps to conceal a crime. His indictment in 2020—considered the first time prosecutors had sought to hold a tech executive criminally liable in a data breach—sent shockwaves through the field of cybersecurity, raising anxiety among chief information security officers that responses to breaches at their own companies could land them in prison. At Sullivan's sentencing, U.S. District Judge William Orrick said the unique nature of the case, as well as Sullivan's strong character, weighed heavily in his decision not to sentence Sullivan to prison time. "I hope everyone in the CISO community takes this as a lesson, and not leniency," Orrick said. Uber hired Sullivan, a widely respected fixture in the security world, to help strengthen its data security after a similar data breach in 2014. Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers. Sullivan said he knew the breach would be embarrassing for Uber if it were made public. Just days before, he'd given a lengthy deposition to the Federal Trade Commission on Uber's progress in tightening security as part of the regulator's continuing investigation into the 2014 incident. So he chose to deal with the situation quietly, paying the two hackers $100,000 in Bitcoin through Uber's white hat bug bounty program while continuing to help Uber's in-house legal team negotiate a settlement that would bring the regulatory agency's investigation to a close. Along with in-house attorney Craig Clark, who got immunity in exchange for his testimony, Sullivan pursued an aggressive legal theory that they believed would settle the matter without having to report the breach to the FTC. Sullivan is being represented by Orrick partner Aravind Swaminathan, who in a statement to Law.com said Sullivan "used tools and strategies that all CISOs utilize to protect the data of hundreds of thousands of Uber drivers, and was prosecuted for doing his job." Sullivan's appeal, filed late Tuesday in the Ninth Circuit, says prosecutors built their case on "innuendo," asking the jury to view Uber's bug bounty program "not as an effective way to protect users, but as hush money. It faulted Mr. Sullivan for not directing Uber's legal department to notify the FTC (a job for Uber's CEO, if anyone), and for not editing submissions to the FTC that Mr. Sullivan had not drafted, signed, and in some instances even read. The government theorized, without proof, that Mr. Sullivan was motivated by a need to protect his own reputation as a cybersecurity professional." Swaminathan said Sullivan's conviction sets a dangerous precedent for other security chiefs who fear they may be targeted for prosecution based on their handling of data breaches. "The misprision conviction—a charge rarely brought by federal prosecutors—criminalized the Uber security team's use of their world-class and leading Bug Bounty program to protect the personal information of hundreds of thousands of Uber drivers," he said. Swaminathan also described the obstruction charge as "profoundly flawed," saying: "Despite the fact that Mr. Sullivan was not responsible at Uber for the FTC's investigation, including the drafting or signing any of the submissions to the FTC, the government singled him out among over 30 of his co-employees who all had information that Mr. Sullivan is alleged to have hidden from the FTC." He added that Sullivan "sets a dangerous precedent for CISOs and CIOs, who now fear criminal liability anytime there is any investigation by any government authority that touches the information technology or security of their company." The case had divided the cybersecurity community—with critics saying he acted selfishly to protect his own reputation and avoid more regulatory scrutiny but supporters calling the government's case overreach. title: Lafayette Attorney Indicted for Role in Alleged DC Solar Ponzi Scheme
description: An East Bay attorney has been charged with bank fraud in what federal prosecutors called the biggest criminal fraud scheme in the history of California’s Eastern District. A federal grand jury on Oct. 5 returned a 23-count indictment against Ari J.…
preview:
An East Bay attorney has been charged with bank fraud in what federal prosecutors called the biggest criminal fraud scheme in the history of California’s Eastern District.

A federal grand jury on Oct. 5 returned a 23-count indictment against Ari J. Lauer of Lafayette for his alleged role in a $912 million conspiracy involving the purported sales and leases of mobile generators, according to documents unsealed Tuesday following Lauer’s arrest. Lauer, a solo practitioner with an office in Walnut Creek, served as outside counsel for the generator company DC Solar.

preview:
A federal judge has set a new trial date for two former tech executives accused of bribing government officials in India, after a witness snafu caused the court to miss its chance to have the trial this year.

Judge Kevin McNulty said the trial, scheduled to open this week, will now have to wait until at least mid-February. Prosecutors had asked for a brief postponement because its star witness was stuck in India. On Friday, a federal prosecutor, Sonali Patel, told McNulty that the witness had been cleared by the Indian government to travel and could be in court as early as the middle of next week, but McNulty said it was too late.

title: 4 Longtime Netflix Legal Execs Out in Restructuring

preview:
Four attorneys who are senior members of Netflix’s legal and business affairs team are exiting as part of a restructuring, including 16-year company veteran Bryony Gagan, who oversaw global content production, acquisition and distribution.

Gagan has the title vice president of legal affairs, as do nine-year company veteran Amy Paquette and 13-year veteran Tim Mizrahi, who also are leaving. The fourth departure is nine-year veteran Stephen Zager, vice president and associate general counsel. The news was first reported by Deadline.

title: Colorado Supreme Court Grants Cert to Bakery Over Refusal to Create Cake Celebrating Transgender Woman
description: The Colorado Supreme Court has granted certification to Masterpiece Cakeshop, the same store that was party to the 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Craig v. Masterpiece Cakeshop, after a decision by the Colorado Court of Appeals rejected the store’s…
preview:
The Colorado Supreme Court has granted certification to Masterpiece Cakeshop, the same store that was party to the 2018 U.S. Supreme Court ruling in Craig v. Masterpiece Cakeshop, after a decision by the Colorado Court of Appeals rejected the store’s arguments and held that the act of baking a pink cake with blue frosting does not constitute protected speech under the First Amendment.

In a published opinion issued last January, the appeals court decided Scardina v. Masterpiece Cakeshop, the second case involving the shop in a claim over whether its owner had the right to refuse service to a customer based on their use of the cake. On June 26, 2017, the U.S. Supreme Court granted certiorari to review an earlier decision in Craig. That same day, Autumn Scardina called Masterpiece to order a cake and told the wife of the store owner that it was for her birthday and to celebrate her transition from male to female, according to the Jan. 26 opinion by Colorado Court of Appeals Judge Timothy J. Schutz.

searchText: California's Data-Deletion Legislation Threatens to Shake Up Digital Ad Industry "We think that this will have a tremendous impact on the small business and startup community in California," said Lartease Tiffith of the Interactive Advertising Bureau. A California privacy bill that will give consumers the power to delete their personal information through a single request may soon become law, and could upend the way data brokers, advertisers and publishers do business in the Golden State. The Delete Act, now on Gov. Gavin Newsom's desk, tasks California's privacy regulator with setting up a "simple" way for people to direct companies to delete their information through a single request by 2026. Data brokers, of which there are about 500 registered with the California Department of Justice, will also have to disclose what kind of information they collect on consumers—including precise geolocation and women's reproductive health data—beginning Jan. 1, 2029. They'll also have to undergo compliance audits every three years, starting in 2028. The California Privacy Protection Agency will have the authority to levy stiff penalties of $200 for each failure to delete, and a $200 fine for each day the data broker fails to register with the CPPA. The law defines "data brokers" as any company that knowingly collects personal information on a consumer with whom it doesn't have a direct relationship to sell to third parties. It would not apply to first-party data, or information that companies collect directly from consumers. Third-party data brokers aggregate public records, mobile apps, social media activity, online purchases and browser cookies to create profiles (third-party data) on consumers that they can sell to others. Some companies, like the credit bureaus Experian and Transunion, operate in the credit and risk mitigation arena, while others work to prevent fraud, perform background checks or build online directories. Many more track consumers' shopping habits and preferences to give other businesses insight to into what products and services they might be interested in buying. CPPA executive director Ashkan Soltani said the bill mirrors an existing state requirement under the California Consumer Privacy Act that businesses honor consumers' requests to opt out of sharing their information with third parties. Last year, retail cosmetics giant Sephora was hit with a $1.2 million fine for failing to process opt-out requests in the first public enforcement action under the state's landmark consumer privacy law. The Delete Act, Soltani said, will make it even easier for consumers to exercise their privacy rights. Ryan O'Leary, a research director at International Data Corp., said there hasn't been much enforcement of the CCPA's opt-out provision apart from the Sephora action, which the Delete Act should help address. "There still leaves a lot to be desired, and this gives them an actual mechanism," he said. The question remains how accessible the mechanism will be for consumers. "The education has to be there for consumers because you can have this law but what if no one requests that their data be deleted?" O'Leary said advertisers and marketing firms will likely lose access to fresh data, but he doesn't see a wholesale crippling of the industry. "I think there will still be a non-negligible amount of people that allow data brokers to sell their data. I don't think there are going to be folks going out of business because of this. They just won't have as much data or they won't be able to be as efficient and narrowly-targeted with their marketing," he said, "The advertising world existed before data was collected. It will exist long after." But the prospect of consumers scrubbing their data en masse has data brokers and digital advertisers on edge, and industry groups have vigorously lobbied in opposition to the bill, saying it will cut off access to free and low-cost digital content and keep small and medium-sized businesses from finding potential customers. "We think that this will have a tremendous impact on the small business and startup community in California," said Lartease Tiffith, executive vice president for public policy for the Interactive Advertising Bureau. Direct-to-consumer businesses may be the most affected, he said, as they rely heavily on third-party data purchased from data brokers for targeted advertising. "Everybody who is using third-party data is using data brokers," Tiffith said. "There's a rush to get more first party data, mostly because there seems to be an anti-third-party data thing going on, but not everyone can afford to." It may also force publishers to put more online content behind a paywall. "If you're a publisher and you rely on advertising and you're realizing you're getting less revenue and advertisers are seeing less conversions, at some point businesses will have to decide whether to keep their content free or go to subscription," Tiffith said. title: AI Study Reveals How Employers Are Using the Tools, and With What Safeguards
description: Littler Mendelson surveyed 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals. The employment law firm found that companies are embracing artificial intelligence's predictive powers, but are cautious about using it for generating content. Most…
preview:
More companies are using artificial intelligence for hiring, recruiting and other human resource-related tasks, but have been slower to adopt generative AI tools such as ChatGPT for creating content, says a new report on AI in the workplace by employment law firm Littler Mendelson.

San Francisco-based Littler’s survey of 399 in-house counsel, HR leaders and other professionals found 56% do not use generative AI at all for HR work. But of those that do, 34% use the technology to write job descriptions, onboarding materials and employee memos. Others use it in much smaller numbers (12%) to answer workplace questions through internal chatbots, and 11% use it for employee development, such as personalized trainings. Only 8% use AI to interact with job candidates.

title: Bill Would Unleash Hackers to Hunt for Federal Contractors' Cybersecurity Flaws
description: Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems.
preview:
Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems.

Vulnerability disclosure policies have been a requirement for federal agencies, along with smartphone, laptop and other device manufacturers and suppliers, since 2020.
excerpt: Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems.
searchText: Bill Would Unleash Hackers to Hunt for Federal Contractors' Cybersecurity Flaws Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems. Federal contractors soon might have to adopt policies that allow ethical hackers to find and report cybersecurity vulnerabilities in their systems. Vulnerability disclosure policies have been a requirement for federal agencies, along with smartphone, laptop and other device manufacturers and suppliers, since 2020. A bill working its way through Congress, the Federal Cybersecurity Vulnerability Reduction Act,, will expand the VDP requirement to all private companies that contract with the government. The lawmaker behind the bill, Rep. Nancy Mace, R-South Carolina, said in a statement that the measure would help shore up the government's digital infrastructure by ensuring a "proactive approach to cybersecurity" and "enabling contractors to identify and address software vulnerabilities promptly." Contractors would have to follow guidelines for setting up VDPs established earlier this year by the National Institute of Standards and Technology. "This legislation, aligned with internationally recognized standards, empowers contractors to stay ahead of malicious actors, preventing potential exploits and protecting sensitive information," said Mace, chair of the House Oversight and Accountability Committee's cybersecurity, information technology and government innovation subcommittee. The bill is supported by HackerOne, a cyberattack-resistance platform and marketplace that matches hackers with companies and facilitates bug bounty payments for ethical hackers. Unlike bug bounties, a more mature cybersecurity program that pays hackers who find vulnerabilities and gives them express permission to do their testing, VDPs mostly provide hackers an avenue for reporting security weaknesses. HackerOne chief legal officer Ilona Cohen said hackers, who take great pride in being able to spot security flaws, are already looking for them in corporate systems. "This work is already being done. People are already looking at these systems. The question is, do you want to create an avenue by which they can report it to you, or would you rather have them tweet it? Personally, I'd rather the former," she said. Cohen, a former legal adviser to President Barack Obama and general counsel of the Office of Management and Budget during the Obama administration, said VDPs are one of most effective ways to fix security flaws and head off cyberattacks. Back in 2015, Cohen's office helped oversee the response to one of the largest data breaches in government history, where hackers posed as posed as an employee of a contractor used by government agencies to perform background checks. "That resulted in a billion records being compromised and 20 million personnel records being compromised. The way the hackers entered the system was through contractors to the agencies," she said. "So if you want to protect these sites, you really have to shore up cybersecurity through all entry points." The Department of Defense already has already embraced the policy, partnering with HackerOne on a pilot program that encouraged hackers to detect software vulnerabilities in its defense industrial base. Cohen said the Defense Department and the participating contractors "were surprised at the number of vulnerabilities identified in their systems and found it quite useful to be able to mitigate and respond to those. Expanding that will be very important to national security." Mace's bill, assigned to the House Armed Services Committee and House Committee on Oversight and Accountability, comes at a time of accelerating cyberattacks targeting a broader swath of companies. "The threat landscape is definitely evolving and it is becoming more sophisticated. They have professionalized ransomware attacks and it can be hugely disruptive to companies," Cohen said. "So the best solution is to prevent it from happening in the first place." NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. International privacy regulators are calling on social media giants to protect their users' publicly available information from web-scraping, a common business practice in the United States, but one that in other jurisdictions could constitute a reportable data breach. "Social media companies have obligations under U.K. data protection law to protect the information people post on their platforms," said Stephen Bonner, head Britain's top privacy watchdog, the Information Commissioner's Office. "We are seeing increased reports of mass data-scraping from social media and remind organisations that such incidents may require reporting to the ICO as a personal data breach." ICO was joined by 11 other data protection authorities from China, Australia, Switzerland, Norway, Jersey, New Zealand, Colombia, Argentina, Mexico and Morocco in a statement that Bonner said should help provide "certainty, and consistency across borders, in how data protection applies to information people post online." It's also a warning that companies must have a lawful reason for collecting personal data, even when it is publicly available. Social media platforms and website operators that host publicly accessible personal data have certain obligations with respect to third-party data-scraping, the statement says. "These obligations will generally apply to personal information whether that information is publicly accessible or not. Mass data-scraping of personal information can constitute a reportable data breach in many jurisdictions." The statement was sent directly to companies running the world's major social media platforms; Alphabet, Meta, ByteDance, Weibo, Microsoft and X Corp. The watchdogs say they are worried about identity fraud, spam marketing, and profiling and surveillance by authorities, and targeted cyberattacks carried about by malicious actors using swathes of personal data posted to hacking forums. Scraped data can also be exploited by foreign governments and intelligence agencies, or harvested without permission for dubious purposes, as with British consulting firm Cambridge Analytica, whose misuse of Facebook data for targeted political advertising triggered one of the most infamous data scandals in recent history. Privacy regulators outlined an array of measures companies should take to mitigate these risks, including cracking down on bots, limiting the number of times per day that an account can visit other account profiles, and dedicating in-house teams to monitor and respond to scraping activity. In an interview with Law.com, privacy scholar Omer Tene, a Goodwin Procter partner and senior fellow at the Future of Privacy Forum, said the statement reflects the attitude "that access to information, even if it's publicly available, if it's done at scale could lead to different harms." It also comes amid a surging commercial demand for data to train and machine learning algorithms and the attendant fight over data ownership. As lawsuits against AI companies alleging copyright and privacy violations pile up, social media platforms are looking to courts to prevent data-scrapers from accessing public information on their sites. "The data is incredibly valuable for the platforms especially today with generative AI and LLMs. A lot of players want to access data to teach algorithms," said Tene, who also noted that entire businesses have been built on scraping publicly accessible information. In his forthcoming "Field Guide to AI Law," scheduled to be published in January 2024, privacy expert Lothar Determann writes that data-scraping has been a longstanding practice. "Companies have been scraping so commonly that the Practicing Law Institute (PLI) hosted a conference in 2014 with the title, 'Everyone's Doing It, But Is It Legal? Web Scraping and Online Data Harvesting.'" He added: "Many online companies scrape content off other sites while complaining about being victims of scraping themselves…. Most companies welcome the robots deployed by search engines to ensure their websites are easily found. At the same time, however, they typically try to protect their sites from scraping and deep-linking that causes users to bypass portal sites (and their advertisements) or that otherwise affects their business interests adversely." In a recent interview, Determann said data-scraping in itself is neither good nor bad. "Accessing a website with automated tools is not per see illegal or problematic—far from it," he said. searchText: California High Court Holds AI Vendors Liable for Biased Job Screening California's highest court has handed down a landmark ruling with major implications for the AI industry: making vendors that use algorithms to perform other employment-related tasks for other companies directly liable for discrimination. California's highest court has handed down a landmark ruling with major implications for the AI industry: making vendors that use algorithms to target job ads, screen out applicants or perform other employment-related tasks for other companies directly liable for discrimination under state law. "The major impact of this is with outsourcing, and that's what a lot of companies are doing for a lot of their employment-related functions," said attorney Randy Erlewine of the San Francisco law firm Phillips, Erlewine, Given & Carlin. "Everyone is being hired these days online, and you've got these major third-party platforms that may have discriminatory biases or metrics, and the employer may not know it is discriminatory." Erlewine represented Kristina Raines in a class action lawsuit against U.S. Healthworks Medical Group, a company that contracts with employers to perform medical screenings of job candidates. Raines's job offer was revoked after she refused to answer a health history survey riddled with questions she considered intrusive about venereal diseases, menstrual cycles, pregnancy and mental illness. Raines settled with her prospective employer, Front Porch Communities and Services, but also went after U.S. Healthworks. After a federal judge dismissed the lawsuit, the Ninth Circuit asked the high court to weigh in on whether California's Fair Housing and Employment Act permits a "business entity acting as an agent of an employer to be held directly liable for employment discrimination." The court on Aug. 21 ruled unanimously that it does. "[W]e recognize as a necessary minimum that, consistent with the FEHA's language and purpose, a business-entity agent can bear direct FEHA liability only when it carries out FEHA-regulated activities on behalf of an employer," Justice Martin Jenkins wrote for the court. Amanda Herron, an attorney in San Diego with Gordon Rees Scully Manusukhani, said the ruling has the potential to impact a variety of industries, from recruiting and background checks to HR and consulting. "Previously, the job applicant who claimed they were discriminated against, their only recourse was to sue the prospective employer directly. Now the California Supreme Court is saying that prospective employers were always on the hook, but now their agents can also be sued," she said. "We can't say for sure what the impact is going to be yet, but it seems like it will double the amount of defendants who can be named in these FEHA suits." Herron said the ruling is a departure from the court's prior decisions where it declined to hold individuals acting on behalf of their employers liable for discrimination under FEHA. But in this case, the court reasoned, business entities with five or more employees are "more likely than an employee agent to have comparable bargaining power to the employer." Companies like U.S. Healthworks operate on national scale. U.S. Healthworks performed 200,000 medical screenings last year, just in California. "These third parties have the expertise to make that portion of the employment related function either cost effective or more expedited. And from a public policy standpoint, they should be the primary ones to bear the cost," Erlewine said. "The employer should be happy for this. If the employer is innocent and in good faith outsourced to a party that was responsible for violating discrimination statutes, that third party is going to be liable." Employers are still on the hook for discrimination, though companies can negotiate "the question of indemnification regarding any potential FEHA liability that might arise." Companies will likely have to re-negotiate their vendor contracts to spread around liability, said Matthew Roberts, an employment law counsel with the California Chamber of Commerce. "What the employer might be able to do here is say, 'If you end up doing something that violates FEHA, we want an indemnity provision here where if we get sued you're paying for it all,'" he said. The ruling also will have a nationwide impact, as business agents need only to work with California companies, not employ California workers themselves, for the law to apply to them. "This is going to be one more impediment when it comes to doing business in California," said Niloy Ray, a shareholder at the labor and employment law firm Littler Mendelson. Ray said the cost of litigating the potential flood of new employment discrimination cases will also rise along with the pool of defendants. title: Leading DEI with Practicality and Purpose
description: The Supreme Court’s affirmative action decisions and the current divisive political landscape have perpetuated skepticism about corporate Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (“DEI”) efforts, and undoubtedly have made corporate DEI programming…
preview:
The Supreme Court’s affirmative action decisions and the current divisive political landscape have perpetuated skepticism about corporate Diversity, Equity and Inclusion (“DEI”) efforts, and undoubtedly have made corporate DEI programming challenging. Corporate counsel should not allow these developments to derail DEI efforts. Instead, corporate counsel should take this opportunity to reinvigorate their companies’ commitments to DEI, in order to create workable and legally defensible programs that achieve robust representation and workforce success.

Corporate counsel are well positioned to play a key role in focusing their companies on the case for DEI, whether premised on fundamental fairness, correcting for historical underrepresentation, or aligning with the shareholder goal of profitability. To do so effectively, they should approach DEI with a view to expanding and not restricting the workforce pipeline. In fact, an effective DEI program should always begin with the message that such programs create new, expansive, and more representative pipelines to the ultimate growth asset: talented people who achieve the corporate mission. Corporate counsel can take a few key steps to help their clients achieve a more diverse and inclusive workforce.

title: Historic NLRB Ruling Gives Workers Path to Unionize Without Having to Vote

In what some attorneys are calling the most significant change in federal labor law in a half-century, the National Labor Relations Board has issued new rules that put employers in the onerous position of being forced to recognize and bargain with a union—unless they take swift action to request an employee election and prevail in that election.

“These changes radically shift the legal landscape for companies,” Morgan, Lewis & Bockius wrote in a note to corporate clients, and “make it much easier for unions to organize.”

title: FTC Shows Willingness to Use Extreme Measures to Tame AI
description: The FTC has grown more aggressive in punishing AI-driven companies that have profited off of customer data. A spate of recent settlements with Amazon, Everalbum and Weight Watchers shows the FTC's growing appetite for ordering companies to delete…
preview:
The Federal Trade Commission has one of the most potent tools to punish artificial intelligence-driven companies that disregard consumer privacy, and it’s not shy about using it. searchText: Ransomware Gangs Are Increasingly Going After Smaller, Easier Targets Ransomware gangs favor smaller companies, as they're more likely to have a smaller IT budget and less cybersecurity expertise. Threat actors are changing their tactics and launching smaller-scale attacks with more frequency. Ransomware attacks have… Ransomware gangs favor smaller companies, as they're more likely to have a smaller IT budget and less cybersecurity expertise. Threat actors are changing their tactics and launching smaller-scale attacks with more frequency. Ransomware attacks have decreased this year compared with the latter half of 2022, but many companies have delayed reporting, and the number of reported attacks is expected to rise in the second half of the year. Small companies beware: You’re more likely to be a victim of a ransomware attack. A new report on the 2023 ransomware threat landscape from cyber-risk quantification platform Kovrr found ransomware actors tend to favor companies with revenue in the $10 million to $50 million range. “Smaller companies have a smaller IT budget and less security expertise. So it makes them easier targets, for sure,” said Guy Propper, head of data for Kovrr. Threat actors are also choosing to forgo larger extortion payments from high-revenue companies in favor of easier and more plentiful targets. “They’re willing to have the smaller ransoms for having easier attacks, and being able to perform more attacks because some of these companies use the same cloud services, the same programs,” Propper said. Preying on smaller companies also minimizes risk as larger targets are more likely to draw swift action from law enforcement, Kovrr’s report says, citing the 2021 attack on Colonial Pipeline. “Attacking smaller companies, while possibly promising lower rewards, also poses a lower risk for ransomware groups, as they are less likely to be prosecuted due to a single attack,” the report says. Propper said the leaked internal communications of one notorious ransomware gang called Conti also warned members to be careful when attacking large companies for this reason. The services sector was the hardest-hit industry, particularly business services, as they make the best targets for extortion, Kovrr’s report says. One reason is because they provide services to other companies, so they are more likely to want to avoid as much downtime as possible. They also rely more on third-party services, such as cloud hosting. And perhaps most important, Propper said, they collect vast amounts of consumer data. Ransomware has developed into a cottage industry in recent years, as threat actors grow more sophisticated and adaptive. Gone are the days of the lone hacker sitting in his mother’s basement. Now ransomware attacks are more likely to be executed by organized groups of individuals each working within their own specialty, whether it’s running the ransomware itself, finding the right target or handling the negotiations. In this way, they operate like small companies themselves, Propper said. Ransomware gangs are also using artificial intelligence tools to perform some of the more laborious work involved in cyber extortion. For example, hackers can use large language models to write ransomware code or hunt for new targets. “It can help you in finding information that might be relevant for your scans,” Propper said. “For example, they could start with a simple question, ‘What are the top 100 health care companies with the most customers, and what are their domains?’ And then they could ask, ‘Which of these domains uses specific technology?’ And then from there, it just saves them a lot of time.” Kovrr found that ransomware attacks dropped by 32% in the first half of 2023, though the firm suspects that this may be caused by delayed reporting by victim companies. Reported attacks may still increase in the second half of the year, following trends over the last two years. “In the previous two years, more attacks have been reported, or have occurred, in the second half of the year compared to the first half,” Kovrr’s report says. Blockchain data analysis firm Chainalysis also reported an uptick in ransomware payments in 2023. “In fact, ransomware attackers are on pace for their second-biggest year ever, having extorted at least $449.1 million through June,” the company says in its midyear crypto crime update. Chainalysis attributes this increase to a rise in both “big-game hunting,” where hackers target deep-pocketed organizations, as well as a rise in successful smaller attacks. “[W]e’re seeing growth in ransomware payments at both ends of the spectrum,” Chainalysis reports. Kovrr looked at data from multiple sources for its study, including data breach notifications from victim companies, news reports of ransomware attacks, and from sites on the dark web, where attackers publish their exploits. Founded in 2011, Fastly helps heavily trafficked websites run faster. Fastly promoted Karen Greenstein to general counsel after she spent more than a year running its 16-person legal department on an interim basis. Greenstein joined the San Francisco-based cloud service provider as an assistant general counsel in 2019. In June 2022, she took over the legal department from chief legal and trust officer Paul Luongo, who resigned to become legal chief at e-commerce platform Narvar. Greenstein jumped into the role overseeing Fastly’s employment, privacy, intellectual property, litigation and commercial legal teams. She was previously general counsel at business news and advice site Business.com, and held senior in-house roles at Viacom, NBCUniversal and CNET. The company did not respond to a request for comment on Greenstein’s promotion. Fastly also hired Mozilla’s Marshall Erwin as chief information security officer and Check Point Software’s Peter Alexander as chief marketing officer. Founded in 2011, Fastly operates an “edge cloud platform” that helps highly trafficked websites run faster. It competes with Amazon Web Services, Cloudflare and Akamai. It had 493 enterprise customers as of year-end, according to a U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission filing. Clients include GitHub, Yelp, Ticketmaster and Stripe, as well as news publishers Gannett and The New York Times. It made headlines in 2021 after an internal glitch brought down a host of major websites for an hour, including Amazon and Reddit.
