title: As Cyberattacks Rise, Including Ga. Case, Firms Face 'Significantly Broadened' Duty to Protect Worker Data
description: Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information. Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally…
preview:
Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information.

Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally bound to mitigate foreseeable risks to employee health and safety. But a ruling out of Georgia last month illustrates how that definition is evolving for the digital age.

Case, Firms Face 'Significantly Broadened' Duty to Protect Worker Data Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information. Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally… Cyberattacks are creating a new litigation battleground, as more courts find that employers have a common-law duty to safeguard employees’ sensitive information. Duty of care is often thought of in the physical context, where employers are legally bound to mitigate foreseeable risks to employee health and safety. But a ruling out of Georgia last month illustrates how that definition is evolving for the digital age. In Ramirez v. The Paradies Shops, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Eleventh Circuit overturned a district court’s dismissal of a class action against a company that suffered a ransomware attack in 2020, where hackers made off with unencrypted Social Security numbers belonging to current and former employees. Employee Carlos Ramirez filed the case in 2021, after Paradies notified him of the attack and after he learned that his Social Security number had been used to file pandemic unemployment assistance claims in Kentucky and Rhode Island. The Eleventh Circuit revived his negligence claim, finding Georgia’s traditional negligence principles “flexible enough to cover Ramirez’s allegations. The court ruled Paradies had a duty under Georgia common law to protect Ramirez’s personal identifying information. In addition, the court found Ramirez had sufficiently shown that he had a “special relationship” with his employer, which has around 10,000 employees and more than $1 billion in sales, and that there was a foreseeable risk of harm as the company kept its employee information unencrypted. The case comes as more appeals courts are ruling in favor of employees in litigation showdowns over personal information swiped by hackers. Last year, the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit found a former biopharmaceutical company employee had standing to bring a negligence class action against her old employer after a hacking group accessed its servers through a phishing attack in 2020, stealing a raft of personal information that the group later posted to the dark web. Get More Information “In an increasingly digitalized world, an employer’s duty to protect its employees’ sensitive information has significantly broadened,” Third Circuit Judge Joseph Greenaway wrote in Clemens v. ExecuPharm, adding that because the employee’s information was posted to the dark web, she faced a substantial risk of identify fraud that was more than hypothetical. These rulings come as ransomware attacks are becoming more sophisticated and frequent, said Becky Baker, a partner at Vinson & Elkins’ labor and employment group. “And the harm that is coming out of the hacking events is also getting worse just because of the development of technology and the way the criminals can use the information that they now have access to in ways that maybe they couldn’t 10 years ago,” she said. “This is making it more risky for employers who hold personal information and don’t have adequate safeguards.” She pointed to yet another case, this one from the Pennsylvania Supreme Court, where the University of Pittsburgh Medical Center’s status as a victim of cyber theft did not absolve it of its duty to ensure the protection the personal and financial information that its 62,000 current and former employees were required to provide as a condition of employment. “I think most employers and particularly large employers that are housing significant amounts of data can reasonably expect to be a target of these types of attacks,” Baker said. “The Supreme Court of Pennsylvania agreed with that and said, ‘Look, this is a relationship where you have a special responsibility. The employee is handing you this information so they can do their job as your employee. And so you have to take reasonable steps to protect it.” Andrew Gray, an associate with the employment law firm Littler Mendelson, said cases such as Ramirez indicate “a broader trend of individuals taking charge of their personal information,” empowered by a wave of state privacy laws that put the onus on companies to notify individuals affected by data breaches. While there isn’t a generally accepted definition for what constitutes reasonable cybersecurity measures, there are plenty of steps an employer can take. That will make it tougher for employers to deny requests than it was in the past. But the ruling doesn't define what would meet the definition of substantial cost. The U.S. Supreme Court’s recent ruling reviving the debate on religious accommodations in the workplace sent a glaring message to employers: They had better have a good reason for denying an employee’s request. But what constitutes a good reason? Experts say the ruling makes that harder to determine, though it does set the bar higher for employers to show that an accommodation would be an “undue hardship.” The high court on June 29 sided with Gerald Groff, an evangelical Christian mail carrier who claimed the postal service discriminated against him by disciplining him when he refused to deliver packages on Sundays. While the justices declined to rule on the merits of his claims, they overturned an appeals court’s dismissal of the case that found Groff’s objection to Sunday work “imposed on his coworkers, disrupted the workplace and workflow, and diminished employee morale.” Since 1977, courts have hewed to the standard set in Trans World Airlines, Inc. v. Hardison that defines an undue hardship as anything that would require an employer to “bear more than a di minimis cost.” Berkeley Law Dean Erwin Chemerinsky said the di minimis standard “made it very difficult for employees to be able to prevail, so it led to some litigation, but not much.” That could be about to change. In a unanimous opinion, Justice Samuel Alito wrote an employer now must show “that the burden of granting an accommodation would result in substantial increased costs in relation to the conduct of its particular business.” Chemerinsky said this heightened burden “dramatically changes the legal standard” for when an employer can deny a religious accommodation. “It used to be from 1977 until the end of June that an employer would not have to bear more than a minimal cost to accommodate an employees’ religious beliefs. Now an employer would have to do it unless it poses a substantial cost,” Chemerinsky said, adding that the ruling “very much favors employees making requests for religious accommodations.” Event Women, Influence & Power in Law Awards (WIPLA) 2023 Women, Influence & Power in Law Awards honors women lawyers who have made a remarkable difference in the legal profession. Get More Information The decision also undoes decades of legal precedent, said Debbie Kaminer a law professor at Baruch College at the City University of New York. “It totally changed the law and pretended it didn’t. Undue hardship has always meant de minimis. No one knows what ‘substantial cost’ means; no one has a clue.” While the ruling largely flew under the radar, overshadowed by the Supreme Court’s monumental decisions on affirmative action and student loan forgiveness, Kaminer said the Groff decision will have an outsized impact in the workplace. “This is a case that is going to be have enormous impact because it affects every workplace with more than 15 employees,” she said. “It’s a huge, huge number.” The court’s opinion gives employers little to go on when trying to assess substantial costs to their businesses. Alioto said the issue will have to be decided by the courts, and each case will be “context-specific.” He wrote, “[C]ourts should resolve whether a hardship would be substantial in the context of an employer’s business in the commonsense manner that it would use in applying any such test.” Chemerinsky said this ambiguity will likely lead to a spike in religious accommodation requests, and more litigation for employers. “Justice Alito’s opinion doesn’t offer a standard for a substantial cost—that in itself is an invitation for requests and litigation,” he said. “I think it’s going to lead to a great deal of litigation and will take a lot of time to clarify the standard.” Employers long have looked to the Equal Employment Opportunity Commission for guidance on whether to grant an employee’s request for religious accommodation. The Supreme Court’s ruling declines to adopt the EEOC’s past interpretations of undue hardship, though it does say it may prompt “little to no change” in the agency’s guidance. A spokesman for the agency said it is in the process of updating that guidance. The company raised nearly $200 million in December, an infusion that rekindled growth. The funding round was at a valuation of $7.4 billion. In-house… What You Need to Know Snyk's legal chief and legal ops chief got the ax in last fall's retrenchment. The company raised nearly $200 million in December, an infusion that rekindled growth. The funding round was at a valuation of $7.4 billion. In-house veteran David Morris joined cybersecurity platform Snyk as general counsel as it continues to rebuild its legal team after a wave of layoffs last year that included its chief legal officer and head of legal operations. Morris shared the news on LinkedIn. “Since 2015, Snyk has led the way for developer security to make the digital world a safer place. I’m proud to take part in their mission to help organizations worldwide develop applications securely,” he wrote. He most recently was general counsel at online-ticketing platform Vivid Seats, which he departed in December. Before that, he spent 13 years as associate general counsel at Tripadvisor. Morris is among a string of executive hires recently announced by Snyk. Also coming aboard are Als Myke Lyons as chief information security officer, Jonaki Egenolf as chief marketing officer and Michael Durso as senior vice president of sales. In a blog post, CEO Peter McKay said the hires will help Snyk further its mission of helping enterprises strengthen their developer security. “Jonaki, Myke, David and Michael each bring an incredibly valuable point of view and the right relevant experience to best position us for growing success as we continue to lead the developer security category we invented,” McKay said. “As DevSecOps becomes increasingly mainstream, together we look forward to helping more global brands shift away from a legacy cybersecurity mindset and fully embrace this cultural revolution,” McKay said. The hires follow a tumultuous year for Snyk, which cut 14% of its global workforce last October in a round of restructuring that McKay said was necessary for the company to operate more efficiently in the face of global economic headwinds. Caught in the layoffs were CLO Karyn Smith, who joined Snyk in January 2022 after seven years as legal chief at San Francisco-based Twilio, and Susan Packal, who stepped down as Twilio’s senior director of legal operations and chief of staff in May 2022 to become vice president of legal operations at Snyk. According to LinkedIn, Smith has not taken a new post while Packal this month become the head of global legal operations for the software firm Atlassian. Snyk shifted back into growth mode after it closed in December on a $196 million Series G funding round at a valuation of $7.4 billion. The round was led by Qatar’s sovereign wealth fund Qatar Investment Authority. Snyk has since added to its legal team, hiring Krista Matthews as vice president of commercial legal in February and Kathryn “Kate” Helin as privacy lead counsel in April. Legal operations specialist Katie Corso joined in March, along with lead counsel Lauren Wilk. On LinkedIn, Morris said a few more additions to the team will be coming soon. “One of the many reasons that I was so enthusiastic about the General Counsel role at Snyk was the opportunity to build a diverse, global team of well rounded legal ‘athletes,’ who are both responsive to a fast moving, growing organization as well as true partners to the business with deep enterprise tech knowledge,” Morris said in an email to Law.com. “As we continue to build the Snyk team and our legal function further matures, I’m personally committed to identifying diverse, passionate candidates who care deeply about building Snyk’s business through a deep understanding of the company’s mission and cybersecurity solutions,” Morris said. He said he’s embraced team-building throughout his career, including at Tripadvisor, where he was the company’s first legal hire in 2008. When he left in 2021, it was publicly traded and had 4,000 employees. Snyk also announced a series of business moves in recent months, including buying the application security management firm Enso Security for more than $50 million. Cooley, which advised Snyk on the last two of its 13 funding rounds, worked on the deal. In April, Snyk launched a series of enhancements to its developer security platform intended to help other businesses create a secure software supply chain. The company made CNBC’s Disruptor 50 List this year, and also was favorably recognized by consulting firms Gartner and Forrester. Morris said Snyk is adding to its legal ranks on the heels of these milestones. “We are adding multiple people to the legal team over the next few months, and expect further growth in the future,” he said. title: Investigating While Under Investigation: Protecting Privilege and Confidentiality in Internal Investigations
description: When corporate misconduct comes to light, corporations often must conduct an internal investigation to effectively assess potential liability, craft remediation, and engage with regulatory scrutiny. Companies rely on investigative findings in…
preview:
When corporate misconduct comes to light, corporations often must conduct an internal investigation to effectively assess potential liability, craft remediation, and engage with regulatory scrutiny.  Companies rely on investigative findings in advocating for DOJ, SEC, and other regulators to forgo charges or enforcement.

Cooperating with regulators, however, requires caution.  Government investigators increasingly rely on the legwork of corporate investigations.  But when company investigators fail to maintain sufficient independence, the company risks becoming embroiled in criminal litigation involving individual wrongdoers, waiving attorney-client privilege and work-product protections, publicly exposing confidential details of its investigation, and, in extreme circumstances, potentially being labelled a member of the government’s prosecution team subject to expansive disclosures.  Corporate counsel must remain vigilant of these risks and maintain appropriate guardrails to protect against them.

title: Hackers Can Steal Encryption Keys From a Distance Using Video
description: On June 13, security researchers disclosed their findings that encryption keys for wireless devices are vulnerable to theft. This research found that cameras in cellular phones or commercial surveillance systems can be used to record power light…
preview:
On June 13, security researchers disclosed their findings that encryption keys for wireless devices are vulnerable to theft. This research found that cameras in cellular phones or commercial surveillance systems can be used to record power light emitting diodes (LEDs) from up to 60 feet away from a device, thus capturing encryption keys.

This new weakness exploits two previously known side-channel attacks, a class of attacks measuring physical effects “leaking” from a device as it performs its operations. Companies should review their systems for this vulnerability, including smart card readers used for access or authentication. All industries are vulnerable to this exploitation; however, health care may be especially hard hit in the future due to the potential to expose electronic medical records. Defense contractors with sensitive information are also highly targeted and should review how this could impact their systems and networks. But the reality is that any secured physical area could be impacted by an attacker’s ability to physically break into buildings and facilities.

Google's long-held dominance in digital advertising is threatened by intensifying legal woes, including a fresh spate of lawsuits that seek to break up its lucrative advertising business. The Mountain View, California-based company is girding for battle on multiple fronts, as the U.S. Department of Justice, major news publishers and 17 state attorneys general have coalesced around allegations that its stranglehold on the technology behind digital advertising represents an abusive monopoly and allows it to undercut rivals and siphon away advertising dollars from website publishers. The advertising battle is the latest flash point in a long-standing assault on the tech giant by regulators alleging it has illegally used its massive scale to gain competitive advantage. Among the highest-stakes legal battles is a 2020 Department of Justice lawsuit alleging Google gained an illegal lock on the internet search business. The case is scheduled for trial later this year. All the scrutiny could make Google reluctant to strike back at competitive threats as aggressively as it otherwise would have, legal scholars and tech analysts say. Similarly, it could distract leadership, putting it a step behind rivals in the quest to innovate. That's what happened to Microsoft after the federal government in the late 1990s brought its landmark antitrust case against the company alleging it abused its stronghold on the personal computer operating system market, said John Lopatka, an antitrust scholar and Penn State law professor. Microsoft lost the case, but the biggest loss was a loss of focus, Lopatka said. Bill Gates later acknowledged that defending the company diverted his attention from what the company should have been working on at the time—an operating system for mobile phones. "The biggest loss for Microsoft wasn't the effect of the judgment; it was that they weren't paying attention to the marketplace and the technology," Lopatka said. The latest potential distraction is the escalating ad-tech litigation claiming Google controls every layer of the process between advertisers and the webpages that display their ads, beginning with the ad servers that inventory the available space for digital ads, and the auctions through which brands compete over that space. When someone opens a webpage, the ad server flags when a slot is available and puts it up for sale, soliciting bids on ad exchanges where brands compete to win the ability to display their ad to users. Advertisers also use buying tools to specify what demographics they want to target and to set the price they are willing to pay for an ad slot. In a lawsuit filed last month, newspaper publisher Gannett contends that Google bought rather than built its way into ad-tech supremacy, starting with its 2008 purchase of leading ad server DoubleClick. The acquisition led to subsequent purchases of other ad server firms, allowing Google to control the tool publishers use to manage their inventory of available slots for digital ads. Google controls 90% of the publisher-ad-server market via its acquisition of DoubleClick, and the auction side through its ad exchange AdX, which controls 60% of the exchange market. Lopatka said the complexity of the ad market will factor into Google's defense. "It's usually pretty clear when an action could have some benefits for consumers and when it isn't really going to have a benefit," he said. "But this is a complicated market and the technology is complicated. The question is if there is some benefit Google can point to. That's what they're going to have to show." Lopatka said Google will also argue that the government has too narrowly defined the markets at issue. "They're going to begin by saying, 'We don't have any monopoly power. You can't define a market for publisher ad servers; it's broader than that,'" he said. Google is also fending off an antitrust probe from across the Atlantic, as the European Commission informed the tech giant in June that it believes it abused its market position by favoring its own ad-tech services. "Google is present at almost all levels of the so-called adtech supply chain," Europe's antitrust chief Margrethe Vestager said in a statement. "Our preliminary concern is that Google may have used its market position to favor its own intermediation services." The commission said past behavioral remedies have been ineffective and that "only the mandatory divestment by Google of part of its services would address its competition concerns." title: Suits Flooding Courts Seize on Decades-Old Wiretapping Laws to Allege Data Breaches
preview:
Data privacy class actions focused on "session replay" software and other ad tech tools that track how users interact with websites are piling up by the day, unabated by a spate of rulings favoring defendants.

Legal observers say the hitch in those defendant victories is that they have largely been on procedural or statute-of-limitation grounds, keeping alive plaintiffs' attorneys hopes that their legal strategy eventually will strike gold.

searchText: Suits Flooding Courts Seize on Decades-Old Wiretapping Laws to Allege Data Breaches  Data privacy class actions focused on "session replay" software and other ad tech tools that track how users interact with websites are piling up by the day, unabated by a spate of rulings favoring defendants. Legal observers say the hitch in those defendant victories is that they have largely been on procedural or statute-of-limitation grounds, keeping alive plaintiffs' attorneys hopes that their legal strategy eventually will strike gold. The plaintiff attorneys are are putting decades-old state wiretap statutes to new use to go after a swath of retailers, insurers, airlines, and other businesses with public-facing websites, arguing that session replay tools—which track consumers' mouse movements, keystrokes, clicks and page visits—constitute illegal wiretapping or eavesdropping. The California Invasion of Privacy Act, which dates back to 1967, has been particularly popular with plaintiff attorneys, but they also have brought cases in Pennsylvania, Florida, Maryland, Illinois and Missouri. Lothar Determann, author of "Determann's Field Guide to Privacy Law," calls the complaints largely bogus, arguing that session replay software doesn't fit the definition of a wiretap, as there is no third-party interception of a communication. "Wiretap is intercepting communications between two parties. This is what it literally means. In these session replay cases, there isn't a third party who is intercepting something," said Determann, who teaches e-commerce law and data privacy law at Berkeley Law, the University of San Francisco Law School and Free University of Berlin. "This is the website operator trying to understand how users use their website to make their communication more effective. I do not think this consists of an an illegal wiretap illegal eavesdropping or illegal recording and I find these lawsuits and threats baseless, meritless and misrepresenting the communication situation and technology and how it works." Courts already have tossed dozens of privacy complaints at the pleading stage on jurisdictional or standing grounds—such as a failure to show plaintiffs actually were harmed by the practice. In another session replay ruling, a district court dismissed a session replay case against the wellness and weigh-loss company Noom, finding it can't be held liable under the California Invasion of Privacy Act for recording communications on its own website. But two recent appellate rulings have given plaintiffs' attorneys renewed confidence in their theories. Last May, the Ninth Circuit reversed a district court's dismissal of a session replay lawsuit, holding that a life insurance company failed to get prior consent from a prospective customer before using a session replay tool called ActiveProspect to record health information he entered into an online questionnaire. That he clicked "view my quote" after filling out the questionnaire and retroactively consented to the company's privacy was not enough, the panel found. The case ended up back before another district judge, who recently dismissed it as barred by CIPA's one-year statute of limitations. In another case, the Third Circuit last August overturned a district judge and revived a woman's claims that she was unlawfully surveilled by marketing platform NaviStone's session replay technology while browsing an online store for pet stairs. The court ruled that NaviStone had "intercepted" the woman's online activities in violation of Pennsylvania's Wiretapping and Electronic Surveillance Control Act. "There are areas of state law that remain untested, and the plaintiffs' bar has been emboldened in the last year or so by a couple of circuit opinions that directly address session replay," said Rebekah Guyon, a Greenberg Traurig shareholder. "Plaintiffs have argued that those decisions opened up potential ambiguity around when the use of session replay could be a wiretap." She added: "For session replay cases as a whole in 2023, we're on track to have more filed cases filed this year than last year, which was a record year for session replay cases nationwide." Plaintiffs have racked up victories in the district courts, as well. This month, U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer ruled against Prudential Financial, upholding privacy claims asserted by a group of consumers who argued that the company used marketing software from ActiveProspect that collected their information without consent while they sought life insurance quotes. District courts also have found that Nike and Lululemon aided and abetted wiretapping by using third-party session replay software. Litigator Michael Bahar, a partner at Eversheds Sutherland, said companies still face a "tremendous risk" from lawsuits based on CIPA and other state wiretapping laws. searchText: Climate Change Will Up Pressure on Tech Over Energy-Hungry Data Centers Data centers, the giant facilities that form the backbone of the internet, soon will fall under more scrutiny as climate risk disclosure rules and investor expectations put more pressure on tech to reduce its environmental footprint. Data centers, the giant facilities that form the backbone of the internet, soon will fall under more scrutiny as climate risk disclosure rules and investor expectations put more pressure on tech to reduce its environmental footprint. With the rise of social media, video streaming, self-driving vehicles and generative artificial intelligence tools, the amount of digital data being created, replicated and processed every year is escalating, and with it the global demand for storage. The market research firm International Data Corp. estimates that the "datasphere" will grow to 175 zettabytes by 2025, likening the world's entire data collection to a stack of DVDs that could circle the Earth 222 times. And the buildings that house the servers on which most of this data sits consume a great deal of energy, accounting for nearly 2% of the electricity use in the U.S., according to the U.S. Department of Energy. They also account for roughly 2% of worldwide greenhouse gas emissions and 3% of the world's electricity supply, twice as much as 10 years ago, according to the Association of Computing Machinery. Data centers also require a tremendous amount of water. A Virginia Tech study says data centers consume water both directly to prevent overheating and indirectly to generate electricity, drawing from 90% of U.S. watersheds. Making matters worse, they disproportionately rely on increasingly scarce water supplies. The researchers noted that "many of the water-sheds in the Western U.S. exhibit high levels of water stress, which is exacerbated by data centers direct and indirect water demands." Communities in both Europe and the western United States have pushed back on new data center construction, even those that purport to use renewable energy. In 2021, a Dutch farming community challenged Meta's plans to build a hyper-scale data center with more than 5,000 servers, culminating in the social media giant's pulling the plug last year. Environmental advocacy groups have also expressed concern over Google's efforts to expand its data center footprint in The Dalles, Oregon. "We have set goals to replenish more water than we consume by 2030 and to support water security in communities where we operate," the company said in its latest 10-K filing with the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission. "We are focused on three areas: enhancing our stewardship of water resources across Google offices and data centers; replenishing our water use and improving watershed health and ecosystems in water-stressed communities; and sharing technology and tools that help everyone predict, prevent, and recover from water stress," the company said. This all comes at a time when regulators, shareholders and consumers are demanding more action from the tech sector on climate change. Beginning in 2024, close to 10,000 American companies with more than $162 million (€150 million) in annual revenue that operate in Europe will have to report how their businesses affect the environment and verify their sustainability efforts under the EU's new climate sustainability reporting directive. The SEC also has a rule in the works that will require companies to detail climate-related risks and emissions data, including any reduction plans or targets. Former SEC Assistant Director Emily Pierce, now an associate general counsel and chief global policy officer at Persefoni, a software firm that helps companies manage climate disclosure requirements, said the pressure will be ramping up. "That pressure is both from existing market forces, as well as market forces that will be accelerated by upcoming regulatory expectations or requirements," she said. "It's sort of like a little infinity loop. You get all this market pressure growing, and now the regulators are stepping in to get more consistent, reliable, comparable disclosures about emissions information, which is just going to further the market pressures on companies to manage their emissions better." Data centers, she said, will be one more crucial element of the broader fight to mitigate the effects of climate change. "There is a lot of energy use associated with data centers. It's going to be an important factor among many factors that a company has to consider when thinking about what data center to use," Pierce said. "Tech is such a fundamental part of our economy. It's one of those things that it has to happen, but can we find ways to do it in a more efficient way? And I think there's absolutely going to be both market pressure and regulatory pressure to try to find ways to do it differently." title: Cyberattacks Are Accelerating With AI's Help
description: Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential.
preview:
Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential.

At last month's RSA Conference, cybersecurity expert Mikko Hyppönen sounded the alarm that AI tools, long used to help bolster corporate security defenses, are now capable of doing real harm. "We are now actually starting to see attacks using large language models," he said.

searchText: Cyberattacks Are Accelerating With AI's Help Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential. Cybercriminals are supercharging their attacks with the help of large language models such as ChatGPT, and security experts warn that they've only scratched the surface of artificial intelligence's threat-acceleration potential. At last month's RSA Conference, cybersecurity expert Mikko Hyppönen sounded the alarm that AI tools, long used to help bolster corporate security defenses, are now capable of doing real harm. "We are now actually starting to see attacks using large language models," he said. In an interview with Information Security Media Group, Hyppönen recounted an email he received from a malware writer boasting that he'd created a "completely new virus" using OpenAI's GPT that can create computer code from instructions written in English. "It's the first malware we've ever seen which uses ChatGPT to rewrite its code," Hyppönen told Information Security's Matthew Schwartz. "It calls GPT to write the code for it, which means every time it's different, and it will be trivial to modify to write it in any other language." Although ChatGPT can blacklist malicious users, Hyppönen said eventually developers might be able to create malware with their own LLMs built in. Though less sophisticated than malware created by human beings, LLMs have expanded the pool of would-be cybercriminals by enabling even novices to develop malicious code, some experts say. Sergey Shykevich, lead ChatGPT researcher at cybersecurity company Check Point, said he's seen hackers bragging in dark web forums about creating malware and ransomware using ChatGPT. "What's important is that ChatGPT allows everyone, even those with zero experience in coding, to develop that skill. Maybe in six months or something, it will be able to also create completely sophisticated malware that we've never before seen," he said. "Now, it mostly allows people who are not software developers to create malware. That makes the threat higher because at the end of the day there will be more malware criminals in the wild and more malware criminals will try and attack corporations." LLMs also can streamline phishing attacks by composing convincing emails impersonating trusted institutions such as a bank or the Internal Revenue Service. "Take, for example, Russian cybercriminals, because most of them don't speak English or their English levels are extremely low. Up until now they used what are called external vendors. They went to graduates of English literature at Russian colleges who wrote them phishing emails in English," Shykevich said. "Now ChatGPT allows them to make their operations much more cost-effective. They just write in ChatGPT, or other similar tools, 'please write an email that looks like it comes from Chase Bank or any other bank' and asks the recipient to provide their bank account information or Social Security number. The chatbot can then generate the email in perfect English," he said. Scott Giordano, general counsel of data loss protection company Spirion, said AI's greatest strength is its ability to quickly pore over mountains of code to find and exploit weaknesses in a company's network before a defender can fix it. "That's the sharpest point that AI has right now. If you're a bad guy and you're not using ChatGPT or other LLMs to go and find vulnerabilities, you're probably not doing your job as a bad guy," Giordano said. "And the converse is true for the good guys. This is an arms race and both sides need to understand how to use this technology for their side," he said. The bad guys, Giordano said, currently have the advantage. "They only have to be right once. They only have to trick you once to start exploiting your network," he said. But companies can combat this by adding AI to their directory of enterprise risks, moving to a zero-trust architecture and training their employees to flag phishing scams or anything else that looks suspicious, Giordano said. title: Will the AI Boom Rewrite the Job Description for General Counsel?
description: The rise of AI hasn't changed the need for GCs to be generalists. But GCs do need to be well-versed on AI's capabilities, as well as its limitations. Legal departments may need to hire AI subject-matter experts, though they also will be relying on…
preview:
In-house experts say artificial intelligence will change the way in-house lawyers work, but GCs do not need to become AI experts. However, having basic AI knowledge and an AI expert on the team will become crucial.

Developing that basic expertise could become a challenge for many legal departments, in part because legal chiefs already have their plates full with other issues, and some are starting out with a low base of tech knowledge. A study of top in-house lawyers from FTI Consulting and software company Relativity last year found that only 33% of the respondents believed lawyers have adequate knowledge about technology.

title: Law Firm Partner Hourly Rates Rose Last Year at Biggest Clip in at Least a Decade
description: What You Need to Know LexisNexis CounselLink analyzed $52 billion in legal spending across 420,000 timekeepers and 1.4 million legal matters. The 50 largest law firms increased their market share to 47.3%. Alternative fee arrangements held steady at…
preview:

searchText: Ex-Uber Security Chief's Impending Sentencing Exposes Divide in Cybersecurity Community "I recognize the costs the case has had on so many—and I believe they all could have been avoided if I had acted differently back in 2016," Joe Sullivan wrote in a letter to the court. A federal judge on Thursday will sentence former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for his role in covering up a 2016 data breach that exposed the personal information of 57 million riders and drivers. His October 2022 conviction, considered the first criminal case brought against a tech executive over a data breach, has divided the cybersecurity community, where Sullivan was a highly respected fixture. Some security experts decry Sullivan's decision to pay two hackers $100,000 through a recently created Uber bug bounty program as a selfish act designed to protect his own reputation and avoid more scrutiny from regulators. Uber already was under investigation by the Federal Trade Commission over lax data security practices that resulted in a similar cyberattack two years earlier. Just 10 days before the hackers contacted him by email to demand a six-figure payment, Sullivan gave a lengthy deposition to the FTC on Uber's progress in tightening security after the 2014 breach. But Sullivan also has a multitude of supporters, many of them security chiefs themselves, who have argued that Sullivan's actions are fairly commonplace, and that a prison sentence would only serve to scare people away from a profession that often requires its leaders to make difficult judgment calls. "We have been closely following Joe Sullivan's trial, the resulting verdict, and the upcoming sentencing. While the trial and the verdict have already had a considerable (and sometimes troubling) impact on our industry, we are particularly concerned about Joe's sentence in this case," says a letter filed by 63 current and former security chiefs. "The CISO job is already hard enough that many professionals do not choose it as their career path, or leave these positions for other professional roles. We are concerned that a prison sentence for Joe will further discourage people from taking these necessary jobs. With the threat of increasing liability, we already see candidates shying away from the role." But given the unique facts of the case, their fears of other security chiefs getting prosecuted might be overblown. Peter Swire, a professor of law and ethics at the Georgia Institute of Technology's Scheller College of Business, said Sullivan's sworn testimony before the FTC about Uber's efforts to beef up security after the 2014 breach and his failure to alert the commission after learning about the much larger breach just days after giving that testimony, were aggravating factors that led to his prosecution. "This new breach was enormous. It was far larger than the previous Uber breach and Uber clearly knew by that time that it was under a legal obligation to report a data breach," he said. "Security chiefs ought to know already that they shouldn't submit sworn testimony that is untrue or seriously misleading. Here we have a combination of a large breach, clear notice to the company of the government's concerns about breaches and a lack of accuracy in the sworn testimony." Swire, a cyberlaw scholar who advised presidents Clinton and Obama on privacy and technology, also emphasized that the breach was not disclosed to the FTC until 2017, when new CEO Dara Khosrowshahi took over the company and fired Sullivan. "A year delay in reporting a massive data breach is egregious behavior," Swire said. Sullivan faces up to eight years in prison. Prosecutors favor a sentence of 15 months, while Sullivan's defense team has asked for leniency, arguing that probation would be appropriate "to promote respect for the law, reflect the seriousness of the offense, and afford adequate deterrence." Sullivan, for his part, says he deeply regrets how he handled things. In a letter to U.S. District Judge William Orrick, Sullivan said not a day has gone by since he was fired in 2017 that he hasn't agonized over the decisions that led up to his prosecution. "I recognize the costs the case has had on so many—and I believe they all could have been avoided if I had acted differently back in 2016," Sullivan wrote. Sullivan said he should have "seen to it that authorities were notified of the incident. preview:

A string of companies, including Samsung, Verizon and JPMorgan Chase, has restricted or barred the use of AI chat bots such as ChatGPT and Google's Bard on work devices, fearing employees might inadvertently share source code or business secrets with these platforms.

It would be like banning email, or Google search, or a reticence to using the Google enterprise suite of products," said Nithya Das, former chie Worries about generative artificial intelligence tools and chatbots show no sign of abating, including the potential for inadvertent leaks of confidential information. A string of companies, including Samsung, Verizon and JPMorgan Chase, has restricted or barred the use of AI chat bots such as ChatGPT and Google's Bard on work devices, fearing employees might inadvertently share source code or business secrets with these platforms. "I think it's shortsighted," said Nithya Das, former chief operating officer and chief legal officer at Olo, a software company that sells online ordering and delivery programs to restaurants. "You can ban it on company equipment but you can't ban it on other devices that employees might be using. It would be like banning email, or Google search, or a reticence to using the Google enterprise suite of products. These are tools that are going to become part of the way people work." Das said she uses ChatGPT for routine queries and contract language, and the results have been a huge time-saver. "I just used it to give me a first draft of some terms of service for a generative AI tool. It wasn't perfect, but it was a good starting point. It saved me a few hours of work and from having to start from scratch," she said. "A lot of colleagues use it for things like that—terms of service, nondisclosure agreements, privacy policies, and using it to give summaries of routine concepts they want to explain to others." Banning new technology is at best a temporary solution to a decadeslong problem around data leaks and intellectual property protection, experts said, especially when employees are already either experimenting with generative AI applications on their own time, or are using them for substantive work. "In a sense, the horse is already somewhat out of the barn. The odds are that employees already are making use of these latest AI tools and have failed to consider the enormous risks involved," said global AI expert and Forbes columnist Lance Eliot. "One thing that is unlikely to work and that can entirely backfire consists of outright banning the use of generative AI. Firms that do this are forsaking the benefits of generative AI. They are also hamstringing the employees that want to save the company time and money by leveraging generative AI. A ban simply says that the top leaders, including the general counsel, are out of touch." Tim Pham, general counsel of Patented.ai, said legal chiefs have long grappled with how to safeguard trade secrets and company knowledge. "I think a lot of the tech companies, in my view, are like the Black Pearl in 'Pirates of the Caribbean,'" Pham said. "Those wooden ships always have leaks. In terms of IP, there's a front door through which you should normally send IP outside, but there are always back doors and side doors; employees leaving, or sending out emails by mistake." AI tools, he said, "have opened up a new category of leaks. And I think the problem is huge." Pham, formerly deputy general counsel and head of IP at Twitter and head of patent prosecution at Google, said that even with training and guidance from security teams, employees can still struggle with identifying and distinguishing confidential company information. "At least with one of the companies I worked at, there was a lot of training and we had a pretty robust InfoSec team. We said what you can and can't do with confidential information and we even labeled certain things as confidential," he said. "But at a tech company you're generating so many documents. And especially if the culture of the company is to share information as much as possible, it is extremely difficult for the average employee to know what is confidential information." Security software designed to prevent users from entering sensitive information and proprietary source code into chatbots offers one solution. Patented.ai created a plug-in called LLM Shield, named after the large language models that serve as the foundational technology behind AI chatbots, to recognize key words and warn users if they're about to inadvertently enter something confidential. "If you are a developer or sales or marketing person and you don't know what's confidential, this provides that co-pilot," Pham said. "It trains itself on all the information that you tell it is confidential. It sees that and can flag it for you." Pham said that for companies such software tools "may help move the risk needle to something that is more acceptable." He added, "I look at the risk needle in terms of IP leaks and sensitive information. The introduction of LLMs have just changed this. title: 'Are You Respecting Their Dignity?': Employee-Surveillance Trend Deeply Splits Employers
description: What You Need to Know More than 500 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals weighed in on employee monitories in a new Littler Mendelson survey. The survey found 45% of companies were using employee surveillance and 41% were not and…
preview:
From keystroke loggers to screenshot-capturing software and webcam eye-trackers, employee-monitoring tools have been on the rise since the COVID-19 pandemic drove white collar workers out of their cubicles and into home offices.

But a new survey from Littler Mendelson found a deep divide among employers on whether the technologies are a good idea. The survey of 515 in-house lawyers, C-suite executives and HR professionals in the U.S. found 45% of companies are using them, but 41% are not and aren’t considering doing so. Twelve percent are considering adoption, and 1% have made the decision to adopt but haven’t yet done so.

title: What Executives Should Take From Ex-Uber Security Chief Joe Sullivan's Sentence
description: "What everyone in the industry wants to understand is, where is the line, and how can we be sure we're not crossing it?" said Ed McAndrew, a former cybercrime prosecutor.
preview:
Even as he spared ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan a prison sentence for concealing a massive data breach from authorities, a federal judge last week delivered a stern warning to the security industry.

"If I had a similar case tomorrow, even if the defendant had the character of Pope Francis, they would be in custody," U.S. District Judge William Orrick said.

searchText: What Executives Should Take From Ex-Uber Security Chief Joe Sullivan's Sentence "What everyone in the industry wants to understand is, where is the line, and how can we be sure we're not crossing it?" said Ed McAndrew, a former cybercrime prosecutor. Even as he spared ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan a prison sentence for concealing a massive data breach from authorities, a federal judge last week delivered a stern warning to the security industry. "If I had a similar case tomorrow, even if the defendant had the character of Pope Francis, they would be in custody," U.S. District Judge William Orrick said. While Sullivan's three-year probation sentence may have been a relief for security chiefs anxious about the outcome of his case, it is little consolation at a time when cyberattacks are increasing, and companies are being squeezed by regulators and law enforcement to report data breaches within short timeframes. "In some ways, Mr. Sullivan benefited from being first," said former cybercrime prosecutor Ed McAndrew, now a partner at BakerHostetler. "If there was another case, the outcome could be very different." Sullivan was convicted of both obstructing the Federal Trade Commission's ongoing investigation into Uber's security practices and misprision of a felony, a rare charge that involves taking active steps to conceal a crime. "I've seen hundreds of cases. I can count on one hand the number of times I even heard the words 'misprision of a felony.' That is seldom-used charge." McAndrew said. "It's a very indirect route to prosecuting failure to disclose a cyberattack. It gave everyone pause. This shows prosecutors have a lot of discretion in what conduct they choose to prosecute." While there were unique elements that differentiated Uber's situation from an everyday incident response, McAndrew said some of the facts of the case, like paying a ransom to hackers to try to secure stolen data, are now fairly commonplace, and cyber insurance policies even provide coverage for extortion payments. "What everyone in the industry wants to understand is, where is the line, and how can we be sure we're not crossing it?" He added that a data breach disclosure often isn't the end of the matter but just the beginning of a new phase of investigation and potential lawsuits over a company's cyber-incident response. "The noncustodial sentence is cold comfort to anyone who faces these types of choices on a daily basis," McAndrew said. Regulators are also demanding more information from companies on their security programs, and bearing down on those who aren't transparent enough. "We've observed several regulatory mandates, both at the state and federal level, with tight notification deadlines in the event of an incident, which indicate the move toward increased transparency," said Devon Ackerman, who was an FBI agent from 2018 to 2016. "This increased scrutiny was happening even during my time as a special agent with the FBI and I continue to see it today." There's also the heightened risk of civil litigation and regulatory penalties for failing to disclose security vulnerabilities. Deputy Attorney General Lisa Monaco has said the Justice Department will target federal contractors that misrepresent their cybersecurity practices with False Claims Act litigation. "That would be another potential line of liability for executives, not to mention shareholder derivative actions and securities actions you'll see in a civil context," said Ed McNicholas, co-leader of Ropes & Gray's data, privacy and cybersecurity practice. And the SEC, with strict data-breach-reporting rules for public companies that are expected to be finalized this year, may be a tougher enforcer than even the DOJ, McNicholas said. "All in all, there's a plethora of potential avenues for executives to be held personally liable both on civil and criminal grounds for failing to report a data breach; the effect of which will make executives much more likely to err on the side of reporting a data breach earlier." McNicholas said that while civil actions, not necessarily criminal charges, will be the primary driver of enforcement against executives, security chiefs will still be tested on how to best to handle data-breach reporting. "I think a security chief will be put in a much more difficult circumstance in terms of not wanting to disclose a vulnerability in their company but needing to comply with the law," he said. "It is, and will remain, a balancing act." It's been seven years since the 2016 hack that led to the DOJ's case against Sullivan, and cyberthreats have only grown in frequency and complexity since. title: How to Stay on Top of Cybersecurity Disclosures as SEC Ramps Up Enforcement
description: It is no secret among public companies and their counsel that the US Securities and Exchange Commission has steadily adopted a more aggressive stance on cybersecurity controls and disclosure and incident response recordkeeping. SEC Senior Counsel…
preview:
It is no secret among public companies and their counsel that the US Securities and Exchange Commission has steadily adopted a more aggressive stance on cybersecurity controls and disclosure and incident response recordkeeping. SEC Senior Counsel Arsen Ablaev recently highlighted the Commission’s cybersecurity priorities at the annual Incident Response Forum Masterclass. SEC Chair Gary Gensler also emphasized risks in cyber and information security in the March 29 budget hearing with the House Appropriations Committee, and endorsed U.S. President Joe Biden’s request to earmark a record $2.4 billion in funding for the regulator in 2024. Last month saw yet another example of the SEC’s mounting focus on cyber disclosures as an enforcement priority with the announcement that cloud computing company Blackbaud agreed to pay a $3-million civil penalty to settle administrative charges for alleged “materially misleading disclosures” about a 2020 ransomware attack.

As we foreshadowed in our 2023 U.S. Cybersecurity and Data Privacy Outlook and Review, the increase in SEC enforcement resources (e.g., doubling the size of its Crypto Assets and Cyber Unit Ablaev sits in), in combination with the promulgation of cybersecurity risk management, strategy, governance, and incident disclosure rules Ablaev confirmed will be finalized in coming months, signal that cybersecurity will continue to be an area of heightened enforcement activity for the SEC. In light of these developments, it is critical companies take stock of their cyber hygiene policies and incident response protocols, and not only manage cybersecurity risks and prevent attacks, but also respond to them with proper disclosures.

title: Cash Is King for Startups as Venture Capital Pulls Back
description: Startups face a more challenging fundraising environment and more scrutiny from investors. Founders used to hold the cards, but the tables have turned. Some observers say this is a healthier environment. The balance of power has shifted in the…
preview:

description: Experts warn that quantum computers are getting closer to being able to crack encryption, putting swaths of sensitive data at risk to digital miscreants as it flows across the internet.

searchText: Supercomputers Soon Will Crack Encryption. Is Your Company Ready? Experts warn that quantum computers are getting closer to being able to crack encryption, putting swaths of sensitive data at risk to digital miscreants as it flows across the internet. Experts warn that quantum computers are getting closer to being able to crack encryption, putting swaths of sensitive data at risk to digital miscreants as it flows across the internet. The Cloud Security Alliance's countdown to "Y2Q" clock will hit zero in 2030, the same year the U.S. Department of Homeland Security predicts that a quantum breakthrough will occur, posing a new threat to the means by which companies secure their customer data, business transactions and confidential communications. The upshot is catastrophic, and affects all data in transit. Everything from internal company emails and Slack messages to health and bank records are at stake, said Rebecca Krauthamer, founder and chief product officer at quantum cybersecurity software firm QuSecure. "Any time you're communicating with somebody else, 99% of the time that's vulnerable," she said. "Any time data is traveling over the internet is when it's at risk." ChatGPT, like any other application, is also at risk of attack. "ChatGPT, that's an application where you're sending and receiving data, so anything you put in ChatGPT is this kind of data that is quantum vulnerable as well." she said, adding that at a recent talk the CIA's chief technology officer likened the potential for breaches to a "potential quantum WikiLeaks." Krauthamer said the timeline for quantum computing is accelerating, citing IBM's ambitious plan for scaling quantum systems. The company says it expects to unveil a 4,158 qubit processor by 2025. Krauthamer said it takes about 4,000 qubits of computing power to break the equivalent of today's encryption. The United States, China, and other foreign governments are also pumping billions of dollars into quantum development. While it remains to be seen when quantum computers will come online, stewards of sensitive data should start preparing for a post-quantum world now, rather than wait for that day to come. Researchers have known about the looming quantum threat since the 1990s, when mathematician Peter Shor demonstrated that quantum computers could do the complex math required to break a widely used encryption method called RSA, named after inventors Ron Rivest, Adi Shamir and Leonard Adleman. RSA is an asymmetric cryptography algorithm, explained technologist Donna Dodson, former director of the National Cybersecurity Center of Excellence. "You have a public key and a private key, and they're mathematically related keys. One is used to lock the door, and the other to unlock the door. Public key cryptography is designed to authenticate who I am and who I claim to be. It's used to create a digital signature which says this message comes from me and nobody else and hasn't been altered since I signed it digitally." Quantum computers will enable digital miscreants to factor large numbers much easier than with classic computers, enabling them to access public and private keys and intercept data traveling between points. "This has been a known problem from a long time, but we've moved from theory more to practice," Dodson said. "A lot of public key infrastructure is based on RSA. That all falls and goes away and it ends up being a really big deal." Krauthamer said the most vulnerable data tends to have a longer shelf life, such as legal and financial records. "The people that have to get ahead of it are in heavily regulated industries," she said, such as health care, finance and insurance—fields where personal information needs to be protected for a number of years. Electronic health records, for example, must be kept private throughout a patient's entire life. Dodson said it's critical that these records be protected from alteration. Otherwise, she said, "you have both a confidentially and an integrity problem." For example, she said, "Let's say you use the RSA algorithm, which is a popular algorithm to sign something. But if the RSA algorithm breaks and somebody else can figure out my private key from my published public key they can reverse the math using a quantum computer. Then they can sign as 'Donna Dodson' all day long. They can put a document out there and say 'Donna Dodson signed this in 2023,' and it's now 2030 and I can't prove that I didn't." One type of attack called "harvest now, decrypt later," involves bad actors collecting encrypted data they can sit on and wait to decrypt at their leisure. Paul Fuegner, head of marketing at QuSecure, said there are a variety of criminal and nefarious actors interested in stealing and decrypting that data, including foreign nation states. title: CEO Favors Building Rapport With Regulators, Rather Than Waiting for Their Call
description: Checkr CEO Daniel Yanisse said his company reached out to regulators—over the objection of his outside counsel. He said it's important for founders to educate themselves on how their industry is regulated. He spoke on a Berkeley Law webinar on…
preview:
Companies generally try to avoid attracting the attention of regulators, especially when they’re in a heavily scrutinized industry. So when Daniel Yanisse, co-founder and CEO of the background-check platform Checkr, decided to ask for a meeting with the Federal Trade Commission, his outside counsel was less than thrilled.

“Our outside counsel took me aside and told me I was crazy to proactively go to regulators, because it’s a dangerous thing to do and businesses don’t do it. They come to you, and you don’t want to be on their radar,” he said. “Initially, she was not very excited about my idea to connect with the regulators and explain what we do to them.”

So when Daniel Yanisse, co-founder and CEO of the background-check platform Checkr, decided to ask for a meeting with the Federal Trade Commission, his outside counsel was less than thrilled. “Our outside counsel took me aside and told me I was crazy to proactively go to regulators, because it’s a dangerous thing to do and businesses don’t do it. They come to you, and you don’t want to be on their radar,” he said. “Initially, she was not very excited about my idea to connect with the regulators and explain what we do to them.” This content has been archived. title: Automated Bias: What Employers Need to Know Before Deployment of AI/ML Technologies
description: The end of 2022 saw the announcement of major layoffs and workforce reductions in the United States, and more fluctuations in the labor market is expected in 2023. In an uncertain job market, employers continue to leverage technologies to streamline…
preview:
The end of 2022 saw the announcement of major layoffs and workforce reductions in the United States, and more fluctuations in the labor market is expected in 2023.  In an uncertain job market, employers continue to leverage technologies to streamline the recruitment, hiring and promotion processes—oftentimes these technologies are based on algorithmic models that quickly analyze vast data sets to rank candidates for hiring, or analyze job performance metrics to recommend promotions. Initial screening interviews may be conducted by AI-backed chatbots or by a fully automated video interview.

The use of artificial intelligence (AI) and machine learning (ML) tools—broadly defined to include any model that processes datasets to detect patterns or make recommendations—in the employment context is not new. What is new, however, is the increasing awareness that AI, ML and automated tools may perpetuate bias based on race, gender or other protected class status. A recent Equal Employment Opportunity Commission (EEOC) enforcement action against iTutorGroup, for example, alleges that the company discriminated against older candidates in violation of the Age Discrimination in Employment Act (ADEA) by automatically rejecting candidates on its hiring platform whose inputted date of birth was over a certain year.

searchText: 'It Was a Bunch of Spooked Wildebeests': How Tech GCs Survived the SVB Panic "This bank was very helpful to the tech community. Dealing with mainstream traditional banks for early stage startups is going to be way more burdensome," said Manuel Martinez-Herrera, GC of BetterCloud. Silicon Valley Bank's astonishingly rapid meltdown tested tech's top in-house lawyers, who flew into emergency response mode to help steer their companies through the chaos. Greg Raiten, co-founder of the general counsel network and platform TechGC, said the upheaval wrought by SVB's collapse within the tech in-house community was on par only with the COVID-19 pandemic. "We saw four or five waves just like this," he said, referring to the early days of the coronavirus. "First, the conversation was about closing offices, transitioning to remote work, impact to business models. Then came layoffs and PPP loans. Then came vaccine mandates and whether/how to go back to office. There were all these spikes of tough and unprecedented questions that the community was navigating together." Raiten said he started closely monitoring SVB on March 9, the day before federal banking regulators took it over, after seeing chatter about the institution's troubles on social media. By the next day, it was clear that circumstances had deteriorated, as murmurs about a possible bank run began to reverberate across Twitter and industry group chats. Raiten started reaching out to the tech and venture fund GCs that comprise TechGC's nearly 4,000 members. His business partner Kiran Lingam, a former GC at equity crowd-funder SeedInvest, rallied industry chief financial officers for an emergency clubhouse session on March 10 through TechGC's sister platform, The F Suite. Raiten said about 250 CFOs participated. Midway through the call, the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. announced it had taken control of the bank. Hungry for clarity and guidance, hundreds of finance and legal chiefs logged on over the weekend to share information. "It was partially group therapy—a lot of this is being with your peers, venting and sharing fear—but it was mostly just how do we figure this out. Everyone wanted to know what everyone else was doing and what they were hearing," Raiten said. TechGC global chair Danielle Sheer added: "When something happens, and nobody knows how to solve it, it's the general counsel that the question lands on. No matter the topic, no matter if it's truly legal in nature, when there's a problem that nobody knows how to solve, the general counsel is at the center of that storm." Even compared with the 2008 financial crisis, the panic that followed SVB's sudden demise was striking. "It was the eight craziest days of my professional career," said Sheer, the chief legal and compliance officer of the privacy software company Commvault. About 300 GCs from across the tech industry convened for a March 11 forum led by Sheer and Manuel Martinez-Herrera, GC of BetterCloud. "It was very hectic for the whole community," Martinez-Herrera said. "Payroll was No. 1 top-of-mind issue over [that] weekend for many members of the community. Then it morphed into, 'Are my customers going to be OK, I need bank accounts at other places, and are my clients going to think I'm in trouble because we were banking at SVB?'" Sheer said GCs worried about the legal ramifications around missing upcoming payroll deadlines, whether wires they'd initiated on Friday would go through, and whether they would have to furlough employees. "There were calls all weekend long for the companies in the greatest amount of pain and stress," Sheer said. "The community rallied to help with thinking through different options, and helping them get creative on inbound financing to keep them afloat." Templates were shared for bridge financing and short-term loan agreements. On March 12, the community hosted an employment webinar with partners from Wilson Sonsini Goodrich & Rosati. Sheer said her company had $1 million at SVB, but did most of its banking at JPMorgan Chase. "I wasn't worried that the lights were going to go out, but I was an SVB customer, so I was going through everything that the rest of the GCs were going through," she said. "And a lot of our GCs had all of their money in Silicon Valley Bank because their lead venture capitalist who gave them that money as an investment insisted that it be held at Silicon Valley Bank." Such was the situation at venture-backed retailer Camp, which had most of its cash in SVB. Sheer said it held a 50% off sale to raise emergency capital, but was left scrambling to find a new bank to process payments. "There was a lot of discussion about how fast it was to open accounts at banks like JPMorgan and Bank of America versus going to other regional banks," she said. Meanwhile, venture fund GCs were grappling with their own unique set of issues, including the regulatory implications of making bridge loans to portfolio companies. title: Litigation Involving Failed Banks: What Litigators and In-House Counsel Should Be Thinking About
description: Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in spectacular fashion earlier this month, with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation putting the bank into a federal receivership. This is the largest collapse of an FDIC-insured bank since the 2008 financial crisis…
preview:
Silicon Valley Bank collapsed in spectacular fashion earlier this month, with the Federal Deposit Insurance Corporation putting the bank into a federal receivership. This is the largest collapse of an FDIC-insured bank since the 2008 financial crisis and the second largest in history, with more than $200 billion in assets involved. FDIC receiverships for two other large banks, Silvergate Bank and Signature Bank, quickly followed. The holding companies for all three banks are expected to enter bankruptcy soon.

Unlike most other businesses, an operating bank cannot seek relief in bankruptcy. (A bank holding company may reorganize in bankruptcy, though.) Rather, an operating bank is subject to its own insolvency regime, namely the FDIC receivership.

searchText: SVB's Failure May Constrict Flow of Capital to Some Startups | Corporate Counsel “The most important thing is it seems like payroll is going to get hit on time, but there are still plenty of things to be concerned about,” said Healy Jones, vice president of financial strategy at the accounting firm Kruze Consulting. The government's move to protect uninsured deposits at Silicon Valley Bank was a relief for many company founders, but the bank's demise likely will leave a trail of challenges for startups, including making cash to fund growth a little harder to come by. "The most important thing is it seems like payroll is going to hit on time, but there are still plenty of things to be concerned about," said Healy Jones, vice president of financial strategy at startup-focused accounting firm Kruze Consulting, which counts nearly 800 venture-backed startups as clients. Though the government guaranteed all deposits at SVB, including those above the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp.'s $250,000 limit, it remains unclear whether companies will be able to draw on funds from venture debt loans. SVB touted itself as the first bank to offer such loans, which startups use to give themselves breathing room before they need more funding from investors. "Many startups were probably planning to use that money to extend their runway and finance operations," Jones said. "It's definitely messing up financing plans and strategy for some clients." The effects will be felt mostly by later stage startups, as 20%-30% of series B to series D companies have some venture debt or have paid a fee to make it available later, Jones said. He estimated that just 10% of those companies actually choose to draw on venture debt. Even so, given that SVB had more than half the market share of venture debt, whether those agreements are still good will be a big concern. "For sure, there will be some companies that it will hurt," he said. "It's important to be able to stretch your runway and grow your valuation, and this is a major partner that has disappeared from the ecosystem." Alex Meshkin, CEO of the tech-enabled medical laboratory FlowHealth, said SVB's collapse calls into question that entire financing tool for startups. "Who wants those loans? They're basically subprime business loans. You're talking about companies that have no credit profile, they're burning cash and are unlikely to raise the same type of capital because of interest rates." Meshkin, who started his company in 2014 without venture backing, said SVB's business model was a turnoff. "I met with SVB many times throughout my career, and I never understood why anyone would bank with them. It was basically social credit. 'If you're backed by Sequoia we're going to lend you money.' That's how it worked." Companies don't need a "friendly bank," he added. "I don't understand why a company with $10 million in funding want more risk than they already have. What do you need as a startup? A bank that you can put your money in that's safe. That's really all you need. SVB provided credit. Do we need credit? VCs have so much money, so why do startups need debt?" Even so, Meshkin said, "SVB was kind of a key aspect of the entire technology ecosystem— not just in Silicon Valley, but other aspiring startup markets as well. Let's just face it, it would do things for startups that very few things other banks would consider doing, because startups are very risky." Jay Jung, founder and managing partner for consulting firm Embarc Advisors, said the VCs' sponsorship of the startups mitigated the risk of the venture debt loans, in addition to making it easier for the companies to raise additional venture rounds. "There's no doubt they were lending to riskier companies, but they were looking at the VC investors when they invest in a startup as well," he said. In cases where a company runs into financial difficulties, Jung said he's seen SVB "work closely with the investors to make the best of the situation and try to salvage what they can. A lot of the people in the startup ecosystem appreciated SVB and liked working with them, and that's why a lot of people are sad to see them go away, at least temporarily." Jung said the venture debt loans that SVB provided aren't necessarily easy to get elsewhere, and alternatives like venture debt funds are more expensive. "It's kind of adding insult to injury because in the last 12 months, it's been a lot lot more difficult to raise equity. They're getting hit on both the equity side and debt side. Equity investors are investing less frequently and in smaller amounts," Jung said. Eighteen months ago, a company that raised $50 million in venture capital might be able to borrow $20 million from SVB, he said. The abrupt collapse of venture capital darling Silicon Valley Bank has exposed several glaring governance and risk management lapses, including that it parted ways with its chief risk officer in April 2022 and appears to have operated without a full-time replacement for nearly the remainder of the year. In its 2023 proxy statement filed March 3, SVB revealed that it initiated talks with chief risk officer Laura Izurieta to leave her job in early 2022. Pursuant to a separation agreement, Izurieta stepped down April 29, 2022, and moved into a "non-executive role focused on certain transition-related duties," which looked to be mostly an advisory role that included helping to find her replacement. The filing did not explain what drove the departure of Izurieta, who'd joined SVB in 2016 after 16 years at Capital One, where she'd risen to executive vice president. She did not respond to a request for comment by ALM. "Given the significance of the position of the Chief Risk Officer, it was important to the Company that the transition be facilitated in a manner that supported continuity and retention within the Risk organization as we searched for a new Chief," SVB wrote in its filing. The filing noted that the new CRO, Kim Olson, started on Dec. 27, 2022. Olson came from Japan-based Sumitomo Mitsui Banking Corp., where she was chief risk officer for the Americas. The CRO's job is to manage the company's risk-valuation process, said Charles Elson, a retired professor of corporate governance at the University of Delaware. "Someone should be there to steward the operation and evaluate how the group is functioning. Without that, it's like having an airplane without a pilot or a ship without a captain. It will move, but to what direction? That's the concern," he said. For a CRO role to sit unfilled for eight months isn't entirely unwonted. Clifford Rossi, a former chief risk officer for Citigroup's Consumer Lending Group, said his role also had been open for eight months before he joined Citigroup in 2007. But the position is so technically complex that such a vacancy can be problematic. "It makes it difficult that risk is being properly managed across the enterprise," Rossi said. Rossi, who is an executive-in-residence at the University of Maryland's Robert H. Smith School of Business, said he also was struck by the apparent lack of risk management expertise among board members on SVB's risk committee, to which the CRO directly reports. Rossi said SVB's board, which represents shareholders, had a responsibility to ensure that management wasn't engaging in risky activities that could lead to a situation as dire and unprecedented as the $42 billion bank run that caused the institution to fail last week. "You need people who can effectively challenge management on those decisions. I have personally been at those meetings at places like Countrywide, Citigroup, and Washington Mutual, where I was managing liaison," he said. At SVB, Rossi said, "few had any level of knowledge around risk management to push back and ask the right questions. If the board can't ask the right questions, how can they represent shareholders?" "He ostensibly has far greater substantive financial services experience than the committee comprised of a Napa vineyard owner, a retired healthcare CIO, a former U.S. Treasury undersecretary, venture capital partners and consulting firm heads," Barsky wrote in an analysis for Forbes.
