title: Everyone Talks About Their Law Firm’s ‘Culture,’ But Is It Possible to Measure It?
description: Cultural inventories have taken a new level of importance at law firms since shifting to remote work and facing recruitment pressures. Another factor driving the importance of culture is the growth of business administrative staff at firms. Legal…
preview:
Legal consultant Marcie Borgal Shunk became certified to use a proprietary tool to measure business culture a decade ago. But it wasn’t until last year that a law firm hired her to measure its culture using the Chicago-based cultural inventory tool developer Human Synergistics.

Cultural inventories have been more of a staple in Fortune 500 companies than the legal industry. In law firms, similar survey-based analyses had the limited purpose of assessing merger prospects or associate retention. But in 2022, Borgal Shunk had three clients—a global law firm, a midsize regional firm and a plaintiffs firm—ask her to assess what it was like for employees to work there.

searchText: SVB's Implosion Has Tech Companies Reeling. Here's What They Should Do "The board, the c-suite, are all going to be looking at the lawyers and my guess is this is a once in a lifetime crisis, so you want to make sure you have people you can count on on your legal team," said three-time general counsel Sterling Miller. The demise of startup financing cornerstone Silicon Valley Bank on Friday sent tech corporate executives and legal department chiefs scrambling to find other sources of financing and immediate solutions. With New York-based Signature Bank becoming the next financial institution to fall, the Federal Reserve moved swiftly over the weekend to stem the fallout. The Fed's measures, announced late Sunday, underscored the potential for the contagion to spread. In the days and weeks ahead, observers said, corporate leaders and in-house legal teams will be racing to identify financial and payroll risks. Some affected companies may want to extend payment terms with vendors, review insurance options as well as lean on outside counsel, they said, with general counsel immediately taking on a mountain of new responsibilities to help their companies regain footing in a shaky financial ecosystem. Companies that had the bulk of their funds deposited with SVB were in a particularly tight spot as the Federal Deposit Insurance Corp. (FDIC) only insures up to $250,000 in deposits, offering a receivership certificate for the rest. "This is an apocalyptic moment for companies," said Foster Sayers, general counsel for software company Pramata on Friday. He said Pramata was able to pull money out of the bank and transfer it to another institution where it had an account just in time. The wire cleared Thursday afternoon. "It was not a moment too soon," he said. Others weren't so fortunate. Streaming company Roku disclosed in an 8-k filing on Friday that 26%, or roughly $487 million of its cash, is currently in uninsured deposits at SVB. "At this time, the company does not know to what extent the company will be able to recover its cash on deposit at SVB." It added that it believes it will be able to meet its obligations with the rest of its $1.4 billion in cash. Biotech company Wave Life Sciences reported that it has $1.5 million in cash at SVB, which is $1.25 million over the FDIC-insured amount, while Oncorus, another biotech company, disclosed that SVB has approximately $10 million, or 23% of its total cash. It also has a standby letter of credit with SVB of about $3.4 million to meet its lease obligations for its Innovation Park offices. By Friday afternoon, SVB's collapse was official, and for many companies, meeting payroll immediately became a top concern, as it wasn't yet certain whether they would be able to access their uninsured deposits on Monday. "The best thing you can do to keep people focused on their work is not having them worried about if they are going to get paid," Sayers said, adding that companies should "figure out and immediately confront any spend that will be going out the door in the next weeks relative to payroll and figure out how they can adjust." He also said that companies left in dire financial straits should temporarily freeze any money going out the door. "You want to talk with anyone in finance, and everyone in procurement, and everyone in legal. Look at contracts to understand what is coming up for renewal and what invoices are coming in so you can put everything on freeze," he said. "A lot of tech companies don't want to deal with invoices and looking at payments, so you want to make sure you lock everything down and immediately communicate with your vendors, especially the ones whose payments are going to be impacted and say, 'I need extended payment terms.'" Sterling Miller, former General Counsel at Travelocity and now CEO and senior counsel at Hilgers Graben, said companies should also be looking for any alternative funding sources to fill their immediate cash needs. "Do I have a line of credit with anyone else? Can I call on private equity to bridge any temporary cash needs I might have? And on the flip side of that, I'm looking at what can I not pay. If I'm in conserve cash flow mode, what are the bills that have to be paid, like payroll, and what can I push out?" Miller also recommended that companies review their insurance policies to see what their coverage options are. "You never know about something that's covered until you pick up the phone and call your broker," he said, adding that companies should also review their contracts for force majeure clauses. "After the pandemic, a lot of companies changed how they define force majeure in ways that are broader than they were before. It's both a shield and a sword." preview:
A Dominion Voting Systems court filing on Wednesday argues that Fox Corp. chief legal and policy officer Viet Dinh should have prevented Fox News from airing false claims that Dominion’s voting machines were rigged.

The filing, a reply brief to Fox’s motion for summary judgment, accuses Dinh of shirking his legal obligations while hiding behind attorney-client privilege. It’s the latest effort by Denver-based Dominion to cast Dinh, a Harvard-educated lawyer and Kirkland & Ellis alum who’s held the legal reins since 2018, as a central figure in the network’s trashing of Dominion in the wake of Donald Trump’s defeat in the 2020 presidential election.

The filing, a reply brief to Fox’s motion for summary judgment, accuses Dinh of shirking his legal obligations while hiding behind attorney-client privilege. Dinh’s deposition, released late Tuesday, added to the mountain of evidence that Fox executives knew or at the very least suspected that claims about a stolen presidential election and rigged voting machines were false. A trove of documents from Dominion’s $1.6 billion defamation lawsuit against Fox News has yielded loads of juicy tidbits for the media to feast on, from Tucker Carlson’s texts expressing his secret hatred of Trump to internal group chats where prime-time stars raged at their Decision Desk colleagues. Dominion’s lawsuit, filed in 2021, accuses Fox News of pushing falsehoods about voter fraud to appease viewers. In his heavily redacted deposition, Dinh acknowledged that executives in the company’s chain of command are obligated to “prevent and correct known falsehoods,” but his deposition raises questions about his level of involvement in the network’s editorial decisions and his role in shielding the network from legal risk. “Generally speaking, a lawyer’s duty can only be to give the client the best legal advice possible, but a lawyer does not have a duty, nor usually even the power, to directly intervene,” Rutgers Law School professor Ronald Chen said in an email to Law.com. Chen said that whether Dinh “should have forcefully advised Fox executives not to broadcast the Dominion story depends a lot on what he knew and when he knew it, particularly regarding the arguably ulterior business motive in catering to some of Trump’s supporters.” In this circumstance, Chen added, a lawyer “might advise the client that the neutral reportage privilege might not be available if Fox is deemed to be serving its own interests and not engaging in neutral reportage of a controversial accusation.” In his deposition, Dinh was cagey in his response to questions from Dominion attorney Stephen Shackelford, a partner at Susman Godfrey, about vetting certain guests appearing on the network. At one point, Shackelford showed him an email from Meade Cooper, head of prime time programming, to senior executive producer Justin Wells saying that there were “obviously some legal concerns” with Rudy Giuliani’s appearance on Tucker Carlson’s show, along with worries that Giuliani “will veer off topic.” Wells responds that he “spoke to Viet right before” the interview, adding, “Nothing to worry about so far.” Dinh said he didn’t recall speaking with Wells. “I would expect that before I’m called, that there has been a consultation with Fox News legal,” Dinh said. “And most of the time, that gets resolved at that level.” Dominion alleges Fox has obscured Dinh’s specific role in discussions about Dominion coverage by refusing to log Dinh’s communications with in-house and outside counsel pertaining to Giuliani, Trump adviser and attorney Sidney Powell, Dominion and election-tech company Smartmatic, “which go directly to when Dinh knew Fox was providing a platform to spread Dominion lies, and thus had the opportunity (as someone in the chain of command for issues involving legal threats) to put a stop to it.” But legal experts say it isn’t so simple. “Generally speaking, a lawyer in a general counsel role only advises a client and does not have the authority to command anything,” Chen said. “A client corporation could give a corporate officer that authority, I suppose, but I have never heard of a general counsel for a media organization being given the authority to directly command the editorial process. “That would be generally inconsistent with the traditional notion that corporate officers should be walled off from editorial officers to prevent undue influence. Of course, that wall of separation does not seem to have been observed by Fox, given communications that have been released in which corporate executives seem to be part of the editorial decision whether to publish or broadcast or not.” Rob Chesnut, former general counsel and chief ethics officer at Airbnb, said it is the job of a legal chief to mitigate business and legal risk. searchText: Former Facebook Security Chief Sounds Off on the Case that Rocked the Cybersecurity World The government's recent prosecution of a former Uber executive for failing to disclose a data breach to law enforcement has company executives, and security chiefs in particular, anxious that they might be next. Companies of all sizes are under assault from sophisticated ransomware groups, and the government's recent prosecution of a former Uber executive for failing to disclose a data breach to law enforcement has company executives, and security chiefs in particular, anxious that they might be next. Alex Stamos, former chief security officer at Facebook and now director at the Stanford Internet Observatory, said Tuesday that the unprecedented criminal case against ex-Uber security chief Joe Sullivan, the first of its kind against a company executive, is problematic on several fronts. "Being breached, paying the attackers, and then not notifying law enforcement is something that happens dozens, or perhaps hundreds, of times a day in the United States," Stamos told Berkeley Law's Irene Liu at a webinar it hosted as part of its executive education program. "Because of the ransomware crisis we're living through, companies of all sizes are being targeted by ransomware groups, they're being breached, and if you're a CEO and one of these hackers comes to you and says, 'For $5 million this problem just goes way,' it is completely in their economic interest and shareholder interest to do so." Stamos said companies will sometimes notify law enforcement about data breaches, but in many cases they do not. Sullivan was found guilty of one count of obstructing the Federal Trade Commission ongoing investigation into Uber's security practices, and one count of misprision of felony for concealing the breach from authorities. Stamos, who is friends with Sullivan and took over his job as security chief at Facebook when Sullivan left for Uber, said the latter charge was the most unsettling. "Joe is being punished for something that actually happens all the time, and for which we don't have good legal guidance," he said. Stamos said he supports a federal standard for reporting breaches to law enforcement, but right now no such law exists at the federal level. "We should not have U.S. attorneys and judges just inventing this really important and impactful precedent on their own with the prosecution of one person." Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers. Prosecutors say the breach looked terrible for Sullivan, who was brought on to help the company beef up its cybersecurity after a similar breach in 2014 in which a hacker accessed unencrypted customer data housed in Uber's Amazon data store using a key Uber engineers had left sitting exposed in GitHub. After one of the hackers reached out to Sullivan's personal email address and demanded a six-figure payment, Sullivan and his security team decided to treat the incident as a routine bug bounty and funneled a $100,000 bitcoin ransom through HackerOne. Sullivan's storied past as one of the nation's first cybercrime prosecutors may have made him an easy target, Stamos said. His law degree, and his career as a high-level in-house lawyer at a number of big tech companies, also made it harder for the jury to swallow his defense that he was following the advice of Uber's in-house counsel when he failed to notify the FTC or law enforcement about the breach. Salle Yoo, who was Uber's general counsel at the time, testified that she was kept in the dark about the hack, while Craig Clark, an in-house lawyer at Uber who worked under Sullivan and was given immunity for his testimony, said Sullivan had asked him to figure out whether the breach could be classified as a bug bounty. Stamos had his own theory of the case, which was that Sullivan, who also kept mum at the behest of former CEO Travis Kalanick, was the sacrificial lamb in a power play between his old boss and Dara Khosrowshahi, who took over after Kalanick left the company under a cloud of scandal. "Uber got a new CEO, the new CEO Travis Kalanick was still on the board and the new CEO wanted him off the board. You had new management come in and look through the history of the company for bad things that happened to try to pin on Travis," Stamos said. "This was a war between millionaires and billionaires, and unfortunately the U.S. attorney's office in Northern California allowed themselves to be used as a weapon in a corporate boardroom war. And they decided to go after Joe as a way to get to Travis Kalanick, and in the end, they didn't get Travis. He's walked away scot-free from this." title: 'This Is a Rocket Ship': How Generative AI Will Transform Legal Departments
description: Generative AI could spur the biggest changes in how legal departments operate since the arrival of the internet. Attorneys will need to stop measuring their performance by the written work they're producing. Legal department leaders who fail to…
preview:
The Goldman Sachs report released this week saying generative AI could automate 44% of legal tasks in the U.S. is a watershed moment for legal departments, according to general counsel and other experts, signaling perhaps the biggest shift in how lawyers work since the arrival of the internet.

In-house attorneys and consultants say the technology will accelerate attorneys’ transition away from rote work to high-value-add tasks. And while it’s difficult to predict exactly how changes will play out, they say legal departments likely will maintain and grow their workforces but in some cases scale back their reliance on pricey outside counsel.

In another sign of increased regulatory crackdowns over privacy breaches in health care, online therapy platform BetterHelp must pay $7.8 million to settle Federal Trade Commission charges that for years it shared users' sensitive mental health information with third parties, such as Facebook and Snapchat, which used it for targeted advertising. Under the settlement, which was approved by the commission 4-0 and announced Thursday, BetterHelp will be banned from sharing health data for advertising. More than 2 million people have signed up with Mountain View, California-based BetterHelp since it launched 2013. The telehealth company requires anyone interested in its counseling service to fill out an online questionnaire with detailed questions about their health history, including whether they've been in therapy, have suicidal thoughts or are on medications. title: In First-of-Kind Case, DOJ Alleges CEO Filed Trading Plans to Pull Off Vast Insider Trading Scheme | Corporate Counsel
description: Few things undermine trust in the markets more than insiders abusing their positions for personal advantage, SEC enforcement division director Gurbir Grewal said.
preview:
The Department of Justice for the first time has charged an executive with fraudulent use of so-called 10b5-1 trading plans to commit criminal insider trading—the latest sign of regulators' concern that the plans, created more than two decades ago to tamp down the potential for illegal trading on nonpublic information, are being abused.

The DOJ on Wednesday unsealed an indictment alleging that Terren Peizer, chairman and former CEO of Los Angeles-based Ontrak, dumped more than $20 million in company stock between May 2021 and August 2021 based on inside knowledge that it was about to lose a contract with Cigna, its largest customer.

searchText: In First-of-Kind Case, DOJ Alleges CEO Filed Trading Plans to Pull Off Vast Insider Trading Scheme | Corporate Counsel Few things undermine trust in the markets more than insiders abusing their positions for personal advantage, SEC enforcement division director Gurbir Grewal said. The Department of Justice for the first time has charged an executive with fraudulent use of so-called 10b5-1 trading plans to commit criminal insider trading—the latest sign of regulators' concern that the plans, created more than two decades ago to tamp down the potential for illegal trading on nonpublic information, are being abused. The DOJ on Wednesday unsealed an indictment alleging that Terren Peizer, chairman and former CEO of Los Angeles-based Ontrak, dumped more than $20 million in company stock between May 2021 and August 2021 based on inside knowledge that it was about to lose a contract with Cigna, its largest customer. Authorities allege that Peizer, 63, dodged more than $12.7 million in losses by creating and trading on two 10b5-1 plans after learning that Cigna was going to cease doing business with Ontrak, which provides behavioral health services to large insurers. title: Noncompete Ban Would Force Companies to Become Smarter About Data-Loss Strategies
description: Companies should focus most on securing data rather than on recovering stolen data. Enforcing a noncompete is time-consuming and expensive. Tracking where data moves can bring to light cyberattacks or questionable conduct by employees. Noncompetes…
preview:
Noncompetes were never a perfect way for companies to try to limit data loss, according to legal observers, who say an outright ban would force businesses to adopt more proactive measures.

“It’s really a blunt instrument, and it’s inherently retrospective,” David Huberman said of noncompetes. Huberman is general counsel of Minneapolis-based Code42, a cybersecurity software company that specializes managing insider risk.

title: In Amicus Briefs, Tech Heavyweights Say Weakening Section 230 Would Be Calamitous
description: SCOTUS will hear arguments Feb. 21 in a case seeking to hold YouTube parent Google liable for third-party content the video-sharing website displays. A band of major tech companies—including Microsoft, Twitter, Yelp and Craigslist—urge the high court…
preview:
Devastating. Disabling. Disastrous. Big Tech is in a panic as Section 230, a long-standing shield against liability for what others post on the internet, is about to have its day in court.

Oral arguments are set for Feb. 21 in Gonzalez v. Google, where the parents of a young woman killed in a 2015 terrorist attack in Paris seek to hold YouTube accountable for hosting and recommending ISIS recruitment videos to users through its algorithm. The U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit decided the case in Google’s favor, but, in a partial dissent, Justice Ronald Gould blasted social media companies for publicizing and proliferating terror attacks, writing the the “so-called ‘neutral’ algorithms created by Facebook, Twitter, and Google, are then transformed into deadly missiles of destruction by ISIS, even though they were not initially intended to be used that way.”

title: The Patent Flywheel: Driving a Culture of Innovation
description: Technology is advancing at a blistering pace. It permeates every area of our modern lives—from the specially-formulated shampoo we use in the shower to fight dandruff, to the fuel-efficient and electric cars in which we drive to work, to the…
preview:
Technology is advancing at a blistering pace. It permeates every area of our modern lives—from the specially-formulated shampoo we use in the shower to fight dandruff, to the fuel-efficient and electric cars in which we drive to work, to the synthetic materials used to create the clothing we wear. Many companies want to be a part of this future by being at the forefront of these advancements in technology. Going from a “good” company to a market leader—a “great” company—requires a culture where innovation is celebrated and efficiently generated systematically.

Jim Collins, in his No. 1 best-selling book Good to Great (Random House Business Books, 2001), introduces an insightful framework for establishing company culture using the image of a mechanical flywheel. The flywheel captures his impression of “the overall feel of what it was like inside companies that went from good to great.” We believe that a particular flywheel architecture including as components the activities of patent filing and strategic portfolio management drives a company’s high performance innovation culture: a culture that systematically and continuously generates market leading technology.

searchText: House Republicans Grill Twitter Legal Brass Over Suppression of Hunter Biden Article What You Need to Know The House Oversight Committee hearing lasted six hours.At issue was why Twitter initially blocked an unflattering New York Post article about Hunter Biden.The hearing was light on probing questions about Twitter's internal… What You Need to Know The House Oversight Committee hearing lasted six hours.At issue was why Twitter initially blocked an unflattering New York Post article about Hunter Biden.The hearing was light on probing questions about Twitter's internal processes and heavy on squabbling between Republicans and Democrats. Three ousted Twitter executives, including two former top lawyers, faced withering criticism from GOP House Oversight Committee members on Wednesday over their handling of a 2020 New York Post article, sourced from files found on Hunter Biden’s laptop, that raised questions about the propriety of Biden family business dealings in the run-up to the 2020 election. The hearing followed the release late last year of a trove of documents by journalist Matt Taibbi that included email discussions among Twitter executives about banning the Hunter Biden article from the platform under its “hacked materials” policy. Former chief legal officer Vijaya Gadde initially said she was “involved” in the decision to censor the story, and under questioning Wednesday from Rep. William Timmons, R-South Carolina, said she “ultimately approved that decision.” She testified, “The New York Post chose not to delete its original tweets, so Twitter made an exception after two weeks to retroactively apply the new policy to the New York Post’s tweets. In hindsight, Twitter should have reinstated the New York Post’s account immediately given the circumstances.” Gadde, former deputy general counsel James Baker and former head of trust and safety Yoel Roth appeared before the committee under subpoena, ostensibly to testify about the temporary removal of the story from the platform, along with the suspension of the New York Post’s Twitter account. But the hearing was light on probing Twitter’s actual decision-making process. At times, it seemed as though the Twitter executives were mere proxies for Republican and Democrat hostilities, as both sides aired a variety of grievances against the social media giant, simultaneously accusing the former Twitter executives of unbounded political bias, fueling the Jan. 6 insurrection, stoking racial hatred, and even conspiring to smother Rep. Marjorie Taylor Greene’s fundraising efforts. “I’m glad you all lost your jobs,” Greene, R-Georgia, seethed. All three were fired from Twitter after Elon Musk bought the San Francisco-based company in October. Baker was the last to be dismissed, leaving in December after Taibbi tweeted that Baker had reviewed the first batch of Twitter documents without Musk’s knowledge, a move Taibbi said contributed to the firing. “In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Musk tweeted about Baker’s departure. Baker referenced his former employer’s tweet in his opening statement, saying he urged caution with respect to Twitter’s blocking of the Biden article and “noted that we needed more information to fully assess what was going on and to decide what to do; hardly a surprising piece of advice from a corporate lawyer.” He added, “I did not destroy or improperly suppress any documents at Twitter regarding information important to the public dialogue. At all times I sought to help my client understand and comply with its legal obligations.” Baker’s contribution to the email chain was that Twitter needed more information to determine whether the story violated Twitter’s “hacked materials” policy. “There are some facts that indicate that the materials may have been hacked,” he wrote, while others indicated that Biden had abandoned the laptop after leaving it at a repair shop or had allowed the shop to access it for some purposes. A number of Republican committee members accused Gadde, Baker and Roth of bending to FBI pressure to squelch the story while also colluding with federal law enforcement and the intelligence community to stifle conservative speech and ensure President Joe Biden’s victory in the 2020 election. “God bless Elon Musk because it was Elon Musk that revealed data that uncovered a disturbing cabal. We’re here today because Twitter got caught, not because people wanted to admit mistakes got made,” said Rep. Pete Sessions, R-Texas. “Or, perhaps they got bought.” Baker, who before joining Twitter had been general counsel of the FBI, invoked attorney-client privilege under questioning from Rep. Jim Jordan, R-Ohio, who grilled him about his opening statement and whether he “properly” suppressed any documents, and whether that suppression occurred “during the time the Twitter files were being released just a few months ago.” Committee

title: 'Risk Management Is a Team Sport': What GCs Should Learn From Uber Cybersecurity Verdict
description: "The CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is," said Donna Gallaher, a data privacy risk adviser.
preview:
The October conviction of former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for concealing a 2016 data breach from government regulators sent ripples of anxiety through the C-suite over the prospect of more executives being held personally liable after a hack.

At a recent panel on what the verdict means for corporate security and legal teams, the consensus was that Sullivan's prosecution was unusual, and his actions egregious. But while companies shouldn't panic, general counsel and security chiefs should band together to tackle cybersecurity incidents with transparency and open communication.
excerpt: "The CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is," said Donna Gallaher, a data privacy risk adviser.
searchText: 'Risk Management Is a Team Sport': What GCs Should Learn From Uber Cybersecurity Verdict "The CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is," said Donna Gallaher, a data privacy risk adviser. The October conviction of former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan for concealing a 2016 data breach from government regulators sent ripples of anxiety through the C-suite over the prospect of more executives being held personally liable after a hack. At a recent panel on what the verdict means for corporate security and legal teams, the consensus was that Sullivan's prosecution was unusual, and his actions egregious. But while companies shouldn't panic, general counsel and security chiefs should band together to tackle cybersecurity incidents with transparency and open communication. "Cyber and privacy is a companywide concern, and that includes the board of directors, all the way down the line," said Cari Robinson, a cybersecurity expert and former Revlon general counsel. "Teamwork is critical. If I don't have a collaborative, transparent and open relationship with my CIO, my CISO, I'm not going to be able to give advice to the company or ultimately to the board of directors." The panel, hosted by the woman-led market network Fourth Floor and moderated by founder Breen Sullivan, also included virtual chief security officer and data privacy risk adviser Donna Gallaher and ClearOPS founder Caroline McCaffery. Robinson, who also headed cybersecurity investigations as an assistant general counsel at IBM, said general counsel should have an "open and collaborative" relationship with security chiefs so that they can fully understand the incident and how to best advise the CEO on what the company's response should be. Sullivan's conviction may have shaken the cybersecurity community, but Robinson said the government is unlikely to turn its sights on executives who act in good faith. Where Sullivan and Uber went wrong, she said, was in confining their handling of the breach to just a handful of top executives, including then-CEO Travis Kalanick, while keeping the general counsel and Uber's legal department in the dark. "It was an easy situation for the government to make an example of," Robinson said. Gallaher said she was struck by the apparent communication gap between Sullivan and Uber's general counsel at the time, Salle Yoo. Rather than keep Yoo in the loop, Sullivan decided, after consulting with another Uber in-house lawyer, that the hack was not disclosable. That lawyer, Craig Clark, also kept the breach from the general counsel and was given immunity for testifying against Sullivan. "Risk management is a team sport," Gallaher said. "And as much as the attorney is playing chess while the CISOs are playing checkers when it comes to navigating the legal processes and how to maneuver the legal system, the CISO knows where all the bodies are buried and where all the evidence is." She said general counsel should cultivate a strong relationship with their company's security chief as a hedge against risk. "Some people might be looking at the Uber case as a general counsel and seeing the CISO got a criminal conviction and thinking, 'That kind of sucks for him.' Well, it's going to suck for you if you end up having to have to do battle with the CISO, who has more technical expertise than you do," Gallaher said. "So just get ahead of that now. Make that person your friend." Legal and security chiefs may speak different languages, but should work together to understand the facts of an incident, Robinson said. "If you told me, 'There's an intrusion in the system and we're in trouble because they have access to all of our stuff,' I'd have to ask you a million questions about what happened, how did it happen, can it be stopped, et cetera. So if you're not having those discussions, then you're not going to be able to make a good decision for the company." Uber was criticized back in 2016 for a lax culture around security that led to two similar data breaches within two years. As cyberattacks grow in sophistication and frequency, Robinson said executives will need to speak up when they spot issues, or walk away from a toxic company culture. "If you find yourself as a CISO or general counsel in an environment that is so toxic that you raise an issue and you're just told to go away and be quiet, and if you don't feel like you can change that culture by opening up the lines of communication, you know what? Free legal advice: Leave," she said. NOT FOR REPRINT © 2024 ALM Global, LLC, All Rights Reserved. Request academic re-use from www.copyright.com. searchText: ChatGPT Might Simplify Life for In-House Counsel—While Also Creating New Risks What You Need to Know ChatGPT can help automate routine communication, but legal experts say it isn't ready for prime time.In-house counsel need to learn how nonlegal employees are using ChatGPT, as they could exposing confidential information.… What You Need to Know ChatGPT can help automate routine communication, but legal experts say it isn't ready for prime time.In-house counsel need to learn how nonlegal employees are using ChatGPT, as they could exposing confidential information. Analysts and academics are already theorizing about how Open AI’s ChatGPT will transform the legal field, with the more bullish of them seeing the AI-powered chatbot as automating routine tasks so that lawyers are freed up to work on more important matters. The discussion is part of a blizzard of debate fueled by the public debut of Open AI’s ChatGPT in November. The powerful tool has sparked speculation and angst, raising questions across industries about its ability to revolutionize communication and potential to lay waste to entire professions. “The reason people are paying so much attention to ChatGPT is it reveals the promise of these types of tools for law practice and what it might be capable of doing in not too long,” said Andrew Perlman, dean of the Suffolk University Law School. “But it’s not ready for prime time in terms of using it for anything important. Open AI’s CEO said that himself, and my own experience using it reveals how imperfect the tool can be,” he said. Perlman said he can envision ChatGPT as a system for answering common, repetitive questions on certain subjects. “It could also be used as a triage tool that could engage people back and forth and get them to the right resources, reducing the demands on the time of in-house lawyers and staff,” he said. “ChatGPT presents us with a way to streamline and make more efficient those kinds of routine communications.” ChatGPT is built on a large language model called text-davincci-003, or GPT-3.5, as it’s colloquially known, that can generate natural-sounding text fit for drafting simple content like an employee handbook, internal corporate policies or anything that requires a standard format. It also can be useful for converting complex legal terminology into plain English. But there are still kinks in the system. Joshua Lenon, a lawyer in residence at the legal software company Clio, said his compliance team recently put ChatGPT to the test, asking it to create a chart of how various state data-breach notification laws define the term “personally identifiable information.” “They are very specific in their drafting, but each state might not be exactly the same. We said, ‘Hey, why not see if ChatGPT could do this chart?’ Well, it couldn’t,” he said. “It wrote back that each state has different definitions but didn’t say what they were.” Lenon, who specializes in compliance, privacy and data security issues, said the experience helped delineate ChatGPT’s abilities and limitations. “It’s good way to transform clear data you already have but not a good way to go out and find data—certainly not to the degree that would be required in a legal environment.” Even for drafting contracts or other documents, Lenon said, ChatGPT requires a sharp human eye to look out for knowledge gaps. “You still have to put in a lot of work. It’s good for marketing and ad copy, but when it looks at legal it might get the format right but not the substance. That’s where it might be tripping for in-house counsel,” he said. Martin Gomez, a partner with Goodwin Procter specializing in intellectual property and tech issues, cautioned against putting blind trust in a generative-AI tool. “For in-house counsel, being able to focus on more high-value tasks or frankly being able to do their job faster, that has value. But we shouldn’t forget that lawyers have a fiduciary duty to their clients—so, for in-house, that’s the company. “They have a duty to get it right. One of the risky things about AI is even the people who make the AI don’t necessarily know where the answers came from. Having an overall understanding that it might get it wrong or could get it wrong and what sort of tasks are appropriate to outsource to an AI and what sort of things should never be trusted to an AI engine, that is something in-house will have to grapple with,” Gomez said. He said ChatGPT can be useful for questions for which there are black-and-white answers, but in-house counsel are often faced with the opposite. “So much of being a lawyer is operating in the gray and making judgment calls,” he said. Technologists note that ChatGPT is only as good as the data on which it is trained, a precept known among programmers as “garbage in, garbage out.” And, for that reason, corporate legal departments shouldn’t rely on the public version of ChatGPT. Legal… What You Need to Know Law firm clients are experiencing 2023 rate increases that generally fall between 5% to 15%.But some hikes are topping 30%.Legal departments are pushing back harder, but many lack a sophisticated rate-review process. Legal departments expressed outrage and girded for battle last fall when their outside law firms rolled out plans for aggressive rate increases for 2023. Yet the showdown that seemed sure to come never really materialized. Legal observers say that while some law departments pushed back on increases more than they had in recent years, and some won larger-than-typical concessions, many departments are ending up with substantial hikes, sometimes more than 15%. And few departments are exercising the nuclear option of firing firms over higher rates. Jason Winmill, a managing partner at the in-house consulting firm Argopoint, said rates have shot upward in 2023, in contrast to the gradual increases of the recent past. “Prior years tended toward 4-6%—with gains accumulating via consistent year-over-year bump-ups vs. single year spikes,” he said. However, 2022 saw increases around 5-7%, and 2023 increases are even loftier, with high-end firms commanding more than 30%. “2023 rate hikes are 7-8% for many. But even steeper hikes are coming from the premium band, where it’s all over the place: sometimes 12% but also sometimes 32%,” he said. “While cracks may be emerging here and there, it’s been a very good time to be outside counsel.” Law firms saw average billing rate increases of 5.8% in 2022, according to Wells Fargo Private Bank Legal Specialty Group. By comparison, firms raised rates by an average of 6.7% in 2021 and 5.9% in 2020. Winmill said the steeper increases could be attributed to demand outstripping supply for the high-end legal services on which Fortune 500 clients depend. “Outside counsel has capitalized on that by ratcheting rates up a few more clicks on top of the normal increases,” he said. The trend was borne out in the yearly letters in-house received from firms. “This year was an avalanche,” said Aarash Darroodi, executive vice president and general counsel of the guitar-maker Fender. “I don’t know if outside counsel couldn’t afford eggs or milk or something. On the receiving end, it’s kind of comedic for us. It’s like, ‘Here it is—the lawyers trying to milk more from us.’” Consulting a price sheet he’d recently received from a firm, Darroodi noticed a marked increase in one associate’s hourly rates. “This one seems to have gone up by about $30 an hour,” he said. During negotiations aimed at ratcheting down proposed law firm increases, “some firms were incredibly flexible … while others drew a hard line,” said Jessica Vander Ploeg, vice president of legal operations for software provider Micro Focus. Vander Ploeg also said she and legal ops executives at other companies have been comparing notes. “More than half saw rate increases of 30% from some of their law firms, and most saw double-digit increases,” she said. “That was their starting point, though; they all negotiated down from that 30%, or most did. It’s not unusual though, to see double-digit increases.” ‘Many Reasons Firms Increase Rates’ Law firms usually begin sending out the dreaded rate-increase notices at the end of the year in the hopes of locking in a new rate as close to Jan. 1 as they can. it’s not unusual for rate negotiations to extend into the first quarter. Vander Ploeg said Micro Focus negotiates rates every two years and when old rates expired at the end of December, her company continued to pay at that level until it reached new agreements. For her company, the average rate increase across all its law firms was 16%. On the low end was a 3% increase, and the high end was 32%, based on attorneys’ roles, recent promotions and the geography they were covering, Vander Ploeg said. The firms’ justifications for increases, she said, ran the gamut—from economic pressures to singular expertise. “I’ve heard inflation, cost-of-living changes, ‘the work we’re doing is specialized,’” she said. “There are many reasons firms increase rates. The key is to evaluate if the increases are reasonable—which is subjective for each in-house department and competitive within the marketplace.” Darroodi noticed the same thing. “Sometimes the increases are justified, like when a senior associate becomes a partner because you’re getting a different level of advice,” he said. “But if they’re just doing it because of inflation, I wonder what sort of inflationary pressures law firms are having. If you’re going to raise the fee, why don’t you improve the way you serve the in-house counsel first?” ‘Trying to Make the Right Moves’

title: Legal Departments Frustrated SCOTUS Sidestepped Attorney-Client Privilege

searchText: Legal Departments Frustrated SCOTUS Sidestepped Attorney-Client Privilege What You Need to Know The U.S. Supreme Court issued a one-sentence order disposing of a case that could have brought clarity to when communication with clients is protected.It was the first time the high court had taken up attorney-client privilege… What You Need to Know The U.S. Supreme Court issued a one-sentence order disposing of a case that could have brought clarity to when communication with clients is protected.It was the first time the high court had taken up attorney-client privilege in 40 years.At issue in the case was so-called dual-purpose communication covering both legal and nonlegal matters. In a blow for in-house counsel seeking clarity on attorney-client privilege, the U.S. Supreme Court tossed what could have been a decisive case for when attorney’s communications with clients are protected. In an unsigned, one-sentence order, the court dismissed an appeal in the case as “improvidently granted” just two weeks after hearing oral arguments, which marked the first time the high court had taken up the issue of attorney-client privilege in 40 years. (Find full coverage of the ruling here.) The case, In re Grand Jury, No. 21-1397, involved a district judge’s denial of attorney-client privilege sought by a law firm hired to prepare tax returns for a client who was “an early promoter of Bitcoin” and left the United States in early 2014, according to a U.S. brief in the case. In a SCOTUS petition In In re Grand Jury, the law firm, which bills itself as specializing in international tax issues, says it provided the client with “legal advice regarding the tax consequences of their anticipated expatriation” and prepared their tax returns and forms to ensure they complied with expatriation tax requirements. A federal grand jury sought records from the firm in its criminal investigation of the client, but the firm refused to hand them over, claiming the communications the grand jury wanted to see were privileged. A federal judge held the firm in contempt for failing to comply with the grand jury’s subpoenas, and the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Ninth Circuit agreed, finding that, while the records addressed both legal and tax matters, they were not privileged, because their “primary purpose” concerned “normal tax return preparation assistance.” In a statement Monday, the Association of Corporate Counsel (ACC) said it was disappointed with the court’s decision to dismiss the case. Susanna McDonald, ACC vice president and chief legal officer, said the court missed an opportunity to weigh in on whether attorney-client privilege applies to “dual purpose” communications that contain advice on multiple legal and nonlegal issues. “In-house counsel need clarity on how all courts will view their client communications so that they can provide the best possible legal advice while also fulfilling their role as a strategic business partner,” McDonald said. In an ACC amicus brief filed jointly with the U.S. Chamber of Commerce, the ACC argued that the demands placed on in-house counsel to advise on compliance, risk mitigation, human resources and government affairs issues require a more predictable standard for determining when attorney-client privilege protections apply. “This predictability is necessary to ensure the full and frank communication between lawyers and their clients that effective legal practice requires,” the groups wrote, shunning the “primary purpose” test used by the appellate court as “completely unworkable for attorneys” and their clients. “Without guidance from the Supreme Court, the legal landscape for dual purpose communications remains murky. In-house counsel routinely engage in communications that have both legal and business purposes that cannot easily be untangled,” McDonald said. “Because the circuit courts are split over which test should be used to determine privilege in these situations, in-house counsel are left wondering what test will apply when so many transactions are across state borders and many companies have operations in multiple states.”

The Federal… What You Need to Know The FTC alleges Credit Karma deceived consumers about their credit-card-approval odds.The order is part of a larger enforcement crackdown on deceptive online tactics.The company could not be reached for comment. The Federal Trade Commission is cracking down on companies it believes use deceptive digital tactics to manipulate consumers into parting with their money, and a consent order requiring Credit Karma to pay $3 million for promoting phony preapproved credit cards offers is the latest example. A complaint the FTC filed in September claims Credit Karma misled consumers into applying for the cards through marketing emails sent between February 2018 and April 2021 that falsely said they were “pre-approved” or had “90% odds of approval.” Instead, the FTC says, consumers wasted their time applying for the cards, and their credit scores took a hit. On Monday, the FTC announced that it had finalized an agreement with the San Francisco-based company to pay $3 million to consumers and stop the misleading practice. Credit Karma did not immediately respond to a request for comment. Misleading or hidden ads, automatic subscription renewals and other web-based designed elements used to steer consumers into buying something or give up their data to businesses have earned the sinister-sounding moniker “dark patterns” from the FTC, which said it will impose stiff penalties on companies that use them. In September, just a week after filing its complaint against Credit Karma, the regulator released a report that found a rise in companies using sophisticated predatory methods to trick consumers into buying their products or share their personal information. Samuel Levine, who heads the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, said in a statement accompanying its complaint against Credit Karma that the agency “will continue its crackdown on digital dark patterns that harm consumers and pollute online commerce.” Things like deceptive marketing emails, ads disguised as independent content, automatic subscription renewals, or burying material information deep within terms of service agreements all count as unscrupulous “dark patterns” in the eyes of regulators. Last week, Jonathan Direnfeld, an Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe partner and expert on regulatory enforcement involving data privacy and unfair and deceptive sales and marketing practices, told Law.com that companies should expect to see even more of a crackdown this year, and not just from the FTC. He said the regulator is increasingly partnering with state attorneys general in bringing consumer protection actions. “The scrutiny and work going on at these agencies is only continuing to ramp up,” he said, noting the use of dark patterns as one of their top priorities for enforcement in 2023.

It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself— but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a profitable manner," said Jonathan Direnfeld, an Orrick, Herrington and Sutcliffe partner. January 20, 2023 at 05:36 AM 4 minute read Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Enforcement actions have increased under the Biden administration.That trend likely will accelerate this year, as the Biden administration enters its third year.Some of the tactics investigators have been targeting have been accepted industry practices. Companies are facing immense pressure from regulators over how they market their services and engage with consumers. Experts say enforcement actions will increase this year, as government agencies zero in on businesses that use deceitful tactics to try to separate consumers from their money or data. “One thing we’ve seen increase in over the last two years is partnerships between the FTC and state attorneys general in bringing actions” said Orrick, Herrington & Sutcliffe partner Jonathan Direnfeld at a recent webinar on regulatory trends jointly hosted by Orrick and the consulting firm Kroll. Direnfeld attributed this shift to the U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in AMG Capital Management, LLC v. FTC, which limited the agency’s ability to seek monetary relief, specifically consumer restitution. This has led the FTC to lean on the broad civil penalty authority enjoyed by state attorneys general. Direnfeld said regulators are becoming more aggressive, pursuing more actions and seeking more money from companies that run afoul of consumer protection rules. He pointed to two large FTC settlements announced last year. In one, internet phone service provider Vonage agreed to pay $100 million in restitution over automatic subscription renewals. It also exacted a whopping $520 million settlement from Fortnite maker Epic Games after alleging it violated the Children’s Online Privacy Protection Act and misled players into making in-game purchases. The Epic Games settlement in particular, Direnfeld said, signals the FTC’s priorities for this year. “First and foremost there’s going to be an increased focused on all things children-directed." This means any kind of marketing aimed at children, be it direct targeted advertising or ads dressed up as entertainment. The FTC also has considered changing its rules around “stealth advertising”—digital media that softens the line between marketing and content by embedding ads in social media, online games and video-sharing platforms. Direnfeld observed that the last two big FTC settlements used the term “dark patterns” to describe tactics that make it easier for unwitting consumers to make purchases. In a post-webinar interview, Direnfeld said the challenge for companies is that some of the things the FTC would classify as a “dark pattern” like automatic renewals and certain user interface designs, have long been commonplace and accepted industry practices. “It poses a lot of challenges to companies—to be able to make decisions on how to potentially modify user flows or sales processes to try to reduce risk while not materially impacting business operations,” he said. Direnfeld, who defends tech and data-driven companies against regulatory enforcement actions, said such decision-making will require general counsel to “go after it with a scalpel, not a cleaver.” "Find the highest-risk pieces to reduce your overall risk profile, particularly if you’re in an industry where where everyone else is doing it,” he said. Should a company find itself the subject of a regulatory investigation, Direnfeld said in-house counsel should immediately start preserving documents. Beyond that, reach out to experienced outside counsel. One thing companies shouldn’t do is try to handle everything in-house, he said. “These are bet-the-company matters. It’s not just on the monetary piece—which can be crippling in itself—but the potential injunctive provision that would require changes for businesses that makes it impossible to continue operating in a profitable manner, Direnfeld said. “Companies that do not find way to effectively navigate through this could easily find themselves out of business.” He said the heat is only to get more intense. “The scrutiny and work going on at these agencies is only continuing to ramp up. January 20, 2023 at 04:48 AM 5 minute read Corporate Governance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Tougher SEC rules on insider trading may result in fewer Rule 10b5-1 plans, experts say.Instead, executives might engage in more open-market transactions.General counsel will have to decide what constitutes material, nonpublic information. General counsel may find themselves pulled into difficult conversations with top executives as the Securities and Exchange Commission tightens its rules on company insiders looking to dump their stock. Insider trading has long been an SEC bugbear. But the steady drumbeat of outrage over high-level executives trading on information ahead of the public has ramped up over the last two decades, said securities law expert Karen Woody, a professor at Washington and Lee University. Suspicion that trades were becoming too well-timed led to unanimous agreement at the SEC that it was time to update its longstanding rule under which corporate insiders are allowed to schedule trades in advance. “There are some old-school theories about why some people are against regulating insider trading—one argument is that insider trading is an employment perk. It’s part of your executive compensation,” Woody said. “But this rule is truly the opposite. It says, ‘We’re not going to let you game the system just because you happen to be working there.’” The misuse of these Rule 10b5-1 plans mostly involved executives trying to take advantage of its flexibility, said former SEC trial attorney Daniel O’Connor, who now co-leads Ropes & Gray’s securities and futures enforcement practice. “Some of the abuses that the staff was talking about have to do with people putting in place multiple plans on either side of a good or bad event—canceling one and then revising another while potentially possessing MNPI [material non-public information],” he said. Now Rule 10b5-1 will only allow one trade plan a year and imposes a 90-to-120 day “cooling off” period for officers and directors between the adoption of the plan and the first trade. Everyone else must adhere to a 30-day waiting period. “That extended cooling off period will help general counsel advise executives on whether certain information is material non-public information,” O’Connor said. The updated rule eliminates Rule 10b5-1 as an affirmative defense against insider trading, and requires directors and officers to certify that their trading plans were made in good faith and that they are not trading on material, nonpublic information. Daniel Taylor, a professor at the University of Pennsylvania’s Wharton School of Business who co-authored an influential study on potential 10b5-1 abuses, said one pressing area of concern will be the rule’s prohibition on executives delaying public disclosure of bad news until after they’ve sold off their shares. “Most people view 10b5-1 as altering the timing of the trades, but there’s also evidence that executives move the timing of the disclosure. Let’s say I learn the company lost a major contract. I may be tempted to delay disclosure of that bad news until after my scheduled sale is complete. The SEC clarified that would be a violation of the good-faith requirement,” Taylor said. He said the new restrictions may lead to less use of 10b5-1 plans. “I do think we will see the use and abuse of these plans decline, but that’s not necessarily a bad thing.” Woody with Washington and Lee said the SEC’s tougher stance also may rectify the perception of executives exploiting loopholes in the existing rules. “Hopefully it will dial down the impression of some funny business around trades,” she said. O’Connor with Ropes & Gray said the revised rule may lead to more executives engaging in open-market transactions, which have their own headaches. “My worry is that the rule makes it less likely people will use 10b5-1 plans and more likely to engage in market transactions where they get pre-clearance, or go ahead and trade without a prior plan. In my experience, that’s the type of trading where things can get more challenging,” he said. “It’s a lot easier to become comfortable about whether a situation is material or not knowing the trade is going to be 90 days off. title: Charlie Rose Lawsuit Sees Several Major Claims Dismissed
description: A state appeals court has thrown out several major claims that a former head makeup artist who spent 22 years working for the Charlie Rose Show had leveled against the once-famed talk show host in a discrimination, harassment and labor lawsuit. Much…
preview:
A state appeals court has thrown out several major claims that a former head makeup artist who spent 22 years working for the Charlie Rose Show had leveled against the once-famed talk show host in a discrimination, harassment and labor lawsuit.

Much of the former makeup artist’s 2019-filed suit, in which she details Rose allegedly “preying” on female staff for years at a TV studio described as a “sexual hunting ground,” is no longer alive. The makeup artist, Gina Riggi, previously withdrew age discrimination and retaliation claims, along with one of her state Labor Law claims, from the action, according to a lower-court ruling.

With the Federal Trade Commission poised to sharply curtail non-compete clauses, litigation experts say now is the time for companies to take stock of their employment agreements. “You want to have a clear message when the FTC or anyone else comes calling and asks, ‘Why do you have these agreements?’” said John Barry, who heads Weil, Gotshal & Manges’ employment litigation practice and co-authored a recent client_briefing on the issue. Barry said companies should audit their agreements to ensure they’re justifiable and reasonable in scope. Legitimate business reasons like protecting trade secrets or preserving customer goodwill can be a shield against antitrust scrutiny. Adding another complication, the FTC’s rule proposes to ban any employment contract language that the FTC views as a “de facto” non-compete clause. Customer non-solicitation agreements, non-disclosure agreements and equity forfeiture provisions could all be interpreted to function as such. “There’s a threshold question about this proposed rule as to whether it would apply to incentive compensation arrangements that contain non-competes,” Barry said. “There’s a possibility that non-competes in connection with equity might still be OK. That’s what we who advise businesses are trying to figure out; are forfeiture for non-competition provisions at risk? If that ability to incentivize talent to come to companies goes away, that’s going to be every problematic for companies, particularly the startups.” Prohibitions on non-compete agreements already are familiar territory to Silicon Valley tech companies, as California already deems them unenforceable. Their disallowance is part of the reason why the Northern District of California is home to the largest docket of trade secret cases in the country. For those outside of California, non-competes are a handy tool to protect against trade secret and intellectual property theft. “If these rules are passed, which is a big if, the companies will certainly have to rely on and follow the California approach,” Barry said, “which is to make sure they’ve identified their trade secrets so if someone does go to work for another company and starts producing a similar product, they’ll be in a better place to enforce and bring an action to try to protect those trade secrets.” Some companies require high-level executives to pay back their vested or unvested equity if they go to work for a competitor. Becky Baker, a partner at Vinson & Elkins’ labor and employment group, said the proposed rule doesn’t directly address whether a clawback would be prohibited, but it does contain language saying agreements requiring a worker to pay damages if they compete against their employer “effect the same restriction.” “Does that mean forfeiting vested shares, or paying back funds would violate this rule? I definitely think it’s potentially on the table from the FTC’s perspective,” Baker said. In the meantime, companies should re-evaluate what type of employees are currently subject to non-competes. “You’re just setting yourself up for a better defense of your non-competes if you’re only using it with a population that requires those restrictions—don’t use it with everyone at the company. The employees who really should have non-compete restrictions are those who have the keys to the kingdom, or who know the secret sauce.” Weil litigation partner Eric Hochstadt said there’s no need to panic. The rule is still in its nascent stage, and the final version could look much different after the close of the 60-day public comment period. The proposal also offers a “safe harbor” for companies to terminate non-competes for 180 days after the rule becomes final. That means the earliest possible date for noncompliance would be in September of this year, though because the FTC will need time to consider comments it likely would be a few months later than that. “You don’t want to overreact and do something rushed,” he said. “This is something you can do with deliberate, careful guidance with counsel within the next few months.” Hochstadt said the FTC has finite resources, and will have to be selective about where it focuses its enforcement efforts. “The disparity in bargaining power is animating the majority of the FTC commissioners who have proposed this rule,” he said, making it all the more likely that regulators will target companies that require non-competes from low-wage wor

searchText: Laid-Off In-House Lawyers Still Finding Jobs, But Could Face Stiffer Competition January 13, 2023 at 10:00 AM 4 minute read Recruiting Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire.Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions. In-house… January 13, 2023 at 10:00 AM 4 minute read Recruiting Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know There are still lots of in-house jobs, though companies are taking longer to hire.Job seekers should capitalize on their networks to find new positions. In-house attorneys have been largely spared in the barrage of layoffs pummeling the tech industry. And while there are still jobs aplenty for those seeking reemployment, legal recruiters warn that the tide could be turning. “We haven’t seen a lot of in-house lawyers desperately looking for jobs,” said Sean Burke, founding partner at legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. However, he added, there’s been a marked increase in applications from law firm lawyers looking to go in-house, leading him to suspect that layoffs have mostly affected the other side. Twitter was an outlier among tech giants when it lost the bulk of its 150-person legal department last year, but Burke noted that most attorneys left willingly after Elon Musk completed his $44 billion purchase of the social media company, installed himself as CEO and demanded employees either work “long hours at high intensity” or walk. “The Twitter attorneys I’ve spoken with left by choice, and they are all very confident in their choice,” Burke said. “They took the money and ran.” But some were also part of a mass layoff that slashed more than 50% of Twitter’s workforce. Ashley Roybal-Reid started as a product counsel at Twitter in February 2022, and by November she was out of a job. In an interview, Roybal-Reid said she received an email announcing “the rumors were true” that Twitter was planning a mass layoff. The following Monday, staff would find out if they were among those cut. “I was trying to wrap up some work that [Thursday] night and my access got cut so I stopped working,” she said. Roybal-Reid said she expected to face some difficulty in trying to land a new job at the end of the year. But after posting about her loss on LinkedIn, she was flooded with messages from colleagues and friends, some of whom she hadn’t spoken with for years. “I was obviously a little bit discouraged. I really liked my job at Twitter and the people I worked with, but fairly quickly I got a sense there was hope out there,” she said. Newly inspired, Roybal-Reid spent the next few weeks on her job search. “I treated it like a 40-hour-a-week job,” she said. This week, Roybal-Reid made another announcement on LinkedIn: she had joined the in-house legal team at Mozilla. Now, she’s the one offering to help her laid-off colleagues find work. “I suspect there are more job seekers than jobs right now, but there are jobs. It’s just a question of finding them,” she said. “It takes a little more legwork. Capitalizing on your network as best you can is probably the No. 1 thing.” John Gilmore, founder and managing partner of the legal recruiting firm BarkerGilmore, said job seekers are having to rely more on their networks and companies are becoming more selective in hiring. “There are still a number of opportunities out there, but companies are being highly selective and they’re moving a bit slower than they ever have to make the hires, so it’s become a bit more of a challenge,” he said. “People are definitely having success in finding new positions, but it’s taking more networking.” Gilmore said using social media to announce you’re looking for a job is a smart move. “I would take advantage of all of that for sure, even reaching out to outside counsel you worked with or law school grads and colleagues,” he said. “Really sit down and exhaust your network.” Burke of Whistler Partners said he expects layoffs to ramp up at outside law firms, which will make competition for in-house jobs more fierce. Lawyers who are already laid off will have a better shot at finding another in-house job now than in a few months. “Somewhere in the near future there’s a dotted line, and if you get laid off after that dotted line, it’s a lot harder because there’s way more competition and not enough jobs,” he said. While that hasn’t happened yet, Burke said things appear to be trending in that direction. “We’re going to see more and more pressure on in-house jobs, and there’s going to be more attorneys from firms looking for them,” he said.

title: As Companies' Fears of Data-Breach Litigation Soar, Legal Terrain Rife With Uncertainty
description: Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to…
preview:
Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to bring claims.

The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TransUnion v. Ramirez—requiring all class members to have an actual, concrete injury beyond the risk of future harm—imposed limits on standing that appeared favorable to companies.
excerpt: Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are...
searchText: As Companies' Fears of Data-Breach Litigation Soar, Legal Terrain Rife With Uncertainty Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to… Companies are entering 2023 with sky-high anxiety over potential legal fallout from data breaches, according to litigation-forecast reports published by law firms this week, and their worries are amplified by uncertainty over who courts will allow to bring claims. The U.S. Supreme Court’s 2021 ruling in TransUnion v. Ramirez—requiring all class members to have an actual, concrete injury beyond the risk of future harm—imposed limits on standing that appeared favorable to companies. But any comfort the ruling, which involved the Fair Credit Reporting Act, brought to attorneys defending data breaches began to fade last year when the U.S. Court of Appeals for the Third Circuit ruled in one such case that the future risk of identity theft is a sufficiently concrete injury. That case, Clemens v. ExecuPharm, involved a known gang of hackers publishing personal data stolen in a ransomware attack on the dark web. The court based its decision on the specific facts of that breach, and what it means for future cases is unclear, Jennifer Romano, a litigation partner for Crowell & Moring in Los Angeles, said in a report issued by her firm this week. Weighing in favor of standing was the fact that it was a cyberattack from a very sophisticated organization. “What other data breach class actions will satisfy the injury requirement under TransUnion? Will it always depend on the facts? This makes it incredibly difficult for parties to assess the risks and potential exposure, which is particularly problematic when the amount of statutory damages could bankrupt a company,” Romano said in the report. Another litigation forecast, this one from Baker McKenzie, included the results of a survey of 600 senior litigation attorneys at large companies on four continents. The attorneys are expecting an action-packed year; just 17% of respondents said they expect the number of disputes this year to decline from 2022. Asked to identify disputes that present a risk to their organizations, 62% of respondents cited cybersecurity/data, putting it at the top of the list. No. 2 was environment, social and governance, at 58%. After that, no dispute type garnered more than 37%. The report noted that cyberattacks are becoming more common, with attackers’ tactics becoming more sinister. Ransomware attacks saw a 13% jump from 2022. The attacks increasingly use “double extortion,” in which cybercriminals not only encrypt files but take a copy and threaten to release them if ransom is not paid, and “triple extortion,” which involves ransom payments from victims’ clients or suppliers whose data was compromised. Scott Giordano, general counsel at data privacy software company Spirion, said the high court’s ruling in TransUnion doesn’t change the dynamic for companies dealing with the aftermath of data breaches, as they will still need to calculate the extent of the harm done. “You’re still going to hire an economist and a data scientist, and have those folks go through the data and find what the potential is for harm,” he said. Giordano said companies should try to reduce their exposure by knowing the type of data they have and paring it down. “First, have a very crisp idea of what sensitive personal information you have inside your information ecosystem, and once you have that, determine what you need and what you can do away with,” he said. “It’s historically been a problem that companies in America collect way more data than they need, thinking they’re going use it down the road. But too often it’s the bad actors who end up using it.” He noted that data encryption can provide a safe harbor for companies under privacy statutes. “Encrypt, encrypt, encrypt,” Giordano said. “If the data is encrypted, in many if not most cases, the statute doesn’t apply. And if the bad guys can’t use it, then it’s harder to articulate the damages you could have.” In an email, Crowell’s Romano said that if companies do suffer a breach, they should gather as much evidence as possible on the incident, and hire experienced forensic teams to investigate. “What happened? When? What information was accessed? What information was exfiltrated? What can you know with certainty? What cannot be determined? Why? These will be key facts in the case, including in opposing class member standing under TransUnion,” Romano said. “Preserving and marshalling the evidence relating to the incident will be central to show that plaintiff has not satisfied that burden.”

searchText: Barrage of New Laws, Regulations Coming in 2023 Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch ANALYSIS "It's going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer. January 11, 2023 at 03:13 PM Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to… Special Reports › Tech Sector Risk Watch ANALYSIS "It's going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer. January 11, 2023 at 03:13 PM Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Amendments to California's consumer-friendly privacy statute are kicking in.An SEC proposed rule would require public companies to disclose material cyber incidents within four days.A U.S. Department of Labor proposed rule would classify more workers as employers rather than contractors. A host of new laws, regulations and reporting requirements are taking effect in 2023 that will keep tech companies on their toes. State laws on pay transparency and data privacy are kicking in, and new Securities and Exchange Commission disclosure rules on climate change and cybersecurity also likely will be in the offing. The Department of Labor also is pushing a rule change that will affect the gig economy. Here is a rundown: Climate Change Disclosures Last March, the Securities and Exchange Commission proposed a rule requiring publicly traded companies to disclose climate change risks. The rule faces strong pushback as Republicans, having retaken control of the House of Representatives, have vowed to probe the SEC’s interest in climate change and other governance issues. “It’s going to be a year with a lot of fireworks and drama,” said Brad Rosen, a senior legal analyst at Wolters Kluwer. Rosen said the rule will likely become final this year despite potential roadblocks, though some of its more contentious provisions may be watered down. “It will not be a total surprise if the final rules are somewhat pared down from the initial proposals,” Rosen said. Michael Littenberg, a partner at Ropes & Gray who advises companies on environmental, social and corporate governance matters, said that while the rule will inevitably face legal challenges, companies will still be expected to comply. He added that it’s unclear whether the final rule will cover indirect emissions that occur in a company’s supply chain, known as “scope 3,” which comprise the bulk of emissions for which tech companies are responsible and can be produced by business travel, commutes and purchased goods and services. Littenberg said such emissions can be hard to quantify. Companies often rely on third-party data sources to calculate those emissions. “If scope 3 disclosures are mandatory for purposes of the rule, that raises the question of what is the liability for that data?” he said. Cybersecurity-Incident Disclosures Another SEC-proposed rule would require publicly traded companies to report “material” cybersecurity incidents within four business days of determining an event has occurred, a tight timeframe that observers say poses some risk. “You’re telling the world you’ve had an incident. If you were wrong or made misleading statements those are some of the risks and pitfalls that could come along with those types of reporting obligations,” said Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts and an expert in cybersecurity and privacy compliance. “It is now public and you cannot unring the bell.” RECOMMENDED FOR YO Whether it’s a failure to disclose or making a false statements, Baker said, “these types of disclosures are going to then be one more thing that plaintiffs and regulators will grab hold of.” Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo said it likely will be difficult for companies to determine whether an incident qualifies as disclosable. “Since the materiality of the incident is the determining factor, that puts a lot of pressure on companies—in a situation that is often very dynamic—to assess and make that determination,” said Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo, who served as regional trial counsel for the SEC. “It calls for companies to do a lot of prep work ahead of time to make that assessment if an incident comes up. It’s a matter of both making sure that information about an incident circulates to the right people on a timely basis and also making sure that they’re getting the kind of information they need.” The requirement that companies disclose their risk management practices and cybersecurity response also could leave them vulnerable to from bad actors, who could access that public information “You could give would-be attackers a road map about how to get around those risk management practices,” Longo said.
