January 11, 2023 at 04:08 PM 6 minute read Risk and Compliance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know The FTC's $520 million penalty against Fortnite over data protection is a sign of cases to come.The SEC's planned climate disclosure rules will be a minefield for companies.The Biden administration stepped up antitrust enforcement in 2022 and likely will escalate those efforts this year. General counsel are entering 2023 facing a raft of global uncertainty, regulatory risks, and legal battles with major implications for the digital economy. Lawmakers, regulators and the courts have all ramped up pressure on the tech industry and show no sign of letting up this year. How companies deal with climate change, compete for business, and collect and protect user data will be top risk areas in 2023. Data Privacy and Protection The consequences for neglecting to protect consumers’ private information are increasing in severity, and enforcement is intensifying. “General counsel can only expect enforcement activity to increase and accelerate in number,” said Todd Ruback, former chief privacy officer and general counsel for ad-blocker and privacy browser Ghostery. He said companies can expect to see more enforcement actions as states continue to adopt their own privacy laws. Companies can also anticipate a rise in class actions over wrongful data collection and third-party tracking. “It’s your obligation to know what third parties are on your website, and that’s where privacy is hard because businesses move fast and are always looking for ways to use data,” Ruback said. “There are headaches galore.” The Federal Trade Commission is also wading in on privacy. Its eye-watering $520 million penalty against Fortnite developer Epic Games for collecting data on children and duping them into making in-game purchases shows the commission is serious about enforcing data protection and privacy laws, said George Washington University Law School professor and former FTC chairman William Kovacic. “These are the largest fines that the FTC has gotten. For most general counsel that’s a significant consideration. What’s evident in just the Epic experience is the commission is making stronger and stronger demands for effective remedies and the price for violations is going up.” General counsel also will be bracing for final approval of new Securities and Exchange Commission cyberattack disclosure rules that would give public companies only four days to disclose a material incident. “Accuracy within the time frame is the risk. If you’ve suffered an incident, your focus is on your business and on identifying potentially compromised information,” said Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts and an expert in cybersecurity and privacy compliance. “Four days will go by in a flash, so to have these reporting obligations going out to the public adds a wrinkle to how you respond to this quickly and correctly.” It can be difficult for general counsels to make sure they’re in the know about privacy vulnerabilities given the pace of business, Ruback said. “Too often the general counsel is looked at as a roadblock and brought in at the 11th hour,” he said. “But the companies that are going to thrive in this new hyper-regulated world we are moving toward in the U.S. are the ones that align their general counsel with the business early and often, so he or she is sitting with the product team and software development folks and providing that sage legal advice that ‘we need to take privacy and data protection into consideration with our products.’” Climate Change Companies also are bracing for final approval of new SEC rules requiring public companies to disclose climate-related risks that could affect their business operations. This is a touchy subject for tech companies, said Will Masters, an ESG and sustainable investments consultant at Arup, as the bulk of their emissions are graded as “scope 3,” which are not produced by the company itself but are derived from intangibles like purchased goods and services, business travel and employee commutes. “Tech companies’ scope 3 emissions are massive,” he said. “And there is no way they can actually prove their scope 3 offsets.” The shift to mandatory disclosures can pose new risks for companies that previously made them voluntarily, Ropes & Gray partner Amy Jane Longo said, as shareholder suits seize on differences between old and new filings. “For companies already making climate disclosures this may impose a requirement to make disclosures in a new way, which c

searchText: Former Deputy GC at EV Company Canoo Among Execs Accused of Corporate Espionage Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology. Canoo, which… Electric vehicle startup Canoo is accusing a swath of its former C-suite executives—including deputy general counsel Michael Fielkow—of stealing trade secrets to form their own competing EV company using Canoo’s proprietary technology. Canoo, which is known for its distinctive egg-shaped auto design, filed a federal lawsuit on Dec. 22 accusing former Canoo CEO John Harris, chief technology officer Phillip Weicker, chief operating officer William Eberts, vice president Alexi Charbonneau and Fielkow of swiping Canoo’s proprietary technology and poaching its employees to create Harbinger Motors in 2021. Canoo’s complaint, first reported by Business Insider, describes the band of higher-ups as a “group of serial grifters” hellbent on owning and controlling their own EV company at any cost. Torrance, California-based Canoo also is suing Gardena, California-based Harbinger’s investors, who the company alleges ”were willing to turn a blind eye to such misconduct to enjoy a shortcut to success.” Harris, Weicker, Eberts and Charbonneau formerly worked together at another EV startup, Los Angeles-based Faraday Future, where Canoo claims the nefarious plot took shape. “Canoo believes it was at Faraday where Harris, Weicker, Eberts, and Charbonneau honed their trade craft of stealing intellectual property for personal financial gain. In lieu of starting an EV company using their own independent work, the four decided that it would be far more expeditious and inexpensive to do so by stealing privileged information and intellectual property while learning what works and doesn’t work—all at the employer’s expense,” its complaint says. Canoo, which launched in 2018, accuses the former executives of pilfering its patented EV technology; a driving platform it calls a “skateboard” that can convert gas-powered vehicles to electric at a minimal cost. The suit also alleges the executives sabotaged Canoo’s deal with step-delivery van maker Morgan Olson to integrate skateboard into that company’s existing fleet. Canoo says Harbinger suspiciously made its own deal with Morgan Olson in 2022. Reached for comment by Law.com, a spokesman for Harbinger dismissed the allegations against Fielkow and the other defendants as “baseless.” The statement said, “Harbinger and its co-founders have always operated with the utmost integrity and have never engaged in any actions that would give rise to this meritless lawsuit.” In the lawsuit, Canoo calls out Fielkow’s conduct as deserving “particular scrutiny” given that he served as Canoo’s deputy general counsel for three years. He rose to vice president of corporate legal, securities and global strategies, leaving the company in March 2022 to become Harbinger’s general counsel. Fielkow oversaw a wide-ranging scope of in-house matters at Canoo, including its “strategic transactions and investments, corporate governance, board advisory, product development, intellectual property and technology licensing, IP litigation, regulatory compliance, securities law, data privacy, and commercial contracts with suppliers and partners,” the lawsuit says. Fielkow also was part of Canoo’s business development team, the complaint notes, “where he assisted in setting and developing plans for business and revenue growth, researching and planning new market initiatives, and meeting with business partners.” This would mean Fielkow had intimate knowledge of Canoo’s business strategy, including its planned partnership with Morgan Olson. Canoo says Filekow and his colleagues “undoubtedly” used confidential information they gleaned from Canoo’s year-and-a-half-long negotiations with Morgan Olson to form the Harbinger-Morgan Olson venture. “Canoo trusted Fielkow to provide counsel free of fraud, theft, and divided loyalty. Fielkow grossly abused that trust, stealing untold amounts of Canoo’s privileged documents and communications, intellectual property, and even misrepresenting on several occasions that he would not join a competitor,” Canoo’s complaint says. It adds, “Unfortunately for Canoo, its trust in Fielkow was misplaced. Fielkow grossly abused his fiduciary position, stealing untold amounts of Canoo’s intellectual property, and even misrepresenting on several occasions that he would not join a competitor. Fielkow knew (or should have known) of the devastating impacts often caused by an attorney violating his ethical and professional responsibilities—yet he intentionally casted them aside.” Reached by Law.com, Fielkow referred questions to the Harbinger spokesman, who would not comment beyond the written statement. According to Canoo, the former executives’ scheme unraveled around March 2022

title: Risks Abound With Twitter In-House Gutting
description: A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple fronts. A legal team that once stood at 150…
preview:
A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple fronts.

A legal team that once stood at 150 employees is now closer to 10 to 20, according to a source familiar with the situation, though that figure could not be independently verified.
excerpt: A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple...
searchText: Risks Abound With Twitter In-House Gutting A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple fronts. A legal team that once stood at 150… A wholesale gutting of Twitter’s legal department in the months following Elon Musk’s $44 billion takeover has reduced its in-house team to a skeleton crew, exposing the company to risk on multiple fronts. A legal team that once stood at 150 employees is now closer to 10 to 20, according to a source familiar with the situation, though that figure could not be independently verified. Nearly all of Twitter’s senior legal leadership has resigned or been fired, leaving the company to face heightened regulatory scrutiny and a raft of federal employment litigation with presumably little guidance from the top. The departure of Twitter’s last remaining deputy general counsel Regina Lima, first reported by Bloomberg, marks the latest in the mass exodus of senior in-house lawyers. Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde was among the first to be axed when Musk took over, along with General Counsel Sean Edgett. Musk dismissed Deputy General Counsel James Baker last week over his possible role in censoring an article about President Joe Biden’s son Hunter. Musk brought in his personal lawyer Alex Spiro to help fill the leadership void, though the New York Times reported this week that Spiro has since decamped. The draining of legal talent has also forced the embattled CEO to draw on senior in-house counsel from his other companies, Tesla and SpaceX. The in-house upheaval has some observers wondering whether the company can live up to the terms of a consent decree it entered into with the Federal Trade Commission after the regulator fined it $150 million this year for continuing to mislead users about privacy protections. Though the FTC doesn’t comment on its investigations, a spokesperson said in November that it’s keeping a close watch on developments at Twitter. Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said a small in-house department isn’t necessarily a liability, but it becomes concerning in a situation such as Twitter’s, where a legal department shrinks in such an abrupt fashion. “The concerning thing is how rapidly this appears to have happened,” he said. “It raises the risk that things are going to fall through the cracks.” Foehl, who also served as general counsel at ACA International and has a long history of working with regulatory bodies, said the FTC has no patience for companies and executive who fail to follow its orders. “I have a lot of experience sitting across the table with regulators, and one of the things that really makes their skin crawl is when their consent orders are not complied with,” he said. “You’re sending the message that you’re not taking the regulator seriously and that’s a big problem because the regulator is much more likely to bring its full enforcement power to bear.” In the last five months, all of the executives on Twitter’s Data Governance Committee responsible for sending quarterly updates to the FTC were fired or left the company, said a source familiar with the committee’s operations. The departures, borne out in media reports, include chief compliance officer Marianne Fogarty, chief information security officer Lea Kissner, and revenue product head Bruce Falck. Former Airbnb general counsel and chief ethics officer Rob Chesnut said Twitter’s regulatory vulnerability bears some similarity to the case of Joseph Sullivan, the former security chief at Uber who is currently fighting his conviction for concealing a 2016 data security breach from authorities and obstructing an FTC investigation of Uber’s security practices. “There are factors in that case that are also present here,” Chesnut said. “Uber had a track record of being close to the edge, in the grey, and even beyond it when it had to deal with regulators. If you have a company like that, you don’t get a break. And if a prosecutor gets a chance to take a shot and there’s any violation of law, you have problem.” Chesnut said the stakes are high for Twitter, whose new owner has a history of contempt for regulators. “Anybody involved in this area at the company has to do everything they can to ensure the FTC order is complied with, and if not, they need to make sure everyone high up at the company is aware of the problem,” he said. Foehl said Musk’s shaky history with regulators, combined with the revolving door of general counsels, is worrisome. “Those two things in combination are really what’s causing the concern here, and the expressed concern from the FTC,” he said.

title: US Judge Disinclined to Overturn Former Uber Security Chief's Conviction in Data Breach Case
description: "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber security chief of concealing a data breach in 2016
preview:
A federal judge said Wednesday that he's inclined to uphold a jury verdict finding former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan guilty of trying to cover up a 2016 data breach, a conviction that rocked the cybersecurity community in October.

Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers.
excerpt: "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber...
searchText: US Judge Disinclined to Overturn Former Uber Security Chief's Conviction in Data Breach Case "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," Joe Sullivan's defense attorney John Cline told a federal judge who said he's not likely to overturn a jury's verdict convicting the former Uber security chief of concealing a data breach in 2016 A federal judge said Wednesday that he's inclined to uphold a jury verdict finding former Uber security chief Joe Sullivan guilty of trying to cover up a 2016 data breach, a conviction that rocked the cybersecurity community in October. Sullivan had only been on the job a few months when two hackers broke into Uber's Amazon data storage server in October 2016 and swiped the personal information of 57 million app users, including names, phone numbers, email addresses and 600,000 driver's license numbers. Assistant U.S. Attorney Andrew Dawson said Sullivan orchestrated the cover-up and hid it from both his employers and the Federal Trade Commission, which was investigating Uber's data security practices in the wake of a different data breach in 2014. Sullivan met with Federal Trade Commission regulators investigating Uber's security practices in 2016, assuring them that Uber had addressed the security vulnerabilities that led up to the 2014 breach, such as reusing passwords and storing data access keys on a public GitHub page. Just 10 days later, hackers breached Uber's AWS servers a second time in a similar fashion. Dawson said that knowing the second hack would "play very badly" with regulators, Sullivan bought the two hackers off with a payment of $100,000 and funneled it through Uber's bug-bounty program. "Sullivan knew exactly what he had done. He covered up a data breach, he covered up a crime and he obstructed the FTC's effort to safeguard user data," Dawson told the jury, describing Sullivan's actions as "comprehensive and calculated." Sullivan also signed off on a letter proposing that the FTC close its two-year investigation and enter into a settlement agreement. "Joe was supportive of proceeding with the recommendation to settle," former in-house attorney Sabrina Ross testified at the trial. Sullivan was fired in 2017, Uber CEO Dara Khosrowshahi said at trial. In 2020 the ex-security chief was charged with one count of obstructing the FTC's investigation and one count of misprision of felony for concealing the breach from authorities. His prosecution is believed to be the first instance of a company executive being held criminally liable for a security breach. Matthew Baker, a partner at Baker Botts specializing in cybersecurity and incident response, said it is rare for the government to charge someone with taking affirmative steps to conceal a felony, but prosecutors could feel emboldened by Sullivan's conviction. "The fact that it was used here—and used successfully—should make any in-house counsel for any company perk their ears up," Baker told ALM. "There's a very interesting legal precedent that will create ripples from a compliance perspective." At a hearing Wednesday on Sullivan's motion for acquittal or a new trial, his attorney John Cline argued that the government failed to show Sullivan had a duty to disclose the breach, and that prosecutors made only a general contention that Uber's in-house counsel relied on Sullivan and his team to keep them updated on any significant security developments that would require disclosure. U.S. District Judge William Orrick, who presided over the nearly monthlong jury trial in September, was unconvinced. "I think there was more than sufficient evidence to sustain a conviction," he said. Dawson said there was much more to Sullivan's obstructive actions than mere omission. "There's misrepresentation, there's concealment, there's hush money, there's a variety of obstructive acts and the Ninth Circuit has recognized the variety with which obstruction can be accomplished," he said. "I would urge the court not to get caught up in just the omission slice. There was a more comprehensive strategy rather than sitting in a corner and staying silent." Cline said he plans to appeal the conviction and will likely rely on the Ninth Circuit's recent ruling in United States v. Kirst to support the argument that Sullivan did not make affirmative misrepresentations to the FTC, and that simply failing to inform authorities of the breach is not enough to support a conviction. "We're flexing our rhetorical muscles for the appeal," he told Orrick. The judge replied, "well-flexed," and took the arguments under submission. In-house legal chiefs already bristling at outside counsel rate hikes may find themselves chafing at Big Law’s rollout of year-end bonuses, many in the six-figure range for eighth year associates. While these events are hardly unexpected, they are also playing out amid widespread tech industry layoffs and an undercurrent of economic precarity that lends an air of insouciance to this year’s parade of bonus announcements. “Law firms face serious pressures to attract and retain talent that is of appropriate quality, and they’re certainly entitled to compensate their professionals appropriately. No one is going to debate that fact. The bigger issue is the context. Many in-house counsel are struggling to retain their teams and they’re only allowed to give out meager pay increases and modest bonuses, so it strikes many reasonable people as just not fair,” said Jason Winmill, managing partner at Argopoint, a consulting firm that advises Fortune 500 legal departments. Shrinking budgets already have legal departments on edge, especially as general counsel are being asked to take on more responsibilities without commensurate pay raises. Frederick Paulmann, a former senior attorney at Pfizer Inc. and founder of The Counsel Management Group, said associate bonuses could be regarded as a questionable decision, given both the general economic climate and reports of law firm and tech industry layoffs. “Against this backdrop, it is by no means clear that associate bonus decisions will sit well with clients,” he said. It could also leave in-house clients wondering whether they’re footing the bill. “A key related question that often occurs but doesn’t always get asked is how are the bonuses funded – from partners’ pockets or on the backs of clients? If law firms choose to issue bonuses, and at the same time are committing to no rate increases into next year, then that’s a much different story. This is especially true if they have found other ways to save, whether it be shrinking their real estate footprint or using technology more effectively. But if law firms seek to grant these bonuses, and at the same time are planning on significant rate increases to fund compensation, then that would not sit as well,” Paulmann said. Some legal chiefs said they didn’t mind the bonuses so much, but noted that excessive base pay for junior associates is often a main driver of high legal bills, particularly when in-house lawyers with years of experience usually make less than lower-level associates. Generous bonus awards have the dual function of retaining top legal talent while signaling a firm’s success and prestige. In-house counsel with outside law firm experience said they understood that the publicity around year-end bonuses can be an incentive for associates who work long hours on high-risk matters. “The announcement of year-end bonuses doesn’t concern me. I come from Big Law myself, so I understand that publishing year-end bonuses is a part of associate talent attraction and retention. December 06, 2022 Elon Musk fired another member of Twitter’s legal top brass, confirming in a tweet on Tuesday that Deputy General Counsel James Baker was “exited from the company” because of his possible role in censoring an article about President Joe Biden’s son Hunter. “In light of concerns about Baker’s possible role in suppression of information important to the public dialogue, he was exited from Twitter today,” Musk wrote. The brouhaha involves a 2020 New York Post article that raised questions about the propriety of Hunter Biden’s business dealings in Ukraine. Musk has been critical of Twitter’s decision to block the article on Twitter, saying last spring that it was “incredibly inappropriate.” The article was sourced from files discovered on Biden’s laptop after he left it at a computer repair shop and never retrieved it. The owner of the shop turned over the laptop to the FBI, but not before copying the hard drive and giving it to former New York City Mayor Rudy Giuliani’s lawyer, Robert Costello, according to the Post’s article. Giuliani later gave a copy to the Post. Musk’s tweet Tuesday came in response to Twitter posts by Matt Taibbi, who publishes the Substack newsletter TK News, that cited emails and other internal documents shedding light on the company’s decision to limit dissemination of certain information before the 2020 presidential election, including the New York Post report. Also on Twitter, Taibbi posted a column by George Washington University School of Law professor Jonathan Turley asserting that Baker had been part of an effort to smother coverage that raised questions about Hunter Biden’s conduct. The disclosures are being widely described by conservative media as the “Twitter files.” The trove of documents posted by Taibbi included email discussions among Twitter executives, including former Chief Legal Officer Vijaya Gadde and former trust and safety chief Yoel Roth about banning the New York Post’s article from the platform under its “hacked materials” policy. “The policy basis is hacked materials—though, as discussed, this is an emerging situation where the facts remain unclear,” Roth wrote. “Can we truthfully claim that this is part of the policy?” former global communications head Brandon Borrman asked. Baker responded in the chain, “I support the conclusion that we need more facts to assess whether the materials were hacked. At this stage however, it is reasonable for us to assume that they may have been and that caution is warranted. “There are some facts that indicate that the materials may have been hacked, while there are others indicating that the computer was either abandoned and/or the owner consented to allow the repair shop to access it for at least some purposes. We simply need more information,” Baker added. Musk on Tuesday said he communicated with Baker about his possible role in censoring information but found his characterization of what occurred “unconvincing.” Baker, a former FBI general counsel and former CNN legal analyst, had been with Twitter as deputy general counsel and vice president of legal since 2020. He is the latest victim of Musk’s housecleaning at Twitter’s legal department since he completed the $44 billion purchase of the San Francisco-based social media giant on Oct. 27. Very excited to join this team!” Jean said in announcing her new position Monday on LinkedIn. Jean has developed extensive expertise in data privacy compliance, coming off a nearly four-year stint at AARP. As senior vice president and chief privacy officer, she helped the Washington, D.C.-based organization protect the data of its 38 million members when it shifted its operations to the virtual realm during the pandemic. “What I appreciate so much about privacy is that you’re doing technical, challenging, and interesting work, but fundamentally, you’re helping protect people,” she told Modern Counsel in an interview earlier this year. She also led data compliance efforts at media giant Bloomberg, including ensuring that it complied with the European Union’s General Data Protection Regulation. Her background makes her well-suited to lead the legal department at 3E, which counts top pharmaceutical and global chemical manufacturers such as Bayer, Dow and SC Johnson among the clients it advises on workplace and product safety, risk management and supply chain regulatory compliance. The company did not respond to a request for comment on its new hire, but noted in a press release earlier this year that it plans to expand its environmental, health, safety, and sustainability footprint worldwide. Earlier this year, Verisk Analytics sold the Carlsbad, California-based company to investment firms New Mountain and Endicott for up to $950 million in cash.

AT&T will pay $6.25 million to settle Securities and Exchange Commission charges that three of its executives in 2016 leaked internal smartphone sales data to Wall Street analysts to avoid falling short of revenue forecasts. It was the largest-ever penalty a case alleging a violation of the agency’s fair-disclosure rule, which bars selective sharing of "material nonpublic information” to market professionals and shareholders. The SEC said AT&T sought to avoid investor disappointment—and a drop in stock price— by getting analysts to lower their revenue forecasts to a number the company could beat when it announced its results to the public on April 26, 2016. AT&T learned in March 2016 that its smartphone sales were lower than expected and that it would likely fail to meet analysts’ revenue estimates for that quarter, according to a complaint the regulator filed in New York federal court last year. According to the SEC, the agency says three investor-relations executives made private calls to analysts at roughly 20 firms, where they gave them details about smartphone sales and their impact on internal revenue metrics. The three executives—Christopher Womack, Michael Black and Kent Evans—also will pay $25,000 each. “The actions allegedly taken by AT&T executives to avoid falling short of analysts’ projections are precisely the type of conduct Regulation FD was designed to prevent,” Gurbir Grewal, director of the SEC’s Division of Enforcement, said in a statement Monday. A company spokesperson said neither AT&T nor its executives admitted or denied any wrongdoing. “We are committed to following all applicable laws and pleased to have resolution with the SEC,” the spokesperson said in an emailed statement.”

The tidal wave of layoffs sweeping through the tech industry is putting legal departments to the test, as in-house counsel seek to mitigate risk and ensure their companies carry out the cuts as humanely as possible. Following years of feverish hiring, tech companies are retrenching. Just in November, 196 companies cut more than 51,000 tech workers, according to Layoffs.fyi, which tracks job losses in the industry. Foster Sayers, general counsel at contract management software company Pramata, said legal chiefs have an important role to play in helping companies implement layoffs thoughtfully while avoiding running afoul of labor laws. Twitter’s recent mass job cuts provide a glaring example of what to avoid. The company is facing at least three class actions alleging the social media giant violated the federal Worker Adjustment and Retraining Notification Act, which requires companies to provide at least 60 days’ notice before cutting at least 50 full-time employees at a single location. Twitter also is facing allegations that it is shorting employees on severance. On top of that, it has faced widespread criticism for locking some employees out of their email before telling them they’d lost their jobs. Sayers said in-house counsel should try to make the best of a bad situation for laid-off employees by ensuring they tailor separation agreements to ensure employees don’t feel cheated. He noted that a friend who was laid off from Twitter revoked his separation agreement because it did not account for the equity that had been part of his compensation. “He felt that he was very clearly promised one outcome, but the severance package offered was not what was promised,” Sayers said. “I’m sure it was drafted from some boilerplate language that outside counsel had. In-house needs to be ready to rise to the occasion and rapidly develop some competency around separation agreements. You have to take the time to own your separation agreement and not just rely on outside counsel.” Sayers said in-house counsel can head off cybersecurity issues by ensuring that separation agreements obligate employees to return their equipment, as well as their logins and credentials. “People just don’t do this, and it’s a huge oversight. Cybersecurity is such a going concern and companies can’t afford to be neglectful,” he said. He added: “Make sure you have a seat at the table, so when your chief technology officer is talking to your head of DevOps and other parts of the business, you can say, ‘Look, this is what we need to be prepared to manage as we off-board employees.’ If you’re not actually at the table, you’re not going to be as effective in getting out in front of these issues.” Des Lafleur, a business attorney and lecturer at the UC Berkeley School of Law who consults with companies on minimizing risk, said cybersecurity is something companies should be thinking about well before employees depart the company. “If you’re worrying about it once the person is departing, you haven’t done enough in the beginning,” she said. Top in-house lawyers in the job market are ratcheting down their appetite for risk, favoring stable, less flashy companies as economic headwinds buffet the tech industry and venture-backed startups. Recruiters say candidates also are seeking more of their compensation in cash instead of stock options. Options can soar if a company hits it big. But many recent grants have slid underwater, amid falling tech stock prices and declining valuations at startups. “Those fly-by-night, Series A companies people would quit their law firm jobs for—no one is quitting for them now,” said Sean Burke, founding partner of the boutique legal recruiting firm Whistler Partners. “There’s definitely right now a huge shift toward prioritizing security and maybe going with a resume builder that has a higher base salary or stock at an actual public company, and not options,” he said. The tech industry has long made equity a significant part of compensation packages, an approach that often makes attorneys, many of them risk-averse by nature, uneasy even in brighter economic environments. That anxiety is even higher these days, recruiters say. “Stock is certainly something candidates think about and worry about as they think about an opportunity. If the company sounds promising and they aren’t as competitive on the cash, sometimes candidates are willing to take a risk on the equity. But given what the current market is, candidates have been a little more hesitant,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “Especially at private companies, candidates are going to be doing as much due diligence as possible every step of the way because it is a real concern that they may be out of the job if there’s not a lot of funding,” Guo said. Mike Evers, president of Evers Legal Search, said job candidates continue to find tech jobs alluring. But the last year has been sobering, amid a deluge of job cuts. Layoffs.fyi tallies that 898 tech companies have laid off 142,942 employees this year. “Nothing has changed with the startup culture, but they are risky and your equity might end up being worthless and you might end up out of a job. The last 12 months have told us that risk is real, and a lot of lawyers have hunkered down into the mindset of risk aversion,” he said. Evers said he recently received a call from an attorney at the e-scooter startup Bird, famous for achieving unicorn status when its valuation hit $1 billion in 2018. But its meteoric rise preceded a swift decent. After going public last year through a special purpose acquisition company merger, its stock has fallen from $8.40 to 23 cents. Evers said positions at startups such as Bird that offered employees a chunk of equity have lost much of their luster. “One of the attorneys who left a major law firm to take one of those sexy, highly competitive jobs just made a change to go work in the legal department at United Airlines. You can’t get more opposite than that,” he said. “We’re now seeing that not every startup situation is a golden job,” he added. “The desire to take those sexy jobs hasn’t changed, but we’re in a period where there are less of them, and there are some lawyers who are proactively looking for exit strategies from startups.” Burke said the challenging environment for tech companies also is spurring lawyers who earlier jumped from law firms to in-house to consider returning to law firms. “Right now there’s more than one IP transaction or SAS licensing attorney who is saying to themselves, ‘I’m working 60-80 hours a week, I’m making less than at a law firm, and now I have stock options that are worth nothing,” he said. “Law firms are steady money, it’s guaranteed, there’s more of a safety net,” he said. “And law firms with tech clients love a lawyer that used to work for a startup, because it shows they are a problem solver—a Wild West lawyer who has handled all kinds of different things. That in-house experience is proof that you’re a bad ass.”

November 23, 2022 at 07:41 AM 6 minute read Corporate Governance Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Horacio Gutierrez must adapt to the new strategies and style of CEO Bob Iger.The board Sunday fired CEO Bob Chapek, the man who hired him.Legal observers say Iger will assess whether he and Gutierrez are on the same page. Horacio Gutierrez landed one of the top legal jobs in the world last December—general counsel of The Walt Disney Co. But just months into the job, the board has fired Bob Chapek—the man who hired him—a sudden shift that presents the first big test for the former Spotify chief legal officer. Legal observers say the big question is whether Gutierrez can conform to new CEO Bob Iger’s vision as he undos some changes by Chapek, whom the board dismissed Sunday after nearly three years at the helm. The change-out occurred after the company reported terrible fiscal fourth-quarter results on Nov. 8, and Chapek was widely criticized for nonetheless striking an upbeat tone during a conference call with analysts later that day. While Iger hasn’t revealed specifics, he said in a staff memo that he will be instituting “organizational and operating changes,” adding, “It is my intention to restructure things in a way that honors and respects creativity as the heart and soul of who we are,” with more control shifting to content-creating teams. Robert Foehl, a professor of law and business ethics at Ohio University, said Iger will assess whether Gutierrez fits into his new vision of the company. “Any time you have a CEO shakeup of any sort, the first idea is, will the general counsel be around? A lot of times when you have CEO changes, the CEO likes to ensure their direct reports and executive management team are all in alignment and can work well together, especially in a situation where you are trying to right the ship,” he said. “The reality of it is, when you’re steering a large ship like this, the executive team needs to be a well-oiled machine and all be on the same page on where the company is going to go and how it’s going to get there. If that’s not the case, the strategy is sort of doomed to failure.” Randy Milch, a former executive vice president and general counsel of Verizon, said Gutierrez has the chops to weather the changes. Gutierrez has more than 35 years of legal experience. He joined Spotify in 2016, starting out as vice president of business and legal affairs. Three years later, the company promoted him to head of global affairs and chief legal officer. He came to Spotify from Microsoft, where he’d spent 17 years, rising to general counsel. This is Iger’s second go-round as Disney CEO. He spent 15 years at the helm of the Burbank, California-based company, a period when it prospered, before retiring in 2020. He remained on the board until stepping down as executive chairman at the end of last year, nine days after the company announced the hiring of Gutierrez as senior executive vice president and general counsel. “Gutierrez has been a senior lawyer at a bunch of companies for quite a long time. I think he’s as well positioned as anyone to understand what happens in the corporate structure when the CEO changes,” Milch said. “The thing that is a little bit different here is that Iger was the CEO for a very long time, very successfully. He had a structure in place and his successor changed that structure, and Iger seems to be saying more or less that he’s going to change the structure back to the way it was.” Gutierrez succeeded Alan Braverman, who retired after nearly two decades as general counsel. Braverman regularly ranked among the highest-paid GCs in the country. In 2021, he received total compensation of $16.6 million. That included $8.8 million in cash—more than any other legal chief. Gutierrez has a rich pay package, as well. His employment agreement shows he could earn more than $22 million in his first year, including an initial stock grant of $10 million and a $2 million signing bonus. Gutierrez, who could not be reached for comment for this story, started his new job in February. He is one of the newer faces on Disney’s leadership roster, which includes longtime executives Alan Bergman, Rebecca Campbell, James Pitaro and Christine McCarthy. Milch, the former Verizon general counsel, said Chapek’s ouster fundamentally changes Gutierrez’s job. “When you’re a new general counsel, you come in and you have a CEO who has not been there very long who is remolding the place. searchText: Senior Attorney at Swiss Re Takes Legal Reins of Climate-Risk Startup Matthew Gabin says he wants to help Arbol "reinvent the way the world manages climate risk." November 22, 2022 at 12:16 PM 2 minute read News Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Arbol has hired Matthew Gabin as chief legal officer and deputy chief… Matthew Gabin says he wants to help Arbol "reinvent the way the world manages climate risk." November 22, 2022 at 12:16 PM 2 minute read News Maria Dinzeo What You Need to Know Arbol has hired Matthew Gabin as chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer.Gabin has extensive experience in insurance products that help companies manage climate risks.Gabin joins Arbol from Swiss Re, where he was a divisional general counsel. Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer. Gabin is a veteran in-house lawyer with expertise in insurance-linked securities, where investors speculate on events like hurricanes or earthquakes, and contracts involving weather risk transfer, where policyholders are compensated for losses stemming from extreme weather. He also has experience in parametric insurance and reinsurance, which offers policyholders a set amount of compensation for trigger events like environmental disasters. At Zurich-based reinsurance group Swiss Re, Gabin was general counsel for its weather risk and commodity trading businesses. He also advised insurers, investment firms and corporates at global white shoe law firm Mayer Brown. Prior to that, he spent nearly 10 years at Allianz Risk Transfer, providing legal and operational advice on alternative risk transfer, a non-traditional insurance product that allows companies to purchase coverage and transfer risk without using commercial insurance. “We are excited to welcome a colleague who has such relevant experience advising some of the world’s leading reinsurers on parametric risk transfer, weather risk and other areas so close to our core business,” Arbol founder and CEO Sid Jha said in a statement. Jha said Gabin’s specialized experience will be critical to the New York City-based company as it broadens its reach into new markets and verticals. In addition to building out Arbol’s legal and compliance teams, Gabin will help oversee the company’s operations and global expansion. According to its website, Arbol uses climate data, blockchain and an AI-powered pricing platform to help its clients “achieve financial climate resilience” through customized insurance to mitigate climate risk. It boasts a rapid settlements and quick payouts based on predetermined data triggers. “Parametric insurance is an indispensable tool for boosting resilience and closing the protection gap, and I’m thrilled to join a team that is driving innovation in the space,” Gabin said in a statement. “Arbol has achieved a lot in a short period of time and is positioning itself as a leader in parametric insurance and climate risk solutions for businesses globally. I look forward to putting my skills to work to help Arbol reinvent the way the world manages climate risk.”

The Federal Trade Commission is taking a tougher stance on companies that fail to safeguard consumer data—and is even going so far as to hold individuals personally accountable for those failings. Two recent cases demonstrate the agency’s willingness to go after individuals. In early October, a federal jury convicted former Uber security chief Joseph Sullivan of concealing a 2016 data breach from law enforcement and obstructing an investigation by the FTC into Uber’s security practices. A federal judge will hear his motion for acquittal next month. The FTC late last month penalized alcohol delivery platform Drizly and its CEO, James Cory Rellas, for a data breach that exposed the personal information of 2.5 million customers. The order personally applies to Rellas. Should he go to another company that collects consumer information, he’d have to follow additional data-security requirements. “CEOs who take shortcuts on security should take note,” Samuel Levine, director of the FTC’s Bureau of Consumer Protection, warned in a statement. “I think there is a gradually developing trend to hold senior officials personally accountable,” said former FTC chairman William Kovacic, now a professor at the George Washington University School of Law. “The source of the trend comes foremost from the concern that the traditional approach, which has emphasized institutional accountability, fails to create incentives for effective compliance.” He said the movement has been accelerated in part by the Cambridge Analytica scandal, where the commission imposed a hefty $5 billion fine and other restrictions on Facebook for collecting and selling users’ personal data. While the FTC did not name CEO Mark Zuckerberg, it required him to periodically certify the company’s compliance with the privacy reforms outlined in its order or face civil and criminal penalties. “I think as we carry this ahead, when the government imposes remedies and accepts settlements though negotiation, these kinds of provisions that require the CEO to sign … are going to be more common,” Kovacic said. The FTC’s order against Drizly carried no fines but threatened Rellas and the company with financial sanctions if they fail to destroy unnecessary customer data or fail to limit data collection and protect against future data breaches. In his statement, the FTC’s Levine said the agency’s action “ensures the CEO faces consequences for the company’s carelessness.” RECOMMENDED FOR YOU Book Internet and Online Law This authoritative work describes the nature and growth of the law of the Internet and explains the legal obligations, opportunities, rights, and risks inherent in this c... title: Senior Attorney at Swiss Re Takes Legal Reins of Climate-Risk Startup
description: Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer. Gabin is a veteran…
preview:
Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer.

Gabin is a veteran in-house lawyer with expertise in insurance-linked securities, where investors speculate on events like hurricanes or earthquakes, and contracts involving weather risk transfer, where policyholders are compensated for losses stemming from extreme weather.

searchText: Senior Attorney at Swiss Re Takes Legal Reins of Climate-Risk Startup Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer. Gabin is a veteran… Arbol, a four-year-old company that helps businesses analyze and manage climate risk, has hired Matthew Gabin, a divisional general counsel at insurance giant Swiss Re, to be chief legal officer and deputy chief operating officer. Gabin is a veteran in-house lawyer with expertise in insurance-linked securities, where investors speculate on events like hurricanes or earthquakes, and contracts involving weather risk transfer, where policyholders are compensated for losses stemming from extreme weather. He also has experience in parametric insurance and reinsurance, which offers policyholders a set amount of compensation for trigger events like environmental disasters. At Zurich-based reinsurance group Swiss Re, Gabin was general counsel for its weather risk and commodity trading businesses. He also advised insurers, investment firms and corporates at global white shoe law firm Mayer Brown. Prior to that, he spent nearly 10 years at Allianz Risk Transfer, providing legal and operational advice on alternative risk transfer, a non-traditional insurance product that allows companies to purchase coverage and transfer risk without using commercial insurance. “We are excited to welcome a colleague who has such relevant experience advising some of the world’s leading reinsurers on parametric risk transfer, weather risk and other areas so close to our core business,” Arbol founder and CEO Sid Jha said in a statement. Jha said Gabin’s specialized experience will be critical to the New York City-based company as it broadens its reach into new markets and verticals. In addition to building out Arbol’s legal and compliance teams, Gabin will help oversee the company’s operations and global expansion. According to its website, Arbol uses climate data, blockchain and an AI-powered pricing platform to help its clients “achieve financial climate resilience” through customized insurance to mitigate climate risk. It boasts a rapid settlements and quick payouts based on predetermined data triggers. “Parametric insurance is an indispensable tool for boosting resilience and closing the protection gap, and I’m thrilled to join a team that is driving innovation in the space,” Gabin said in a statement. “Arbol has achieved a lot in a short period of time and is positioning itself as a leader in parametric insurance and climate risk solutions for businesses globally. I look forward to putting my skills to work to help Arbol reinvent the way the world manages climate risk.”

The staggering degree of mismanagement and laxity called out in a court filing by new FTX CEO John Ray sent shockwaves through the legal community, raising the question of what level of culpability, if any, may rest with the platform’s legal division. “Never in my career have I seen such a complete failure of corporate controls and such a complete absence of trustworthy financial information as occurred here,” wrote the new CEO, who past experience includes supervising Enron’s notorious bankruptcy. “From compromised systems integrity and faulty regulatory oversight abroad, to the concentration of control in the hands of a very small group of inexperienced, unsophisticated and potentially compromised individuals, this situation is unprecedented.” While the extent of the implosion underway at FTX may be unprecedented, the chaos serves as a cautionary tale for in-house attorneys on how to avoid a similar crisis. “If you are a general counsel or an in-house lawyer—you don’t have to be in crypto trading—anybody in these roles can be thinking, ‘Could I be in this situation where management is engaged in doing something inappropriate, and what is my responsibility, based on what I directly knew or the red flags that should have led me to ask questions, to have detected that?” Baker Botts partner Michael Ward said. “And if I was aware or didn’t ask reasonable questions, what is my personal liability?’ ” said Ward, a former federal prosecutor who also worked for years as a chief compliance officer at companies like Adobe, Cisco and Juniper Networks. Ward added: “The best strategy is not to put your head in the sand but to be diligent and proactive to identify problems and solve them. You wouldn’t want to rely on a lack of knowledge as a strategy. Be attentive to red flags and follow up on them.” Little is known publicly so far about what went on behind the scenes with FTX’s legal team, other than the bulk of its compliance and legal staff quit earlier this week, including General Counsel Can Sun, whose LinkedIn page shows him now working at a stealth mode blockchain startup. Ryne Miller, general counsel for FTX’s U.S. subsidiary, is still with the company, and in a Slack message reviewed by the Wall Street Journal, he bemoaned the opacity of its top brass. “I have very limited transparency, and more is not possible without full cooperation from the founders,” he wrote. “I thought of that as a takeaway,” Jennifer Judge, former in-house attorney and general counsel who co-hosts the Lawyers Behaving Badly podcast, said of Miller’s admission. Neither Miller nor Sun responded to messages from Law.com. Lack of transparency from the top is a major headache for in-house counsel. For Judge, it’s a red flag. “I would be really wary of working with a business team where you felt like you didn’t have the full picture, especially when it comes to financials and holding other people’s money,” she said. “You hope when you’re hired, especially as a general counsel, you are hired on not to just provide legal advice but as a strategic spot leader. If the CEO clearly doesn’t want your legal advice or strategic judgment, there’s only so far you can go in terms of being at that company.” Foster Sayers, the general counsel at contract management software company Pramata, echoed that point. “Attorneys need to be as involved as they can be to be successful as in-house counsel,” he said. “If you want to be an effective in-house counsel, then you make yourself a seat at the table.” Sayers said it’s problematic when a general counsel is in the dark about business decisions. “It’s in those meetings where you hear the things that come up, when you can be proactive. Often we are too reactive. They come to us when things go sideways. In-house legal… What You Need to Know Companies face an increasingly risky regulatory landscape.They'll continue to need specialized expertise in areas like antitrust and privacy.Indiscriminate legal cuts would be short-sighted, legal observers say. In-house legal teams across big tech are feeling the pinch as companies put the brakes on their legal hiring sprees in response to economic concerns, but they will still need attorneys with specialized skills to see them through the tough regulatory road ahead. “The tech industry experienced unprecedented growth over the last couple of years, which is the reason for the incredible volume of hiring,” said Lina Guo, a managing director for Major, Lindsey & Africa’s in-house counsel recruiting team in San Francisco. “The current layoffs in the industry have been more of a market correction given the hiring frenzy over the last couple of years.” That rapid expansion includes e-commerce giant Amazon, whose legal team grew from 800 in 2017 to a LinkedIn directory listing more than 1,800 people employed in some corporate counsel capacity. Facebook parent Meta Platforms also went on a hiring spree last year in the face of tightening privacy regulations. Now both companies have moved to cut staffing levels amid a business slump. “In the last year and a half, all the big tech companies—Facebook, Twitter, Google, Apple, Netflix—they’ve all grown explosively. Now no one is growing,” observed one Bay Area recruiter who spoke on the condition of anonymity. “There’s no ‘we need to hire lawyers to keep up with the growing demand of business.’ Any hiring is very strategic.” Guo with Major, Lindsey & Africa also said in-house hiring has fallen off, but there’s still a demand for attorneys with specialized expertise. “We have seen a slowdown in terms of legal hiring, but we are still having companies and clients coming to us looking for skilled attorneys. We haven’t seen a huge slash in legal departments. That’s not to say lawyers aren’t being laid off, but, at the end of the day, any company that’s looking to grow or pivot is going to need great lawyers.” Guo said attorneys with privacy, compliance or transactional experience will have more favorable prospects. “Privacy attorneys are still very much in demand, and attorneys with specific transaction experience will continue to be fine, even if they have been laid off, given that skills set its very marketable,” she said. “Also attorneys with general corporate and securities experience. Although not as many companies are going public, at the end of the day, if you’re a public company or private company looking to go public, having corporate securities experience is valuable.” As regulators continue to bear down on tech companies over privacy, antitrust and corporate governance, cuts to in-house legal teams may be shortsighted, legal observers say. “I would think it would be at least pretty risky,” said Joshua Davis, a research professor at UC Hastings College of the Law and an expert in antitrust litigation. “There was a perfect storm where Republicans perceived many of these companies as anti-Republican, and Democrats are concerned with market power. And that means really big companies like Facebook and Amazon and Apple—the true monsters—they’ve been really vulnerable. I don’t think that’s changed. Credit… What You Need to Know S&P did not admit or deny the allegations but agreed to a censure.The ratings agency had self-reported the conduct.This is the SEC's second conflict-of-interest enforcement action against a ratings agency this year. Credit ratings giant S&P Global on Monday agreed to pay the U.S. Securities and Exchange Commission $2.5 million to settle charges that it violated the regulator’s rules against conflicts of interest. The SEC found that over five days in August 2017, S&P commercial employees, who are responsible for maintaining relationships with the companies that hire S&P to rate their debt, tried several times to influence colleagues who were determining the rating for a company’s jumbo residential mortgage-backed securities. The regulator says that while correspondence went through S&P’s compliance department, some emails commercial employees sent to the S&P analytical team contained statements conveying sales and marketing considerations. In a statement, the SEC said it found that “as a result of the content, urgent nature, high volume, and compressed timing of the communications, the S&P commercial employees became participants in the rating process during a time when they were influenced by sales and marketing considerations.” SEC rules prohibit ratings agencies from allowing sales and marketing considerations to influence credit ratings. New York-based S&P self-reported its employees’ conduct to the SEC, cooperated with the regulator’s investigation, and took steps to bolster its conflicts-of-interest policies. S&P did not admit or deny the charges but agreed to the entry of a cease-and-desist order, a censure, and other compliance measures on top of the $2.5 million penalty. While it declined to comment specifically on the settlement, S&P said in a statement that it “takes compliance with regulatory obligations very seriously and is committed to the integrity of its ratings process and high-quality independent credit ratings,” and that it is “pleased to have concluded this matter.” This is the SEC’s second enforcement action against a credit rating agency this year. In June, it alleged that Egan-Jones Rating Co. and its CEO, Sean Egan, were influenced by a client’s marketing activities while determining its credit rating, creating a conflict of interest. The firm settled the charges for $1.7 million, without an admission of any wrongdoing, and Egan agreed to pay $300,000.

The attack happened in the… SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Paul Pelosi, real estate investor and husband of House Speaker Nancy Pelosi, was violently assaulted in his San Francisco home in what appeared to be a targeted home invasion early Friday morning. The attack happened in the Pelosi’s home on Broadway Street in the tony neighborhood of Pacific Heights. At a press conference Friday, San Francisco Police Chief Bill Scott identified the assailant as 42-year-old David Depape. He declined to answer questions about how Depape was able to get into the home. Scott said the attack happened at roughly 2:30 a.m. Friday. When officers arrived at the home, they found Depape and Mr. Pelosi in the midst of a struggle. "Our officers observed and Mr. Pelosi both holding a hammer. The suspect pulled the hammer away from Mr. Pelosi and violently assaulted him with it. Our officers immediately tackled the suspect, disarmed him, took him into custody, requested emergency backup and rendered medical aid." The Associated Press has reported that Pelosi, 82, suffered blunt force trauma to his head and body. According to the AP, Depape shouted “Where is Nancy, where is Nancy?” during the attack. Scott said both the suspect and Pelosi were taken to the hospital for treatment. "The motive for this attack is still being determined," he said, adding that Depape will be booked on charges of attempted homicide, assault with deadly weapon, elder abuse, burglary and "several other additional felonies." "This is an active investigation currently being led by the SFPD's special investigation's division," Scott said. The Capitol Police said in a statement that Speaker Pelosi was in Washington with her protective detail at the time of the break-in. While “the motivation for the attack is still under investigation,” Capitol Police said it is assisting the FBI and the San Francisco Police Department with its investigation. In an evening press conference Friday, Scott said the attack was not intentional but could not give more information. He also clarified that a neighbor called 911, not Paul Pelosi as previously reported. Scott said the department could offer no new information, and referred inquiries about Pelosi's condition to a statement released by Pelosi's spokesperson Drew Hammill, which offered scant details. “Early this morning, an assailant broke into the Pelosi residence in San Francisco and violently assaulted Mr. Pelosi. The assailant is in custody and the motivation for the attack is under investigation. Mr. Pelosi was taken to the hospital, where he is receiving excellent medical care and is expected to make a full recovery. The Speaker was not in San Francisco at the time. “The Speaker and her family are grateful to the first responders and medical professionals involved, and request privacy at this time." searchText: McKinsey & Company remains on hook in class action over opioid crisis SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Global consulting firm McKinsey & Company must face multidistrict litigation seeking to hold it accountable for its part in fueling a nationwide opioid crisis with aggressive marketing strategies, after a federal judge found it… SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — Global consulting firm McKinsey & Company must face multidistrict litigation seeking to hold it accountable for its part in fueling a nationwide opioid crisis with aggressive marketing strategies, after a federal judge found it cannot use jurisdictional grounds to escape liability. McKinsey is accused of devising strategies for its client, Oxycontin maker Purdue Pharma, that boosted sales of high-dose pills with deceptive messaging to doctors that downplayed the risks of addiction. The plaintiffs are private citizens, city governments, Native American tribes, school districts, and children with neonatal abstinence syndrome from opioid exposure in the womb. They are from 19 states: Alaska, Arizona, Colorado, Hawai’i, Indiana, Kentucky, Louisiana, Maryland, Mississippi, Montana, New Mexico, Oklahoma, Oregon, Tennessee, Utah, Virginia, Washington, West Virginia, and Wisconsin, and the cases have been consolidated into a multidistrict litigation. The plaintiffs argued that McKinsey consultants conducted extensive research that helped Purdue carry out a targeted marketing plan to increase sales. “McKinsey’s documents contain email after email describing its consultants riding along with Purdue’s sales team visiting doctors, including in Tennessee, Maryland, Indiana, Louisiana, and other states where McKinsey claims it did not work. For example, Purdue arranged to have a McKinsey consultant spend a day working with a sales representative in Tennessee,” a recent court filing says. “Don’t think McKinsey didn’t know the consequences of its field research and doctor targeting. McKinsey analyzed those, too, developing a method for Purdue to identify abuse and diversion hot spots — but without ever acting to address them. McKinsey knew exactly the places it was targeting and where the harms of its work impacted communities.” U.S. District Judge Charles Breyer, who is overseeing the sprawling case, sided with the plaintiffs in a ruling Thursday. “Plaintiffs have established that McKinsey committed intentional acts directed toward the subject states,” he wrote. “McKinsey performed numerous acts directed at the subject states. These acts included creating granular analyses of market attractiveness of the subject states, creating target lists of prescribers in the subject states, working alongside Purdue sales representatives in the subject states, and working with Purdue to implement sales strategies in the subject states.” In its bid to fend off negligence, fraud, public nuisance, and state consumer protection claims, McKinsey claimed it never manufactured, distributed or sold prescription painkillers in any of these states, nor has it ever interacted with any of the plaintiffs, “much less made any representations to them about opioids.” Accordingly, “McKinsey is not subject to expansive nationwide personal jurisdiction in the same way that other defendants in other opioid-related litigation may be," the company said. In rejecting that argument, Breyer wrote, “McKinsey effectively contends that it can help Purdue develop and manage strategies to increase opioid sales in the subject states, but that it cannot be subject to jurisdiction when those strategies result in increased opioid sales that cause harm in the subject states.” The judge determined the plaintiffs showed more than random negligence. “To the contrary, plaintiffs plausibly allege that McKinsey’s actions significantly contributed to the wide-ranging harms that have affected the subject states,” he wrote. "McKinsey is more akin to an advertising agency that advised a manufacturer on how to sell boilers to residents of specific states, despite knowing that the boilers carried a significant risk of exploding. There is no random or attenuated chain of contacts here. Plaintiffs have plausibly alleged that McKinsey intentionally and purposefully directed contacts at the subject states for several years.” He also found the plaintiffs had adequately asserted that McKinsey's methods to increase opioid sales caused foreseeable harm because their consultants delivered presentations to Purdue that mentioned prescribers' concerns about opioid abuse, and even worked with Purdue to “counter emotional messages from mothers with teenagers that overdosed in [sic] OxyContin.” Breyer’s ruling allows the litigation to move forward, though McKinsey will likely try to get it dismissed on the merits. Attorneys for the parties did not respond to requests for comment by press time. The case concerns multi-unit buildings bought jointly by several people who collectively own the building and share a single mortgage, what’s known as a tenancy-in-common, or TIC. San Francisco has a notoriously lengthy and expensive process to convert a TIC into condominium — where each person owns his or her own piece of the building — due to a lottery process that allows only 200 units to be converted citywide each year. Ohio residents Peyman Pakdel and Sima Chegini bought a tenancy-in-common interest in a six-unit building in San Francisco’s Russian Hill neighborhood in 2009, signing an agreement with the other owners to to take all necessary steps to convert the building to condominiums. The couple has had a tenant in their unit since 2010, but intended to move in when they retired. The city of San Francisco upended their plans in 2013 by passing an ordinance that put a 10-year halt on the city’s unpopular condo conversion lottery and allowed about 2,200 tenancy-in-common owners to convert their interests into condos under an “expedited conversion program” that also gives tenants the right to take a lifetime lease for the unit they rent. Pakdel and Chegini offered their tenant $100,000 to move out, but he refused. Pakdel and Chegini rejected the tenant’s counteroffer to purchase the unit for $1.03 million and forged ahead with participation in the program, agreeing to provide the tenant with a lifetime lease, a deal he took in May 2017. One month later, the couple decided they wanted to move in to the unit and asked the city for an exemption to the lifetime lease provision. The city denied the couple’s belated request, resulting in the lawsuit. "The tenant is still living in the unit,” their attorney Jeffrey McCoy of the Pacific Legal Foundation said in an email to Courthouse News. “The Pakdels would still like to retire to San Francisco, whether it is in the unit they now own or a similar one. But whether they can will depend on the outcome of the case.” In March 2020, a Ninth Circuit panel upheld U.S. District Judge Richard Seeborg’s dismissal of the couple’s lawsuit, finding they failed to fulfill an administrative prerequisite to apply for an exemption before the condo conversion was complete. The U.S. Supreme Court reversed that decision and reinstated the case in a 7-page per curiam opinion that found property owners need not exhaust administrative remedies to sue a government for unlawful taking. The only requirement is that the government decision be final, the high court wrote. It also suggested that the Ninth Circuit re-evaluate the case in light of its ruling in Cedar Point Nursery v. Hassid that a regulation requiring farm owners to allow union organizers on to their properties to meet with workers constituted a per se physical taking. Now, over a year later, Seeborg dismissed the couple’s regulatory and physical takings claims. “Plaintiffs have an uphill battle to state a plausible claim for a private taking. They have not met their burden,” Seeborg wrote in his Tuesday ruling. He found the city’s actions “were clearly rationally related to the purpose of preventing tenant displacement” and were not merely intended to take private property from one person and give it to another without benefiting the general public. Seeborg also ruled the law isn’t a regulatory taking under a four-factor test laid out in Penn Central Transportation Co. v. City of New York that balances economic impacts of the regulation, the extent to which it interferes with investment-backed expectations, and the character of the government action. The judge found the lifetime lease did not significantly diminish the value of the property, and that the Pakdels were well aware that their condo conversion could be approved at any time after they offered their tenant the lease. “Indeed, it would be unreasonable for them to have believed they could avoid the lifetime lease requirement once they submitted their application,” he wrote. Little compared Alsup’s work to “Anatomy of a Murder,” John Voelker’s acclaimed courtroom drama based on the author’s real-life experience as a defense attorney. Voelker, who wrote under the pen name Robert Traver, would later became an associate justice of the Michigan Supreme Court. One difference between the works, Little noted, was that Alsup wrote his while handling a full caseload in the Northern District of California. It also isn’t his first book — his other works include a memoir about growing up in segregated Mississippi, and “Missing in the Minarets,” a non-fiction work about prominent San Francisco attorney Peter Starr, who disappeared in 1933 while hiking in the Sierra. Alsup was a student at Mississippi State University in 1963 when Kennedy was fatally shot on Nov. 22 as his presidential motorcade drove through Dealey Plaza in downtown Dallas. He was in his dormitory’s common area when his dorm mother delivered the news. As they watched Walter Cronkite take off his glasses and gravely announce that president Kennedy had died at 1:00PM that afternoon, Alsup said he was “heartsick and shocked.” What followed made for a disturbing memory, as a throng of students ran up and down the quad, ringing cow bells in celebration. “They were celebrating the death of JFK. That’s how much he was hated in Mississippi,” Alsup said. “I’m sad to say that was not a good memory.” Alsup’s interest was reinvigorated with the 50th anniversary of the JFK assassination in 2013, which led him to seek out the Warren Commission’s report and its 26 volumes of testimony from the federal court’s library. He was later told that he’d been the first to ever request it. “As a trial lawyer and judge, I’ve spent years evaluating evidence. But I was so absorbed with these people,” Alsup said, referring to the testimony of everyday witnesses — a waitress, a cab driver on his way to work. “Halfway through, I began to see a possible defense for Lee Harvey Oswald. I wanted to write something to help the reader feel like they had parachuted in to 1963 and they were sitting at the elbow of these investigators and lawyers.” The novel follows fictional protagonist Abe Summer, a Department of Justice attorney from Washington, D.C., and Elaine Navarro, a federal prosecutor out of Dallas. Both are brought in to assist real-life Dallas District Attorney Henry Wade, (the “Wade” in Roe v. The… SAN FRANCISCO (CN) — The long-running legal fight between abortion foe David Daleiden and Planned Parenthood took another turn Friday, as a Ninth Circuit panel found Daleiden’s undercover videos are not entitled to First Amendment protections. The panel’s ruling largely upheld a jury’s 2019 verdict finding Daleiden and his antiabortion group the Center for Medical Progress substantially harmed Planned Parenthood by recording secret videos of abortion providers and posting them online, and awarding Planned Parenthood more than $2 million in compensatory and statuary damages. Using fake IDs to gain access, Daleiden and fellow activist Sandra Merritt used fake IDs an infiltrated abortion industry conferences from 2013 to 2015, by posing as exhibitors with a phony human tissue procurement company called BioMax. Daleiden and Merritt maintained they were citizen journalists investigating “violent felonies” based on a belief that infants were being born alive at Planned Parenthood clinics and that Planned Parenthood was illegally profiting from the sale of fetal tissue for medical research. While the panel said it had no view on whether the tactics were legitimate journalism or part of a smear campaign as Planned Parenthood contended, it was nonetheless illegal and the First Amendment does not preclude the award of damages to reimburse Planned Parenthood for security costs and changes to their vetting procedures. "Invoking journalism and the First Amendment does not shield individuals from liability for violations of laws applicable to all members of society,” U.S. Circuit Judge Ronald Gould, a Bill Clinton appointee, wrote for the unanimous panel. “Appellants have been held to the letter of the law, just like all other members of our society. Appellants have no special license to break laws of general applicability in pursuit of a headline.” Gould noted that the decision does not chill investigative journalism, writing, “Our decision does not impose a new burden on journalists or undercover investigations using lawful means. From the beginning of their scheme, appellants engaged in illegal conduct — including forging signatures, creating and procuring fake driver’s licenses, and breaching contracts — that the jury found so objectionable as to award Planned Parenthood punitive damages.” He continued, “Journalism and investigative reporting have long served a critical role in our society. But journalism and investigative reporting do not require illegal conduct. In affirming Planned Parenthood’s compensatory damages from appellants’ First Amendment challenge, we simply reaffirm the established principle that the pursuit of journalism does not give a license to break laws of general applicability.” The panel reversed the jury's finding that Daleiden and his cohort violated the Federal Wiretap Act by recording Planned Parenthood staff 42 times at conferences, lunches, and health clinics without their consent. Planned Parenthood had claimed the recordings were made in furtherance of civil racketeering scheme to destroy the organization, but the panel found Planned Parenthood could not reuse the same criminal purpose to support a Federal Wiretap Act claim. In a separate memorandum, the panel upheld U.S. District Judge William Orrick's ruling in favor of Planned Parenthood on its contract, trespass and racketeering claims. Gould was joined by Chief U.S Circuit Judge Mary Murguia, a Barack Obama appointee, and U.S. Circuit Judge Nancy Freudenthal, an Obama appointee sitting by designation from the District of Wyoming. "We are thrilled with today’s ruling," Helene Krasnoff, the vice president of public policy litigation and law at Planned Parenthood, said in a statement to Courthouse News Friday morning. "In 2019, a jury — with all of the facts fully presented to it — determined that David Daleiden and the Center for Medical Progress intentionally broke the law in a multiyear campaign to advance their antiabortion agenda and prevent Planned Parenthood from serving the patients who depend on us. Daleiden was ordered to pay millions of dollars in damages as a result. Today, the Ninth Circuit Court of Appeals affirmed those holdings, once again making clear that the only people who engaged in wrongdoing were those behind this malicious fraud." Krasnoff added, "This was never about monetary gain; this was about exposing the fraudulent and illegal actions of Daleiden and those who conspired with him, and ensuring that Planned Parenthood providers are able to continue serving the 2.4 million patients who rely on us for high-quality health care every year."
